paragraphs: The Creation · 1:1–2:3
In the beginning, God creates the heavens and the earth.
The earth is formless and empty. Darkness is over the face of the deep. And the Spirit of God is hovering over the face of the waters.
The First Day · 1:3–5
And God says, “Let there be light.” And there is light.
And God sees that the light is good. And God separates the light from the darkness.
God calls the light Day, and the darkness he calls Night.
And there is evening and there is morning — the first day.
The Second Day · 1:6–8
And God says, “Let there be an expanse in the midst of the waters, and let it separate waters from waters.”
And God makes the expanse and separates the waters below the expanse from the waters above the expanse. And it is so.
And God calls the expanse Sky.
And there is evening and there is morning — the second day.
The Third Day · 1:9–13
And God says, “Let the waters below the sky be gathered to one place, and let the dry ground appear.” And it is so.
And God calls the dry ground Earth, and the gathered waters he calls Seas. And God sees that it is good.
And God says, “Let the earth sprout vegetation — plants bearing seed, and fruit trees bearing fruit according to their kinds, with their seed in them, on the earth.” And it is so.
And the earth brings forth vegetation — plants bearing seed according to their kinds, and trees bearing fruit with their seed in them according to their kinds. And God sees that it is good.
And there is evening and there is morning — the third day.
The Fourth Day · 1:14–19
And God says, “Let there be lights in the expanse of the sky to separate the day from the night. And let them be for signs and for appointed times, and for days and years.
And let them be lights in the expanse of the sky to give light on the earth.” And it is so.
And God makes the two great lights — the greater light to rule the day and the lesser light to rule the night — and the stars.
And God sets them in the expanse of the sky to give light on the earth,
to rule over the day and over the night, and to separate the light from the darkness. And God sees that it is good.
And there is evening and there is morning — the fourth day.
The Fifth Day · 1:20–23
And God says, “Let the waters swarm with swarms of living creatures, and let birds fly above the earth across the face of the expanse of the sky.”

And God creates the great sea creatures and every living creature that moves, with which the waters swarm, according to their kinds, and every winged bird according to its kind. And God sees that it is good.
And God blesses them, saying, “Be fruitful and multiply and fill the waters in the seas, and let birds multiply on the earth.”
And there is evening and there is morning — the fifth day.
The Sixth Day · 1:24–30
And God says, “Let the earth bring forth living creatures according to their kinds — livestock and creeping things and wild animals according to their kinds.” And it is so.
And God makes the wild animals according to their kinds and the livestock according to their kinds and everything that creeps on the ground according to its kind. And God sees that it is good.

And God says, “Let us make the human in our image, after our likeness. And let them have dominion over the fish of the sea and over the birds of the sky and over the livestock and over all the earth and over every creeping thing that creeps on the earth.”
And God creates the human in his own image —
in the image of God he creates him —
male and female he creates them.

And God blesses them. And God says to them, “Be fruitful and multiply and fill the earth and subdue it. Rule over the fish of the sea and over the birds of the sky and over every living thing that moves on the earth.”
And God says, “Look — I give you every plant bearing seed that is on the face of all the earth, and every tree that has fruit bearing seed. They shall be food for you.
And to every wild animal and to every bird of the sky and to everything that creeps on the earth — everything that has the breath of life — I give every green plant for food.” And it is so.
And God sees everything he has made — and look, it is very good.
And there is evening and there is morning — the sixth day.
The Seventh Day · 2:1–3
And the heavens and the earth and all their host are completed.
And on the seventh day God finishes his work that he has done. And he rests on the seventh day from all his work that he has done.
And God blesses the seventh day and makes it holy — because on it he rests from all his work that God has created by making.
The Seventh Day · 2:1–3

So the heavens and the earth are finished, with everything that fills them. On the seventh day God finishes the work he has been doing, and on the seventh day he rests from all the work he has done. God blesses the seventh day and makes it holy, because on it he rests from all his work of creating.
The Toledot of the Heavens and the Earth · 2:4–7

This is the story of the generations of the heavens and the earth when they are created. On the day YHWH God makes the earth and the heavens, there is not a single shrub of the field on the earth yet, and not a single plant of the field has sprouted. YHWH God has not sent rain on the earth, and there is no human to work the ground. But a mist rises up from the earth and waters the whole face of the ground. Then YHWH God shapes the man from the dust of the ground. He breathes into his nostrils the breath of life, and the man becomes a living creature.
The Garden · 2:8–17

YHWH God plants a garden in Eden, off in the east, and there he puts the man he has shaped. Out of the ground YHWH God makes every kind of tree grow, trees lovely to look at and good for food. In the middle of the garden stands the tree of life, and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil.

A river flows out of Eden to water the garden. From there it splits and becomes four rivers. The first is named Pishon. It winds through the whole land of Havilah, where there is gold. The gold of that land is good, and there is fragrant resin there too, and onyx stone. The second river is named Gihon. It winds through the whole land of Cush. The third river is named Tigris. It runs east of Assyria. And the fourth river is the Euphrates.

YHWH God takes the man and sets him in the garden of Eden to work it and to keep it. And YHWH God gives the man a command: “You may eat freely from every tree in the garden, except the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. Don’t eat from that one. On the day you eat from it, you will surely die.”
The Forming of the Woman · 2:18–25

Then YHWH God says, “It’s not good for the man to be on his own. I will make him a helper to be his counterpart.” So out of the ground YHWH God shapes every animal of the field and every bird of the sky, and he brings them to the man to see what he will call them. Whatever the man calls each living creature, that is its name. The man gives names to all the livestock, to the birds of the sky, and to every animal of the field. But for the man himself, no helper is found to be his counterpart. So YHWH God puts the man into a deep sleep, and while he sleeps, God takes one of his sides and closes up the flesh in its place. Out of the side he has taken from the man, YHWH God builds a woman, and he brings her to the man. And the man cries out, “This one, at last, is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh! She will be called Woman, because out of Man she was taken.”
So it is that a man leaves his father and his mother and clings to his wife, and the two of them become one flesh. The man and his wife are both naked, and they feel no shame.
The Temptation · 3:1–7
Now the serpent is craftier than any wild animal YHWH God has made. He says to the woman, “Did God really say, ‘You must not eat from any tree in the garden’?”

The woman tells the serpent, “We can eat fruit from the trees in the garden. It’s only the fruit of the tree in the middle of the garden. God said, ‘Don’t eat it, and don’t touch it, or you will die.’”
“You won’t die,” the serpent tells the woman. “Not at all. God knows that on the day you eat it, your eyes will be opened, and you will be like God, knowing good and evil.”

The woman looks at the tree. It is good for food. It is a delight to the eyes. And it is desirable, a tree to make a person wise. So she takes some of its fruit and eats. She gives some to her husband, who is there with her, and he eats too. Then the eyes of both of them are opened, and they know they are naked. So they sew fig leaves together and make coverings for themselves.
The Reckoning · 3:8–13
Then they hear the sound of YHWH God walking in the garden in the cool breeze of the day. The man and his wife hide from YHWH God among the trees of the garden.
But YHWH God calls to the man. “Where are you?”
“I heard the sound of you in the garden,” the man says, “and I was afraid, because I’m naked. So I hid.”
“Who told you that you were naked?” God asks. “Have you eaten from the tree I commanded you not to eat from?”
The man says, “The woman you put here with me, she gave me fruit from the tree, and I ate.”
Then YHWH God says to the woman, “What is this you have done?” And the woman says, “The serpent tricked me, and I ate.”
The Judgments · 3:14–19

So YHWH God says to the serpent, “Because you have done this, cursed are you above all the livestock and above every wild animal. On your belly you will crawl, and dust you will eat, all the days of your life. I will put hostility between you and the woman, between your offspring and her offspring. He will strike at your head, and you will strike at his heel.”
To the woman he says, “I will greatly increase your pain in bearing children. In pain you will bring children into the world. You will long for your husband, and he will rule over you.”

And to Adam he says, “Because you listened to your wife and ate from the tree I commanded you about when I said, ‘Don’t eat from it,’ the ground is cursed because of you. With hard labor you will eat from it all the days of your life. It will grow thorns and thistles for you, and you will eat the plants of the field. By the sweat of your face you will eat your bread, until you go back to the ground, because out of it you were taken. You are dust, and to dust you go back.”
Naming, Clothing, and Exile · 3:20–24
The man names his wife Eve. In Hebrew it is Havvah, Life, because she is to be the mother of all who live. And YHWH God makes garments out of animal skins for Adam and his wife, and he clothes them.

Then YHWH God says, “Look, the man has become like one of us, knowing good and evil. Now he might reach out his hand and take from the tree of life too, and eat, and live forever.” So YHWH God sends him out of the garden of Eden to work the ground he was taken from. He drives the man out. And on the east side of the garden of Eden he stations the cherubim, with a sword of flame that whirls and turns every way, to guard the road to the tree of life.
Cain and Abel · 4:1–16

The man lies with Eve his wife, and she conceives and gives birth to Cain. “I have gotten a man,” she says, “with YHWH’s help!” (The name Cain sounds like the Hebrew for “gotten.”) Later she gives birth to his brother Abel. Abel becomes a keeper of sheep, and Cain a worker of the ground.

In the course of time Cain brings some of the fruit of the ground as an offering to YHWH. Abel brings one too: some of the firstborn of his flock, and the fattest portions. And YHWH looks with favor on Abel and his offering. But on Cain and his offering he does not look with favor. Cain is furious, and his face falls. So YHWH says to Cain, “Why are you so angry? Why has your face fallen? If you do what is right, won’t your face be lifted up? But if you don’t do what is right, sin is crouched at the doorway like an animal ready to spring. It wants you. But you are to master it.”
Cain says to his brother Abel, “Let’s go out to the field.” And while they are out in the field, Cain rises up against his brother Abel and kills him.
Then YHWH says to Cain, “Where is Abel, your brother?” “I don’t know,” he says. “Am I my brother’s keeper?”

“What have you done?” YHWH says. “Listen! The voice of your brother’s blood is crying to me from the ground. Now you are cursed, cursed from the ground that opened its mouth to take in your brother’s blood from your hand. When you work the ground, it will no longer give you its strength. You will be a restless wanderer on the earth.”

Cain says to YHWH, “My punishment is more than I can carry. Look, today you are driving me off the face of the ground, and I will be hidden from your face. I will be a restless wanderer on the earth, and whoever finds me will kill me.”

But YHWH says to him, “Not so. If anyone kills Cain, vengeance will fall on him seven times over.” And YHWH puts a mark on Cain, so that no one who finds him will strike him down. So Cain goes out from the presence of YHWH and settles in the land of Nod, the land of Wandering, east of Eden.
The Line of Cain · 4:17–24

Cain lies with his wife, and she conceives and gives birth to Enoch. Cain is building a city, and he names the city after his son, Enoch. Enoch has a son named Irad. Irad is the father of Mehujael, Mehujael is the father of Methushael, and Methushael is the father of Lamech.

Lamech takes two wives. One is named Adah and the other Zillah. Adah gives birth to Jabal. He is the father of all who live in tents and keep livestock. His brother’s name is Jubal. He is the father of all who play the harp and the pipe. Zillah also has a son, Tubal-Cain, who forges every kind of tool out of bronze and iron. Tubal-Cain’s sister is Naamah.

And Lamech sings this to his wives: “Adah and Zillah, hear my voice! Wives of Lamech, listen to what I say! I have killed a man for wounding me, a young man for striking me. If Cain is avenged seven times, then Lamech seventy-seven times!”
The Line of Seth · 4:25–26

Adam lies with his wife again, and she gives birth to a son and names him Seth. “God has granted me another child in place of Abel,” she says, “since Cain killed him.” (Seth sounds like the Hebrew for “granted.”) Seth too has a son, and he names him Enosh. It is in those days that people begin to call on the name of YHWH.
The Book of the Generations of Adam · 5:1–32

This is the book of the generations of Adam. On the day God creates humankind, he makes them in the likeness of God. Male and female he creates them, and he blesses them. On the day they are created, he names them Adam, which means Human.

Adam lives a hundred and thirty years. Then he has a son in his own likeness, after his own image, and names him Seth. After Seth is born, Adam lives eight hundred years more and has other sons and daughters. Adam lives nine hundred and thirty years in all, and then he dies.

Seth lives a hundred and five years, and then he has Enosh. After Enosh is born, Seth lives eight hundred and seven years more and has other sons and daughters. Seth lives nine hundred and twelve years in all, and then he dies.

Enosh lives ninety years, and then he has Kenan. After Kenan is born, Enosh lives eight hundred and fifteen years more and has other sons and daughters. Enosh lives nine hundred and five years in all, and then he dies.

Kenan lives seventy years, and then he has Mahalalel. After Mahalalel is born, Kenan lives eight hundred and forty years more and has other sons and daughters. Kenan lives nine hundred and ten years in all, and then he dies.

Mahalalel lives sixty-five years, and then he has Jared. After Jared is born, Mahalalel lives eight hundred and thirty years more and has other sons and daughters. Mahalalel lives eight hundred and ninety-five years in all, and then he dies.

Jared lives a hundred and sixty-two years, and then he has Enoch. After Enoch is born, Jared lives eight hundred years more and has other sons and daughters. Jared lives nine hundred and sixty-two years in all, and then he dies.

Enoch lives sixty-five years, and then he has Methuselah. After Methuselah is born, Enoch walks with God three hundred years and has other sons and daughters. Enoch lives three hundred and sixty-five years in all. Enoch walks with God, and then he is gone, because God takes him.

Methuselah lives a hundred and eighty-seven years, and then he has Lamech. After Lamech is born, Methuselah lives seven hundred and eighty-two years more and has other sons and daughters. Methuselah lives nine hundred and sixty-nine years in all, and then he dies.

Lamech lives a hundred and eighty-two years, and then he has a son. He names him Noah. “This one will bring us comfort,” he says, “from our work and from the painful toil of our hands on the ground YHWH has cursed.” (Noah sounds like the Hebrew for “comfort.”) After Noah is born, Lamech lives five hundred and ninety-five years more and has other sons and daughters. Lamech lives seven hundred and seventy-seven years in all, and then he dies.
When Noah is five hundred years old, he has three sons: Shem, Ham, and Japheth.
The Sons of God and the Daughters of Humanity · 6:1–4

Now people begin to multiply over the face of the ground, and daughters are born to them. And the sons of God see that the daughters of humankind are beautiful, and they take as wives any of them they choose. Then YHWH says, “My Spirit will not stay with humankind forever, for they are flesh. Their days will be a hundred and twenty years.” The Nephilim, the Fallen Ones, are on the earth in those days, and afterward too, whenever the sons of God go in to the daughters of humankind and they bear them children. These are the mighty men of long ago, the men with a name.
The Wickedness of Humanity · 6:5–8

YHWH sees that human wickedness on the earth is great. Every scheme their hearts can dream up is nothing but evil, all day long. And YHWH is sorry he ever made humankind on the earth. It grieves him to the heart. So YHWH says, “I will wipe the humans I have created off the face of the ground: people and animals, creeping things and birds of the sky. I am sorry I ever made them.” But Noah finds favor in the eyes of YHWH.
Noah and the Ark · 6:9–22
Here is the story of the generations of Noah. Noah is a righteous man, blameless among the people of his time. Noah walks with God. Noah has three sons: Shem, Ham, and Japheth.
The earth is ruined in God’s sight, and the earth is full of violence. God looks at the earth, and he sees how ruined it is, because all flesh has ruined its way on the earth.

So God says to Noah, “I have decided to bring an end to all flesh, because through them the earth is full of violence. Look, I am going to destroy them along with the earth. Build yourself an ark of gopher wood. Make rooms in it, and coat it with pitch inside and out. This is how you are to build it: three hundred cubits long, fifty cubits wide, and thirty cubits high. That is about four hundred fifty feet long, seventy-five feet wide, and forty-five feet high. Make a roof for the ark, and finish it a cubit from the top. Put the door in the side of the ark, and build it with a lower deck, a second deck, and a third. And I, yes I, am bringing the flood, the waters over the earth, to destroy all flesh under the sky that has the breath of life in it. Everything on the earth will die. But with you I will establish my covenant. You will go into the ark, you and your sons, your wife and your sons’ wives with you. And from every living thing, from all flesh, you are to bring two of every kind into the ark, to keep them alive with you. They are to be male and female. Two of every kind will come to you to be kept alive: birds of every kind, livestock of every kind, and every kind of creature that creeps on the ground. And take with you every kind of food that is eaten, and store it up. It will be food for you and for them.”
And Noah does it. Everything God commands him, Noah does.
Entering the Ark · 7:1–24

Then YHWH says to Noah, “Go into the ark, you and all your household, because I have seen that you are righteous before me in this generation. Take seven pairs of every clean animal with you, a male and its mate, and of the animals that are not clean, one pair, a male and its mate. And of the birds of the sky, take seven pairs, male and female, to keep their kind alive on the face of the whole earth. Seven days from now I will send rain on the earth for forty days and forty nights, and I will wipe every living thing I have made off the face of the ground.”
And Noah does everything YHWH commands him.

Noah is six hundred years old when the flood comes, the waters over the earth. Noah goes into the ark to escape the floodwaters, with his sons, his wife, and his sons’ wives. Clean animals and unclean animals, birds and everything that creeps on the ground, come to Noah two by two, male and female, and go into the ark, just as God commanded Noah. And after the seven days, the floodwaters come over the earth.

In the six hundredth year of Noah’s life, in the second month, on the seventeenth day of the month, on that very day, all the springs of the great deep burst open, and the windows of the sky are flung wide. And the rain falls on the earth forty days and forty nights.

On that same day Noah goes into the ark, with his sons Shem, Ham, and Japheth, and Noah’s wife, and the three wives of his sons. With them go every wild animal of every kind, all the livestock of every kind, every creeping thing of every kind that creeps on the earth, and every bird of every kind, everything with wings. They come to Noah and go into the ark two by two, from all flesh that has the breath of life in it. In they go, male and female of all flesh, just as God commanded him. And YHWH shuts him in.

For forty days the flood keeps coming on the earth. The waters rise and lift the ark, and it rises high above the earth. The waters swell and rise higher and higher over the earth, and the ark floats on the face of the waters. The waters swell more and more over the earth, until all the high mountains under the whole sky are covered. The waters rise fifteen cubits, more than twenty feet, above the mountains, and the mountains are covered.

And all flesh that moves on the earth dies: birds, livestock, wild animals, every creature that swarms on the earth, and every human being. Everything on dry land with the breath of the spirit of life in its nostrils dies. He wipes out every living thing on the face of the ground: people and animals, creeping things and birds of the sky. They are wiped off the earth. Only Noah is left, and those who are with him in the ark. And the waters swell over the earth for a hundred and fifty days.
God Remembers Noah · 8:1–5

But God remembers Noah, and all the wild animals and all the livestock with him in the ark. And God sends a wind over the earth, and the waters begin to go down. The springs of the deep and the windows of the sky are shut, and the rain from the sky is held back. Little by little the waters pull back from the earth. By the end of the hundred and fifty days the waters have gone down. In the seventh month, on the seventeenth day of the month, the ark comes to rest on the mountains of Ararat. The waters keep going down until the tenth month. And on the first day of the tenth month, the tops of the mountains can be seen.
The Birds · 8:6–12

At the end of forty days, Noah opens the window he has made in the ark, and he sends out a raven. It flies back and forth, back and forth, until the waters have dried up from the earth. Then he sends out a dove, to see whether the waters have gone down from the face of the ground. But the dove finds no resting place for the sole of her foot, and she comes back to him in the ark, because water still covers the face of the whole earth. So he reaches out his hand, takes her, and brings her back inside the ark with him. He waits seven more days, and again he sends the dove out from the ark. The dove comes back to him in the evening, and look, there in her beak is an olive leaf, freshly plucked! Then Noah knows the waters have gone down from the earth. He waits seven more days and sends out the dove again, and this time she does not come back to him.
Leaving the Ark · 8:13–19

In the six hundred and first year, on the first day of the first month, the waters have dried up from the earth. Noah takes the covering off the ark and looks out, and the face of the ground is drying. By the twenty-seventh day of the second month, the earth is dry.

Then God speaks to Noah: “Come out of the ark, you and your wife, your sons and your sons’ wives with you. Bring out with you every living thing of all flesh that is with you, the birds, the livestock, and every creature that creeps on the earth, so they can swarm over the earth and be fruitful and multiply on it.”
So Noah comes out, with his sons, his wife, and his sons’ wives. Every animal, every creeping thing, every bird, everything that moves on the earth comes out of the ark, family by family.
Noah’s Altar and YHWH’s Promise · 8:20–22

Then Noah builds an altar to YHWH. He takes some of every clean animal and every clean bird, and he offers burnt offerings on the altar. YHWH smells the soothing aroma, and YHWH says in his heart, “I will never again curse the ground because of humankind, even though every scheme of the human heart is evil from youth. Never again will I strike down every living thing, as I have done. While the earth remains, planting and harvest, cold and heat, summer and winter, day and night will not stop.”
The New Commission · 9:1–7

God blesses Noah and his sons and says to them, “Be fruitful and multiply, and fill the earth. Every animal of the earth and every bird of the sky will fear you and dread you, along with everything that creeps on the ground and all the fish of the sea. They are put into your hands. Every living thing that moves will be food for you. Just as I once gave you the green plants, now I give you everything. Only, you must not eat flesh with its life still in it, that is, with its blood. For your own lifeblood I will surely demand an accounting. I will demand it from every animal. And from every human being I will demand an accounting for the life of another human, his brother. Whoever spills human blood, by a human his own blood will be spilled, because God made humankind in his own image. As for you, be fruitful and multiply. Swarm over the earth and multiply on it.”
The Covenant with Noah · 9:8–17

Then God says to Noah and to his sons with him, “As for me, look, I am establishing my covenant with you, and with your offspring after you, and with every living creature that is with you: the birds, the livestock, and every wild animal with you, everything that came out of the ark, every animal on earth. I establish my covenant with you: never again will all flesh be cut off by the waters of a flood. Never again will there be a flood to destroy the earth.”

And God says, “This is the sign of the covenant I am making between me and you and every living creature with you, for all generations to come: I hang my bow in the cloud, and it will be the sign of my covenant with the earth. Whenever I bring clouds over the earth and the bow appears in the cloud, I will remember my covenant between me and you and every living creature of all flesh. And never again will the waters become a flood to destroy all flesh. When the bow is in the cloud, I will look at it and remember the everlasting covenant between God and every living creature of all flesh on the earth.” And God says to Noah, “This is the sign of the covenant I have established between me and all flesh on the earth.”
Noah’s Sons · 9:18–29
The sons of Noah who come out of the ark are Shem, Ham, and Japheth. Ham is the father of Canaan. These three are the sons of Noah, and from them the whole earth is peopled.

Noah, a man of the soil, is the first to plant a vineyard. He drinks some of the wine and gets drunk, and he lies uncovered inside his tent. Ham, the father of Canaan, sees his father’s nakedness and goes out and tells his two brothers. But Shem and Japheth take a cloak, lay it across their shoulders, and walk in backward to cover their father’s nakedness. Their faces are turned away, so they do not see their father naked.
When Noah wakes up from his wine and learns what his youngest son has done to him, he says, “Cursed be Canaan! He will be the lowest of servants to his brothers.”
And he says, “Blessed be YHWH, the God of Shem! Let Canaan be his servant. May God make room for Japheth, and let him live in the tents of Shem. Let Canaan be his servant.”
After the flood Noah lives three hundred and fifty years. Noah lives nine hundred and fifty years in all, and then he dies.
The Table of Nations · 10:1
Here is the story of the generations of Noah’s sons, Shem, Ham, and Japheth. Sons are born to them after the flood.
The Sons of Japheth · 10:2–5

The sons of Japheth: Gomer, Magog, Madai, Javan, Tubal, Meshech, and Tiras. The sons of Gomer: Ashkenaz, Riphath, and Togarmah. The sons of Javan: Elishah, Tarshish, the Kittim, and the Dodanim. From these the peoples of the coastlands spread out into their lands, each with its own language, by their clans, in their nations.
The Sons of Ham · 10:6–20
The sons of Ham: Cush, Egypt, Put, and Canaan. The sons of Cush: Seba, Havilah, Sabtah, Raamah, and Sabteca. The sons of Raamah: Sheba and Dedan.

Cush is the father of Nimrod, who becomes the first mighty warrior on the earth. He is a mighty hunter before YHWH. That is why people say, “Like Nimrod, a mighty hunter before YHWH.” His kingdom begins with Babel, Erech, Akkad, and Calneh, in the land of Shinar. From that land he goes out into Assyria and builds Nineveh, Rehoboth-Ir, Calah, and Resen, which lies between Nineveh and Calah. That is the great city.
Egypt is the father of the Ludim, the Anamim, the Lehabim, the Naphtuhim, the Pathrusim, the Casluhim (from whom the Philistines come), and the Caphtorim.

Canaan is the father of Sidon his firstborn, and of Heth, and of the Jebusites, the Amorites, the Girgashites, the Hivites, the Arkites, the Sinites, the Arvadites, the Zemarites, and the Hamathites. Later the clans of the Canaanites spread out. The territory of the Canaanites runs from Sidon toward Gerar, as far as Gaza, and then toward Sodom, Gomorrah, Admah, and Zeboiim, as far as Lasha. These are the sons of Ham, by their clans and their languages, in their lands and their nations.
The Sons of Shem · 10:21–32

Sons are born to Shem too, the older brother of Japheth. Shem is the ancestor of all the sons of Eber. The sons of Shem: Elam, Asshur, Arpachshad, Lud, and Aram. The sons of Aram: Uz, Hul, Gether, and Mash. Arpachshad is the father of Shelah, and Shelah is the father of Eber. Two sons are born to Eber. One is named Peleg, which means Division, because in his days the earth is divided. His brother is named Joktan. Joktan is the father of Almodad, Sheleph, Hazarmaveth, Jerah, Hadoram, Uzal, Diklah, Obal, Abimael, Sheba, Ophir, Havilah, and Jobab. All these are sons of Joktan. The land where they live stretches from Mesha toward Sephar, the hill country of the east. These are the sons of Shem, by their clans and their languages, in their lands and their nations.
These are the clans of Noah’s sons, by their generations, in their nations. From them the nations spread out over the earth after the flood.
The Tower of Babel · 11:1–9

Now the whole earth has one language and the same words. As people travel out of the east, they come upon a plain in the land of Shinar, and they settle there. And they say to one another, “Come on, let’s make bricks and fire them hard.” So they use brick instead of stone, and tar instead of mortar. Then they say, “Come on, let’s build ourselves a city, with a tower whose top is in the sky. Let’s make a name for ourselves, so we won’t be scattered over the face of the whole earth.”

And YHWH comes down to see the city and the tower the humans are building. YHWH says, “Look, they are one people, and they all have one language, and this is only the beginning of what they will do. Nothing they set out to do will be out of their reach. Come on, let’s go down and mix up their language there, so they can’t understand each other’s speech.” So YHWH scatters them from there over the face of the whole earth, and they stop building the city. That is why it is called Babel, because there YHWH mixes up the language of the whole earth. (Babel sounds like the Hebrew for “mix up.”) And from there YHWH scatters them over the face of the whole earth.
The Generations of Shem to Abram · 11:10–26

Here is the story of the generations of Shem. Two years after the flood, when Shem is a hundred years old, he has Arpachshad. After Arpachshad is born, Shem lives five hundred years more and has other sons and daughters.
Arpachshad lives thirty-five years, and then he has Shelah. After Shelah is born, Arpachshad lives four hundred and three years more and has other sons and daughters.
Shelah lives thirty years, and then he has Eber. After Eber is born, Shelah lives four hundred and three years more and has other sons and daughters.
Eber lives thirty-four years, and then he has Peleg. After Peleg is born, Eber lives four hundred and thirty years more and has other sons and daughters.
Peleg lives thirty years, and then he has Reu. After Reu is born, Peleg lives two hundred and nine years more and has other sons and daughters.
Reu lives thirty-two years, and then he has Serug. After Serug is born, Reu lives two hundred and seven years more and has other sons and daughters.
Serug lives thirty years, and then he has Nahor. After Nahor is born, Serug lives two hundred years more and has other sons and daughters.
Nahor lives twenty-nine years, and then he has Terah. After Terah is born, Nahor lives a hundred and nineteen years more and has other sons and daughters.
Terah lives seventy years, and then he has Abram, Nahor, and Haran.
Terah’s Family and Journey · 11:27–32

Here is the story of the generations of Terah. Terah is the father of Abram, Nahor, and Haran. And Haran is the father of Lot. Haran dies while his father Terah is still alive, in the land where he was born, in Ur of the Chaldeans. Abram and Nahor both marry. Abram’s wife is named Sarai, and Nahor’s wife is named Milcah. She is the daughter of Haran, who is also the father of Iscah. And Sarai is barren. She has no child. Terah takes his son Abram, his grandson Lot the son of Haran, and his daughter-in-law Sarai, the wife of his son Abram, and together they set out from Ur of the Chaldeans to go to the land of Canaan. But when they come to Haran, they settle there. Terah lives two hundred and five years, and Terah dies in Haran.
The Call of Abram · 12:1–9

Then YHWH says to Abram, “Get yourself going! Leave your land, your kin, and your father’s house, and go to the land that I will show you. I will make a great nation out of you. I will bless you. I will make your name great, and you will be a blessing. Those who bless you, I will bless, and whoever treats you with contempt, I will curse. And in you all the families of the ground will be blessed.”

So Abram goes, just as YHWH has told him, and Lot goes with him. Abram is seventy-five years old when he sets out from Haran. He takes his wife Sarai, his nephew Lot, all the wealth they have gathered, and all the people they have gained in Haran, and they set out for the land of Canaan. And they come into the land of Canaan. Abram travels through the land as far as the place called Shechem, to the oak of Moreh. The Canaanites are in the land at that time.
Then YHWH appears to Abram and says, “To your offspring I will give this land.” So Abram builds an altar there to YHWH, who has appeared to him.

From there he moves on to the hill country east of Bethel and pitches his tent, with Bethel to the west and Ai to the east. There he builds an altar to YHWH and calls on the name of YHWH. Then Abram keeps moving, stage by stage, toward the Negev, the dry south country.
Abram in Egypt · 12:10–20

Now a famine comes on the land. So Abram goes down to Egypt to live there for a while, because the famine in the land is severe. As he is about to enter Egypt, he says to his wife Sarai, “Listen. I know what a beautiful woman you are. When the Egyptians see you, they’ll say, ‘That’s his wife.’ Then they’ll kill me and let you live. Please, say you’re my sister, so that things go well for me because of you, and I stay alive thanks to you.”

And sure enough, when Abram comes into Egypt, the Egyptians see that the woman is very beautiful. Pharaoh’s officials see her too, and they sing her praises to Pharaoh, and the woman is taken into Pharaoh’s house. Pharaoh treats Abram well for her sake. Abram gets sheep and cattle, male and female donkeys, male and female servants, and camels. But YHWH strikes Pharaoh and his household with great plagues because of Sarai, Abram’s wife. So Pharaoh summons Abram. “What have you done to me?” he says. “Why didn’t you tell me she was your wife? Why did you say, ‘She’s my sister,’ so that I took her to be my wife? Now, here is your wife. Take her and go!”
And Pharaoh gives his men orders about him, and they send him on his way, with his wife and everything he has.
Abram and Lot Part Ways · 13:1–13

So Abram goes up out of Egypt into the Negev, he and his wife and everything he has, and Lot with him. Abram is very rich now, heavy with livestock, silver, and gold. From the Negev he travels on, stage by stage, as far as Bethel, to the place between Bethel and Ai where his tent stood at the beginning, the place where he first built the altar. And there Abram calls on the name of YHWH.

Lot, who is traveling with Abram, also has flocks and herds and tents. The land can’t support them both living side by side. They own too much to stay together. So quarrels break out between Abram’s herdsmen and Lot’s herdsmen. And the Canaanites and the Perizzites are living in the land at that time. So Abram says to Lot, “Please, let’s not have any quarreling between you and me, or between your herdsmen and mine. We are family. Isn’t the whole land in front of you? Let’s part ways. If you go left, I’ll go right. If you go right, I’ll go left.”

Lot looks up and sees the whole plain of the Jordan, watered everywhere like the garden of YHWH, like the land of Egypt, all the way to Zoar. (This is before YHWH destroys Sodom and Gomorrah.) So Lot chooses the whole plain of the Jordan for himself and travels east. And so they part from each other. Abram settles in the land of Canaan, while Lot settles among the cities of the plain and pitches his tent as far as Sodom. Now the men of Sodom are wicked, great sinners against YHWH.
The Promise Renewed · 13:14–18

After Lot has parted from him, YHWH says to Abram, “Lift up your eyes. From the place where you are standing, look north and south, east and west. All the land you see I will give to you and to your offspring forever. I will make your offspring like the dust of the earth. If anyone could count the dust of the earth, then your offspring could be counted too. Get up! Walk the length and the breadth of the land, because I am giving it to you.”
So Abram moves his tent and comes to live by the oaks of Mamre, at Hebron. And there he builds an altar to YHWH.
The War of the Kings · 14:1–12

In the days of Amraphel king of Shinar, Arioch king of Ellasar, Chedorlaomer king of Elam, and Tidal king of Goiim, these kings go to war against Bera king of Sodom, Birsha king of Gomorrah, Shinab king of Admah, Shemeber king of Zeboiim, and the king of Bela (that is, Zoar). These five join forces in the Valley of Siddim, where the Salt Sea is now. For twelve years they have served Chedorlaomer, and in the thirteenth year they rebel. In the fourteenth year Chedorlaomer and the kings allied with him come and strike down the Rephaim in Ashteroth-karnaim, the Zuzim in Ham, the Emim in Shaveh-kiriathaim, and the Horites in their hill country of Seir, as far as El-paran at the edge of the wilderness. Then they turn back and come to En-mishpat (that is, Kadesh), and they conquer the whole country of the Amalekites, and also the Amorites who live in Hazazon-tamar. Then the king of Sodom, the king of Gomorrah, the king of Admah, the king of Zeboiim, and the king of Bela (that is, Zoar) march out and draw up their battle lines in the Valley of Siddim, against Chedorlaomer king of Elam, Tidal king of Goiim, Amraphel king of Shinar, and Arioch king of Ellasar. Four kings against five. Now the Valley of Siddim is full of tar pits. As the kings of Sodom and Gomorrah run, some of their men fall into them, and the rest escape to the hills. The enemy takes all the goods of Sodom and Gomorrah and all their food, and goes on their way. They also take Lot, Abram’s nephew, who is living in Sodom, along with his goods, and off they go.
Abram Rescues Lot · 14:13–16

Then someone who has escaped comes and tells Abram the Hebrew. Abram is living by the oaks of Mamre the Amorite, brother of Eshcol and Aner. These men are Abram’s allies. When Abram hears that his kinsman has been taken captive, he calls out his trained men, born in his own household, three hundred and eighteen of them, and he chases the raiders as far as Dan. At night he splits his forces against them, he and his servants, and he strikes them and chases them as far as Hobah, north of Damascus. He brings back all the goods. He brings back his kinsman Lot and his goods too, and the women and the other people.
Melchizedek · 14:17–24

After Abram comes back from defeating Chedorlaomer and the kings with him, the king of Sodom goes out to meet him in the Valley of Shaveh (that is, the King’s Valley). And Melchizedek king of Salem brings out bread and wine. He is a priest of God Most High. He blesses Abram and says, “Blessed be Abram by God Most High, maker of heaven and earth. And blessed be God Most High, who has handed your enemies over to you.” And Abram gives him a tenth of everything.
The king of Sodom says to Abram, “Give me the people, and keep the goods for yourself.”

But Abram tells the king of Sodom, “I have raised my hand in an oath to YHWH, God Most High, maker of heaven and earth, that I won’t take a thread or a sandal strap or anything at all that is yours. You will never be able to say, ‘I made Abram rich.’ I’ll take nothing except what the young men have eaten, and the share that belongs to the men who went with me, Aner, Eshcol, and Mamre. Let them take their share.”
The Word of YHWH · 15:1–6
After these things the word of YHWH comes to Abram in a vision: “Don’t be afraid, Abram. I am your shield. Your reward is going to be great, very great.”

But Abram says, “Lord YHWH, what will you give me? I am going through life childless, and the one who will inherit my household is Eliezer of Damascus.” And Abram says, “Look, you haven’t given me any offspring, so a servant born in my house will be my heir.”

Then the word of YHWH comes to him again: “This man will not be your heir. A son who comes from your own body will be your heir.” And he takes him outside and says, “Look up there, at the sky. Count the stars, if you are able to count them.” Then he says to him, “That is how many your offspring will be.” And Abram puts his trust in YHWH, and YHWH reckons that trust to him as righteousness.
The Land Promise Confirmed · 15:7–11
Then he says to Abram, “I am YHWH, who brought you out of Ur of the Chaldeans to give you this land to possess.”
“Lord YHWH,” Abram says, “how can I know that I will possess it?”

So he tells him, “Bring me a heifer three years old, a female goat three years old, a ram three years old, a turtledove, and a young pigeon.” Abram brings him all these. He cuts them in two and lays each half facing the other, but the birds he does not cut in half. Then birds of prey swoop down on the carcasses, and Abram drives them away.
The Covenant of the Pieces · 15:12–21

As the sun is going down, a deep sleep falls on Abram. And look, a terror, a great darkness, comes down on him. Then YHWH says to Abram, “Know this for certain: your offspring will be strangers in a land that is not theirs. They will be slaves there and be oppressed for four hundred years. But I will bring judgment on the nation they serve, and afterward they will come out with great wealth. As for you, you will go to your fathers in peace. You will be buried at a good old age. And in the fourth generation they will come back here, because the guilt of the Amorites has not yet run full.”

When the sun has set and it is dark, look! A smoking firepot and a blazing torch pass between the pieces. On that day YHWH cuts a covenant with Abram: “To your offspring I give this land, from the river of Egypt to the great river, the river Euphrates, the land of the Kenites, the Kenizzites, the Kadmonites, the Hittites, the Perizzites, the Rephaim, the Amorites, the Canaanites, the Girgashites, and the Jebusites.”
Hagar and Ishmael · 16:1–16

Now Sarai, Abram’s wife, has borne him no children. But she has a servant girl, an Egyptian named Hagar. So Sarai says to Abram, “Look, YHWH has kept me from having children. Please, go in to my servant. Maybe I can build a family through her.” And Abram listens to Sarai. So after Abram has lived ten years in the land of Canaan, his wife Sarai takes Hagar the Egyptian, her servant, and gives her to her husband Abram as a wife. He goes in to Hagar, and she conceives. And when she sees that she is pregnant, her mistress becomes small in her eyes. Then Sarai says to Abram, “This wrong done to me is on you! I put my servant in your arms, and now that she sees she’s pregnant, I am nothing in her eyes. May YHWH judge between you and me!”
“Look,” Abram tells Sarai, “your servant is in your hands. Do with her whatever you think best.” Then Sarai treats her harshly, and Hagar runs away from her.

The messenger of YHWH finds her by a spring of water in the wilderness, the spring on the road to Shur. “Hagar, servant of Sarai,” he says, “where have you come from, and where are you going?” “I’m running away from my mistress Sarai,” she says.

Then the messenger of YHWH tells her, “Go back to your mistress, and put yourself under her hand.” And the messenger of YHWH says to her, “I will give you so many offspring that they will be too many to count.” The messenger of YHWH says to her, “Look, you are pregnant, and you will have a son. Name him Ishmael, God Hears, because YHWH has heard your misery. He will be a wild donkey of a man. His hand will be against everyone, and everyone’s hand against him. He will live at odds with all his brothers.”

So she gives a name to YHWH, who has spoken to her: “You are El-Roi, the God who sees me.” For she says, “Have I truly seen the One who sees me, and lived to tell it?” That is why the well is called Beer-lahai-roi, the Well of the Living One who sees me. It is still there, between Kadesh and Bered.
Hagar bears Abram a son, and Abram names the son Hagar has borne him Ishmael. Abram is eighty-six years old when Hagar bears him Ishmael.
El Shaddai and the Covenant of Circumcision · 17:1–14

When Abram is ninety-nine years old, YHWH appears to him and says, “I am El Shaddai. Walk before my face, and be whole. I will set my covenant between me and you, and I will multiply you greatly, greatly.”

Abram falls on his face, and God speaks with him: “As for me, look, this is my covenant with you: you will be the father of a crowd of nations. No longer will your name be Abram, Exalted Father. Your name will be Abraham, Father of a Crowd, because I am making you the father of a crowd of nations. I will make you fruitful, very fruitful. I will make nations come from you, and kings will come out of you. I will establish my covenant between me and you and your offspring after you, generation after generation, as an everlasting covenant, to be your God and the God of your offspring after you. And to you and your offspring after you I will give the land where you are now a stranger, the whole land of Canaan, to hold forever. And I will be their God.”

Then God says to Abraham, “As for you, you must keep my covenant, you and your offspring after you, generation after generation. This is my covenant that you are to keep, between me and you and your offspring after you: every male among you must be circumcised. You will circumcise the flesh of your foreskin, and that will be the sign of the covenant between me and you. Every male among you who is eight days old must be circumcised, generation after generation, whether he is born in your house or bought with money from a foreigner who is not of your offspring. Born in your house or bought with your money, he must be circumcised. So my covenant will be in your flesh, an everlasting covenant. Any uncircumcised male, who has not been circumcised in the flesh of his foreskin, will be cut off from his people. He has broken my covenant.”
The Renaming of Sarai and the Promise of Isaac · 17:15–27

God also says to Abraham, “As for Sarai your wife, don’t call her Sarai anymore. Her name is Sarah, Princess. I will bless her, and I will give you a son by her too. Yes, I will bless her, and she will become nations. Kings of peoples will come from her.”

Abraham falls on his face, and he laughs. He says to himself, “Can a son be born to a man a hundred years old? Can Sarah have a child at ninety?” And Abraham says to God, “If only Ishmael might live under your blessing!”

But God says, “No. Your wife Sarah will bear you a son, and you will name him Isaac, He Laughs. I will establish my covenant with him as an everlasting covenant, for his offspring after him. And as for Ishmael, I have heard you. Look, I will bless him. I will make him fruitful and multiply him greatly, greatly. He will father twelve princes, and I will make him a great nation. But my covenant I will establish with Isaac, whom Sarah will bear to you at this time next year.”

When he has finished speaking with him, God goes up from Abraham. That very day Abraham takes his son Ishmael and every male in his household, everyone born in his house and everyone bought with his money, and he circumcises the flesh of their foreskins, just as God has told him. Abraham is ninety-nine years old when the flesh of his foreskin is circumcised, and his son Ishmael is thirteen years old when the flesh of his foreskin is circumcised. On that very day Abraham and his son Ishmael are circumcised. And all the men of his household, those born in his house and those bought with money from foreigners, are circumcised with him.
Three Visitors at Mamre · 18:1–15

YHWH appears to Abraham by the oaks of Mamre, while he is sitting at the entrance of his tent in the heat of the day. He looks up, and there are three men standing near him. When he sees them, he runs from the tent entrance to meet them and bows down to the ground. “My lord,” he says, “if I have found favor in your eyes, please don’t pass your servant by. Let me have a little water brought, so you can wash your feet and rest under the tree. And let me fetch a bite of bread so you can refresh yourselves. Then you can go on your way, since you have come to your servant.” “All right,” they say. “Do as you have said.”

So Abraham hurries into the tent to Sarah. “Quick!” he says. “Take three measures of fine flour, a good twenty quarts, and knead it and bake some bread.” Then Abraham runs to the herd, picks out a calf, tender and choice, and gives it to a servant, who hurries to get it ready. Then he takes curds and milk and the calf he has had prepared, and he sets it before them. And while they eat, he stands nearby under the tree.
“Where is Sarah, your wife?” they ask him. “There, in the tent,” he says.
Then one of them says, “I will surely come back to you this time next year, and your wife Sarah will have a son!” Now Sarah is listening at the tent entrance, right behind him.

Abraham and Sarah are old, far along in years, and Sarah is long past the age for having children. So Sarah laughs to herself. “Now that I’m worn out,” she thinks, “am I to know delight? And my lord is old too!”

Then YHWH says to Abraham, “Why did Sarah laugh and say, ‘Will I really have a baby, now that I’m old?’ Is anything too wonderful for YHWH? At the appointed time I will come back to you, this time next year, and Sarah will have a son.”
But Sarah denies it. “I didn’t laugh,” she says, because she is afraid. “Oh yes,” he says. “You did laugh.”
Abraham Intercedes for Sodom · 18:16–33

Then the men get up to leave and look down toward Sodom, and Abraham walks along with them to see them on their way. And YHWH says, “Should I hide from Abraham what I am about to do? Abraham is surely going to become a great and mighty nation, and in him all the nations of the earth will be blessed. I have known him, so that he will teach his children and his household after him to keep the way of YHWH by doing what is right and just. That way YHWH can bring about for Abraham what he has promised him.” Then YHWH says, “The outcry against Sodom and Gomorrah is so great, and their sin so very heavy, that I will go down and see whether what they have done is as bad as the outcry that has reached me. And if not, I will know.”

So the men turn and head toward Sodom, but Abraham is still standing before YHWH. Abraham comes near and says, “Will you really sweep away the righteous along with the wicked? What if there are fifty righteous people in the city? Will you really sweep it away and not spare the place for the sake of the fifty righteous inside it? Far be it from you to do such a thing, to kill the righteous with the wicked, so that the righteous fare the same as the wicked! Far be it from you! Won’t the Judge of all the earth do what is just?”

And YHWH says, “If I find fifty righteous people in the city of Sodom, I will spare the whole place for their sake.” Abraham answers, “Look, I have dared to speak to the Lord, I who am nothing but dust and ashes. What if the fifty righteous are five short? Will you destroy the whole city for lack of five?” “If I find forty-five there,” he says, “I will not destroy it.”
Once again Abraham speaks to him: “What if only forty are found there?” “For the sake of the forty, I won’t do it,” he says.
“Please, don’t let the Lord be angry, but let me speak,” Abraham says. “What if only thirty are found there?” “If I find thirty there,” he says, “I won’t do it.”
“Look, I have dared to speak to the Lord,” Abraham says. “What if only twenty are found there?” “For the sake of the twenty,” he says, “I won’t destroy it.”
“Please, don’t let the Lord be angry, and let me speak just one more time,” Abraham says. “What if only ten are found there?” “For the sake of the ten,” he says, “I won’t destroy it.”
When YHWH has finished speaking with Abraham, he goes on his way, and Abraham goes back home.
The Two Angels Come to Sodom · 19:1–11

The two messengers come to Sodom in the evening, while Lot is sitting in the gate of Sodom. When Lot sees them, he gets up to meet them and bows with his face to the ground. “Please, my lords,” he says, “turn aside to your servant’s house. Spend the night and wash your feet. Then you can get up early and be on your way.” “No,” they say. “We’ll spend the night in the town square.”

But he presses them hard, so they turn aside with him and come into his house. He makes them a meal and bakes bread without yeast, and they eat. But before they lie down, the men of the city, the men of Sodom, surround the house, young and old, every last man from every part of the city. They shout to Lot, “Where are the men who came to you tonight? Bring them out to us, so we can have sex with them!”

Lot goes out to them at the doorway and shuts the door behind him. “Please, my brothers,” he says, “don’t do this evil thing. Look, I have two daughters who have never been with a man. Let me bring them out to you, and you can do with them whatever you like. Only don’t do anything to these men, because they have come under the shelter of my roof.”

“Get out of the way!” they say. And they say, “This fellow came here as a foreigner, and now he wants to play judge! Now we’ll do worse to you than to them!” They push hard against Lot and move in to break down the door. But the men inside reach out, pull Lot into the house with them, and shut the door. Then they strike the men at the door of the house with blindness, young and old alike, so that they wear themselves out groping for the door.
The Destruction of Sodom · 19:12–29

Then the men say to Lot, “Who else do you have here? Sons-in-law, sons, daughters, anyone you have in the city, get them out of this place. We are about to destroy this place, because the outcry against its people has grown so great before YHWH that YHWH has sent us to destroy it.”

So Lot goes out and speaks to his sons-in-law, the men pledged to marry his daughters. “Get up! Get out of this place, because YHWH is about to destroy the city!” But his sons-in-law think he is joking.

As dawn breaks, the messengers urge Lot on. “Hurry! Take your wife and your two daughters who are here, or you will be swept away when the city is punished.” But he lingers. So the men grab his hand, and his wife’s hand, and the hands of his two daughters, because YHWH has pity on him, and they bring him out and set him down outside the city. As soon as they have brought them out, one of them says, “Run for your lives! Don’t look back, and don’t stop anywhere in the plain. Run for the hills, or you will be swept away!”

But Lot says to them, “Oh no, my lord, please! Look, your servant has found favor in your eyes, and you have shown me great steadfast love in saving my life. But I can’t run as far as the hills. The disaster will catch up with me, and I’ll die. Look, there’s a town near enough to run to, and it’s only a small one. Please, let me run there. It’s only small, isn’t it? And my life will be saved.”

“Very well,” he says. “I will grant this request too. I won’t overthrow the town you are talking about. Hurry! Run there, because I can’t do anything until you get there.” That is why the town is called Zoar, Small Town.

The sun has risen over the land by the time Lot reaches Zoar. Then YHWH rains down sulfur and fire on Sodom and Gomorrah, from YHWH, out of the sky. He overthrows those cities and the whole plain, everyone living in the cities, and everything that grows on the ground. But Lot’s wife, behind him, looks back, and she becomes a pillar of salt.

Early the next morning Abraham gets up and goes to the place where he stood before YHWH. He looks down toward Sodom and Gomorrah and the whole land of the plain, and he sees smoke rising from the land like smoke from a furnace.
So it is that when God destroys the cities of the plain, God remembers Abraham. He sends Lot out of the middle of the overthrow when he overthrows the cities where Lot has lived.
Lot and His Daughters · 19:30–38

Lot goes up out of Zoar and settles in the hills with his two daughters, because he is afraid to stay in Zoar. He and his two daughters live in a cave. The older daughter says to the younger, “Our father is old, and there isn’t a man left in the land to come to us, the way it’s done all over the world. Come on, let’s get our father drunk on wine and lie with him, so we can keep our father’s family line alive.” So that night they get their father drunk on wine, and the older one goes in and lies with her father. He doesn’t know when she lies down or when she gets up. The next day the older says to the younger, “Look, last night I lay with my father. Let’s get him drunk on wine again tonight, and you go in and lie with him, so we can keep our father’s family line alive.” So that night too they get their father drunk on wine, and the younger one goes in and lies with him. He doesn’t know when she lies down or when she gets up. And so both of Lot’s daughters become pregnant by their father. The older one has a son and names him Moab, From Father. He is the father of the Moabites to this day. The younger one also has a son, and she names him Ben-ammi, Son of My People. He is the father of the Ammonites to this day.
Abraham and Abimelech · 20:1–18

From there Abraham moves on toward the Negev and settles between Kadesh and Shur. For a while he lives as a foreigner in Gerar. And Abraham says of his wife Sarah, “She’s my sister.” So Abimelech king of Gerar sends for Sarah and takes her. But God comes to Abimelech in a dream by night and says to him, “Look, you are a dead man, because of the woman you have taken. She is another man’s wife.”

Now Abimelech has not gone near her. “Lord,” he says, “will you kill people who are innocent? Didn’t he tell me himself, ‘She’s my sister’? And she said too, ‘He’s my brother.’ I did this with a clear heart and clean hands.”

Then God says to him in the dream, “Yes, I know you did this with a clear heart. In fact, it was I who held you back from sinning against me. That is why I didn’t let you touch her. Now give the man back his wife. He is a prophet, and he will pray for you, and you will live. But if you don’t give her back, know for certain that you will die, you and everyone who belongs to you.”

Early the next morning Abimelech gets up and calls all his servants together and tells them everything, and the men are terrified. Then Abimelech summons Abraham and says to him, “What have you done to us? How have I wronged you, that you would bring such great guilt on me and my kingdom? You have done things to me that should never be done.” And Abimelech asks Abraham, “What were you thinking, to do a thing like this?”

Abraham says, “I thought to myself, ‘There is no fear of God in this place at all. They’ll kill me because of my wife.’ Besides, she really is my sister, my father’s daughter, though not my mother’s. And she became my wife. So when God sent me wandering from my father’s house, I said to her, ‘This is the steadfast love you can show me: everywhere we go, say of me, “He’s my brother.”’”

Then Abimelech takes sheep and cattle, male and female servants, and gives them to Abraham, and he gives his wife Sarah back to him. And Abimelech says, “Look, my land lies open in front of you. Settle wherever you like.” And to Sarah he says, “Look, I am giving your brother a thousand pieces of silver. Let it be a covering for the eyes of everyone with you, so that before them all you are cleared.”

Then Abraham prays to God, and God heals Abimelech, and his wife, and his servant women, so that they can have children again. For YHWH had closed every womb in Abimelech’s household because of Sarah, Abraham’s wife.
The Birth of Isaac · 21:1–7

YHWH comes to Sarah, just as he said he would, and YHWH does for Sarah what he promised. Sarah conceives and bears Abraham a son in his old age, at the very time God told him. Abraham names the son Sarah has borne him Isaac, He Laughs. And when his son Isaac is eight days old, Abraham circumcises him, just as God commanded him. Abraham is a hundred years old when his son Isaac is born to him. And Sarah says, “God has made laughter for me! Everyone who hears will laugh along with me.” And she says, “Who would ever have told Abraham that Sarah would nurse children? Yet I have borne him a son in his old age!”
Hagar and Ishmael Sent Away · 21:8–21

The child grows and is weaned, and on the day Isaac is weaned, Abraham throws a great feast. But Sarah sees the son that Hagar the Egyptian bore to Abraham laughing, playing the part of Isaac. So she says to Abraham, “Throw out this slave woman and her son! The son of this slave woman will never share the inheritance with my son Isaac.”

This troubles Abraham deeply, because it concerns his son. But God says to Abraham, “Don’t be troubled about the boy and your servant. Whatever Sarah tells you, listen to her, because it is through Isaac that your offspring will carry your name. And I will make a nation out of the servant’s son too, because he is your child.”

So early the next morning Abraham takes some bread and a skin of water and gives them to Hagar. He sets them on her shoulder, gives her the boy, and sends her away. And she goes off and wanders, lost, in the wilderness of Beersheba. When the water in the skin is gone, she leaves the boy under one of the bushes. Then she goes and sits down across from him, about a bowshot away, because she says, “I can’t watch the boy die.” And as she sits there, she lifts up her voice and weeps. But God hears the voice of the boy. And the messenger of God calls to Hagar from the sky and says to her, “What’s wrong, Hagar? Don’t be afraid. God has heard the voice of the boy, right there where he is. Get up, lift the boy up, and hold him by the hand, because I will make him into a great nation.”

Then God opens her eyes, and she sees a well of water. She goes and fills the skin with water and gives the boy a drink. And God is with the boy as he grows up. He lives in the wilderness and becomes an archer. He makes his home in the wilderness of Paran, and his mother finds him a wife from the land of Egypt.
The Covenant with Abimelech · 21:22–34

About that time Abimelech and Phicol, the commander of his army, say to Abraham, “God is with you in everything you do. So swear to me here by God that you won’t deal falsely with me, or with my children, or with my descendants. Show me and the land where you have been living the same steadfast love I have shown you.”

“I swear it,” Abraham says. But Abraham complains to Abimelech about a well that Abimelech’s servants have seized. “I don’t know who did this,” Abimelech says. “You never told me, and I never heard about it until today.”

So Abraham takes sheep and cattle and gives them to Abimelech, and the two of them cut a covenant. Then Abraham sets seven ewe lambs from the flock apart by themselves. “What are these seven ewe lambs you have set apart?” Abimelech asks Abraham.

“Take these seven ewe lambs from my hand,” he says, “as a witness for me that I dug this well.” That is why that place is called Beersheba, Well of the Oath, or Well of Seven, because there the two of them swear an oath. So they cut a covenant at Beersheba. Then Abimelech and Phicol, the commander of his army, get up and go back to the land of the Philistines. And Abraham plants a tamarisk tree in Beersheba, and there he calls on the name of YHWH, El Olam, the Everlasting God. And Abraham lives as a foreigner in the land of the Philistines for a long time.
The Binding of Isaac · 22:1–19
After these things God tests Abraham. “Abraham!” he says. And Abraham says, “Here I am.”
“Take your son,” he says, “your only son, the one you love, Isaac, and get yourself going to the land of Moriah. Offer him there as a burnt offering on one of the mountains I will show you.”

So Abraham gets up early in the morning and saddles his donkey. He takes two of his young men with him, and his son Isaac. He splits the wood for the burnt offering, and he sets out for the place God has told him about. On the third day Abraham looks up and sees the place in the distance. Abraham says to his young men, “Stay here with the donkey. The boy and I will go on over there. We will worship, and then we will come back to you.” Abraham takes the wood for the burnt offering and lays it on his son Isaac, and he carries the fire and the knife in his own hand. And the two of them walk on together. Then Isaac speaks to his father Abraham. “My father?” “Here I am, my son,” he says. “Here’s the fire and the wood,” Isaac says, “but where is the lamb for the burnt offering?”

Abraham says, “God will see to the lamb for the burnt offering himself, my son.” And the two of them walk on together. They come to the place God has told him about, and Abraham builds the altar there and lays out the wood. He binds his son Isaac and lays him on the altar, on top of the wood. Then Abraham reaches out his hand and takes the knife to slaughter his son.
But the messenger of YHWH calls to him from the sky: “Abraham! Abraham!” “Here I am,” he says.
“Don’t lay a hand on the boy,” he says. “Don’t do anything to him. Now I know that you fear God, because you have not held back your son, your only son, from me.”

Abraham looks up, and look, behind him there is a ram, its horns caught in a thicket. Abraham goes and takes the ram and offers it up as a burnt offering in place of his son. And Abraham names that place YHWH Yireh, YHWH Sees to It. That is why people still say today, “On the mountain of YHWH it will be seen to.”

Then the messenger of YHWH calls to Abraham a second time from the sky and says, “By myself I have sworn, says YHWH: because you have done this, and have not held back your son, your only son, I will bless you richly. I will make your offspring as many as the stars of the heavens and the sand on the shore of the sea. Your offspring will take possession of the gates of their enemies. And in your offspring all the nations of the earth will be blessed, because you have listened to my voice.”
Then Abraham goes back to his young men, and they get up and go together to Beersheba. And Abraham stays in Beersheba.
The Family of Nahor · 22:20–24

After these things, word comes to Abraham: “Listen, Milcah has borne children too, to your brother Nahor: Uz his firstborn, Buz his brother, Kemuel the father of Aram, Chesed, Hazo, Pildash, Jidlaph, and Bethuel.” Bethuel is the father of Rebekah. These eight Milcah bears to Nahor, Abraham’s brother. And his concubine, whose name is Reumah, also bears sons: Tebah, Gaham, Tahash, and Maacah.
The Death and Burial of Sarah · 23:1–20

Sarah lives a hundred and twenty-seven years. These are the years of Sarah’s life. And Sarah dies at Kiriath-arba, that is, Hebron, in the land of Canaan. And Abraham goes in to mourn for Sarah and to weep over her.

Then Abraham rises from beside his dead wife and speaks to the Hittites, the sons of Heth. “I am a stranger and a foreigner living among you,” he says. “Sell me some ground among you for a grave, so I can bury my dead out of my sight.”
The Hittites answer Abraham, “Listen to us, my lord. You are a prince of God among us. Bury your dead in the finest of our tombs. Not one of us will refuse you his tomb for burying your dead.”

Abraham rises and bows low to the people of the land, the Hittites. And he says to them, “If you are willing for me to bury my dead out of my sight, then hear me, and speak to Ephron son of Zohar for me. Ask him to sell me the cave of Machpelah that belongs to him, at the far end of his field. Let him sell it to me here among you for the full price, as a burial place of my own.”

Now Ephron is sitting right there among the Hittites. And Ephron the Hittite answers Abraham in the hearing of the Hittites, of everyone who comes in at the gate of his city: “No, my lord, listen to me. I give you the field, and I give you the cave that is in it. Before the eyes of my own people I give it to you. Bury your dead.”

Again Abraham bows low before the people of the land, and he says to Ephron in the hearing of the people of the land, “If only you will listen to me! I will pay the price of the field. Take it from me, so I can bury my dead there.”
Ephron answers Abraham, “My lord, listen to me. A piece of land worth four hundred shekels of silver, what is that between you and me? Bury your dead.”
Abraham agrees to Ephron’s terms. He weighs out for Ephron the silver he named in the hearing of the Hittites: four hundred shekels of silver, by the weight the merchants use, about ten pounds.

So Ephron’s field at Machpelah, near Mamre, the field and the cave in it, and all the trees in the field, all within its borders, become Abraham’s property, in the presence of the Hittites, before everyone who comes in at the gate of his city. After this, Abraham buries his wife Sarah in the cave of the field of Machpelah near Mamre, that is, Hebron, in the land of Canaan. So the field and the cave in it pass from the Hittites to Abraham as a burial place of his own.
The Servant’s Commission · 24:1–9

Abraham is old now, far along in years, and YHWH has blessed Abraham in every way. Abraham says to his servant, the oldest of his household, the one in charge of everything he owns, “Please put your hand under my thigh. I want you to swear by YHWH, the God of heaven and the God of the earth, that you won’t take a wife for my son from the daughters of the Canaanites I am living among. Instead, go to my own country and my own kin, and take a wife for my son Isaac there.”
The servant says to him, “What if the woman isn’t willing to come back with me to this land? Should I then take your son back to the land you came from?”

“Make sure you never take my son back there,” Abraham tells him. “YHWH, the God of heaven, took me from my father’s house and from the land of my birth. He spoke to me and swore to me, ‘To your offspring I will give this land.’ He will send his messenger ahead of you, and you will take a wife for my son from there. If the woman isn’t willing to come back with you, then you will be free of this oath of mine. Only don’t take my son back there.”
So the servant puts his hand under the thigh of Abraham his master and swears to him about this.
The Journey and the Prayer at the Well · 24:10–27

Then the servant takes ten of his master’s camels and sets out, with all sorts of fine gifts from his master in hand. He travels to Aram of the Two Rivers, to the city of Nahor. He has the camels kneel down outside the city by the well. It is evening, the time when the women go out to draw water. And he prays, “YHWH, God of my master Abraham, please let it happen for me today. Show steadfast love to my master Abraham. Look, I am standing here by the spring, and the daughters of the townspeople are coming out to draw water. Let it be like this: the young woman I say to, ‘Please tip your jar so I can have a drink,’ and who answers, ‘Drink, and I’ll water your camels too,’ let her be the one you have chosen for your servant Isaac. That is how I will know you have shown steadfast love to my master.”

He has not even finished speaking when look, out comes Rebekah with her jar on her shoulder. She is the daughter of Bethuel, son of Milcah, the wife of Abraham’s brother Nahor. The young woman is very beautiful to look at, and unmarried. No man has ever been with her. She goes down to the spring, fills her jar, and comes back up. The servant runs to meet her. “Please,” he says, “let me sip a little water from your jar.”

“Drink, my lord,” she says. And quickly she lowers her jar onto her hand and gives him a drink. When she has given him enough, she says, “I’ll draw water for your camels too, until they have had their fill.” So she quickly empties her jar into the trough and runs back to the well to draw more, and she draws enough for all his camels.

All the while the man is gazing at her in silence, waiting to learn whether YHWH has made his journey a success or not. When the camels have finished drinking, the man takes out a gold ring weighing half a shekel and two gold bracelets for her wrists weighing ten shekels, and he says, “Whose daughter are you? Please tell me. Is there room in your father’s house for us to spend the night?”
She tells him, “I am the daughter of Bethuel, the son Milcah bore to Nahor.” And she adds, “We have plenty of straw and feed, and room for you to spend the night.”

Then the man bows down and worships YHWH. “Blessed be YHWH,” he says, “the God of my master Abraham, who has not let go of his steadfast love and his faithfulness toward my master. As for me, YHWH has led me on the road straight to the house of my master’s kin.”
At the House of Laban · 24:28–67

The young woman runs and tells her mother’s household all about it. Now Rebekah has a brother named Laban. And Laban runs out to the man at the spring. He has seen the ring, and the bracelets on his sister’s wrists, and he has heard his sister Rebekah say, “This is what the man said to me.” So he goes out to the man, and there he is, standing by the camels at the spring. “Come in, you who are blessed by YHWH!” Laban says. “Why are you standing out here? I have the house ready, and a place for the camels.”

So the man comes into the house, and the camels are unloaded. Straw and feed are brought for the camels, and water to wash his feet and the feet of the men with him. Then food is set before him. But he says, “I won’t eat until I have said what I came to say.” “Go ahead, speak,” says Laban.

“I am Abraham’s servant,” he says. “YHWH has blessed my master richly, and he has become a great man. YHWH has given him flocks and herds, silver and gold, male and female servants, camels and donkeys. And Sarah, my master’s wife, bore my master a son when she was old, and my master has given him everything he owns. My master made me swear an oath. He said, ‘Don’t take a wife for my son from the daughters of the Canaanites, whose land I live in. Go to my father’s house, to my own clan, and take a wife for my son there.’ I said to my master, ‘What if the woman won’t come back with me?’ And he said to me, ‘YHWH, before whom I walk, will send his messenger with you and make your journey a success. You will take a wife for my son from my own clan, from my father’s house. Then you will be free of my oath, once you have gone to my clan. Even if they won’t give her to you, you will be free of my oath.’ So today I came to the spring, and I prayed, ‘YHWH, God of my master Abraham, if you will, please make this journey I’m on a success. Look, I am standing by this spring. Let it be that the young woman who comes out to draw water, the one I say to, “Please give me a little water from your jar,” and who says to me, “Drink, and I’ll draw water for your camels too,” let her be the woman YHWH has chosen for my master’s son.’ And before I had finished speaking in my heart, look, out came Rebekah with her jar on her shoulder. She went down to the spring and drew water, and I said to her, ‘Please give me a drink.’ She quickly lowered her jar from her shoulder and said, ‘Drink, and I’ll water your camels too.’ So I drank, and she watered the camels too. Then I asked her, ‘Whose daughter are you?’ And she said, ‘The daughter of Bethuel, Nahor’s son, whom Milcah bore to him.’ So I put the ring in her nose and the bracelets on her wrists. And I bowed down and worshiped YHWH. I blessed YHWH, the God of my master Abraham, who led me on the right road to take the daughter of my master’s kinsman for his son. Now then, if you mean to show steadfast love and faithfulness to my master, tell me. And if not, tell me, so I’ll know which way to turn.”

Laban and Bethuel answer, “This comes from YHWH. We can’t say anything to you, one way or the other. Look, here is Rebekah. Take her and go, and let her be the wife of your master’s son, just as YHWH has said.”

When Abraham’s servant hears what they say, he bows down to the ground before YHWH. Then the servant brings out jewelry of silver and gold, and clothing, and gives them to Rebekah. He also gives costly gifts to her brother and her mother. Then he and the men with him eat and drink and spend the night. When they get up in the morning, he says, “Send me on my way back to my master.”
But her brother and her mother say, “Let the girl stay with us a while, ten days or so. Then she can go.”
“Don’t hold me back,” he tells them, “now that YHWH has made my journey a success. Send me on my way, so I can go to my master.”
“Let’s call the girl,” they say, “and ask her.” So they call Rebekah and ask her, “Will you go with this man?” “I will go,” she says.
