So they send their sister Rebekah on her way with her nurse, and with Abraham’s servant and his men. And they bless Rebekah and say to her, “Our sister, may you become thousands upon tens of thousands! And may your offspring take possession of the gates of those who hate them!”

Then Rebekah and her young women get up, mount the camels, and follow the man. So the servant takes Rebekah and sets out. Now Isaac has just come back from Beer-lahai-roi, for he is living in the Negev. One evening Isaac goes out into the field to think and pray, and he looks up, and look, there are camels coming! Rebekah looks up too, and when she sees Isaac, she slips down from her camel. “Who is that man walking across the field to meet us?” she asks the servant. “That is my master,” the servant says. So she takes her veil and covers herself.

Then the servant tells Isaac everything he has done. And Isaac brings her into the tent of his mother Sarah. He takes Rebekah, and she becomes his wife, and he loves her. And so Isaac is comforted after his mother’s death.
The Death of Abraham · 25:1–11

Abraham takes another wife, and her name is Keturah. She bears him Zimran, Jokshan, Medan, Midian, Ishbak, and Shuah. Jokshan is the father of Sheba and Dedan. The descendants of Dedan are the Asshurim, the Letushim, and the Leummim. The sons of Midian are Ephah, Epher, Hanoch, Abida, and Eldaah. All these are descendants of Keturah. Abraham leaves everything he owns to Isaac. But to the sons of his concubines Abraham gives gifts, and while he is still alive he sends them away from his son Isaac, eastward, to the land of the east. These are the years of Abraham’s life: a hundred and seventy-five years. Then Abraham breathes his last and dies at a good old age, an old man, full of years, and he is gathered to his people. His sons Isaac and Ishmael bury him in the cave of Machpelah near Mamre, in the field of Ephron son of Zohar the Hittite, the field Abraham bought from the Hittites. There Abraham is buried with his wife Sarah. After Abraham’s death, God blesses his son Isaac. And Isaac settles near Beer-lahai-roi.
The Sons of Ishmael · 25:12–18

Here is the story of the generations of Ishmael, Abraham’s son, whom Hagar the Egyptian, Sarah’s servant, bore to Abraham. These are the names of Ishmael’s sons, listed in the order of their birth: Nebaioth, Ishmael’s firstborn, then Kedar, Adbeel, Mibsam, Mishma, Dumah, Massa, Hadad, Tema, Jetur, Naphish, and Kedemah. These are the sons of Ishmael, and these are their names, by their villages and their encampments: twelve princes of their tribes. These are the years of Ishmael’s life: a hundred and thirty-seven years. He breathes his last and dies, and he is gathered to his people. His descendants settle from Havilah to Shur, near the border of Egypt, on the way to Assyria. He lives at odds with all his kin.
The Birth of Esau and Jacob · 25:19–28

Here is the story of the generations of Isaac, Abraham’s son. Abraham is the father of Isaac. Isaac is forty years old when he takes Rebekah as his wife, the daughter of Bethuel the Aramean from Paddan-aram, and the sister of Laban the Aramean. Isaac pleads with YHWH for his wife, because she is barren. And YHWH answers his plea, and his wife Rebekah conceives. But the children crash against each other inside her, and she says, “If it’s going to be like this, why am I alive?” So she goes to ask YHWH. And YHWH tells her, “Two nations are in your womb. Two peoples will be parted from your body. One people will overpower the other, and the elder will serve the younger.”

When her time comes to give birth, look, there are twins in her womb. The first comes out red, his whole body like a hairy cloak, so they name him Esau, Hairy. After that his brother comes out, with his hand gripping Esau’s heel, so he is named Jacob, Heel-Grabber. Isaac is sixty years old when she gives birth to them.

The boys grow up. Esau becomes a skilled hunter, a man of the open country, while Jacob is a quiet man who stays among the tents. Isaac loves Esau, because he has a taste for wild game, but Rebekah loves Jacob.
The Selling of the Birthright · 25:29–34

One day Jacob is cooking stew when Esau comes in from the open country, worn out and starving. Esau says to Jacob, “Quick, let me gulp down some of that red stuff, that red stew there. I’m starving!” That is why he is also called Edom, Red.
“First sell me your birthright,” Jacob says.
“Look, I’m about to die,” Esau says. “What good is a birthright to me?”
“Swear to me first,” Jacob says. So he swears to him and sells his birthright to Jacob.
Then Jacob gives Esau bread and lentil stew. He eats and drinks, then gets up and leaves. So Esau treats his birthright as worthless.
Isaac and Abimelech · 26:1–33

Now there is a famine in the land, another one besides the earlier famine in Abraham’s day. So Isaac goes to Abimelech king of the Philistines, at Gerar. YHWH appears to him and says, “Don’t go down to Egypt. Settle in the land I tell you about. Stay in this land as a foreigner, and I will be with you and bless you. To you and to your offspring I will give all these lands, and I will keep the oath I swore to your father Abraham. I will make your offspring as many as the stars in the sky, and I will give your offspring all these lands. And in your offspring all the nations of the earth will be blessed, because Abraham listened to my voice and kept my charge: my commands, my decrees, and my teachings.”

So Isaac settles in Gerar. When the men of the place ask about his wife, he says, “She’s my sister.” He is afraid to say, “She’s my wife,” because he thinks, “The men here might kill me over Rebekah, since she is so beautiful.” After he has been there a long time, Abimelech king of the Philistines happens to look down from a window, and what does he see but Isaac laughing and playing with Rebekah, his wife! So Abimelech summons Isaac. “Look, she is obviously your wife!” he says. “So why did you say, ‘She’s my sister’?” Isaac tells him, “Because I thought I might die on account of her.”
“What have you done to us?” Abimelech says. “One of the men might easily have slept with your wife, and you would have brought guilt down on us!”
So Abimelech gives an order to all the people: “Whoever touches this man or his wife will surely be put to death.”

Isaac sows seed in that land, and that same year he reaps a hundred times what he planted. YHWH blesses him. The man grows rich, and keeps growing richer and richer, until he is very rich indeed. He has flocks and herds and a great household of servants, and the Philistines envy him. So the Philistines stop up all the wells his father’s servants dug in his father Abraham’s day, filling them in with dirt. Then Abimelech says to Isaac, “Move away from us. You have grown far too strong for us.”
So Isaac leaves there, pitches his tents in the valley of Gerar, and settles there.

Isaac digs out again the wells that were dug in the days of his father Abraham, which the Philistines stopped up after Abraham died. And he gives them the same names his father gave them. Isaac’s servants dig in the valley and find a well of fresh, flowing water there. But the herdsmen of Gerar quarrel with Isaac’s herdsmen. “The water is ours!” they say. So he names the well Esek, Quarrel, because they quarreled with him. Then they dig another well, and they fight over that one too. So he names it Sitnah, Accusation. He moves on from there and digs another well, and no one fights over that one. So he names it Rehoboth, Wide Places. “Now YHWH has made room for us,” he says, “and we will be fruitful in the land.”

From there he goes up to Beersheba. That night YHWH appears to him and says, “I am the God of your father Abraham. Don’t be afraid, because I am with you. I will bless you and multiply your offspring for the sake of my servant Abraham.”
So Isaac builds an altar there and calls on the name of YHWH. He pitches his tent there, and his servants dig a well there.
Then Abimelech comes to him from Gerar, with Ahuzzath his adviser and Phicol the commander of his army. Isaac asks them, “Why have you come to me, when you hate me and sent me away from you?”

“We can see plainly that YHWH is with you,” they say. “So we said, ‘Let there be an oath between us, between us and you.’ Let us cut a covenant with you that you won’t do us any harm, just as we haven’t touched you, and have done nothing but good to you, and sent you away in peace. Now you are the blessed of YHWH.”

So Isaac throws a feast for them, and they eat and drink. Early the next morning they get up and swear an oath to one another. Then Isaac sends them on their way, and they leave him in peace. That same day Isaac’s servants come and tell him about the well they have been digging. “We’ve found water!” they say. He names it Shibah, Oath. That is why the name of the city is Beersheba to this day.
Esau’s Wives · 26:34–35
When Esau is forty years old, he marries Judith daughter of Beeri the Hittite, and Basemath daughter of Elon the Hittite. And they make life bitter for Isaac and Rebekah.
The Stolen Blessing · 27:1–40
When Isaac is old and his eyes have grown so dim he can no longer see, he calls for Esau, his older son. “My son,” he says. “Here I am,” Esau answers.

“Look,” Isaac says, “I am old now, and I don’t know the day of my death. So take your gear, your quiver and your bow, and go out into the open country and hunt some game for me. Make me a tasty dish, the kind I love, and bring it to me to eat, so that with my whole soul I can bless you before I die.”

Now Rebekah is listening while Isaac speaks to his son Esau. So when Esau goes off into the open country to hunt game and bring it back, Rebekah says to her son Jacob, “Listen, I just heard your father talking to your brother Esau. He said, ‘Bring me some game and make me a tasty dish to eat, so I can bless you in the presence of YHWH before I die.’ Now, my son, listen to me, and do exactly what I tell you. Go out to the flock and bring me two good young goats, and I’ll make them into a tasty dish for your father, the kind he loves. Then you take it to your father to eat, so that he will bless you before he dies.”

But Jacob says to his mother Rebekah, “Look, my brother Esau is a hairy man, and I’m a smooth man. What if my father touches me? I’ll look like I’m making a fool of him, and I’ll bring a curse on myself instead of a blessing.”
“Let the curse fall on me, my son,” his mother says. “Just listen to me. Go and get them for me.”

So he goes and gets them and brings them to his mother, and his mother makes a tasty dish, the kind his father loves. Then Rebekah takes the best clothes of Esau, her older son, which she has in the house, and she puts them on Jacob, her younger son. And she covers his hands and the smooth part of his neck with the skins of the young goats. Then she hands her son Jacob the tasty dish and the bread she has made.
He goes in to his father and says, “My father.” “Here I am,” he says. “Which one are you, my son?”
Jacob tells his father, “I am Esau, your firstborn. I’ve done what you told me. Please, sit up and eat some of my game, so that you can bless me with your whole soul.”
“How did you find it so fast, my son?” Isaac asks. “Because YHWH your God sent it my way,” he says.
Then Isaac says to Jacob, “Come close, so I can feel you, my son, and know whether you really are my son Esau or not.”

So Jacob comes close to his father Isaac, and Isaac feels him and says, “The voice is the voice of Jacob, but the hands are the hands of Esau.” He does not recognize him, because his hands are hairy like his brother Esau’s hands. So he blesses him. “Are you really my son Esau?” he asks. “I am,” he says.
“Then bring it to me,” Isaac says, “and I will eat some of my son’s game, so that with my whole soul I can bless you.” So Jacob brings it to him, and he eats, and he brings him wine, and he drinks.

Then his father Isaac says to him, “Come here and kiss me, my son.” So he comes close and kisses him. And when Isaac smells the smell of his clothes, he blesses him: “Ah, the smell of my son is like the smell of a field that YHWH has blessed! May God give you the dew of the sky and the richness of the earth, plenty of grain and new wine. May peoples serve you and nations bow down to you. Be master over your brothers, and may your mother’s sons bow down to you. Cursed be everyone who curses you, and blessed be everyone who blesses you!”

No sooner has Isaac finished blessing Jacob, and Jacob has barely left his father Isaac’s presence, than his brother Esau comes in from his hunting. He too makes a tasty dish and brings it to his father. “Let my father sit up and eat some of his son’s game,” he says, “so that you can bless me with your whole soul.”
“Who are you?” his father Isaac asks. “I’m your son,” he says, “your firstborn, Esau.”
Then Isaac begins to shake, trembling from head to foot. “Who was it, then,” he says, “who hunted game and brought it to me? I ate it all before you came, and I blessed him. And blessed he will be!”
When Esau hears his father’s words, he lets out a loud and bitter cry, a cry without end. “Bless me,” he says to his father. “Me too, my father!”
But Isaac says, “Your brother came in with deceit and took your blessing.”

“Isn’t he rightly named Jacob, Heel-Grabber?” Esau says. “He has grabbed my heel twice now! He took my birthright, and look, now he has taken my blessing!” Then he says, “Haven’t you saved a blessing for me?”
Isaac answers Esau, “Look, I have made him your master, and I have given him all his brothers as his servants, and I have sustained him with grain and new wine. So what can I do for you, my son?”
Esau says to his father, “Do you have only one blessing, my father? Bless me, me too, my father!” And Esau lifts up his voice and weeps.

Then his father Isaac answers him, “Look, your home will be far from the richness of the earth, and far from the dew of the sky above. By your sword you will live, and you will serve your brother. But when you grow restless, you will break his yoke off your neck.”
Jacob Flees · 27:41–46
Esau holds a grudge against Jacob because of the blessing his father gave him. And Esau says to himself, “The days of mourning for my father are coming. Then I will kill my brother Jacob.”

But word of what Esau, her older son, has said reaches Rebekah. So she sends for Jacob, her younger son, and tells him, “Listen, your brother Esau is consoling himself with the thought of killing you. So now, my son, listen to me. Get up and run to my brother Laban in Haran. Stay with him for a while, until your brother’s fury cools, until your brother’s anger turns away from you and he forgets what you did to him. Then I will send for you and bring you back from there. Why should I lose you both in one day?”
Then Rebekah says to Isaac, “I am sick to death of these Hittite women! If Jacob marries one of the Hittite women, one of the women of this land like these, what good will my life be to me?”
Isaac Sends Jacob to Paddan-aram · 28:1–9

So Isaac calls for Jacob and blesses him, and he gives him this command: “Don’t marry any of the women of Canaan. Get up and go to Paddan-aram, to the house of Bethuel, your mother’s father. Find yourself a wife there, from among the daughters of Laban, your mother’s brother. May El Shaddai bless you and make you fruitful and multiply you, so that you become a whole gathering of peoples. May he give the blessing of Abraham to you and to your offspring with you, so that you take possession of the land where you now live as a foreigner, the land God gave to Abraham.”
So Isaac sends Jacob on his way, and he goes to Paddan-aram, to Laban son of Bethuel the Aramean, the brother of Rebekah, the mother of Jacob and Esau.

Now Esau sees that Isaac has blessed Jacob and sent him off to Paddan-aram to find a wife there, and that when he blessed him, he commanded him, “Don’t marry any of the women of Canaan,” and that Jacob has listened to his father and mother and gone to Paddan-aram. So Esau realizes how little his father Isaac thinks of the women of Canaan. So Esau goes to Ishmael and marries Mahalath, the daughter of Abraham’s son Ishmael and the sister of Nebaioth, in addition to the wives he already has.
Jacob’s Dream at Bethel · 28:10–22

Jacob leaves Beersheba and sets out for Haran. He comes to a certain place and stops there for the night, because the sun has gone down. He takes one of the stones of the place, puts it under his head, and lies down in that place to sleep. And he dreams. Look, a stairway is standing on the ground, its top touching the sky, and look, God’s messengers are going up and coming down on it! And look, YHWH is standing over him, and he says, “I am YHWH, the God of your father Abraham and the God of Isaac. The land you are lying on I will give to you and to your offspring. Your offspring will be like the dust of the earth, and you will spread out to the west and the east, to the north and the south. In you and in your offspring all the families of the ground will be blessed. Look, I am with you. I will guard you wherever you go, and I will bring you home to this land. I will never leave you, not until I have done everything I have told you.”

Then Jacob wakes up from his sleep. “YHWH is truly in this place,” he says, “and I didn’t know it!” And he is afraid, and he says, “What an awesome place this is! This is nothing less than the house of God. This is the gate of heaven.”

Early in the morning Jacob gets up, takes the stone he put under his head, and sets it up as a standing pillar. And he pours oil on top of it. He names that place Bethel, House of God, though the town used to be called Luz. Then Jacob makes a vow: “If God will be with me and guard me on this road I am traveling, and give me bread to eat and clothes to wear, so that I come back to my father’s house in peace, then YHWH will be my God, and this stone I have set up as a pillar will be God’s house. And of everything you give me, I will surely give a tenth back to you.”
Jacob Arrives at Laban’s House · 29:1–14

Jacob picks up his feet and goes on, and he comes to the land of the people of the east. He looks around, and there in the open country is a well, with three flocks of sheep lying beside it, because the flocks are watered from that well. The stone over the mouth of the well is a big one. When all the flocks have gathered there, the shepherds roll the stone off the mouth of the well and water the sheep. Then they put the stone back in its place over the mouth of the well. Jacob says to them, “Friends, where are you from?” “We’re from Haran,” they say.
“Do you know Laban, Nahor’s grandson?” he asks. “We know him,” they say.
“Is he well?” he asks. “He’s well,” they say. “And look, here comes his daughter Rachel with the sheep.”
“Look,” he says, “it’s still broad daylight. It isn’t time yet to gather the animals in. Water the sheep, and take them back out to graze.”
“We can’t,” they say, “not until all the flocks are gathered and the stone is rolled off the mouth of the well. Then we water the sheep.”

He is still talking with them when Rachel arrives with her father’s sheep, because she is a shepherd. And when Jacob sees Rachel, the daughter of his mother’s brother Laban, with the sheep of his mother’s brother Laban, Jacob steps up, rolls the stone off the mouth of the well all by himself, and waters the flock of his mother’s brother Laban. Then Jacob kisses Rachel, and he lifts up his voice and weeps. Jacob tells Rachel that he is her father’s kinsman, Rebekah’s son, and she runs and tells her father.

As soon as Laban hears the news about Jacob, his sister’s son, he runs to meet him. He hugs him and kisses him and brings him to his house, and Jacob tells Laban all that has happened. “You really are my own bone and flesh!” Laban says to him. And Jacob stays with him a whole month.
Jacob, Leah, and Rachel · 29:15–30
Then Laban says to Jacob, “Just because you’re my kinsman, should you work for me for nothing? Tell me, what should your wages be?”

Now Laban has two daughters. The older is named Leah, and the younger is named Rachel. Leah has tender eyes, but Rachel is lovely in form and lovely to look at. Jacob is in love with Rachel. So he says, “I’ll work for you seven years for your younger daughter Rachel.”
“Better I give her to you than to some other man,” Laban says. “Stay with me.”
So Jacob works seven years for Rachel, and they seem to him like only a few days, because he loves her so.
Then Jacob says to Laban, “Give me my wife. My time is up, and I want to go in to her.”

So Laban gathers all the people of the place and throws a feast. But in the evening he takes his daughter Leah and brings her to Jacob, and Jacob goes in to her. And Laban gives his servant Zilpah to his daughter Leah as her servant. And in the morning, look, it’s Leah! “What have you done to me?” Jacob says to Laban. “Didn’t I work for you for Rachel? Why have you tricked me?”

“It isn’t done here,” Laban says, “to give the younger in marriage before the firstborn. Finish out the wedding week with this one, and we’ll give you the other one too, in return for another seven years of work for me.”

And Jacob does so. He finishes out the week with Leah, and then Laban gives him his daughter Rachel as his wife. Laban gives his servant Bilhah to his daughter Rachel as her servant. So Jacob goes in to Rachel too, and he loves Rachel more than Leah. And he works for Laban another seven years.
Leah’s Sons · 29:31–35

When YHWH sees that Leah is hated, he opens her womb, but Rachel is barren. Leah conceives and has a son, and she names him Reuben, See, a Son! “Because YHWH has seen my misery,” she says. “Surely now my husband will love me.” She conceives again and has a son, and she says, “Because YHWH has heard that I am hated, he has given me this one too.” So she names him Simeon, Heard. Again she conceives and has a son, and she says, “Now this time my husband will be joined to me, because I have borne him three sons.” So he is named Levi, Joined. And again she conceives and has a son, and she says, “This time I will praise YHWH.” So she names him Judah, Praise. Then she stops having children.
The Children of Jacob · 30:1–24
When Rachel sees that she is not bearing Jacob any children, she is jealous of her sister. “Give me children,” she says to Jacob, “or I’ll die!”
Jacob’s anger blazes up at Rachel. “Am I in the place of God,” he says, “who has kept you from bearing children?”

“Here’s my servant Bilhah,” she says. “Go in to her, so that she can give birth on my knees, and I can build a family through her too.” So she gives him her servant Bilhah as a wife, and Jacob goes in to her. Bilhah conceives and bears Jacob a son. And Rachel says, “God has judged in my favor. He has heard my voice and given me a son.” So she names him Dan, He Judged. Rachel’s servant Bilhah conceives again and bears Jacob a second son. And Rachel says, “I have wrestled God-sized wrestlings with my sister, and I have won.” So she names him Naphtali, My Wrestling.

When Leah sees that she has stopped having children, she takes her servant Zilpah and gives her to Jacob as a wife. Leah’s servant Zilpah bears Jacob a son. “What good fortune!” Leah says. So she names him Gad, Fortune. Leah’s servant Zilpah bears Jacob a second son. “How happy I am!” Leah says. “The women will call me happy.” So she names him Asher, Happy.
During the wheat harvest Reuben goes out and finds some mandrakes, love apples, in the field and brings them to his mother Leah. Rachel says to Leah, “Please give me some of your son’s mandrakes.”

But she says to her, “Wasn’t it enough that you took my husband? Now you want to take my son’s mandrakes too?” “All right,” Rachel says. “He can sleep with you tonight in exchange for your son’s mandrakes.”
When Jacob comes in from the field that evening, Leah goes out to meet him. “You’re sleeping with me tonight,” she says. “I’ve hired you with my son’s mandrakes.” So he sleeps with her that night.

And God listens to Leah, and she conceives and bears Jacob a fifth son. Leah says, “God has given me my wages, because I gave my servant to my husband.” So she names him Issachar, Wages. Leah conceives again and bears Jacob a sixth son. And Leah says, “God has given me a precious gift. Now my husband will honor me, because I have borne him six sons.” So she names him Zebulun, Honor. Later she has a daughter and names her Dinah.

Then God remembers Rachel. God listens to her and opens her womb. She conceives and has a son, and she says, “God has taken away my disgrace.” She names him Joseph, May He Add, and says, “May YHWH add another son for me.”
Jacob’s Bargain with Laban · 30:25–43

After Rachel has given birth to Joseph, Jacob says to Laban, “Send me on my way, so I can go home to my own place and my own country. Give me my wives and my children, the ones I have worked for, and let me go. You know how hard I have worked for you.”
But Laban says to him, “Please, if I have found favor in your eyes, stay. I have learned by divination that YHWH has blessed me because of you.” And he says, “Name your wages, and I’ll pay them.”

Jacob says to him, “You know how I have worked for you, and how your livestock have done in my care. You had little before I came, and it has burst out into a great deal. YHWH has blessed you at my every step. But now, when will I do something for my own household?”
“What should I give you?” Laban asks. “Don’t give me anything,” Jacob says. “If you will do this one thing for me, I will go back to pasturing your flock and keeping it.

Let me go through all your flocks today and take out every speckled or spotted sheep, every dark lamb, and every spotted or speckled goat. They will be my wages. Then in days to come my honesty will speak for me. Whenever you come to check on my wages, any goat in my care that isn’t speckled or spotted, or any lamb that isn’t dark, will count as stolen.”
“Agreed,” Laban says. “Let it be as you say.”

But that same day Laban takes out the male goats that are streaked or spotted, and all the female goats that are speckled or spotted, every one with white on it, and all the dark lambs, and he puts them in the care of his sons. Then he puts three days’ journey between himself and Jacob, while Jacob goes on pasturing the rest of Laban’s flocks.

Then Jacob takes fresh-cut branches of poplar, almond, and plane trees, and peels white stripes in them, laying bare the white wood under the bark. He sets the peeled branches in the troughs, in the water channels, right in front of the flocks where they come to drink. And the animals mate when they come to drink. So the flocks mate in front of the branches, and they bear young that are streaked, speckled, and spotted. Jacob sets the lambs apart, and he turns the flocks to face the streaked and dark animals in Laban’s flock. So he builds up flocks of his own and keeps them apart from Laban’s flock. Whenever the stronger animals are mating, Jacob lays the branches in the troughs in front of their eyes, so that they mate among the branches. But when the animals are weak, he doesn’t put them there. So the weak ones go to Laban, and the strong ones to Jacob. And so the man grows very rich, with large flocks, male and female servants, camels and donkeys.
Jacob Flees from Laban · 31:1–21

Now Jacob hears what Laban’s sons are saying: “Jacob has taken everything our father had. He’s made all this wealth out of what belonged to our father.” And Jacob sees the look on Laban’s face. Laban doesn’t look at him the way he used to. Then YHWH says to Jacob, “Go back to the land of your fathers and to your kin, and I will be with you.”

So Jacob sends for Rachel and Leah to come out to the field where his flock is, and he says to them, “I can see from your father’s face that he doesn’t look at me the way he used to. But the God of my father has been with me. You know I have worked for your father with all my strength. Yet your father has cheated me and changed my wages ten times. But God hasn’t let him harm me. If he said, ‘The speckled ones will be your wages,’ then the whole flock bore speckled young. And if he said, ‘The streaked ones will be your wages,’ then the whole flock bore streaked young. So God has taken your father’s livestock away from him and given them to me. Once, in the season when the flocks were mating, I looked up and saw in a dream that the male goats mating with the flock were streaked, speckled, and mottled. And the messenger of God said to me in the dream, ‘Jacob!’ And I said, ‘Here I am.’ He said, ‘Look up and see: all the male goats mating with the flock are streaked, speckled, and mottled, because I have seen everything Laban is doing to you. I am the God of Bethel, where you anointed a pillar and made a vow to me. Now get up, leave this land, and go back to the land where you were born.’”

Rachel and Leah answer him, “Is there any share or inheritance left for us in our father’s house? Doesn’t he treat us like foreigners? He sold us, and then he spent every bit of the money paid for us! All the wealth God has taken away from our father belongs to us and our children anyway. So now, whatever God has told you, do it.”

So Jacob gets up and puts his children and his wives on camels, and he drives off all his livestock and all the goods he has gathered, the livestock he has acquired in Paddan-aram, to go to his father Isaac in the land of Canaan. Laban has gone off to shear his sheep, and Rachel steals her father’s household gods.

And Jacob steals Laban the Aramean’s heart: he slips away without telling him he is running. So he runs off with everything he has. He sets out, crosses the Euphrates River, and heads for the hill country of Gilead.
Laban Pursues Jacob · 31:22–42

On the third day Laban is told that Jacob has run away. He takes his kinsmen with him and chases after Jacob for seven days, and catches up with him in the hill country of Gilead. But God comes to Laban the Aramean in a dream by night and tells him, “Be careful not to say anything to Jacob, good or bad.”

Laban catches up with Jacob. Jacob has pitched his tent in the hill country, and Laban and his kinsmen pitch theirs in the hill country of Gilead. Then Laban says to Jacob, “What have you done? You’ve stolen my heart and carried off my daughters like prisoners of war! Why did you run off in secret and steal away from me? Why didn’t you tell me? I would have sent you off with celebration and songs, with tambourines and harps. You didn’t even let me kiss my grandchildren and my daughters goodbye! That was a foolish thing you did. I have the power to do you harm. But last night the God of your father said to me, ‘Be careful not to say anything to Jacob, good or bad.’ Now, you had to go, because you were homesick for your father’s house. But why did you steal my gods?”

Jacob answers Laban, “I was afraid. I thought you would take your daughters away from me by force. But if you find your gods with anyone here, that person won’t live. Here in front of our kinsmen, look for yourself, and if you find anything of yours with me, take it.” Jacob doesn’t know that Rachel has stolen them.

So Laban goes into Jacob’s tent, and Leah’s tent, and the tent of the two servant women, but he doesn’t find them. He comes out of Leah’s tent and goes into Rachel’s tent. Now Rachel has taken the household gods, put them inside her camel’s saddle, and sat down on them. Laban feels his way through the whole tent but doesn’t find them. She says to her father, “Don’t be angry, my lord, that I can’t get up for you. I’m having my period.” So he searches, but he doesn’t find the household gods.

Then Jacob gets angry and takes Laban to task. “What is my crime?” Jacob says to Laban. “What is my sin, that you come chasing after me in a rage? You’ve felt your way through all my things. What have you found that belongs to your house? Set it out here in front of my kinsmen and yours, and let them judge between the two of us.

Twenty years now I have been with you. Your ewes and your nanny goats have never lost their young, and I have never eaten the rams of your flock. I never brought you an animal torn by wild beasts. I took the loss myself. You made me pay for anything stolen, by day or by night. This is how it was for me: by day the heat ate me up, and by night the cold, and sleep ran away from my eyes. Twenty years I have been in your household. I worked for you fourteen years for your two daughters and six years for your flock, and you changed my wages ten times. If the God of my father, the God of Abraham, the Fear of Isaac, had not been on my side, you would have sent me away empty-handed by now. But God has seen my misery and the work of my hands, and last night he set you straight.”
The Covenant at Galeed · 31:43–55

Laban answers Jacob, “The daughters are my daughters, the children are my children, the flocks are my flocks. Everything you see is mine! But what can I do today about these daughters of mine, or the children they have borne? So come, let’s cut a covenant, you and I, and let it stand as a witness between us.”

So Jacob takes a stone and sets it up as a pillar. And Jacob says to his kinsmen, “Gather stones.” So they take stones and make a heap, and they eat there beside the heap. Laban calls it Jegar-sahadutha, and Jacob calls it Galeed. Both names mean Heap of Witness, one in Aramaic and one in Hebrew. “This heap is a witness between you and me today,” Laban says. That is why it is named Galeed, and also Mizpah, Watchtower, because he says, “May YHWH keep watch between you and me when we are out of each other’s sight. If you mistreat my daughters, or if you take other wives besides my daughters, even though no one else is with us, look, God is witness between you and me.” Then Laban says to Jacob, “Look at this heap, and look at this pillar I have set up between you and me. This heap is a witness, and this pillar is a witness, that I won’t cross over past this heap to you, and you won’t cross over past this heap and this pillar to me, to do harm. May the God of Abraham and the God of Nahor, the God of their father, judge between us.” So Jacob swears by the Fear of his father Isaac. Then Jacob offers a sacrifice there in the hill country and invites his kinsmen to the meal. They eat, and they spend the night in the hill country. Early in the morning Laban gets up, kisses his grandchildren and his daughters, and blesses them. Then Laban leaves and goes back home.
Messengers and Fear · 32:1–21
Jacob goes on his way, and God’s messengers meet him. When Jacob sees them, he says, “This is God’s camp!” So he names that place Mahanaim, Two Camps.

Jacob sends messengers ahead of him to his brother Esau in the land of Seir, the country of Edom. He gives them these orders: “This is what you are to say to my lord Esau: ‘Your servant Jacob says this: I have been living with Laban as a foreigner, and I have stayed until now. I have cattle and donkeys, flocks, and male and female servants. I am sending word to my lord, in hope of finding favor in your eyes.’” The messengers come back to Jacob and say, “We went to your brother Esau. He is coming to meet you, and four hundred men are with him.” Jacob is terrified and sick with worry. So he splits the people with him into two camps, along with the flocks and herds and camels. He thinks, “If Esau comes to one camp and attacks it, the camp that is left can get away.”

Then Jacob prays, “God of my father Abraham and God of my father Isaac, YHWH, you told me, ‘Go back to your country and your kin, and I will do you good.’ I am too small for all the acts of steadfast love and all the faithfulness you have shown your servant. When I crossed this Jordan, all I had was my staff, and now I have become two camps. Please, rescue me from the hand of my brother, from the hand of Esau. I am afraid of him. I am afraid he will come and attack me, mothers and children alike. But you said, ‘I will surely do you good, and I will make your offspring like the sand of the sea, too many to count.’”

He spends the night there. Then from what he has with him he picks out a gift for his brother Esau: two hundred nanny goats and twenty billy goats, two hundred ewes and twenty rams, thirty nursing camels with their young, forty cows and ten bulls, twenty female donkeys and ten male donkeys. He puts each herd in the care of one of his servants, and he tells his servants, “Go on ahead of me, and keep some space between one herd and the next.” He gives the one in front these orders: “When my brother Esau meets you and asks, ‘Who do you belong to? Where are you going? And whose animals are these in front of you?’ then say, ‘They belong to your servant Jacob. They are a gift sent to my lord Esau. And look, he is right behind us.’” He gives the same orders to the second and the third and to everyone driving the herds: “This is what you are to say to Esau when you meet him. And be sure to say, ‘Look, your servant Jacob is right behind us.’” For he thinks, “I will soothe his face with the gift that goes ahead of me, and after that I will look him in the face. Maybe he will welcome me.”
So the gift goes on ahead of him, while he himself spends that night in the camp.
The Wrestling at the Jabbok · 32:22–32

That same night he gets up and takes his two wives, his two servant women, and his eleven sons, and crosses the ford of the Jabbok. He takes them and sends them across the stream, and he sends across everything he has. And Jacob is left alone. And a man wrestles with him there until the break of day. When the man sees that he cannot overpower him, he strikes the socket of Jacob’s hip, and Jacob’s hip is wrenched as he wrestles with him. Then the man says, “Let me go, because the day is breaking.” But Jacob says, “I won’t let you go, not until you bless me.”
“What is your name?” the man asks. “Jacob,” he says.
“Your name will no longer be Jacob,” the man says, “but Israel, Wrestles with God, because you have wrestled with God and with men, and you have won.”
Then Jacob asks him, “Please, tell me your name.” But he says, “Why do you ask my name?” And he blesses him there.

So Jacob names the place Peniel, Face of God. “I have seen God face to face,” he says, “and I am still alive.” The sun rises on him as he passes Peniel, limping because of his hip. That is why to this day the people of Israel do not eat the sinew of the thigh that is on the hip socket, because he struck Jacob’s hip socket on the sinew of the thigh.
Jacob Meets Esau · 33:1–11

Jacob looks up, and there is Esau coming, with four hundred men. So he divides the children among Leah and Rachel and the two servant women. He puts the servant women and their children in front, Leah and her children next, and Rachel and Joseph at the back. He himself goes on ahead of them, bowing down to the ground seven times as he comes near his brother.

But Esau runs to meet him. He throws his arms around him, falls on his neck, and kisses him, and the two of them weep. Then Esau looks up and sees the women and children. “Who are these with you?” he asks. “The children God has graciously given your servant,” Jacob says.
Then the servant women come forward with their children and bow down. Leah and her children come forward too and bow down. And last of all Joseph and Rachel come forward and bow down.
“What do you mean by this whole camp I met?” Esau asks. “To find favor in my lord’s eyes,” Jacob says.
But Esau says, “I have plenty, my brother. Keep what is yours for yourself.”

“No, please,” Jacob says. “If I have found favor in your eyes, then take my gift from my hand. Seeing your face is like seeing the face of God, now that you have welcomed me. Please accept my blessing that has been brought to you, because God has been gracious to me, and I have everything I need.” And because Jacob keeps urging him, Esau takes it.
The Parting of Ways · 33:12–20
Then Esau says, “Let’s get going. I’ll go along ahead of you.”

But Jacob says to him, “My lord knows the children are tender, and I have to care for the ewes and cows that are nursing their young. If they are driven hard even for one day, all the flocks will die. Let my lord go on ahead of his servant, and I will come along slowly, at the pace of the livestock in front of me and at the pace of the children, until I come to my lord in Seir.”
“Then let me leave some of my men with you,” Esau says. “Why do that?” Jacob says. “Just let me find favor in my lord’s eyes.”

So that same day Esau starts back on his way to Seir. But Jacob travels to Succoth. He builds himself a house there and makes shelters for his livestock. That is why the place is called Succoth, Shelters.

So Jacob, coming from Paddan-aram, arrives safe and sound at the city of Shechem in the land of Canaan, and he camps just outside the city. He buys the plot of ground where he has pitched his tent from the sons of Hamor, Shechem’s father, for a hundred pieces of silver. And there he sets up an altar and calls it El-Elohe-Israel, God, the God of Israel.
The Violation of Dinah · 34:1–24

Now Dinah, the daughter Leah bore to Jacob, goes out to visit the women of the land. And Shechem, son of Hamor the Hivite, the chief of the region, sees her. He seizes her, lies with her, and violates her. But his heart clings to Dinah, Jacob’s daughter. He loves the girl, and he speaks tenderly to her heart. And Shechem says to his father Hamor, “Get me this girl for my wife.”

Jacob hears that Shechem has defiled his daughter Dinah. But his sons are out in the field with his livestock, so Jacob keeps quiet until they come home. Then Hamor, Shechem’s father, comes out to Jacob to talk with him. Jacob’s sons come in from the field as soon as they hear. The men are wounded to the heart and furious, because Shechem has done an outrage in Israel by lying with Jacob’s daughter, a thing that must never be done. But Hamor talks with them. “My son Shechem’s heart is set on your daughter,” he says. “Please, give her to him as his wife. Marry into our families. Give us your daughters, and take our daughters for yourselves. Settle among us. The land is open to you. Live in it, trade in it, and get property in it.”

And Shechem says to her father and her brothers, “Let me find favor in your eyes, and I will give you whatever you ask. Set the bride-price and the gift as high as you like, and I will pay whatever you tell me. Only give me the girl as my wife.”

But because he has defiled their sister Dinah, Jacob’s sons answer Shechem and his father Hamor with deceit. “We can’t do this,” they tell them. “We can’t give our sister to a man who isn’t circumcised. That would be a disgrace for us. There is only one condition on which we will agree: that you become like us, and every male among you is circumcised. Then we will give you our daughters and take your daughters for ourselves. We will settle among you and become one people. But if you won’t listen to us and be circumcised, then we will take our daughter and go.”

Their offer seems good to Hamor and to his son Shechem. And the young man doesn’t waste any time doing it, because he is delighted with Jacob’s daughter. And he is the most honored man in his father’s whole household. So Hamor and his son Shechem go to the gate of their city and speak to the men of their city. “These men are friendly toward us,” they say. “Let them settle in the land and trade in it. Look, the land has room enough for them. We can marry their daughters, and we can give them ours. But there is just one condition on which the men will agree to live with us and become one people: every male among us must be circumcised, just as they are. Won’t their livestock and their property and all their animals become ours? Let’s just agree with them, and they will settle among us.”
And everyone who goes out through the city gate listens to Hamor and his son Shechem, and every male is circumcised, every man who goes out through the gate of his city.
Simeon and Levi · 34:25–31

Then on the third day, while they are still in pain, two of Jacob’s sons, Simeon and Levi, Dinah’s brothers, take their swords, walk into the unsuspecting city, and kill every male. They kill Hamor and his son Shechem with the sword, take Dinah out of Shechem’s house, and leave. Then Jacob’s other sons come upon the dead and loot the city, because their sister has been defiled. They take their flocks and herds and donkeys, and everything else in the city and in the fields. They carry off all their wealth, all their little ones, and their wives, and they plunder everything in the houses. Then Jacob says to Simeon and Levi, “You have brought trouble on me! You have made me stink to the people of the land, the Canaanites and the Perizzites. We are few in number. If they band together against me and attack me, I will be destroyed, I and my household.”
But they say, “Should he have treated our sister like a prostitute?”
The Return to Bethel · 35:1–15
God says to Jacob, “Get up, go up to Bethel, and settle there. Build an altar there to the God who appeared to you when you were running from your brother Esau.”

So Jacob says to his household and to everyone with him, “Get rid of the foreign gods you have among you. Make yourselves clean, and change your clothes. Then let’s get up and go up to Bethel. I will build an altar there to the God who answered me on the day of my trouble and has been with me on every road I have traveled.”

So they give Jacob all the foreign gods they have, and the rings from their ears, and Jacob buries them under the oak near Shechem. Then they set out, and a terror from God falls on the towns all around them, so that no one chases after the sons of Jacob. And Jacob comes to Luz, that is, Bethel, in the land of Canaan, he and all the people with him. He builds an altar there and calls the place El-Bethel, God of Bethel, because it was there that God revealed himself to him when he was running from his brother. Then Deborah, Rebekah’s nurse, dies, and she is buried under the oak below Bethel. So it is called Allon-bacuth, Oak of Weeping.

God appears to Jacob again after he comes back from Paddan-aram, and he blesses him. God says to him, “Your name is Jacob. But you will not be called Jacob anymore. Israel will be your name.” So he names him Israel. And God says to him, “I am El Shaddai. Be fruitful and multiply. A nation, and a whole gathering of nations, will come from you, and kings will come from your own body. The land I gave to Abraham and Isaac I will give to you, and to your offspring after you I will give the land.”

Then God goes up from him, from the place where he spoke with him. And Jacob sets up a pillar in the place where God spoke with him, a pillar of stone. He pours out a drink offering on it, and he pours oil on it. And Jacob names the place where God spoke with him Bethel.
The Death of Rachel and the Birth of Benjamin · 35:16–20

Then they set out from Bethel. While they are still some distance from Ephrath, Rachel goes into labor, and her labor is hard. In the worst of her labor the midwife says to her, “Don’t be afraid. You have another son!”

And as her life is slipping away, for she is dying, she names him Ben-oni, Son of My Sorrow. But his father names him Benjamin, Son of the Right Hand. So Rachel dies, and she is buried beside the road to Ephrath, that is, Bethlehem. Jacob sets up a pillar over her grave. It is the pillar of Rachel’s grave, and it stands there to this day.
The Sons of Jacob and the Death of Isaac · 35:21–29

Israel travels on and pitches his tent beyond Migdal-eder, the Tower of the Flock. While Israel is living in that land, Reuben goes and lies with Bilhah, his father’s concubine, and Israel hears about it. Now Jacob has twelve sons.

The sons of Leah: Reuben, Jacob’s firstborn, then Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, and Zebulun. The sons of Rachel: Joseph and Benjamin. The sons of Bilhah, Rachel’s servant: Dan and Naphtali. The sons of Zilpah, Leah’s servant: Gad and Asher. These are the sons of Jacob born to him in Paddan-aram. And Jacob comes home to his father Isaac at Mamre, near Kiriath-arba, that is, Hebron, where Abraham and Isaac lived as foreigners.
Isaac lives a hundred and eighty years. Then Isaac breathes his last and dies, and he is gathered to his people, old and full of days. And his sons Esau and Jacob bury him.
The Generations of Esau · 36:1–8

Here is the story of the generations of Esau, that is, Edom. Esau takes his wives from the women of Canaan: Adah daughter of Elon the Hittite, and Oholibamah daughter of Anah and granddaughter of Zibeon the Hivite, and Basemath, Ishmael’s daughter, the sister of Nebaioth. Adah bears Esau a son, Eliphaz. Basemath bears Reuel. And Oholibamah bears Jeush, Jalam, and Korah. These are the sons of Esau born to him in the land of Canaan. Then Esau takes his wives and his sons and daughters, everyone in his household, his livestock and all his animals, and all the goods he has gathered in the land of Canaan, and he moves to a land away from his brother Jacob. Their wealth is too great for them to live together. The land where they are living as foreigners can’t support them both, because of all their livestock. So Esau settles in the hill country of Seir. Esau is Edom.
Chiefs and Kings of Edom · 36:9–43

Here is the story of the generations of Esau, the father of the Edomites, in the hill country of Seir. These are the names of Esau’s sons: Eliphaz, the son of Esau’s wife Adah, and Reuel, the son of Esau’s wife Basemath. The sons of Eliphaz: Teman, Omar, Zepho, Gatam, and Kenaz. Timna is a concubine of Esau’s son Eliphaz, and she bears Eliphaz a son, Amalek. These are the descendants of Esau’s wife Adah. These are the sons of Reuel: Nahath, Zerah, Shammah, and Mizzah. These are the descendants of Esau’s wife Basemath. And these are the sons of Esau’s wife Oholibamah, daughter of Anah and granddaughter of Zibeon. She bears Esau Jeush, Jalam, and Korah.

These are the clan chiefs among the sons of Esau. The sons of Eliphaz, Esau’s firstborn: chief Teman, chief Omar, chief Zepho, chief Kenaz, chief Korah, chief Gatam, and chief Amalek. These are the chiefs descended from Eliphaz in the land of Edom. They are the descendants of Adah. These are the sons of Esau’s son Reuel: chief Nahath, chief Zerah, chief Shammah, and chief Mizzah. These are the chiefs descended from Reuel in the land of Edom. They are the descendants of Esau’s wife Basemath. These are the sons of Esau’s wife Oholibamah: chief Jeush, chief Jalam, and chief Korah. These are the chiefs descended from Esau’s wife Oholibamah, the daughter of Anah. These are the sons of Esau, that is, Edom, and these are their chiefs.

These are the sons of Seir the Horite, the people living in the land: Lotan, Shobal, Zibeon, Anah, Dishon, Ezer, and Dishan. These are the chiefs of the Horites, the sons of Seir, in the land of Edom. The sons of Lotan: Hori and Heman. Lotan’s sister is Timna. The sons of Shobal: Alvan, Manahath, Ebal, Shepho, and Onam. The sons of Zibeon: Aiah and Anah. This is the Anah who finds the hot springs in the wilderness while he is pasturing the donkeys of his father Zibeon. The children of Anah: Dishon, and Oholibamah daughter of Anah. The sons of Dishon: Hemdan, Eshban, Ithran, and Cheran. The sons of Ezer: Bilhan, Zaavan, and Akan. The sons of Dishan: Uz and Aran. These are the chiefs of the Horites: chief Lotan, chief Shobal, chief Zibeon, chief Anah, chief Dishon, chief Ezer, and chief Dishan. These are the chiefs of the Horites, clan by clan, in the land of Seir.

These are the kings who reign in the land of Edom before any king reigns over the people of Israel. Bela son of Beor reigns in Edom, and the name of his city is Dinhabah. When Bela dies, Jobab son of Zerah from Bozrah reigns in his place. When Jobab dies, Husham from the land of the Temanites reigns in his place. When Husham dies, Hadad son of Bedad, who defeats Midian in the country of Moab, reigns in his place. The name of his city is Avith. When Hadad dies, Samlah of Masrekah reigns in his place. When Samlah dies, Shaul of Rehoboth on the River reigns in his place. When Shaul dies, Baal-hanan son of Achbor reigns in his place. When Baal-hanan son of Achbor dies, Hadar reigns in his place. The name of his city is Pau, and his wife’s name is Mehetabel, the daughter of Matred and granddaughter of Mezahab.

These are the names of the chiefs descended from Esau, by their clans and their places, name by name: chief Timna, chief Alvah, chief Jetheth, chief Oholibamah, chief Elah, chief Pinon, chief Kenaz, chief Teman, chief Mibzar, chief Magdiel, and chief Iram. These are the chiefs of Edom, by their settlements in the land they hold. This is Esau, the father of Edom.
Joseph and His Brothers · 37:1–11

Jacob settles in the land where his father lived as a foreigner, the land of Canaan. Here is the story of the generations of Jacob. Joseph is seventeen years old, and he is shepherding the flock with his brothers. He is just a boy, helping the sons of Bilhah and Zilpah, his father’s wives. And Joseph brings their father a bad report about them. Now Israel loves Joseph more than all his other sons, because he is the son of his old age. And he has a special robe made for him, a long robe with sleeves. When his brothers see that their father loves him more than all of them, they hate him, and they can’t say a kind word to him.

Then Joseph has a dream, and when he tells it to his brothers, they hate him even more. “Listen to this dream I had,” he says to them. “There we were, binding sheaves of grain out in the field, and look, my sheaf stood up and stayed standing, and look, your sheaves gathered around it and bowed down to my sheaf!”

“So you’re going to be our king, are you?” his brothers say. “You’re going to rule over us?” And they hate him even more, because of his dreams and because of what he says. Then he has another dream, and he tells it to his brothers. “Look,” he says, “I had another dream. And look, the sun and the moon and eleven stars were bowing down to me!” When he tells it to his father as well as his brothers, his father scolds him. “What kind of dream is this you’ve had?” he says. “Are your mother and I and your brothers really going to come and bow down to the ground before you?” His brothers are jealous of him, but his father keeps the matter in mind.
The Pit · 37:12–30

One day his brothers go off to graze their father’s flock near Shechem. And Israel says to Joseph, “Your brothers are grazing the flock near Shechem, aren’t they? Come, I’m going to send you to them.” “Here I am,” Joseph says.

“Go and see how your brothers are doing and how the flock is doing,” he tells him, “and bring me back word.” So he sends him off from the valley of Hebron, and Joseph comes to Shechem. A man finds him wandering around in the countryside and asks him, “What are you looking for?”
“I’m looking for my brothers,” Joseph says. “Can you tell me where they are grazing the flock?”
“They’ve moved on from here,” the man says. “I heard them say, ‘Let’s go to Dothan.’” So Joseph goes after his brothers and finds them at Dothan.

They see him far off, and before he reaches them, they plot to kill him. “Look,” they say to one another, “here comes that master of dreams! Come on, let’s kill him and throw him into one of these pits. We’ll say a wild animal ate him. Then we’ll see what becomes of his dreams!”

But when Reuben hears this, he tries to rescue him from their hands. “Let’s not take his life,” he says. “Don’t shed any blood,” Reuben tells them. “Throw him into this pit here in the wilderness, but don’t lay a hand on him.” He means to rescue him from them and bring him back to his father. So when Joseph reaches his brothers, they strip him of his robe, the special robe he is wearing, and they take him and throw him into the pit. The pit is empty. There is no water in it.

Then they sit down to eat their meal. And they look up, and there is a caravan of Ishmaelites coming from Gilead, their camels loaded with spices, balm, and myrrh, on their way down to Egypt. Judah says to his brothers, “What do we gain if we kill our brother and cover up his blood? Come on, let’s sell him to the Ishmaelites and not lay a hand on him. After all, he is our brother, our own flesh.” And his brothers agree. So when the Midianite traders come by, they pull Joseph up out of the pit and sell him to the Ishmaelites for twenty pieces of silver. And they take Joseph to Egypt.
When Reuben comes back to the pit, Joseph isn’t in the pit! And he tears his clothes. He goes back to his brothers and says, “The boy is gone! And I, where can I go now?”
The Robe and Jacob’s Grief · 37:31–36

Then they take Joseph’s robe, slaughter a young goat, and dip the robe in the blood. They send the special robe to their father with this message: “We found this. Please look closely. Is it your son’s robe or not?”

He recognizes it. “It’s my son’s robe!” he says. “A wild animal has eaten him! Joseph has been torn to pieces, torn to pieces!” Jacob tears his clothes, wraps sackcloth around his waist, and mourns for his son for a long time. All his sons and all his daughters try to comfort him, but he refuses to be comforted. “No,” he says, “I will go down to Sheol, to the grave, still mourning for my son.” And his father weeps for him. Meanwhile the Midianites sell Joseph in Egypt to Potiphar, one of Pharaoh’s officials, the captain of the guard.
Judah and Tamar · 38:1–30

About that time Judah goes down, away from his brothers, and pitches his tent near a man of Adullam named Hirah. There Judah sees the daughter of a Canaanite man named Shua. He marries her and goes in to her. She conceives and has a son, and he names him Er. She conceives again and has a son, and she names him Onan. And once more she has a son, and she names him Shelah. Judah is at Chezib when she gives birth to him. Judah gets a wife for Er, his firstborn, and her name is Tamar. But Er, Judah’s firstborn, is evil in the eyes of YHWH, and YHWH puts him to death. Then Judah says to Onan, “Go in to your brother’s wife. Do your duty to her as a brother-in-law, and raise up offspring for your brother.” But Onan knows the offspring won’t be counted as his. So whenever he goes in to his brother’s wife, he spills his seed on the ground, so as not to give his brother offspring. What he does is evil in the eyes of YHWH, and YHWH puts him to death too. Then Judah says to his daughter-in-law Tamar, “Live as a widow in your father’s house until my son Shelah grows up.” For he thinks, “He might die too, like his brothers.” So Tamar goes and lives in her father’s house.

A long time passes, and Judah’s wife, the daughter of Shua, dies. When Judah’s time of mourning is over, he goes up to Timnah to the men shearing his sheep, he and his friend Hirah the Adullamite. Tamar is told, “Look, your father-in-law is going up to Timnah to shear his sheep.” So she takes off her widow’s clothes, covers herself with a veil, wraps herself up, and sits down at the entrance to Enaim, on the road to Timnah. She can see that Shelah has grown up, and yet she has not been given to him as his wife. When Judah sees her, he takes her for a prostitute, because she has covered her face. He turns aside to her by the road and says, “Come on, let me sleep with you.” He doesn’t know she is his daughter-in-law. “What will you give me for sleeping with you?” she asks.
“I’ll send you a young goat from the flock,” he says. “Will you give me something to hold until you send it?” she asks.
“What should I give you?” he says. “Your seal on its cord,” she says, “and the staff in your hand.” So he gives them to her and sleeps with her, and she conceives by him.

Then she gets up and leaves. She takes off her veil and puts her widow’s clothes back on. Judah sends the young goat with his friend the Adullamite to get back the pledge from the woman, but he can’t find her. He asks the men of the place, “Where is the shrine woman who was by the road at Enaim?” “There hasn’t been any shrine woman here,” they say.

So he goes back to Judah and says, “I couldn’t find her. And the men of the place said, ‘There hasn’t been any shrine woman here.’” “Let her keep the things,” Judah says, “or we’ll become a laughingstock. After all, I sent this young goat, and you couldn’t find her.”
About three months later Judah is told, “Your daughter-in-law Tamar has played the prostitute, and look, she’s pregnant from it.” “Bring her out,” Judah says, “and let her be burned!”

As she is being brought out, she sends word to her father-in-law: “I am pregnant by the man these things belong to.” And she says, “Please look closely. Whose are these, this seal, this cord, and this staff?”
Judah recognizes them, and he says, “She is more in the right than I am, because I didn’t give her to my son Shelah.” And he never sleeps with her again.

When the time comes for her to give birth, look, there are twins in her womb. As she is giving birth, one of them puts out a hand, and the midwife takes a scarlet thread and ties it on his hand. “This one came out first,” she says. But as he pulls his hand back, look, out comes his brother! “What a breakout you have made for yourself!” she says. So he is named Perez, Breakout. Afterward his brother comes out, the one with the scarlet thread on his hand, and he is named Zerah, Bright Dawn.
Joseph in Potiphar’s House · 39:1–18

Now Joseph has been taken down to Egypt. And Potiphar, an Egyptian, one of Pharaoh’s officials, the captain of the guard, buys him from the Ishmaelites who brought him down there. YHWH is with Joseph, and he becomes a man who succeeds at everything. He lives in the house of his Egyptian master. His master sees that YHWH is with him, and that YHWH makes everything he does succeed in his hands. So Joseph finds favor in his eyes and becomes his personal servant. Potiphar puts him in charge of his household and places everything he owns in his hands. From the time he puts him in charge of his household and everything he owns, YHWH blesses the Egyptian’s household because of Joseph. The blessing of YHWH is on everything he has, in the house and in the field. So he leaves everything he has in Joseph’s hands, and with Joseph there he doesn’t give a thought to anything except the food he eats. And Joseph is fine in form and fine to look at.
After a while his master’s wife sets her eyes on Joseph. “Sleep with me,” she says.

But he refuses. “Look,” he says to his master’s wife, “with me here, my master doesn’t give a thought to anything in the house. He has put everything he owns in my hands. No one in this house is greater than I am. He has held nothing back from me except you, because you are his wife. So how could I do such a great evil and sin against God?”

And though she keeps after Joseph day after day, he won’t listen to her or lie beside her or even be with her. Then one day he goes into the house to do his work, and none of the household servants are inside. She grabs him by his cloak. “Sleep with me!” she says. But he leaves his cloak in her hand and runs out of the house.

When she sees that he has left his cloak in her hand and run out of the house, she calls her household servants. “Look!” she says. “My husband has brought in a Hebrew to make sport of us! He came in to sleep with me, and I screamed at the top of my voice. And when he heard me screaming, he left his cloak beside me and ran out of the house.” She keeps his cloak beside her until his master comes home. Then she tells him the same story: “That Hebrew slave you brought us came in to make sport of me. But when I screamed, he left his cloak beside me and ran out of the house.”
Joseph in Prison · 39:19–23

When his master hears the story his wife tells him, “This is what your slave did to me,” he burns with anger. So Joseph’s master takes him and puts him in prison, the place where the king’s prisoners are kept. And there he stays, in prison. But YHWH is with Joseph and shows him steadfast love. He gives him favor in the eyes of the warden of the prison. So the warden puts Joseph in charge of all the prisoners there. Whatever is done there, Joseph is the one who does it. The warden doesn’t give a thought to anything in Joseph’s care, because YHWH is with him. And whatever he does, YHWH makes it succeed.
The Dreams of the Cupbearer and the Baker · 40:1–23

Some time later, the king of Egypt’s cupbearer and his baker offend their lord, the king of Egypt. Pharaoh is furious with his two officials, the chief cupbearer and the chief baker, and he puts them in custody in the house of the captain of the guard, in the same prison where Joseph is held. The captain of the guard assigns Joseph to them, and he looks after them. They are in custody for some time. Then one night the two of them, the cupbearer and the baker of the king of Egypt who are held in the prison, each have a dream, and each dream has its own meaning. When Joseph comes to them in the morning, he sees that they are upset. So he asks Pharaoh’s officials who are in custody with him in his master’s house, “Why do you look so gloomy today?”
“We each had a dream,” they tell him, “and there’s no one to tell us what they mean.” “Don’t interpretations belong to God?” Joseph says. “Please, tell me your dreams.”

So the chief cupbearer tells Joseph his dream. “In my dream,” he says, “look, there was a vine in front of me. On the vine were three branches. As soon as it budded, out came its blossoms, and its clusters ripened into grapes. Pharaoh’s cup was in my hand. So I took the grapes, squeezed them into Pharaoh’s cup, and put the cup in Pharaoh’s hand.”

“This is what it means,” Joseph tells him. “The three branches are three days. Within three days Pharaoh will lift up your head and give you back your post. You will put Pharaoh’s cup in his hand, just as you used to when you were his cupbearer. But remember me when things go well for you. Please, show me steadfast love. Mention me to Pharaoh, and get me out of this place. I was kidnapped from the land of the Hebrews, and even here I have done nothing to deserve being thrown into this pit.”

When the chief baker sees that the interpretation is good, he says to Joseph, “I had a dream too. Look, there were three baskets of white bread on my head. In the top basket were all kinds of baked goods for Pharaoh, but the birds were eating them out of the basket on my head.”

“This is what it means,” Joseph answers. “The three baskets are three days. Within three days Pharaoh will lift up your head, right off you! He will hang you on a pole, and the birds will eat the flesh off your bones.”

And on the third day, which is Pharaoh’s birthday, he throws a feast for all his officials, and he lifts up the head of the chief cupbearer and the head of the chief baker in front of all his officials. He gives the chief cupbearer back his post, and once more he puts the cup in Pharaoh’s hand. But the chief baker he hangs, just as Joseph told them. Yet the chief cupbearer does not remember Joseph. He forgets him.
Pharaoh’s Dreams · 41:1–36

Two full years later, Pharaoh has a dream. He is standing by the Nile, and look, up out of the Nile come seven cows, sleek and fat, and they graze among the reeds. And look, after them seven other cows come up out of the Nile, ugly and thin, and they stand beside the other cows on the riverbank. And the ugly, thin cows eat up the seven sleek, fat cows. Then Pharaoh wakes up. He falls asleep again and has a second dream. Look, seven heads of grain, plump and good, are growing on a single stalk. And look, after them seven other heads of grain sprout, thin and scorched by the east wind. And the thin heads of grain swallow up the seven plump, full heads. Then Pharaoh wakes up, and it was a dream! In the morning his spirit is troubled. So he sends for all the magicians and all the wise men of Egypt, and Pharaoh tells them his dreams. But no one can tell Pharaoh what they mean.

Then the chief cupbearer says to Pharaoh, “Today I must mention my own failings. Pharaoh was angry with his servants, and he put me and the chief baker in custody in the house of the captain of the guard. One night we each had a dream, he and I, and each dream had its own meaning. A young Hebrew was there with us, a servant of the captain of the guard. We told him our dreams, and he told us what they meant, each man’s dream and its meaning. And it all turned out exactly as he told us. I was given back my post, and the baker was hanged.”

Jacob lives in the land of Egypt seventeen years, and the years of Jacob’s life come to a hundred and forty-seven. When the time draws near for Israel to die, he calls for his son Joseph and says to him, “If I have found favor in your eyes, put your hand under my thigh and promise to show me steadfast love and faithfulness. Please don’t bury me in Egypt. When I lie down with my fathers, carry me out of Egypt and bury me in their burial place.” “I will do as you say,” Joseph tells him.
“Swear it to me,” Jacob says. So Joseph swears it to him. And Israel bows down at the head of his bed.
The Blessing of Ephraim and Manasseh · 48:1–22

Some time later Joseph is told, “Listen, your father is ill.” So he takes his two sons Manasseh and Ephraim with him. When Jacob is told, “Look, your son Joseph has come to you,” Israel gathers his strength and sits up in bed. Jacob says to Joseph, “El Shaddai appeared to me at Luz in the land of Canaan, and he blessed me. He said to me, ‘Look, I am going to make you fruitful and multiply you. I will make you a gathering of peoples, and I will give this land to your offspring after you to hold forever.’ So now your two sons, who were born to you in the land of Egypt before I came to you here, are mine. Ephraim and Manasseh will be mine, just as Reuben and Simeon are. Any children you have after them will be yours. They will be listed under the names of their brothers when it comes to their inheritance. As for me, when I was coming back from Paddan, to my sorrow Rachel died in the land of Canaan while we were still on the road, a little way from Ephrath. And I buried her there beside the road to Ephrath, that is, Bethlehem.”
When Israel sees Joseph’s sons, he asks, “Who are these?”
“They are my sons,” Joseph tells his father, “the ones God has given me here.” “Please bring them to me,” he says, “so I can bless them.”

Now Israel’s eyes are dim with age, and he can hardly see. So Joseph brings them close to him, and he kisses them and hugs them. And Israel says to Joseph, “I never expected to see your face again, and look, God has let me see your children too!” Then Joseph takes them from his father’s knees and bows down with his face to the ground. And Joseph takes them both, Ephraim with his right hand toward Israel’s left, and Manasseh with his left hand toward Israel’s right, and brings them close to him. But Israel reaches out his right hand and lays it on the head of Ephraim, the younger, and his left hand on Manasseh’s head. He crosses his hands on purpose, though Manasseh is the firstborn. And he blesses Joseph and says, “May the God before whom my fathers Abraham and Isaac walked, the God who has been my shepherd all my life long to this day, the messenger who has been my redeemer from every harm, may he bless these boys. May my name live on in them, and the names of my fathers Abraham and Isaac. And may they grow into a great crowd on the earth.”

When Joseph sees his father laying his right hand on Ephraim’s head, he doesn’t like it. So he takes hold of his father’s hand to move it from Ephraim’s head to Manasseh’s head. “Not that way, my father,” Joseph tells him. “This one is the firstborn. Put your right hand on his head.”

But his father refuses. “I know, my son, I know,” he says. “He too will become a people, and he too will be great. But his younger brother will be greater than he is, and his offspring will become a whole world of nations.” So he blesses them that day and says, “By you Israel will speak its blessings, saying, ‘May God make you like Ephraim and Manasseh.’” So he puts Ephraim ahead of Manasseh. Then Israel says to Joseph, “Look, I am about to die. But God will be with you and will bring you back to the land of your fathers. And to you, more than to your brothers, I give one shoulder of land, Shechem, the ridge I took from the Amorites with my sword and my bow.”
Jacob’s Blessing of His Sons · 49:1–27
Then Jacob calls for his sons and says, “Gather around, so I can tell you what will happen to you in the days to come.”
Gather together and listen, you sons of Jacob.
Listen to Israel, your father.
Reuben, you are my firstborn,
my strength, the first fruit of my manhood,
first in honor and first in power.
But you boil over like water,
and you will be first no longer,
because you climbed into your father’s bed.
You defiled it. He climbed onto my couch!
Simeon and Levi are brothers.
Their swords are weapons of violence.
Let my soul never enter their council.
Let my heart never join their gathering.
In their anger they killed men,
and on a whim they crippled oxen.
Cursed be their anger, so fierce,
and their fury, so cruel!
I will scatter them through Jacob
and disperse them through Israel.
Judah, your brothers will praise you.
Your hand will be on the neck of your enemies.
Your father’s sons will bow down to you.
Judah is a lion’s cub.
You come up from the kill, my son.
He crouches, he lies down like a lion,
like a lioness. Who dares to wake him?
The scepter will not leave Judah,
nor the ruler’s staff from between his feet,
until Shiloh comes, the one to whom it belongs,
and the obedience of the peoples is his.
He ties his donkey to the vine,
his colt to the choicest vine.
He washes his clothes in wine,
his robes in the blood of grapes.
His eyes are darker than wine,
his teeth whiter than milk.
Zebulun will live by the seashore.
He will be a harbor for ships,
and his border will reach to Sidon.
Issachar is a strong-boned donkey,
lying down between the saddlebags.
He sees how good a resting place is,
how pleasant the land is.
So he bends his shoulder to the load
and becomes a slave at forced labor.
Dan will judge his people
as one of the tribes of Israel.
Dan will be a snake by the roadside,
a viper on the path,
that bites the horse’s heels
so its rider falls backward.
I wait for your salvation, YHWH.
Gad will be raided by raiders,
but he will raid at their heels.
Asher’s food will be rich.
He will provide delicacies fit for a king.
Naphtali is a doe running free,
who brings forth lovely fawns.
Joseph is a fruitful vine,
a fruitful vine beside a spring,
whose branches run over the wall.
The archers attacked him fiercely.
They shot at him and hounded him.
But his bow stayed steady,
and his arms stayed strong,
by the hands of the Mighty One of Jacob,
by the name of the Shepherd, the Rock of Israel,
by the God of your father, who helps you,
by Shaddai, who blesses you
with blessings of the sky above,
blessings of the deep that lies below,
blessings of the breasts and of the womb.
The blessings of your father
are greater than the blessings of the ancient mountains,
the bounty of the everlasting hills.
May they rest on the head of Joseph,
on the brow of the one set apart from his brothers.
Benjamin is a ravenous wolf.
In the morning he devours the prey,
and in the evening he divides the plunder.
Jacob’s Death and Burial Instructions · 49:28–33

These are the twelve tribes of Israel, and this is what their father says to them as he blesses them. He blesses each of them with the blessing that fits him. Then he gives them his instructions: “I am about to be gathered to my people. Bury me with my fathers in the cave in the field of Ephron the Hittite, the cave in the field of Machpelah, near Mamre, in the land of Canaan. Abraham bought it along with the field from Ephron the Hittite as a burial place of his own. There they buried Abraham and his wife Sarah. There they buried Isaac and his wife Rebekah. And there I buried Leah. The field and the cave in it were bought from the Hittites.” When Jacob has finished giving his sons their instructions, he draws his feet up into the bed, breathes his last, and is gathered to his people.
Jacob’s Burial · 50:1–14

Joseph throws himself on his father’s face, weeps over him, and kisses him. Then Joseph orders the physicians in his service to embalm his father, and the physicians embalm Israel. It takes them forty full days, because that is how long embalming takes. And the Egyptians weep for him seventy days.

When the days of weeping for him are over, Joseph speaks to Pharaoh’s household. “If I have found favor in your eyes,” he says, “please speak to Pharaoh for me and tell him this: ‘My father made me swear an oath. He said, “Look, I am dying. Bury me in the tomb I dug for myself in the land of Canaan.” So now please let me go up and bury my father. Then I will come back.’”
And Pharaoh says, “Go up and bury your father, just as he made you swear.”

So Joseph goes up to bury his father, and with him go all Pharaoh’s officials, the elders of his household, and all the elders of the land of Egypt, and all of Joseph’s household, and his brothers, and his father’s household. Only their little ones and their flocks and herds are left behind in the land of Goshen. Chariots and horsemen go up with him too. It is a very great procession. When they reach the threshing floor of Atad, beyond the Jordan, they lament there with a great and bitter lament. And Joseph mourns for his father seven days. When the people who live in the land, the Canaanites, see the mourning at the threshing floor of Atad, they say, “This is a solemn mourning for the Egyptians!” That is why the place beyond the Jordan is called Abel-mizraim, Mourning of Egypt. So Jacob’s sons do for him just as he commanded them. His sons carry him to the land of Canaan and bury him in the cave in the field of Machpelah, near Mamre, the field Abraham bought from Ephron the Hittite as a burial place of his own. After he has buried his father, Joseph goes back to Egypt, he and his brothers and everyone who went up with him to bury his father.
Joseph Reassures His Brothers · 50:15–21

Now that their father is dead, Joseph’s brothers begin to worry. “What if Joseph holds a grudge against us,” they say, “and pays us back in full for all the evil we did to him?” So they send word to Joseph: “Before he died, your father left this command: ‘This is what you are to say to Joseph: Please, forgive your brothers for the wrong they did, their sin, for the evil they did to you.’ So now, please forgive the wrong done by the servants of your father’s God.” And Joseph weeps when their message comes to him. Then his brothers come themselves and fall down before him. “Look,” they say, “we are your slaves.” But Joseph says to them, “Don’t be afraid. Am I in the place of God? You planned evil against me, but God planned it for good, to keep a great many people alive, as you see today. So don’t be afraid. I will provide for you and your little ones.” And he comforts them and speaks to their hearts.
The Death of Joseph · 50:22–26

So Joseph stays in Egypt, he and his father’s household. Joseph lives a hundred and ten years. He lives to see Ephraim’s children to the third generation. And the children of Machir, Manasseh’s son, are born on Joseph’s knees. Then Joseph says to his brothers, “I am about to die.
