But God will surely come to you, and he will bring you up out of this land to the land he swore to give to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob.” And Joseph makes the sons of Israel swear an oath. “God will surely come to you,” he says, “and then you must carry my bones up from here.” So Joseph dies, a hundred and ten years old. They embalm him, and he is laid in a coffin in Egypt.
Israel Multiplies in Egypt · 1:1–7

These are the names of the sons of Israel who come to Egypt with Jacob, each man with his household: Reuben, Simeon, Levi, and Judah, Issachar, Zebulun, and Benjamin, Dan and Naphtali, Gad and Asher. All the descendants of Jacob number seventy in all. Joseph is already in Egypt. Then Joseph dies, and all his brothers, and that whole generation. But the people of Israel are fruitful. They swarm and multiply and grow strong, very, very strong, until the land is full of them.
The New King · 1:8–14

Then a new king rises over Egypt, a king who does not know Joseph. “Look,” he says to his people, “the people of Israel are too many and too strong for us. Come on, let’s be clever with them, or they will keep multiplying. Then if war breaks out, they will join our enemies, fight against us, and leave the land.” So they put slave drivers over them to crush them under heavy loads. And they build supply cities for Pharaoh: Pithom and Rameses. But the more they crush them, the more they multiply and the more they spread, until the Egyptians dread the people of Israel. So the Egyptians work the people of Israel without mercy. They make their lives bitter with hard labor, with mortar and brick and every kind of work in the fields. All of it they force on them without mercy.
The Midwives · 1:15–22

Then the king of Egypt speaks to the Hebrew midwives. One is named Shiphrah, and the other Puah. “When you help the Hebrew women give birth,” he says, “watch as they deliver. If it’s a son, kill him. If it’s a daughter, let her live.” But the midwives fear God. They do not do what the king of Egypt tells them. They let the boys live. So the king of Egypt summons the midwives. “Why have you done this?” he says. “Why have you let the boys live?”
“Because Hebrew women aren’t like Egyptian women,” the midwives tell Pharaoh. “They are full of life! They give birth before the midwife even gets there.”

So God is good to the midwives, and the people multiply and grow very strong. And because the midwives fear God, he gives them families of their own. Then Pharaoh gives an order to all his people: “Every son born to the Hebrews, throw him into the Nile. But let every daughter live.”
The Birth and Preservation of Moses · 2:1–10

Now a man from the house of Levi marries a Levite woman. She conceives and gives birth to a son. When she sees how good he is, a fine child, she hides him for three months. When she can’t hide him any longer, she gets him a little ark woven of papyrus. She coats it with tar and pitch, puts the child in it, and sets it among the reeds at the edge of the Nile. His sister stands at a distance to see what will happen to him. Then Pharaoh’s daughter comes down to bathe at the Nile, while her young women walk along the riverbank. She sees the little ark among the reeds and sends her servant girl to get it. She opens it and sees the child, and look, the baby is crying! She feels sorry for him. “This is one of the Hebrew children,” she says.
Then his sister says to Pharaoh’s daughter, “Should I go and get a nurse for you from the Hebrew women, to nurse the baby for you?”
“Go,” Pharaoh’s daughter tells her. So the girl goes and gets the baby’s mother.
Pharaoh’s daughter says to her, “Take this child and nurse him for me, and I will pay you.” So the woman takes the child and nurses him.

When the child is older, she brings him to Pharaoh’s daughter, and he becomes her son. She names him Moses. “Because I drew him out of the water,” she says. (Moses sounds like the Hebrew for “draw out.”)
Moses Flees to Midian · 2:11–22

Years later, when Moses has grown up, he goes out to his own people and watches them at their hard labor. And he sees an Egyptian beating a Hebrew, one of his own people. He looks this way and that, and when he sees no one, he strikes the Egyptian down and hides him in the sand.
The next day he goes out again, and look, two Hebrew men are fighting. He says to the one in the wrong, “Why are you hitting your fellow Hebrew?”
“Who made you a prince and a judge over us?” the man says. “Are you planning to kill me, the way you killed the Egyptian?” Then Moses is afraid. “Surely the thing is known,” he thinks.
When Pharaoh hears about it, he tries to kill Moses. But Moses runs from Pharaoh and settles in the land of Midian. And he sits down by a well.

Now the priest of Midian has seven daughters. They come to draw water and fill the troughs to water their father’s flock. But some shepherds come and drive them away. So Moses gets up, comes to their rescue, and waters their flock. When the girls come home to their father Reuel, he asks, “Why are you home so early today?”
“An Egyptian rescued us from the shepherds,” they say. “He even drew water for us and watered the flock!”
“Then where is he?” he asks his daughters. “Why did you leave the man out there? Invite him to eat with us.”

So Moses agrees to stay with the man, and he gives Moses his daughter Zipporah as a wife. She gives birth to a son, and Moses names him Gershom. “Because I have become a stranger in a strange land,” he says. (Gershom sounds like the Hebrew for “a stranger there.”)
God Hears · 2:23–25

A long time passes, and the king of Egypt dies. The people of Israel groan under their slavery, and they cry out, and their cry for help rises up to God from their slavery. And God hears their groaning, and God remembers his covenant with Abraham, with Isaac, and with Jacob. And God sees the people of Israel, and God knows.
The Burning Bush · 3:1–10

Now Moses is tending the flock of his father-in-law Jethro, the priest of Midian. He leads the flock to the far side of the wilderness and comes to Horeb, the mountain of God. There the messenger of YHWH appears to him in a flame of fire from the middle of a bush. Moses looks, and look, the bush is on fire, but the bush is not burning up! “I’ll turn aside,” Moses says, “and see this amazing sight. Why isn’t the bush burning up?”
When YHWH sees that he has turned aside to look, God calls to him from the middle of the bush. “Moses! Moses!” “Here I am,” he says.

“Don’t come any closer,” God says. “Take your sandals off your feet, because the place you are standing on is holy ground.” And he says, “I am the God of your father, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob.” And Moses hides his face, because he is afraid to look at God.

Then YHWH says, “I have seen, I have truly seen how my people in Egypt are suffering. I have heard their cry under the whips of their taskmasters. I know their pain. So I have come down to rescue them from the hand of the Egyptians and bring them up out of that land, to a good and roomy land, a land flowing with milk and honey, the home of the Canaanites, Hittites, Amorites, Perizzites, Hivites, and Jebusites. And now, listen: the cry of the people of Israel has reached me, and I have seen how the Egyptians are crushing them. So come now. I am sending you to Pharaoh, to bring my people, the people of Israel, out of Egypt.”
The Commission and the Divine Name · 3:11–22
But Moses says to God, “Who am I, that I should go to Pharaoh? Who am I to bring the people of Israel out of Egypt?”
“I will be with you,” God says. “Here is your sign that I am the one sending you: once you lead the people out of Egypt, you will all serve God right here on this mountain.”
Then Moses says to God, “Suppose I go to the people of Israel and tell them, ‘The God of your fathers has sent me to you,’ and they ask me, ‘What is his name?’ What should I tell them?”

And God says to Moses, “Ehyeh asher ehyeh: I am who I am, I will be who I will be.” And he says, “Tell the people of Israel this: ‘Ehyeh, I AM, has sent me to you.’” And God says to Moses, “Tell the people of Israel this: ‘YHWH, the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, has sent me to you.’ This is my name forever, and this is how I am to be remembered, generation after generation. Go, gather the elders of Israel together and tell them, ‘YHWH, the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, has appeared to me. He says, “I have come to you, and I have seen what is being done to you in Egypt. And I have promised to bring you up out of your misery in Egypt to the land of the Canaanites, Hittites, Amorites, Perizzites, Hivites, and Jebusites, a land flowing with milk and honey.”’ They will listen to you. Then you and the elders of Israel will go to the king of Egypt and tell him, ‘YHWH, the God of the Hebrews, has met with us. Now please let us go three days’ journey into the wilderness, so we can offer sacrifices to YHWH our God.’ But I know the king of Egypt won’t let you go, not unless a mighty hand makes him. So I will stretch out my hand and strike Egypt with all the wonders I will do there. After that he will let you go. And I will make the Egyptians look kindly on this people, so that when you go, you won’t go empty-handed. Every woman will ask her neighbor, and any woman living in her house, for silver and gold jewelry and for clothing. You will put them on your sons and daughters. And so you will strip Egypt bare.”
The Signs and Moses’ Objections · 4:1–17
Moses answers, “But what if they don’t believe me or listen to me? What if they say, ‘YHWH didn’t appear to you’?”
“What is that in your hand?” YHWH asks him. “A staff,” he says.
“Throw it on the ground,” YHWH says. So he throws it on the ground, and it becomes a snake, and Moses runs from it.
Then YHWH says to Moses, “Reach out your hand and grab it by the tail.” So he reaches out and catches it, and it becomes a staff in his hand again.

“This is so they will believe that YHWH, the God of their fathers, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, has appeared to you.” Then YHWH says to him, “Put your hand inside your cloak.” So he puts his hand inside his cloak, and when he takes it out, look, his hand is diseased, white as snow.
“Put your hand back inside your cloak,” he says. So he puts his hand back inside his cloak, and when he takes it out, look, it is healthy again, like the rest of his skin.

“If they don’t believe you or pay attention to the first sign, they will believe the second. And if they don’t believe even these two signs or listen to you, take some water from the Nile and pour it on the dry ground. The water you take from the Nile will turn to blood on the dry ground.”
But Moses says to YHWH, “Please, Lord, I have never been a man of words, not before, and not since you have spoken to your servant. My mouth is heavy and my tongue is heavy.”
YHWH says to him, “Who gave humans their mouths? Who makes them unable to speak or hear, to see or not see? Isn’t it I, YHWH? So now go. I will be with your mouth, and I will teach you what to say.”
But he says, “Please, Lord, send someone else. Send whoever you want.”

Then YHWH’s anger blazes against Moses. “What about your brother Aaron the Levite?” he says. “I know he can speak well. And look, he is already on his way out to meet you, and when he sees you, his heart will be glad. You will speak to him and put the words in his mouth. I will be with your mouth and with his mouth, and I will teach you both what to do. He will speak to the people for you. He will be a mouth for you, and you will be like God to him. And take this staff in your hand. With it you will do the signs.”
The Return to Egypt · 4:18–31
Then Moses goes back to his father-in-law Jethro and says to him, “Please let me go back to my people in Egypt to see whether they are still alive.” “Go in peace,” Jethro tells Moses.
And YHWH says to Moses in Midian, “Go back to Egypt. All the men who wanted to kill you are dead.”

So Moses takes his wife and his sons, puts them on a donkey, and starts back to the land of Egypt. And Moses carries the staff of God in his hand. And YHWH says to Moses, “When you go back to Egypt, make sure you do before Pharaoh all the wonders I have put in your power. But I will harden his heart, and he won’t let the people go. Then say to Pharaoh, ‘This is what YHWH says: Israel is my son, my firstborn. I told you, “Let my son go, so he can worship me.” But you refused to let him go. So now I will kill your son, your firstborn.’”

On the journey, at a place where they stop for the night, YHWH meets Moses and tries to kill him. But Zipporah takes a flint knife, cuts off her son’s foreskin, and touches his feet with it. “Surely you are a bridegroom of blood to me!” she says.
So he lets him alone. It is then she says, “A bridegroom of blood,” because of the circumcision.
Meanwhile YHWH says to Aaron, “Go out into the wilderness to meet Moses.” So he goes, and he meets him at the mountain of God and kisses him.

Moses tells Aaron everything YHWH has sent him to say, and all the signs he has commanded him to do. Then Moses and Aaron go and gather all the elders of the people of Israel. Aaron tells them everything YHWH has said to Moses, and he does the signs in front of the people. And the people believe. When they hear that YHWH has come to the people of Israel and has seen their misery, they bow their heads and worship.
Moses and Aaron Before Pharaoh · 5:1–9
Afterward Moses and Aaron go to Pharaoh and say, “This is what YHWH, the God of Israel, says: ‘Let my people go, so they can hold a festival for me in the wilderness.’”
“Who is YHWH,” Pharaoh says, “that I should listen to him and let Israel go? I don’t know YHWH, and I won’t let Israel go.”
“The God of the Hebrews has met with us,” they say. “Please let us go three days’ journey into the wilderness to offer sacrifices to YHWH our God, or he may strike us with disease or the sword.”

But the king of Egypt says to them, “Moses and Aaron, why are you taking the people away from their work? Get back to your loads!” And Pharaoh says, “Look, there are so many of these people in the land now, and you want them to stop working!” That same day Pharaoh gives orders to the slave drivers over the people and to their foremen: “Don’t give the people straw for making bricks anymore. Let them go and gather their own straw. But demand the same number of bricks they made before. Don’t reduce it at all. They’re lazy. That’s why they keep crying, ‘Let us go and offer sacrifices to our God.’ Make the work heavier for the men. Keep them busy at it, so they pay no attention to lies.”
The People’s Complaint · 5:10–21

So the slave drivers and the foremen go out and tell the people, “This is what Pharaoh says: ‘I won’t give you any straw. Go and get your own straw wherever you can find it. But your work won’t be reduced one bit.’” So the people scatter all over the land of Egypt to gather stubble to use for straw. And the slave drivers keep pushing them: “Finish your work, the same quota every day, just as when you had straw!” And the Israelite foremen, whom Pharaoh’s slave drivers have put in charge of them, are beaten. “Why haven’t you made your quota of bricks yesterday or today, the way you did before?”

So the Israelite foremen go and cry out to Pharaoh. “Why are you treating your servants like this? No straw is given to your servants, yet they tell us, ‘Make bricks!’ Look, your servants are being beaten, but the fault is with your own people.”

“Lazy, that’s what you are! Lazy!” Pharaoh says. “That’s why you keep saying, ‘Let us go and offer sacrifices to YHWH.’ Now get back to work! You won’t be given any straw, and you will still deliver the full number of bricks.”
The Israelite foremen can see they are in trouble when they are told, “You must not reduce the number of bricks you make each day.”

When they leave Pharaoh, they find Moses and Aaron waiting to meet them, and they say to them, “May YHWH look on you and judge you! You have made us stink in the eyes of Pharaoh and his officials. You have put a sword in their hand to kill us.”
Moses’ Lament · 5:22–23

Then Moses turns back to YHWH and says, “Lord, why have you brought trouble on this people? Why did you ever send me? Ever since I came to Pharaoh to speak in your name, he has brought trouble on this people, and you haven’t rescued your people at all.”
YHWH Answers Moses · 6:1
Then YHWH says to Moses, “Now you will see what I will do to Pharaoh. By a mighty hand he will let them go. By a mighty hand he will drive them out of his land.”
The Covenant Name Declared · 6:2–13

God speaks to Moses and says to him, “I am YHWH. I appeared to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob as El Shaddai, but by my name YHWH I did not make myself known to them. I also established my covenant with them, to give them the land of Canaan, the land where they lived as foreigners. And I have heard the groaning of the people of Israel, whom the Egyptians are holding as slaves, and I have remembered my covenant. So tell the people of Israel: ‘I am YHWH. I will bring you out from under the loads of the Egyptians. I will rescue you from slavery to them. I will redeem you with an outstretched arm and with mighty acts of judgment. I will take you as my own people, and I will be your God. And you will know that I am YHWH your God, who brings you out from under the loads of the Egyptians. I will bring you into the land I raised my hand and swore to give to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob. I will give it to you as your own. I am YHWH.’”
Moses tells this to the people of Israel, but they won’t listen to him, because their spirits are crushed and their slavery is cruel.
Then YHWH says to Moses, “Go and tell Pharaoh king of Egypt to let the people of Israel go out of his land.”

But Moses says to YHWH, “Look, the people of Israel haven’t listened to me. So how will Pharaoh listen to me, when my lips are uncircumcised?” Yet YHWH speaks to Moses and Aaron, and he gives them orders about the people of Israel and about Pharaoh king of Egypt, to bring the people of Israel out of the land of Egypt.
The Genealogy of Moses and Aaron · 6:14–27

These are the heads of their families. The sons of Reuben, Israel’s firstborn: Hanoch, Pallu, Hezron, and Carmi. These are the clans of Reuben. The sons of Simeon: Jemuel, Jamin, Ohad, Jachin, Zohar, and Shaul, the son of a Canaanite woman. These are the clans of Simeon. These are the names of the sons of Levi by their generations: Gershon, Kohath, and Merari. Levi lives a hundred and thirty-seven years. The sons of Gershon, by their clans: Libni and Shimei. The sons of Kohath: Amram, Izhar, Hebron, and Uzziel. Kohath lives a hundred and thirty-three years. The sons of Merari: Mahli and Mushi. These are the clans of the Levites by their generations. Amram marries Jochebed, his father’s sister, and she bears him Aaron and Moses. Amram lives a hundred and thirty-seven years. The sons of Izhar: Korah, Nepheg, and Zichri. The sons of Uzziel: Mishael, Elzaphan, and Sithri. Aaron marries Elisheba, daughter of Amminadab and sister of Nahshon, and she bears him Nadab and Abihu, Eleazar and Ithamar. The sons of Korah: Assir, Elkanah, and Abiasaph. These are the clans of the Korahites. Aaron’s son Eleazar marries one of the daughters of Putiel, and she bears him Phinehas. These are the heads of the Levite families, clan by clan. This is the same Aaron and Moses to whom YHWH says, “Bring the people of Israel out of the land of Egypt, company by company.” They are the ones who speak to Pharaoh king of Egypt about bringing the people of Israel out of Egypt. This is that same Moses and Aaron.
The Commission Renewed · 6:28–30
On the day YHWH speaks to Moses in the land of Egypt, YHWH says to Moses, “I am YHWH. Tell Pharaoh king of Egypt everything I tell you.”
But Moses says to YHWH, “Look, my lips are uncircumcised. How will Pharaoh ever listen to me?”
Aaron’s Staff · 7:1–13

Then YHWH says to Moses, “See, I have made you like God to Pharaoh, and your brother Aaron will be your prophet. You are to say everything I command you, and your brother Aaron will tell Pharaoh to let the people of Israel go out of his land. But I will make Pharaoh’s heart stubborn, and I will multiply my signs and my wonders in the land of Egypt. Pharaoh won’t listen to you. Then I will lay my hand on Egypt, and with mighty acts of judgment I will bring my companies, my people, the people of Israel, out of the land of Egypt. And the Egyptians will know that I am YHWH, when I stretch out my hand over Egypt and bring the people of Israel out from among them.”
And Moses and Aaron do just that. They do exactly as YHWH commands them. Moses is eighty years old and Aaron eighty-three when they speak to Pharaoh.
YHWH says to Moses and Aaron, “When Pharaoh says to you, ‘Show me a wonder,’ then tell Aaron, ‘Take your staff and throw it down in front of Pharaoh,’ and it will become a serpent.”

So Moses and Aaron go in to Pharaoh and do just as YHWH has commanded. Aaron throws his staff down in front of Pharaoh and his officials, and it becomes a serpent. Then Pharaoh calls for his wise men and sorcerers, and the magicians of Egypt do the same thing with their secret arts. Each one throws down his staff, and they become serpents. But Aaron’s staff swallows up their staffs. Still Pharaoh’s heart is hardened, and he won’t listen to them, just as YHWH said.
The First Plague — Blood · 7:14–25

Then YHWH says to Moses, “Pharaoh’s heart is heavy. He refuses to let the people go. Go to Pharaoh in the morning, just as he is going out to the water. Stand on the bank of the Nile to meet him, and take in your hand the staff that turned into a snake. Tell him, ‘YHWH, the God of the Hebrews, has sent me to you to say: Let my people go, so they can worship me in the wilderness. But so far you have not listened. This is what YHWH says: By this you will know that I am YHWH. Look, with the staff in my hand I will strike the water of the Nile, and it will turn to blood. The fish in the Nile will die, and the Nile will stink, and the Egyptians won’t be able to bear drinking its water.’” And YHWH says to Moses, “Tell Aaron, ‘Take your staff and stretch out your hand over the waters of Egypt, over their rivers, their canals, their ponds, and all their pools of water, so they turn to blood.’ There will be blood all through the land of Egypt, even in the buckets of wood and the jars of stone.”

Moses and Aaron do just as YHWH has commanded. In front of Pharaoh and his officials, Aaron raises the staff and strikes the water of the Nile, and all the water of the Nile turns to blood. The fish in the Nile die, and the Nile stinks so badly that the Egyptians can’t drink its water. There is blood all through the land of Egypt. But the magicians of Egypt do the same thing with their secret arts. So Pharaoh’s heart is hardened, and he won’t listen to them, just as YHWH said. Pharaoh turns and goes into his palace, and he doesn’t take even this to heart. All the Egyptians dig along the Nile for water to drink, because they can’t drink the water of the Nile. Seven days pass after YHWH has struck the Nile.
The Second Plague — Frogs · 8:1–15

Then YHWH says to Moses, “Go to Pharaoh and tell him, ‘This is what YHWH says: Let my people go, so they can worship me. If you refuse to let them go, look, I will plague your whole country with frogs. The Nile will swarm with frogs. They will come up into your palace and your bedroom and onto your bed, into the houses of your officials and onto your people, into your ovens and your kneading bowls. The frogs will climb all over you and your people and all your officials.’” And YHWH says to Moses, “Tell Aaron, ‘Stretch out your hand with your staff over the rivers, the canals, and the ponds, and make frogs come up over the land of Egypt.’” So Aaron stretches out his hand over the waters of Egypt, and the frogs come up and cover the land of Egypt. But the magicians do the same with their secret arts, and they bring up frogs on the land of Egypt too.
Then Pharaoh summons Moses and Aaron. “Pray to YHWH to take the frogs away from me and my people,” he says, “and I will let the people go to offer sacrifices to YHWH.”

“The honor is yours,” Moses tells Pharaoh. “Just tell me when I should pray for you and your officials and your people, so that the frogs will be gone from you and your houses and be left only in the Nile.”

“Tomorrow,” Pharaoh says. “It will be as you say,” Moses replies, “so that you will know there is no one like YHWH our God. The frogs will leave you and your houses, your officials and your people. They will be left only in the Nile.”

Then Moses and Aaron leave Pharaoh, and Moses cries out to YHWH about the frogs he has brought on Pharaoh. And YHWH does what Moses asks. The frogs die in the houses, in the courtyards, and in the fields. They pile them up in heaps, and the whole land stinks. But when Pharaoh sees that he has room to breathe, he makes his heart heavy and won’t listen to them, just as YHWH said.
The Third Plague — Gnats · 8:16–19

Then YHWH says to Moses, “Tell Aaron, ‘Stretch out your staff and strike the dust of the ground, and it will become gnats all through the land of Egypt.’” And they do it. Aaron stretches out his hand with his staff and strikes the dust of the ground, and gnats swarm over people and animals. All the dust of the ground becomes gnats all through the land of Egypt. The magicians try to bring out gnats with their secret arts, but they can’t. And the gnats are on people and animals alike. So the magicians say to Pharaoh, “This is the finger of God!” But Pharaoh’s heart is hardened, and he won’t listen to them, just as YHWH said.
The Fourth Plague — Flies · 8:20–32

Then YHWH says to Moses, “Get up early in the morning and stand in front of Pharaoh as he goes out to the water. Tell him, ‘This is what YHWH says: Let my people go, so they can worship me. If you don’t let my people go, look, I will send swarms of flies on you and your officials and your people and into your houses. The houses of the Egyptians will be full of swarms of flies, and so will the very ground they stand on. But on that day I will set apart the land of Goshen, where my people live. No swarms of flies will be there, so that you will know that I, YHWH, am right here in the midst of the land. I will draw a line between my people and your people. This sign will happen tomorrow.’” And YHWH does it. Thick swarms of flies pour into Pharaoh’s palace and into his officials’ houses. All through the land of Egypt the land is ruined by the flies.
Then Pharaoh summons Moses and Aaron. “Go,” he says, “offer sacrifices to your God here in the land.”

“That wouldn’t be right,” Moses says. “The sacrifices we offer to YHWH our God are detestable to the Egyptians. If we offer sacrifices the Egyptians find detestable right before their eyes, won’t they stone us? We must go three days’ journey into the wilderness and offer sacrifices to YHWH our God, as he tells us.”
“I will let you go,” Pharaoh says, “to offer sacrifices to YHWH your God in the wilderness. Only don’t go very far. Now pray for me.”

“As soon as I leave you,” Moses says, “I will pray to YHWH, and tomorrow the swarms of flies will leave Pharaoh and his officials and his people. Only Pharaoh must not play us false again by refusing to let the people go to offer sacrifices to YHWH.” So Moses leaves Pharaoh and prays to YHWH. And YHWH does what Moses asks. He takes the swarms of flies away from Pharaoh and his officials and his people. Not one is left. But this time too Pharaoh makes his heart heavy, and he won’t let the people go.
The Fifth Plague — Livestock · 9:1–7

Then YHWH says to Moses, “Go to Pharaoh and tell him, ‘This is what YHWH, the God of the Hebrews, says: Let my people go, so they can worship me. If you refuse to let them go and keep holding on to them, look, the hand of YHWH will fall on your livestock in the fields, on your horses and donkeys and camels, your herds and your flocks, with a terrible disease. But YHWH will draw a line between the livestock of Israel and the livestock of Egypt, and nothing that belongs to the people of Israel will die.’” And YHWH sets a time. “Tomorrow,” he says, “YHWH will do this in the land.” And the next day YHWH does it. All the livestock of Egypt die, but not one animal belonging to the people of Israel dies. Pharaoh sends men to look, and sure enough, not a single animal of Israel’s has died. But Pharaoh’s heart is heavy, and he won’t let the people go.
The Sixth Plague — Boils · 9:8–12

Then YHWH says to Moses and Aaron, “Take handfuls of soot from a kiln, and let Moses toss it into the air in front of Pharaoh. It will become fine dust over the whole land of Egypt, and it will break out in festering boils on people and animals all through the land of Egypt.”

So they take soot from a kiln and stand in front of Pharaoh, and Moses tosses it into the air. And it breaks out in festering boils on people and animals. The magicians can’t even stand in front of Moses because of the boils, because the boils are on the magicians and on all the Egyptians. But YHWH hardens Pharaoh’s heart, and he won’t listen to them, just as YHWH told Moses.
The Seventh Plague — Hail · 9:13–35

Then YHWH says to Moses, “Get up early in the morning, stand in front of Pharaoh, and tell him, ‘This is what YHWH, the God of the Hebrews, says: Let my people go, so they can worship me. This time I am going to send all my plagues against you yourself, against your officials and your people, so that you will know there is no one like me in all the earth. By now I could have stretched out my hand and struck you and your people with disease, and you would have been wiped off the earth. But I have let you stand for this very reason: to show you my power, and so that my name will be told throughout all the earth. You still set yourself up against my people and won’t let them go. So look, about this time tomorrow I will rain down hail, the heaviest hail Egypt has ever seen, from the day it was founded until now. So now send word to bring your livestock and everything you have in the fields under shelter. Every person and animal caught out in the field and not brought inside will die when the hail comes down on them.’”

Those among Pharaoh’s officials who fear the word of YHWH hurry their servants and their livestock inside. But those who pay no attention to the word of YHWH leave their servants and their livestock out in the field.
Then YHWH says to Moses, “Stretch out your hand toward the sky, so that hail falls on the whole land of Egypt, on people and animals and every plant of the field throughout the land of Egypt.”

So Moses stretches out his staff toward the sky, and YHWH sends thunder and hail, and fire streaks down to the ground. YHWH rains hail on the land of Egypt. Hail falls, with fire flashing back and forth through it, hail so heavy that nothing like it has been seen in all the land of Egypt since it became a nation. All through the land of Egypt the hail strikes down everything in the fields, people and animals alike. The hail beats down every plant of the field and shatters every tree. Only in the land of Goshen, where the people of Israel are, is there no hail.

Then Pharaoh summons Moses and Aaron. “This time I have sinned,” he tells them. “YHWH is in the right, and I and my people are in the wrong. Pray to YHWH. We have had enough of God’s thunder and hail. I will let you go. You don’t have to stay any longer.”

Moses says to him, “As soon as I have gone out of the city, I will spread out my hands to YHWH. The thunder will stop, and there will be no more hail, so that you will know that the earth belongs to YHWH. But as for you and your officials, I know that you still do not fear YHWH God.”
(The flax and the barley are ruined, because the barley is in the ear and the flax is in bloom. But the wheat and the spelt are not ruined, because they come up later.)

So Moses leaves Pharaoh and goes out of the city, and he spreads out his hands to YHWH. The thunder and the hail stop, and the rain no longer pours down on the land. But when Pharaoh sees that the rain and hail and thunder have stopped, he sins again. He makes his heart heavy, he and his officials. So Pharaoh’s heart is hardened, and he won’t let the people of Israel go, just as YHWH said through Moses.
The Eighth Plague — Locusts · 10:1–20

Then YHWH says to Moses, “Go to Pharaoh. I have made his heart heavy, and the hearts of his officials, so that I can show these signs of mine among them, and so that you can tell your children and your grandchildren the story of how I made fools of the Egyptians, and of the signs I did among them. Then you will know that I am YHWH.”

So Moses and Aaron go to Pharaoh and say to him, “This is what YHWH, the God of the Hebrews, says: ‘How long will you refuse to bow down before me? Let my people go, so they can worship me. If you refuse to let my people go, look, tomorrow I will bring locusts into your country. They will cover the face of the ground until no one can see the ground. They will eat whatever little is left to you after the hail, and they will eat every tree growing in your fields. They will fill your palace and the houses of all your officials and all the Egyptians, something your fathers and your grandfathers never saw, from the day they came into this land until now.’” Then he turns and leaves Pharaoh.
Pharaoh’s officials say to him, “How long will this man be a trap for us? Let the men go, so they can worship YHWH their God. Don’t you know yet that Egypt is ruined?”
So Moses and Aaron are brought back to Pharaoh. “Go, worship YHWH your God,” he says to them. “But just who will be going?”
“We will go with our young and our old,” Moses says. “We will go with our sons and daughters, with our flocks and herds, because we must hold a festival to YHWH.”

“YHWH be with you, then,” Pharaoh says, “if I ever let you go with your little ones! You can see you are plotting something evil. No! Only the men can go and worship YHWH, since that is what you are asking for.” And they are driven out of Pharaoh’s presence.

Then YHWH says to Moses, “Stretch out your hand over the land of Egypt for the locusts, so that they swarm over the land of Egypt and eat every plant in the land, everything the hail has left.” So Moses stretches out his staff over the land of Egypt, and YHWH drives an east wind across the land all that day and all that night. By morning the east wind has brought the locusts. The locusts swarm over the whole land of Egypt and settle down in every part of it, a terrible horde. There has never been such a swarm of locusts before, and there never will be again. They cover the face of the whole land until the land is black with them. They eat every plant in the land and all the fruit on the trees that the hail has left. Nothing green is left on tree or plant in all the land of Egypt. Pharaoh quickly summons Moses and Aaron. “I have sinned against YHWH your God and against you,” he says. “Now please forgive my sin just this once, and pray to YHWH your God to take this deadly plague away from me.”

So Moses leaves Pharaoh and prays to YHWH. And YHWH turns the wind into a very strong west wind, which picks up the locusts and drives them into the Red Sea. Not a single locust is left anywhere in Egypt. But YHWH hardens Pharaoh’s heart, and he won’t let the people of Israel go.
The Ninth Plague — Darkness · 10:21–29

Then YHWH says to Moses, “Stretch out your hand toward the sky, so that darkness spreads over the land of Egypt, a darkness so thick it can be felt.” So Moses stretches out his hand toward the sky, and a deep darkness covers the whole land of Egypt for three days. No one can see anyone else, and no one moves from where he is for three days. But all the people of Israel have light where they live.
Then Pharaoh summons Moses. “Go, worship YHWH,” he says. “Even your little ones can go with you. Only leave your flocks and herds behind.”

But Moses says, “You must also let us have animals for sacrifices and burnt offerings to offer to YHWH our God. Our livestock must go with us too. Not a hoof can be left behind. We have to take some of them to worship YHWH our God, and until we get there, we won’t know what we will need to worship YHWH.”
But YHWH hardens Pharaoh’s heart, and he won’t let them go. “Get out of my sight!” Pharaoh tells him. “Make sure you never see my face again! The day you see my face, you will die!”
“You have said it,” Moses answers. “I will never see your face again.”
The Final Plague Announced · 11:1–10

Now YHWH has said to Moses, “One more plague I will bring on Pharaoh and on Egypt. After that he will let you go from here. And when he lets you go, he will drive you out of here altogether. Tell the people that every man and every woman is to ask their neighbors for silver and gold jewelry.” And YHWH makes the Egyptians look kindly on the people. And the man Moses himself is highly regarded in the land of Egypt, by Pharaoh’s officials and by the people.

So Moses says, “This is what YHWH says: ‘About midnight I will go out through the middle of Egypt, and every firstborn in the land of Egypt will die, from the firstborn of Pharaoh, who sits on his throne, to the firstborn of the slave girl at her hand mill, and every firstborn of the livestock too. There will be loud wailing through the whole land of Egypt, worse than there has ever been or ever will be again. But among the people of Israel not even a dog will growl at any person or animal, so that you will know that YHWH draws a line between Egypt and Israel.’ Then all these officials of yours will come down to me and bow low before me and say, ‘Go, you and all the people who follow you!’ After that I will go.” And Moses leaves Pharaoh, burning with anger.

YHWH has told Moses, “Pharaoh won’t listen to you, so that my wonders will multiply in the land of Egypt.” Moses and Aaron have done all these wonders before Pharaoh, but YHWH has hardened Pharaoh’s heart, and he won’t let the people of Israel go out of his land.
The Institution of the Passover · 12:1–28

YHWH says to Moses and Aaron in the land of Egypt, “This month will be the head of the months for you. It will be the first month of your year. Tell the whole community of Israel: ‘On the tenth day of this month, each man is to take a lamb for his family, one lamb for each household. If a household is too small for a whole lamb, they are to share one with their nearest neighbor, depending on how many people there are. Count how much each person will eat when you choose the lamb. Your lamb must be a year-old male without any defect. You may take it from the sheep or the goats. Keep it until the fourteenth day of this month. Then the whole assembly of the community of Israel is to slaughter it at twilight. They are to take some of the blood and put it on the two doorposts and the top of the doorframe of the houses where they eat it. That same night they are to eat the meat, roasted over the fire, with bread made without yeast and with bitter herbs. Don’t eat it raw or boiled in water, but roasted over the fire, head, legs, and insides. Don’t leave any of it until morning. If any is left until morning, burn it. And this is how you are to eat it: with your belt fastened, your sandals on your feet, and your staff in your hand. Eat it in a hurry. It is YHWH’s Passover. That night I will pass through the land of Egypt and strike down every firstborn in the land of Egypt, people and animals alike. And on all the gods of Egypt I will bring judgment. I am YHWH. The blood will be a sign for you on the houses where you are. When I see the blood, I will pass over you, and no plague will fall on you to destroy you when I strike the land of Egypt. This day will be a day for you to remember. You are to keep it as a festival to YHWH, generation after generation, as a rule for all time.

For seven days you are to eat bread made without yeast. On the very first day, clear the yeast out of your houses, because whoever eats anything with yeast in it from the first day through the seventh will be cut off from Israel. On the first day hold a holy assembly, and on the seventh day another holy assembly. No work is to be done on those days, except to prepare what each person needs to eat. That is all you may do. Keep the Festival of Unleavened Bread, because on this very day I brought your companies out of the land of Egypt. Keep this day generation after generation, as a rule for all time. In the first month, from the evening of the fourteenth day until the evening of the twenty-first day, you are to eat bread made without yeast. For seven days no yeast is to be found in your houses. Whoever eats anything with yeast in it will be cut off from the community of Israel, whether a foreigner or someone born in the land. Eat nothing made with yeast. Wherever you live, eat bread made without yeast.’”

Then Moses calls all the elders of Israel together and says to them, “Go and pick out lambs for your families, and slaughter the Passover lamb. Take a bunch of hyssop, dip it in the blood in the basin, and brush some of the blood from the basin on the top of the doorframe and on both doorposts. Then none of you is to go out the door of his house until morning. When YHWH passes through to strike the Egyptians, he will see the blood on the top of the doorframe and on the two doorposts, and YHWH will pass over that door. He won’t let the destroyer come into your houses to strike you down. You are to keep this as a rule for you and your children forever. When you come into the land YHWH will give you, as he has promised, keep this service. And when your children ask you, ‘What does this service mean to you?’ then tell them, ‘It is the Passover sacrifice to YHWH, who passed over the houses of the people of Israel in Egypt when he struck down the Egyptians, and spared our homes.’” Then the people bow their heads and worship.
And the people of Israel go and do it. They do just as YHWH has commanded Moses and Aaron.
The Tenth Plague and the Departure · 12:29–42

At midnight YHWH strikes down every firstborn in the land of Egypt, from the firstborn of Pharaoh, who sits on his throne, to the firstborn of the prisoner in the dungeon, and every firstborn of the livestock too. Pharaoh gets up in the night, he and all his officials and all the Egyptians, and there is loud wailing in Egypt, because there is not a house without someone dead. Pharaoh summons Moses and Aaron in the night. “Get up!” he says. “Get out from among my people, you and the people of Israel! Go, worship YHWH, as you have asked. Take your flocks and your herds, as you have asked, and go! And bless me too!”

The Egyptians urge the people to hurry and leave the land. “Otherwise,” they say, “we will all be dead!” So the people take their dough before the yeast is added, with their kneading bowls wrapped up in their cloaks on their shoulders. The people of Israel have done as Moses told them, and they have asked the Egyptians for silver and gold jewelry and for clothing. And YHWH has made the Egyptians look kindly on the people, so they give them whatever they ask. And so they strip Egypt bare.

The people of Israel set out from Rameses toward Succoth, about six hundred thousand men on foot, not counting the children. A great mixed crowd of other people goes up with them too, with flocks and herds, a great many animals. With the dough they brought out of Egypt they bake flat cakes without yeast. The dough has no yeast in it, because they were driven out of Egypt and couldn’t wait, and they haven’t prepared any food for the journey.

The people of Israel have lived in Egypt four hundred and thirty years. And at the end of four hundred and thirty years, on that very day, all the companies of YHWH go out from the land of Egypt. It is a night of watching for YHWH, to bring them out of the land of Egypt. This same night is a night of watching for YHWH, for all the people of Israel, generation after generation.
Passover Regulations · 12:43–51

YHWH says to Moses and Aaron, “This is the rule for the Passover: no foreigner is to eat it. But any slave who has been bought with money may eat it once you have circumcised him. A temporary resident or a hired worker may not eat it. It must be eaten inside one house. Don’t take any of the meat outside the house, and don’t break any of its bones. The whole community of Israel must keep it. If a foreigner living among you wants to keep the Passover to YHWH, all the males in his household must be circumcised. Then he may come and keep it, and he will be like someone born in the land. But no uncircumcised man may eat it. The same law applies to the one born in the land and to the foreigner living among you.”
And all the people of Israel do it. They do just as YHWH has commanded Moses and Aaron. And on that very day YHWH brings the people of Israel out of the land of Egypt, company by company.
Consecration of the Firstborn · 13:1–16
YHWH says to Moses, “Set apart for me as holy every firstborn, the first to open the womb among the people of Israel, both human and animal. It is mine.”

Then Moses says to the people, “Remember this day, the day you came out of Egypt, out of the house of slavery, because YHWH brought you out of here by the strength of his hand. Nothing with yeast in it is to be eaten. Today, in the month of Abib, the month of new grain, you are going out. When YHWH brings you into the land of the Canaanites, Hittites, Amorites, Hivites, and Jebusites, the land he swore to your fathers to give you, a land flowing with milk and honey, you are to keep this service in this month. For seven days eat bread made without yeast, and on the seventh day hold a festival to YHWH. Bread made without yeast is to be eaten for the seven days. Nothing with yeast in it is to be seen among you. No yeast is to be seen anywhere in your territory. On that day tell your son, ‘This is because of what YHWH did for me when I came out of Egypt.’ It will be like a sign on your hand and a reminder on your forehead, so that the teaching of YHWH will be on your lips. For with a mighty hand YHWH brought you out of Egypt. So keep this rule at its set time, year after year.

When YHWH brings you into the land of the Canaanites, as he swore to you and to your fathers, and gives it to you, you are to hand over to YHWH everything that first opens the womb. Every firstborn male of your animals belongs to YHWH. Every firstborn donkey you must buy back with a lamb. If you don’t buy it back, break its neck. And every firstborn son among your children you must redeem. And in days to come, when your son asks you, ‘What does this mean?’ tell him, ‘By the strength of his hand YHWH brought us out of Egypt, out of the house of slavery. When Pharaoh made himself stubborn and refused to let us go, YHWH killed every firstborn in the land of Egypt, both human and animal. That is why I sacrifice to YHWH every male that first opens the womb, but every firstborn among my sons I redeem.’ It will be like a sign on your hand and a band on your forehead, because by the strength of his hand YHWH brought us out of Egypt.”
The Pillar of Cloud and Fire · 13:17–22

When Pharaoh lets the people go, God doesn’t lead them along the road through Philistine country, even though that way is shorter. For God says, “If they face war, the people might change their minds and go back to Egypt.” So God leads the people around by the wilderness road toward the Red Sea. And the people of Israel go up out of the land of Egypt ready for battle. Moses takes the bones of Joseph with him, because Joseph made the sons of Israel swear an oath. He said, “God will surely come to you, and then you must carry my bones up from here with you.” They set out from Succoth and camp at Etham, at the edge of the wilderness. And YHWH goes ahead of them, by day in a pillar of cloud to lead them along the road, and by night in a pillar of fire to light their way, so they can travel by day or by night. The pillar of cloud by day and the pillar of fire by night never leave their place in front of the people.
Pharaoh Pursues Israel · 14:1–20

Then YHWH says to Moses, “Tell the people of Israel to turn back and camp in front of Pi-hahiroth, between Migdol and the sea. Camp by the sea, right across from Baal-zephon. Pharaoh will think, ‘The people of Israel are wandering around lost. The wilderness has closed in on them.’ And I will harden Pharaoh’s heart, and he will chase after them. Then I will win glory for myself over Pharaoh and his whole army, and the Egyptians will know that I am YHWH.” And they do it.

When the king of Egypt is told that the people have run away, Pharaoh and his officials change their minds about the people. “What have we done?” they say. “We’ve let Israel go, and lost our slaves!” So he has his chariot harnessed and takes his army with him. He takes six hundred of the best chariots, and all the other chariots of Egypt, with officers over all of them. And YHWH hardens the heart of Pharaoh king of Egypt, and he chases after the people of Israel, while the people of Israel are marching out with their hands held high. The Egyptians chase after them, all Pharaoh’s horses and chariots, his horsemen and his army, and they catch up with them as they are camped by the sea near Pi-hahiroth, across from Baal-zephon.

As Pharaoh draws near, the people of Israel look up, and there are the Egyptians, marching after them! And they are terrified. The people of Israel cry out to YHWH. And they say to Moses, “Weren’t there enough graves in Egypt, that you had to bring us out here to die in the wilderness? What have you done to us, bringing us out of Egypt? Didn’t we tell you in Egypt, ‘Leave us alone and let us serve the Egyptians’? We would be better off serving the Egyptians than dying in the wilderness!”

But Moses says to the people, “Don’t be afraid. Stand your ground and watch YHWH rescue you today. These Egyptians you see today, you will never see again, ever. YHWH will fight for you. All you have to do is keep still.”

Then YHWH says to Moses, “Why are you crying out to me? Tell the people of Israel to move on. And you, lift up your staff and stretch out your hand over the sea and split it apart, so that the people of Israel can go through the middle of the sea on dry ground. And I, look, I will harden the hearts of the Egyptians, and they will go in after them. Then I will win glory for myself over Pharaoh and his whole army, his chariots and his horsemen. And the Egyptians will know that I am YHWH, when I have won glory for myself over Pharaoh, his chariots, and his horsemen.” Then the messenger of God, who has been going ahead of Israel’s camp, moves and goes behind them. The pillar of cloud moves from in front of them and stands behind them. It comes between the camp of Egypt and the camp of Israel. There is the cloud and the darkness, and yet it lights up the night. So neither one comes near the other all night long.
The Crossing of the Sea · 14:21–31

Then Moses stretches out his hand over the sea, and all night long YHWH pushes the sea back with a fierce east wind, and the seabed becomes dry land. The waters are split apart. And the people of Israel go through the middle of the sea on dry ground, with the waters standing like a wall on their right and on their left. The Egyptians chase them and follow them into the middle of the sea, all Pharaoh’s horses, his chariots, and his horsemen. Then in the last watch of the night, just before morning, YHWH looks down on the Egyptian army from the pillar of fire and cloud, and throws the Egyptian army into a panic. He jams the wheels of their chariots so that they drive heavily. “Let’s get away from Israel!” the Egyptians say. “YHWH is fighting for them against Egypt!”

Then YHWH says to Moses, “Stretch out your hand over the sea, so the waters come back over the Egyptians, over their chariots and their horsemen.” So Moses stretches out his hand over the sea, and as morning breaks, the sea rushes back to its usual depth. The Egyptians run straight into it, and YHWH shakes the Egyptians off into the middle of the sea. The waters come back and cover the chariots and the horsemen, Pharaoh’s whole army that followed them into the sea. Not one of them is left. But the people of Israel walk on dry ground through the middle of the sea, with the waters standing like a wall on their right and on their left. That day YHWH saves Israel from the hand of the Egyptians, and Israel sees the Egyptians lying dead on the seashore. And when Israel sees the great power YHWH has used against the Egyptians, the people fear YHWH, and they put their trust in YHWH and in his servant Moses.
The Song of the Sea · 15:1–21
Then Moses and the people of Israel sing this song to YHWH: “I will sing to YHWH, for he has triumphed, triumphed gloriously! Horse and rider he has hurled into the sea.”
Yah is my strength and my song,
and he has become my rescue.
This is my God, and I will praise him,
my father’s God, and I will lift him high.
YHWH is a warrior.
YHWH is his name.
Pharaoh’s chariots and his army
he has flung into the sea.
His finest officers
are drowned in the Red Sea.
The deep waters cover them.
They sank to the bottom like a stone.
Your right hand, YHWH,
is glorious in power.
Your right hand, YHWH,
smashes the enemy to pieces.
In your great majesty
you throw down those who rise against you.
You send out your burning anger,
and it eats them up like straw.
At the blast of your nostrils
the waters piled up.
The surging waves stood up like a wall.
The deep waters hardened in the heart of the sea.
The enemy said, “I will chase them,
I will catch them,
I will divide the plunder.
I will have my fill of them.
I will draw my sword.
My hand will destroy them.”
But you blew with your breath,
and the sea covered them.
They sank like lead
in the mighty waters.
Who is like you, YHWH, among the gods?
Who is like you, glorious in holiness,
awesome in praises,
working wonders?
You stretched out your right hand,
and the earth swallowed them.
In your steadfast love you lead
the people you have redeemed.
In your strength you guide them
to your holy dwelling.
The peoples hear and tremble.
Pain grips the people of Philistia.
The chiefs of Edom are shaken.
Trembling seizes the leaders of Moab.
All the people of Canaan melt away.
Terror and dread fall on them.
Because of the might of your arm
they stand as still as stone
until your people pass by, YHWH,
until the people you have made your own pass by.
You will bring them in and plant them
on the mountain that is your own,
the place, YHWH, you have made your home,
the sanctuary, Lord, your hands have built.
YHWH will reign forever and ever!

When Pharaoh’s horses, with his chariots and horsemen, went into the sea, YHWH brought the waters of the sea back over them. But the people of Israel walked on dry ground through the middle of the sea. Then Miriam the prophet, Aaron’s sister, takes a tambourine in her hand, and all the women follow her with tambourines, dancing. And Miriam sings back to them, “Sing to YHWH, for he has triumphed, triumphed gloriously! Horse and rider he has hurled into the sea.”
Bitter Water Made Sweet · 15:22–27

Then Moses leads Israel on from the Red Sea, and they go out into the wilderness of Shur. For three days they travel through the wilderness and find no water. When they come to Marah, they can’t drink its water, because it is bitter. That is why it is called Marah, Bitter. So the people grumble against Moses. “What are we going to drink?” they say. Then Moses cries out to YHWH, and YHWH shows him a piece of wood. He throws it into the water, and the water turns sweet. There YHWH gives them a rule and a law, and there he tests them. He says, “If you will listen closely to the voice of YHWH your God, and do what is right in his eyes, and pay attention to his commands, and keep all his decrees, I won’t bring on you any of the diseases I brought on the Egyptians. For I am YHWH who heals you.”
Then they come to Elim, where there are twelve springs of water and seventy palm trees, and they camp there beside the water.
Manna and Quail in the Wilderness · 16:1–36

They set out from Elim, and the whole community of Israel comes into the wilderness of Sin, between Elim and Sinai, on the fifteenth day of the second month after they came out of the land of Egypt. And there in the wilderness the whole community of Israel grumbles against Moses and Aaron. “If only we had died by YHWH’s hand in the land of Egypt!” the people of Israel tell them. “There we sat around pots of meat and ate all the bread we wanted. But you have brought us out into this wilderness to starve this whole crowd to death!”

Then YHWH says to Moses, “Look, I am going to rain down bread from the sky for you. The people are to go out each day and gather enough for that day. In this way I will test them, to see whether they will walk in my teaching or not. On the sixth day, when they prepare what they bring in, it will be twice as much as they gather on other days.”

So Moses and Aaron say to all the people of Israel, “This evening you will know that it was YHWH who brought you out of the land of Egypt, and in the morning you will see the glory of YHWH, because he has heard your grumbling against YHWH. Who are we, that you grumble against us?” And Moses says, “YHWH will give you meat to eat in the evening and all the bread you want in the morning, because YHWH has heard the grumbling you grumble against him. Who are we? Your grumbling isn’t against us. It is against YHWH.” Then Moses says to Aaron, “Tell the whole community of Israel, ‘Come near before YHWH, because he has heard your grumbling.’” And while Aaron is speaking to the whole community of Israel, they look toward the wilderness, and there is the glory of YHWH, shining in the cloud! And YHWH says to Moses, “I have heard the grumbling of the people of Israel. Tell them, ‘At twilight you will eat meat, and in the morning you will be filled with bread. Then you will know that I am YHWH your God.’”

That evening quail fly in and cover the camp, and in the morning a layer of dew lies all around the camp. When the dew lifts, there on the face of the wilderness is something thin and flaky, fine as frost on the ground. When the people of Israel see it, they ask each other, “Man hu? What is it?” because they don’t know what it is. And Moses tells them, “It is the bread YHWH has given you to eat. This is what YHWH has commanded: ‘Each of you is to gather as much as you need to eat, an omer for each person, about two quarts. Gather for everyone living in your tent.’” The people of Israel do it. Some gather more, some less. But when they measure it by the omer, the one who gathered much has nothing left over, and the one who gathered little has no shortage. Each has gathered just as much as he needs to eat. And Moses tells them, “No one is to keep any of it until morning.” But they don’t listen to Moses. Some of them keep part of it until morning, and it breeds worms and stinks. And Moses is angry with them. So morning after morning they gather it, each as much as he needs to eat. And when the sun grows hot, it melts away.

On the sixth day they gather twice as much bread, two omers for each person. And all the leaders of the community come and tell Moses. He tells them, “This is what YHWH has said: ‘Tomorrow is a day of rest, a holy Sabbath to YHWH. Bake what you want to bake, and boil what you want to boil, and set aside whatever is left over and keep it until morning.’” So they set it aside until morning, as Moses has told them, and it doesn’t stink, and there are no worms in it. “Eat it today,” Moses says, “because today is a Sabbath to YHWH. Today you won’t find any out in the field. Six days you are to gather it, but on the seventh day, the Sabbath, there won’t be any.” Even so, on the seventh day some of the people go out to gather it, and they find none. Then YHWH says to Moses, “How long will you refuse to keep my commands and my teachings? Look, YHWH has given you the Sabbath. That is why on the sixth day he gives you bread for two days. Each of you stay where you are. No one is to leave his place on the seventh day.” So the people rest on the seventh day.

The house of Israel names it manna. It is white, like coriander seed, and it tastes like wafers made with honey. Moses says, “This is what YHWH has commanded: ‘Keep an omer of it for generations to come, so they can see the bread I fed you in the wilderness when I brought you out of the land of Egypt.’” So Moses says to Aaron, “Take a jar, put a full omer of manna in it, and set it before YHWH, to be kept for generations to come.” As YHWH commanded Moses, Aaron sets it in front of the Testimony to be kept. The people of Israel eat manna for forty years, until they come to a land where people live. They eat manna until they reach the border of the land of Canaan. (An omer is a tenth of an ephah.)
Water from the Rock · 17:1–7

The whole community of Israel sets out from the wilderness of Sin, traveling stage by stage as YHWH commands, and they camp at Rephidim. But there is no water for the people to drink. So the people quarrel with Moses. “Give us water to drink!” they say. “Why are you quarreling with me?” Moses says to them. “Why are you testing YHWH?”
But the people are thirsty there, and they grumble against Moses. “Why did you bring us up out of Egypt,” they say, “to kill us and our children and our livestock with thirst?”
Then Moses cries out to YHWH, “What am I going to do with these people? Any minute now they will stone me!”

YHWH says to Moses, “Go on ahead of the people, and take some of the elders of Israel with you. Take in your hand the staff you struck the Nile with, and go. Look, I will stand there before you on the rock at Horeb. Strike the rock, and water will come out of it for the people to drink.” And Moses does so, before the eyes of the elders of Israel. And he names the place Massah and Meribah, Testing and Quarreling, because the people of Israel quarreled there, and because they tested YHWH, saying, “Is YHWH among us or not?”
The Battle with Amalek · 17:8–16

Then Amalek comes and attacks Israel at Rephidim. Moses says to Joshua, “Pick out some men for us and go out and fight Amalek. Tomorrow I will stand on top of the hill with the staff of God in my hand.” So Joshua does as Moses tells him and fights Amalek, while Moses, Aaron, and Hur go up to the top of the hill. Whenever Moses holds up his hand, Israel gets the upper hand. And whenever he lets his hand down, Amalek gets the upper hand. But Moses’ hands grow heavy. So they take a stone and put it under him, and he sits on it. Aaron and Hur hold up his hands, one on one side and one on the other, and his hands stay steady until the sun goes down. And Joshua cuts down Amalek and his army with the sword. Then YHWH says to Moses, “Write this down in a scroll to be remembered, and read it aloud to Joshua: I will wipe out the memory of Amalek from under the sky.” And Moses builds an altar and names it YHWH Nissi, YHWH Is My Banner. “A hand is raised against the throne of Yah,” he says. “YHWH will be at war with Amalek generation after generation.”
Jethro’s Visit · 18:1–12

Now Jethro, the priest of Midian and Moses’ father-in-law, hears about everything God has done for Moses and for his people Israel, how YHWH has brought Israel out of Egypt. Moses has sent his wife Zipporah back home, and Jethro, Moses’ father-in-law, has taken her in, along with her two sons. One son is named Gershom, because Moses said, “I have become a stranger in a strange land.” The other is named Eliezer, My God Is Help, because he said, “The God of my father has been my help and has rescued me from Pharaoh’s sword.” So Jethro, Moses’ father-in-law, comes with Moses’ sons and wife to Moses in the wilderness, where he is camped at the mountain of God. He sends word to Moses: “I, your father-in-law Jethro, am coming to you, with your wife and her two sons.”

So Moses goes out to meet his father-in-law. He bows down and kisses him, and they ask how each other is doing, and they go into the tent. Then Moses tells his father-in-law everything YHWH has done to Pharaoh and the Egyptians for Israel’s sake, all the hardships they have met along the way, and how YHWH has rescued them. And Jethro is overjoyed at all the good YHWH has done for Israel in rescuing them from the hand of the Egyptians. “Blessed be YHWH,” Jethro says, “who has rescued you from the hand of the Egyptians and from the hand of Pharaoh, who has rescued the people from under the hand of the Egyptians! Now I know that YHWH is greater than all the gods, because of what happened when they treated Israel with such arrogance.” Then Jethro, Moses’ father-in-law, brings a burnt offering and sacrifices to God. And Aaron comes with all the elders of Israel to eat bread with Moses’ father-in-law in the presence of God.
Jethro’s Counsel · 18:13–27

The next day Moses takes his seat to judge the people, and the people stand around Moses from morning till evening. When Moses’ father-in-law sees all he is doing for the people, he says, “What is this you are doing for the people? Why are you sitting here alone, with all the people standing around you from morning till evening?”

Moses says to his father-in-law, “Because the people come to me to seek God’s will. Whenever they have a dispute, they come to me, and I judge between one person and another, and I teach them God’s decrees and teachings.” Moses’ father-in-law says to him, “What you are doing is not good. You will wear yourself out, you and these people with you. The load is too heavy for you. You can’t carry it alone. Now listen to me. Let me give you some advice, and may God be with you. You stand before God for the people, and you bring their cases to God. Teach them the decrees and the teachings, and show them the road they are to walk and the work they are to do. But pick out capable men from all the people, men who fear God, trustworthy men who hate a bribe, and put them over the people as leaders of thousands, of hundreds, of fifties, and of tens. Let them judge the people all the time. Let them bring every big case to you, but let them decide every small case themselves. That will make your load lighter, because they will carry it with you. If you do this, and God so commands you, you will be able to stand the strain, and all these people will go home at peace.”

So Moses listens to his father-in-law and does everything he says. Moses picks out capable men from all Israel and makes them heads over the people, leaders of thousands, of hundreds, of fifties, and of tens. They judge the people all the time. The hard cases they bring to Moses, but every small case they decide themselves. Then Moses sends his father-in-law on his way, and Jethro goes back to his own country.
Israel at Sinai · 19:1–9

In the third month after the people of Israel came out of the land of Egypt, on that very day, they come into the wilderness of Sinai. They have set out from Rephidim, and they come into the wilderness of Sinai and camp in the wilderness. And there Israel camps in front of the mountain. Then Moses goes up to God, and YHWH calls to him from the mountain: “This is what you are to say to the house of Jacob, and tell the people of Israel: ‘You have seen for yourselves what I did to the Egyptians, and how I lifted you up on eagles’ wings and carried you here to be with me. So now, if you truly listen to my voice and keep my covenant, you will be my own treasure out of all the peoples, for the whole earth is mine. You will be a kingdom of priests to me, a holy nation.’ These are the words you are to speak to the people of Israel.”

So Moses comes and calls together the elders of the people and sets before them all these words YHWH has commanded him. And all the people answer together, “Everything YHWH has spoken, we will do!” And Moses carries the people’s words back to YHWH.

YHWH says to Moses, “Look, I am going to come to you in a thick cloud, so that the people will hear when I speak with you, and will trust you forever after.” And Moses tells YHWH what the people have said.
The Consecration of the People · 19:10–25

Then YHWH says to Moses, “Go to the people and make them holy today and tomorrow. Have them wash their clothes, and be ready by the third day, because on the third day YHWH will come down on Mount Sinai before the eyes of all the people. Set a boundary for the people all around the mountain and tell them, ‘Be careful not to go up the mountain or even touch its edge. Whoever touches the mountain will surely be put to death. No hand is to touch that one. He must be stoned or shot with arrows. Animal or human, he must not live.’ When the ram’s horn sounds a long blast, then they may come up to the mountain.”
So Moses goes down from the mountain to the people and makes the people holy, and they wash their clothes. And he tells the people, “Be ready by the third day. Don’t go near a woman.”

On the morning of the third day there is thunder and lightning, and a heavy cloud on the mountain, and a blast of the ram’s horn, very loud. And all the people in the camp tremble. Then Moses leads the people out of the camp to meet God, and they take their stand at the foot of the mountain. Mount Sinai is all smoke, because YHWH has come down on it in fire. The smoke billows up like smoke from a kiln, and the whole mountain shakes violently. As the blast of the ram’s horn grows louder and louder, Moses speaks, and God answers him in thunder. YHWH comes down on Mount Sinai, onto the top of the mountain, and YHWH calls Moses to the top of the mountain, and Moses goes up.

Then YHWH says to Moses, “Go down and warn the people not to force their way through to YHWH to look, or many of them will die. Even the priests who come near YHWH must make themselves holy, or YHWH will break out against them.”
But Moses says to YHWH, “The people can’t come up Mount Sinai, because you yourself warned us, ‘Set a boundary around the mountain and keep it holy.’”
“Go down,” YHWH tells him, “and then come back up, and bring Aaron with you. But don’t let the priests and the people force their way through to come up to YHWH, or he will break out against them.”
So Moses goes down to the people and tells them.
The Ten Words · 20:1
And God speaks all these words:
The Prologue · 20:2
“I am YHWH your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery.
The First Word · 20:3
You must have no other gods before my face.
The Second Word · 20:4–6

You must not make yourself a carved image, or a likeness of anything in the sky above or on the earth below or in the waters under the earth. You must not bow down to them or serve them, because I, YHWH your God, am a jealous God. I bring the guilt of the fathers down on the children, to the third and fourth generation of those who hate me, but I show steadfast love to thousands, to those who love me and keep my commands.
The Third Word · 20:7
You must not carry the name of YHWH your God as an empty thing, because YHWH will not let anyone go unpunished who carries his name emptily.
The Fourth Word · 20:8–11

Remember the Sabbath day, to keep it holy. Six days you are to work and do all your work, but the seventh day is a Sabbath to YHWH your God. On it you must not do any work, not you, or your son or daughter, or your male or female servant, or your livestock, or the foreigner living within your gates. For in six days YHWH made the heavens and the earth, the sea, and everything in them, and on the seventh day he rested. That is why YHWH blessed the Sabbath day and made it holy.
The Fifth Word · 20:12
Honor your father and your mother, so that you may live long on the land YHWH your God gives you.
The Sixth Word · 20:13
You must not murder.
The Seventh Word · 20:14
You must not commit adultery.
The Eighth Word · 20:15
You must not steal.
The Ninth Word · 20:16
You must not give false testimony against your neighbor.
The Tenth Word · 20:17
You must not crave your neighbor’s house. You must not crave your neighbor’s wife, or his male or female servant, or his ox or his donkey, or anything that belongs to your neighbor.”
The People’s Fear · 20:18–21

All the people see the thunder and the lightning, and hear the blast of the ram’s horn, and see the mountain smoking. And when the people see it, they shake with fear and keep their distance. “You speak to us,” they say to Moses, “and we will listen. But don’t let God speak to us, or it will be the death of us!”

“Don’t be afraid,” Moses tells the people. “God has come to test you, so that the fear of him will stay with you and keep you from sinning.” So the people keep their distance, while Moses goes near the thick darkness where God is.
The Altar Law · 20:22–26

Then YHWH says to Moses, “This is what you are to tell the people of Israel: ‘You have seen for yourselves that I have spoken with you from the heavens. Don’t make any gods of silver or gold to stand alongside me. Don’t make them for yourselves. Make an altar of earth for me, and sacrifice on it your burnt offerings and your peace offerings, your sheep and your cattle. Wherever I cause my name to be remembered, I will come to you and bless you. If you make me an altar of stone, don’t build it with cut stones, because if you use a chisel on it, you will defile it. And don’t go up to my altar by steps, so that your nakedness isn’t exposed on it.’”
The Covenant Code Begins · 21:1–6
“These are the rulings you are to set before them.

If you buy a Hebrew slave, he is to serve six years, and in the seventh he goes free, without paying anything. If he came in single, he goes out single. If he had a wife, his wife goes out with him. If his master gives him a wife and she bears him sons or daughters, the wife and her children belong to her master, and he goes out alone. But if the slave declares, ‘I love my master, my wife, and my children. I don’t want to go free,’ then his master is to bring him before God. He is to bring him to the door or the doorpost and pierce his ear with an awl, and he will serve him for life.
Laws on Personal Injury · 21:7–36

If a man sells his daughter as a servant, she does not go free the way the male slaves do. If she doesn’t please the master who chose her for himself, he must let her be bought back. He has no right to sell her to foreigners, because he has broken faith with her. If he chooses her for his son, he must treat her as a daughter. If he takes another wife for himself, he must not cut back on her food, her clothing, or her rights as a wife. If he doesn’t provide her these three things, she may go free, without paying any money.

Whoever strikes someone a deadly blow must be put to death. But if he didn’t lie in wait for him, and God let it happen, I will appoint a place where he can flee. But if someone schemes and kills his neighbor on purpose, take him even from my altar to be put to death.
Whoever strikes his father or his mother must be put to death.
Whoever kidnaps someone, whether he has sold him or is still holding him, must be put to death.
Whoever curses his father or his mother must be put to death.

If men quarrel and one strikes the other with a stone or his fist, and he doesn’t die but is laid up in bed, and if he gets up again and walks around outside with his staff, then the one who struck him will not be punished. He must only pay for the time he lost and see that he is fully healed.

If a man strikes his male or female slave with a rod and the slave dies under his hand, he must be punished. But if the slave gets up after a day or two, he is not to be punished, since the slave is his property.

If men are fighting and hit a pregnant woman so that her child comes out, but there is no further harm, the one responsible must be fined whatever the woman’s husband demands and the judges allow. But if there is harm, then you are to give life for life, eye for eye, tooth for tooth, hand for hand, foot for foot, burn for burn, wound for wound, bruise for bruise.

If a man strikes his male or female slave in the eye and destroys it, he must let the slave go free because of the eye. If he knocks out the tooth of his male or female slave, he must let the slave go free because of the tooth.

If an ox gores a man or a woman to death, the ox must be stoned, and its meat must not be eaten. But the owner of the ox is not liable. But if the ox has had a habit of goring, and its owner has been warned but has not kept it penned up, and it kills a man or a woman, the ox must be stoned, and its owner must also be put to death. If a ransom is set for him instead, he must pay whatever is demanded to redeem his life. If the ox gores a son or a daughter, the same ruling applies. If the ox gores a male or female slave, the owner must pay thirty shekels of silver to their master, and the ox must be stoned.
If a man leaves a pit open, or digs a pit and doesn’t cover it, and an ox or a donkey falls into it, the owner of the pit must make it good. He must pay its owner, and the dead animal is his.

If one man’s ox injures another man’s ox and it dies, they are to sell the live ox and split the money, and split the dead animal too. But if it was known that the ox had a habit of goring, and its owner didn’t keep it penned up, he must pay ox for ox, and the dead animal is his.”
Theft and Restitution · 22:1–15

“If a man steals an ox or a sheep and slaughters it or sells it, he must pay back five oxen for the ox and four sheep for the sheep. If a thief is caught breaking in at night and is struck and dies, there is no bloodguilt for the one who struck him. But if it happens after sunrise, there is bloodguilt. A thief must make full restitution. If he has nothing, he must be sold to pay for what he stole. If the stolen animal is found alive in his possession, whether ox or donkey or sheep, he must pay back double.
If a man lets his animal graze in a field or vineyard, and it strays and grazes in someone else’s field, he must make it good from the best of his own field and the best of his own vineyard.
If a fire breaks out and spreads into thornbushes, and stacked grain or standing grain or a whole field is burned up, the one who started the fire must make it good.

If a man gives his neighbor silver or goods to keep safe, and they are stolen from that man’s house, the thief, if he is caught, must pay back double. If the thief isn’t caught, the owner of the house must come before God to settle whether he laid his own hand on his neighbor’s property. In every case of disputed property, whether ox, donkey, sheep, clothing, or anything lost, where someone says, ‘This is mine,’ both parties are to bring their case before God. The one God declares guilty must pay back double to his neighbor.

If a man gives his neighbor a donkey, an ox, a sheep, or any animal to keep, and it dies or is injured or is carried off while no one is looking, an oath before YHWH will settle it between them, that he did not lay his hand on his neighbor’s property. The owner must accept it, and no restitution is owed. But if it was actually stolen from him, he must make it good to the owner. If it was torn apart by a wild animal, let him bring the remains as evidence. He does not have to make good what was torn.

If a man borrows an animal from his neighbor, and it is injured or dies while the owner isn’t there, he must make it good. If the owner was there, he does not have to make it good. If it was hired, the hiring fee covers the loss.
