But his wife says to him, “If YHWH were pleased to kill us, he wouldn’t have received a burnt offering and a meal offering at our hand, and he wouldn’t have shown us all these things, nor would he have told us such things as these at this time.”
The Boy Grows · 13:24–25
The woman bears a son, and names him Samson. The child grows, and YHWH blesses him. YHWH’s Spirit begins to move him in Mahaneh Dan, between Zorah and Eshtaol.
The Woman at Timnah · 14:1–4

Samson goes down to Timnah, and sees a woman in Timnah of the daughters of the Philistines. He comes up, and tells his father and his mother, and says, “I have seen a woman in Timnah of the daughters of the Philistines. Now therefore get her for me as my wife.”
Then his father and his mother say to him, “Isn’t there a woman among your brothers’ daughters, or among all my people, that you go to take a wife of the uncircumcised Philistines?”
Samson says to his father, “Get her for me, for she pleases me well.”
But his father and his mother don’t know that it is of YHWH; for he seeks an occasion against the Philistines. Now at that time the Philistines rules over Israel.
The Lion and the Honey · 14:5–9

Then goes Samson down with his father and his mother to Timnah, and comes to the vineyards of Timnah; and look, a young lion roared against him. YHWH’s Spirit comes mightily on him, and he tears him as he would have torn a young goat; and he has nothing in his hand, but he doesn’t tell his father or his mother what he has done. He goes down, and talks with the woman, and she pleases Samson well. After a while he returns to take her; and he goes over to see the carcass of the lion; and look, there is a swarm of bees in the body of the lion, and honey. He takes it into his hands, and goes on, eating as he goes. He comes to his father and mother, and gives to them, and they eat, but he doesn’t tell them that he has taken the honey out of the lion’s body.
The Riddle · 14:10–14
His father goes down to the woman; and Samson makes a feast there, for the young men used to do so. When they see him, they bring thirty companions to be with him.

Samson says to them, “Let me tell you a riddle now. If you can declare it to me within the seven days of the feast, and find it out, then I will give you thirty linen garments and thirty changes of clothing; but if you can’t declare it to me, then you will give me thirty linen garments and thirty changes of clothing.”
They say to him, “Tell us your riddle, that we may hear it.” He says to them,
“Out of the eater came out food.
Out of the strong came out sweetness.”
They can’t in three days declare the riddle.
The Pressure on His Wife · 14:15–17

On the seventh day, they say to Samson’s wife, “Entice your husband, that he may declare to us the riddle, lest we burn you and your father’s house with fire. Have you called us to impoverish us? Isn’t that so?”
Samson’s wife weeps before him, and says, “You just hate me, and don’t love me. You’ve told a riddle to the children of my people, and haven’t told it to me.”
He says to her, “Look, I haven’t told my father or my mother, so why should I tell you?”
She weeps before him the seven days, while their feast lasts; and on the seventh day, he tells her, because she presses him severely; and she tells the riddle to the children of her people.
The Answer · 14:18–20
The men of the city say to him on the seventh day before the sun goes down, “What is sweeter than honey? What is stronger than a lion?”
He says to them,
“If you hadn’t plowed with my heifer,
you wouldn’t have found out my riddle.”

YHWH’s Spirit comes mightily on him, and he goes down to Ashkelon, and strikes thirty men of them, and takes their plunder, then gives the changes of clothing to those who declare the riddle. His anger burns, and he goes up to his father’s house. But Samson’s wife is given to his companion who has been his friend.
The Foxes · 15:1–5
But after a while, in the time of wheat harvest, Samson visits his wife with a young goat. He says, “I will go in to my wife’s room.”

But her father wouldn’t allow him to go in. Her father says, “I most certainly thought that you utterly hated her; therefore I gave her to your companion. Isn’t her younger sister more beautiful than she? Please take her, instead.”

Samson says to them, “This time I will be blameless in the case of the Philistines, when I harm them.” Samson goes and catches three hundred foxes, and takes torches, and turns tail to tail, and puts a torch in the middle between every two tails. When he has set the torches on fire, he lets them go into the standing grain of the Philistines, and burns up both the shocks and the standing grain, and also the olive groves.
Hip and Thigh · 15:6–8
Then the Philistines says, “Who has done this?”
They say, “Samson, the son-in-law of the Timnite, because he has taken his wife, and given her to his companion.” The Philistines comes up, and burns her and her father with fire.

Samson says to them, “If you behave like this, surely I will take revenge on you, and after that I will cease.” He strikes them hip and thigh with a great slaughter; and he goes down and lives in the cave in Etam’s rock.
Bound and Brought Out · 15:9–13
Then the Philistines goes up, encamps in Judah, and spreads themselves in Lehi.
The men of Judah say, “Why have you come up against us?”
They say, “We have come up to bind Samson, to do to him as he has done to us.”
Then three thousand men of Judah go down to the cave in Etam’s rock, and say to Samson, “Don’t you know that the Philistines are rulers over us? What then is this that you have done to us?”
He says to them, “As they did to me, so I have done to them.”
They say to him, “We have come down to bind you, that we may deliver you into the hand of the Philistines.”
Samson says to them, “Swear to me that you will not attack me yourselves.”
They speak to him, saying, “No; but we will bind you securely, and deliver you into their hands; but surely we will not kill you.” They bind him with two new ropes, and bring him up from the rock.
The Jawbone · 15:14–17

When he comes to Lehi, the Philistines shouts as they meet him. Then YHWH’s Spirit comes mightily on him, and the ropes that are on his arms become as flax that are burned with fire, and his bands drop from off his hands. He finds a fresh jawbone of a donkey, puts out his hand, takes it, and strikes a thousand men with it. Samson says, “With the jawbone of a donkey, heaps on heaps; with the jawbone of a donkey I have struck a thousand men.” When he has finished speaking, he throws the jawbone out of his hand; and that place is called Ramath Lehi.
The Spring at Lehi · 15:18–20
He is very thirsty, and calls on YHWH, and says, “You have given this great deliverance by the hand of your servant; and now should I die of thirst, and fall into the hands of the uncircumcised?”

But God splits the hollow place that is in Lehi, and water comes out of it. When he has drunk, his spirit comes again, and he revives. Therefore its name is called En Hakkore, which is in Lehi, to this day. He judges Israel twenty years in the days of the Philistines.
The Gates of Gaza · 16:1–3

Samson goes to Gaza, and sees there a prostitute, and goes in to her. The Gazites are told, “Samson is here!” They surround him, and lay wait for him all night in the gate of the city, and are quiet all the night, saying, “Wait until morning light, then we will kill him.” Samson lies until midnight, and arises at midnight, and lays hold of the doors of the gate of the city, and the two posts, and plucks them up, bar and all, and puts them on his shoulders, and carries them up to the top of the mountain that is before Hebron.
Delilah · 16:4–14

It comes to pass afterward, that he loves a woman in the valley of Sorek, whose name is Delilah. The lords of the Philistines come up to her, and say to her, “Entice him, and see in which his great strength lies, and by what means we may prevail against him, that we may bind him to afflict him; and we will each give you eleven hundred pieces of silver.”
Delilah says to Samson, “Please tell me where your great strength lies, and what you might be bound to afflict you.”
Samson says to her, “If they bind me with seven green cords that were never dried, then should I become weak, and be as another man.”

Then the lords of the Philistines bring up to her seven green cords which have not been dried, and she binds him with them. Now she has an ambush waiting in the inner room. She says to him, “The Philistines are on you, Samson!” He breaks the cords, as a string of tow is broken when it touches the fire. So his strength is not known.
Delilah says to Samson, “Look, you have mocked me, and told me lies: now please tell me with which you might be bound.”
He says to her, “If they only bind me with new ropes with which no work has been done, then should I become weak, and be as another man.”
So Delilah takes new ropes, and binds him therewith, and says to him, “The Philistines are on you, Samson!” The ambush is waiting in the inner room. He breaks them off his arms like a thread.
Delilah says to Samson, “Until now, you have mocked me and told me lies. Tell me with what you might be bound.”
He says to her, “If you weave the seven locks of my head with the web.”
She fastens it with the pin, and says to him, “The Philistines are on you, Samson!” He awakens out of his sleep, and plucks away the pin of the beam, and the web.
The Telling · 16:15–20
She says to him, “How can you say, ‘I love you,’ when your heart is not with me? You have mocked me these three times, and have not told me where your great strength lies.”

When she presses him daily with her words, and urges him, his soul is troubled to death. He tells her all his heart, and says to her, “No razor has ever come on my head; for I have been a Nazirite to God from my mother’s womb. If I am shaved, then my strength will go from me, and I will become weak, and be like any other man.”

When Delilah sees that he has told her all his heart, she sends and calls for the lords of the Philistines, saying, “Come up this once, for he has told me all his heart.” Then the lords of the Philistines come up to her, and bring the money in their hand. She makes him sleep on her knees; and she calls for a man, and shaves off the seven locks of his head; and she begins to afflict him, and his strength goes from him. She says, “The Philistines are upon you, Samson!”
He awakes out of his sleep, and says, “I will go out as at other times, and shake myself free.” But he doesn’t know that YHWH has departed from him.
Bound and Blinded · 16:21–22

The Philistines lays hold on him, and puts out his eyes; and they bring him down to Gaza, and bind him with fetters of brass; and he grinds at the mill in the prison. However the hair of his head begins to grow again after he is shaved.
The House of Dagon · 16:23–27

The lords of the Philistines gather them together to offer a great sacrifice to Dagon their god, and to rejoice; for they say, “Our god has delivered Samson our enemy into our hand.” When the people see him, they praise their god; for they say, “Our god has delivered our enemy and the destroyer of our country, who has slain many of us, into our hand.”

When their hearts are merry, they say, “Call for Samson, that he may entertain us.” They call for Samson out of the prison; and he performs before them. They set him between the pillars; and Samson says to the boy who holds him by the hand, “Allow me to feel the pillars whereupon the house rests, that I may lean on them.”
Now the house is full of men and women; and all the lords of the Philistines are there; and there are on the roof about three thousand men and women, who see while Samson performs.
The Last Prayer · 16:28–31

Samson calls to YHWH, and says, “Lord YHWH, remember me, please, and strengthen me, please, only this once, God, that I may be at once avenged of the Philistines for my two eyes.” Samson takes hold of the two middle pillars on which the house rests, and leans on them, the one with his right hand, and the other with his left. Samson says, “Let me die with the Philistines!” He bows himself with all his might; and the house falls on the lords, and on all the people who are therein. So the dead that he kills at his death are more than those who he kills in his life. Then his brothers and all the house of his father come down, and take him, and bring him up, and bury him between Zorah and Eshtaol in the burial site of Manoah his father. He judges Israel twenty years.
The Silver and the Image · 17:1–6

There is a man of the hill country of Ephraim, whose name is Micah. He says to his mother, “The eleven hundred pieces of silver that were taken from you, about which you uttered a curse, and also spoke it in my ears, look, the silver is with me. I took it.”
His mother says, “May YHWH bless my son!”

He restores the eleven hundred pieces of silver to his mother, then his mother says, “I most certainly dedicate the silver to YHWH from my hand for my son, to make a carved image and a molten image. Now therefore I will restore it to you.”

When he restores the money to his mother, his mother takes two hundred pieces of silver, and gives them to a silversmith, who makes a carved image and a molten image out of it. It is in the house of Micah.

The man Micah has a house of gods, and he makes an ephod, and teraphim, and consecrates one of his sons, who become his priest. In those days there is no king in Israel. Everyone does that which is right in his own eyes.
The Wandering Levite · 17:7–13

There is a young man out of Bethlehem Judah, of the family of Judah, who is a Levite; and he lives there. The man departs out of the city, out of Bethlehem Judah, to live where he can find a place, and he comes to the hill country of Ephraim, to the house of Micah, as he travels. Micah says to him, “Where did you come from?”

He says to him, “I am a Levite of Bethlehem Judah, and I am looking for a place to live.” Micah says to him, “Dwell with me, and be to me a father and a priest, and I will give you ten pieces of silver per year, a suit of clothing, and your food.” So the Levite goes in. The Levite is content to dwell with the man; and the young man is to him as one of his sons. Micah consecrates the Levite, and the young man becomes his priest, and is in the house of Micah. Then Micah says, “Now know I that YHWH will do good to me, since I have a Levite as my priest.”
The Danites Spy Out the Land · 18:1–10

In those days there is no king in Israel. In those days the tribe of the Danites seeks an inheritance to dwell in; for to that day, their inheritance has not fallen to them among the tribes of Israel. The children of Dan send five men of their family from their whole number, men of valor, from Zorah, and from Eshtaol, to spy out the land, and to search it. They say to them, “Go, explore the land!”

They come to the hill country of Ephraim, to the house of Micah, and lodge there. When they are by the house of Micah, they know the voice of the young man the Levite; so they go over there, and say to him, “Who brought you here? What do you do in this place? What do you have here?”
He says to them, “Thus and thus has Micah dealt with me, and he has hired me, and I am become his priest.”
They say to him, “Please ask counsel of God, that we may know whether our way which we go will be prosperous.”
The priest says to them, “Go in peace. Your way in which you go is before YHWH.”

Then the five men depart, and come to Laish, and see the people who are there, how they live in safety, in the way of the Sidonians, quiet and secure; for there is no one in the land, possessing authority, that might put them to shame in anything, and they are far from the Sidonians, and have no dealings with anyone else. They come to their brothers at Zorah and Eshtaol; and their brothers ask them, “What do you say?”

They say, “Arise, and let us go up against them; for we have seen the land, and look, it is very good. Do you stand still? Don’t be slothful to go and to enter in to possess the land. When you go, you will come to an unsuspecting people, and the land is large; for God has given it into your hand, a place where there is no lack of anything that is in the earth.”
Six Hundred Set Out · 18:11–13

The family of the Danites set out from Zorah and Eshtaol, with six hundred men armed with weapons of war. They go up and encamp in Kiriath Jearim, in Judah. Therefore they call that place Mahaneh Dan, to this day. Look, it is behind Kiriath Jearim. They pass from there to the hill country of Ephraim, and come to the house of Micah.
They Take Micah’s Gods and Priest · 18:14–20

Then the five men who go to spy out the country of Laish answer, and say to their brothers, “Do you know that there is in these houses an ephod, and teraphim, and a carved image, and a molten image? Now therefore consider what you have to do.” They go over there, and come to the house of the young Levite man, even to the house of Micah, and ask him how he is doing. The six hundred men armed with their weapons of war, who are of the children of Dan, stand by the entrance of the gate. The five men who go to spy out the land go up, and come in there, and take the engraved image, the ephod, the teraphim, and the molten image; and the priest stands by the entrance of the gate with the six hundred men armed with weapons of war.
When these go into Micah’s house, and take the engraved image, the ephod, the teraphim, and the molten image, the priest says to them, “What are you doing?”

They say to him, “Hold your peace, put your hand on your mouth, and go with us, and be to us a father and a priest. Is it better for you to be priest to the house of one man, or to be priest to a tribe and a family in Israel?”
The priest’s heart is glad, and he takes the ephod, the teraphim, and the engraved image, and goes with the people.
Micah Pursues · 18:21–26

So they turn and depart, and put the little ones, the livestock, and the goods before them. When they are a good way from the house of Micah, the men who are in the houses near Micah’s house gather together and overtook the children of Dan. As they cry to the children of Dan, they turn their faces, and say to Micah, “What ails you, that you come with such a company?”
He says, “You have taken away my gods which I made, and the priest, and have gone away! What more do I have? How can you ask me, ‘What ails you?’”
The children of Dan say to him, “Don’t let your voice be heard among us, lest angry fellows fall on you, and you lose your life, with the lives of your household.”
The children of Dan go their way; and when Micah sees that they are too strong for him, he turns and goes back to his house.
The Sack of Laish · 18:27–31

They take that which Micah has made, and the priest whom he has, and come to Laish, to a people quiet and unsuspecting, and strike them with the edge of the sword; then they burn the city with fire. There is no deliverer, because it is far from Sidon, and they have no dealings with anyone else; and it is in the valley that lies by Beth Rehob. They build the city, and live in it. They call the name of the city Dan, after the name of Dan their father, who is born to Israel; however the name of the city used to be Laish. The children of Dan set up for themselves the engraved image; and Jonathan, the son of Gershom, the son of Moses, and his sons are priests to the tribe of the Danites until the day of the captivity of the land. So they set up for themselves Micah’s engraved image which he makes, and it remains all the time that God’s house is in Shiloh.
A Levite and His Concubine · 19:1–9

In those days, when there is no king in Israel, there is a certain Levite living on the farther side of the hill country of Ephraim, who takes for himself a concubine out of Bethlehem Judah. His concubine plays the prostitute against him, and goes away from him to her father’s house to Bethlehem Judah, and is there for four months. Her husband arises, and goes after her, to speak kindly to her, to bring her again, having his servant with him, and a couple of donkeys. She brings him into her father’s house; and when the father of the young lady sees him, he rejoices to meet him. His father-in-law, the young lady’s father, keeps him there; and he stays with him three days. So they eat and drank, and stay there.

On the fourth day, they get up early in the morning, and he rises up to depart. The young lady’s father says to his son-in-law, “Strengthen your heart with a morsel of bread, and afterward you will go your way.” So they sit down, ate, and drank, both of them together. Then the young lady’s father says to the man, “Please be pleased to stay all night, and let your heart be merry.” The man rises up to depart; but his father-in-law urges him, and he stays there again. He arises early in the morning on the fifth day to depart; and the young lady’s father says, “Please strengthen your heart and stay until the day declines”; and they both eat.

When the man rises up to depart, he, and his concubine, and his servant, his father-in-law, the young lady’s father, says to him, “Look, now the day draws toward evening, please stay all night. Look, the day is ending. Stay here, that your heart may be merry; and tomorrow go on your way early, that you may go home.”
They Reach Gibeah · 19:10–15
But the man wouldn’t stay that night, but he rises up and departed, and toward Jebus (also called Jerusalem). With him are a couple of saddled donkeys. His concubine also is with him.
When they are by Jebus, the day is far spent; and the servant says to his master, “Please come and let us enter into this city of the Jebusites, and stay in it.”

His master says to him, “We won’t enter into the city of a foreigner that is not of the children of Israel; but we will pass over to Gibeah.” He says to his servant, “Come and let us draw near to one of these places; and we will lodge in Gibeah, or in Ramah.” So they pass on and go their way; and the sun goes down on them near Gibeah, which belongs to Benjamin. They go over there, to go in to stay in Gibeah. He goes in, and sits down in the street of the city; for there is no one who takes them into his house to stay.
An Old Man Takes Them in · 19:16–21

Look, an old man comes from his work out of the field at evening. Now the man is from the hill country of Ephraim, and he lives in Gibeah; but the men of the place are Benjamites. He lifts up his eyes, and sees the wayfaring man in the street of the city; and the old man says, “Where are you going? Where did you come from?”

He says to him, “We are passing from Bethlehem Judah to the farther side of the hill country of Ephraim. I am from there, and I went to Bethlehem Judah. I am going to YHWH’s house; and there is no one who has taken me into his house. Yet there is both straw and feed for our donkeys; and there is bread and wine also for me, and for your servant, and for the young man who is with your servants. There is no lack of anything.”

The old man says, “Peace be to you; how ever let me supply all your needs. Just don’t sleep in the street.” So he brings him into his house, and gives the donkeys fodder. Then they wash their feet, and eat and drank.
The Outrage at Gibeah · 19:22–26

As they are making their hearts merry, look, the men of the city, certain wicked fellows, surround the house, beating at the door; and they speak to the master of the house, the old man, saying, “Bring out the man who came into your house, that we can have sex with him!”

The man, the master of the house, goes out to them, and says to them, “No, my brothers, please don’t act so wickedly; since this man has come into my house, don’t do this folly. Look, here is my virgin daughter and his concubine. I will bring them out now. Humble them, and do with them what seems good to you; but to this man don’t do any such folly.”

But the men wouldn’t listen to him: so the man lays hold of his concubine, and brings her out to them; and they have sex with her, and abuse her all night until the morning. When the day begins to dawn, they let her go. Then the woman comes in the dawning of the day, and falls down at the door of the man’s house where her lord is, until it is light.
The Knife and the Twelve Pieces · 19:27–30

Her lord rises up in the morning, and opens the doors of the house, and goes out to go his way; and look, the woman his concubine has fallen down at the door of the house, with her hands on the threshold.
He says to her, “Get up, and let us be going!” but no one answers. Then he takes her up on the donkey; and the man rises up, and goes to his place.

When he has come into his house, he takes a knife, and cuts up his concubine, and divides her, limb by limb, into twelve pieces, and sends her throughout all the borders of Israel. It is so, that all who see it says, “Such a deed has not been done or seen from the day that the children of Israel came up out of the land of Egypt to this day! Consider it, take counsel, and speak.”
All Israel as One Man · 20:1–7

Then all the children of Israel go out, and the congregation is assembled as one man, from Dan even to Beersheba, with the land of Gilead, to YHWH at Mizpah. The chiefs of all the people, even of all the tribes of Israel, present themselves in the assembly of the people of God, four hundred thousand footmen who draw sword. (Now the children of Benjamin hear that the children of Israel have gone up to Mizpah.) The children of Israel say, “Tell us, how did this wickedness happen?”

The Levite, the husband of the woman who is murdered, answers, “I came into Gibeah that belongs to Benjamin, I and my concubine, to spend the night. The men of Gibeah rose against me, and surrounded the house by night. They intended to kill me, and they raped my concubine, and she is dead. I took my concubine, and cut her in pieces, and sent her throughout all the country of the inheritance of Israel; for they have committed lewdness and folly in Israel. Look, you children of Israel, all of you, give here your advice and counsel.”
Israel Resolves to Punish Gibeah · 20:8–11

All the people arise as one man, saying, “None of us will go to his tent, neither will any of us turn to his house. But now this is the thing which we will do to Gibeah: we will go up against it by lot; and we will take ten men of one hundred throughout all the tribes of Israel, and one hundred of one thousand, and a thousand out of ten thousand, to get food for the people, that they may do, when they come to Gibeah of Benjamin, according to all the folly that they have worked in Israel.” So all the men of Israel are gathered against the city, knit together as one man.
Benjamin Refuses to Surrender the Men · 20:12–17

The tribes of Israel send men through all the tribe of Benjamin, saying, “What wickedness is this that has happened among you? Now therefore deliver up the men, the wicked fellows, who are in Gibeah, that we may put them to death, and put away evil from Israel.”

But Benjamin would not listen to the voice of their brothers the children of Israel. The children of Benjamin gather themselves together out of the cities to Gibeah, to go out to battle against the children of Israel. The children of Benjamin are counted on that day out of the cities twenty-six thousand men who draw the sword, besides the inhabitants of Gibeah, who are counted seven hundred chosen men. Among all these soldiers there are seven hundred chosen men who are left-handed. Every one of them can sling a stone at a hair and not miss. The men of Israel, besides Benjamin, are counted four hundred thousand men who draw sword. All these are men of war.
Two Defeats · 20:18–25
The children of Israel arise, go up to Bethel, and ask counsel of God. They ask, “Who will go up for us first to battle against the children of Benjamin?”
YHWH says, “Judah first.”

The children of Israel rise up in the morning, and encamp against Gibeah. The men of Israel go out to battle against Benjamin; and the men of Israel set the battle in array against them at Gibeah. The children of Benjamin come out of Gibeah, and on that day destroy twenty-two thousand of the Israelite men down to the ground. The people, the men of Israel, encourage themselves, and set the battle again in array in the place where they set themselves in array the first day. The children of Israel go up and weep before YHWH until evening; and they ask of YHWH, saying, “Should I again draw near to battle against the children of Benjamin my brother?”
YHWH says, “Go up against him.”

The children of Israel come near against the children of Benjamin the second day. Benjamin goes out against them out of Gibeah the second day, and destroys down to the ground of the children of Israel again eighteen thousand men. All these draw the sword.
Weeping at Bethel · 20:26–28

Then all the children of Israel, and all the people, go up, and come to Bethel, and weep, and sit there before YHWH, and fast that day until evening; then they offer burnt offerings and peace offerings before YHWH. The children of Israel ask YHWH (for the ark of the covenant of God are there in those days, and Phinehas, the son of Eleazar, the son of Aaron, stands before it in those days), saying, “Should I yet again go out to battle against the children of Benjamin my brother, or should I cease?”
YHWH says, “Go up; for tomorrow I will deliver him into your hand.”
The Ambush · 20:29–43

Israel sets ambushes all around Gibeah. The children of Israel go up against the children of Benjamin on the third day, and set themselves in array against Gibeah, as at other times. The children of Benjamin go out against the people, and are drawn away from the city; and they begin to strike and kill of the people, as at other times, in the highways, of which one goes up to Bethel, and the other to Gibeah, in the field, about thirty men of Israel.
The children of Benjamin say, “They are struck down before us, as at the first.” But the children of Israel say, “Let us flee, and draw them away from the city to the highways.”

All the men of Israel rise up out of their place, and set themselves in array at Baal Tamar. Then the ambushers of Israel break out of their place, even out of Maareh Geba. Ten thousand chosen men out of all Israel come over against Gibeah, and the battle is severe; but they don’t know that disaster is close to them. YHWH strikes Benjamin before Israel; and the children of Israel destroyed of Benjamin that day twenty-five thousand one hundred men. All these draw the sword. So the children of Benjamin see that they are struck; for the men of Israel yield to Benjamin, because they trust the ambushers whom they have set against Gibeah. The ambushers hurry, and rush on Gibeah; then the ambushers spread out, and strike all the city with the edge of the sword. Now the appointed sign between the men of Israel and the ambushers is that they should make a great cloud of smoke rise up out of the city. The men of Israel turn in the battle, and Benjamin begins to strike and kill of the men of Israel about thirty persons; for they say, “Surely they are struck down before us, as in the first battle.” But when the cloud begins to arise up out of the city in a pillar of smoke, the Benjamites look behind them; and look, the whole city goes up in smoke to the sky. The men of Israel turn, and the men of Benjamin are dismayed; for they see that disaster has come on them. Therefore they turn their backs before the men of Israel to the way of the wilderness; but the battle follows hard after them; and those who come out of the cities destroy them in the middle of it. They surround the Benjamites, chase them, and trod them down at their resting place, as far as near Gibeah toward the sunrise.
The Six Hundred at Rimmon · 20:44–48

Eighteen thousand men of Benjamin fall; all these are men of valor. They turn and flee toward the wilderness to the rock of Rimmon; and they glean five thousand men of them in the highways, and follow hard after them to Gidom, and strike two thousand men of them. So that all who fall that day of Benjamin are twenty-five thousand men who draw the sword. All these are men of valor. But six hundred men turn and flee toward the wilderness to the rock of Rimmon, and stay in the rock of Rimmon four months. The men of Israel turn again on the children of Benjamin, and strike them with the edge of the sword, both the entire city, and the livestock, and all that they find. Moreover all the cities which they find they set on fire.
The Oath at Mizpah · 21:1–7

Now the men of Israel have sworn in Mizpah, saying, “None of us will give his daughter to Benjamin as a wife.” The people come to Bethel, and sit there until evening before God, and lift up their voices, and weep severely. They say, “YHWH, the God of Israel, why has this happened in Israel, that there should be one tribe lacking in Israel today?”

On the next day, the people rise early, and build an altar there, and offer burnt offerings and peace offerings. The children of Israel say, “Who is there among all the tribes of Israel who didn’t come up in the assembly to YHWH?” For they have made a great oath concerning him who doesn’t come up to YHWH to Mizpah, saying, “He will surely be put to death.” The children of Israel grieve for Benjamin their brother, and say, “There is one tribe cut off from Israel today. How should we provide wives for those who remain, since we have sworn by YHWH that we will not give them of our daughters to wives?”
Jabesh-gilead · 21:8–14

They say, “What one is there of the tribes of Israel who didn’t come up to YHWH to Mizpah?” Look, no one comes from Jabesh Gilead to the camp to the assembly. For when the people are counted, look, there are none of the inhabitants of Jabesh Gilead there. The congregation sends twelve thousand of the most valiant men there, and commands them, saying, “Go and strike the inhabitants of Jabesh Gilead with the edge of the sword, with the women and the little ones. This is the thing that you will do: you will utterly destroy every male, and every woman who has lain with a man.” They find among the inhabitants of Jabesh Gilead four hundred young virgins, who have not known man by lying with him; and they bring them to the camp to Shiloh, which is in the land of Canaan.

The whole congregation sends and speaks to the children of Benjamin who are in the rock of Rimmon, and proclaims peace to them. Benjamin returns at that time; and they give them the women whom they have saved alive of the women of Jabesh Gilead. There still aren’t enough for them.
The Dancers of Shiloh · 21:15–23

The people grieve for Benjamin, because YHWH has made a breach in the tribes of Israel. Then the elders of the congregation say, “How should we provide wives for those who remain, since the women are destroyed out of Benjamin?” They say, “There must be an inheritance for those who are escaped of Benjamin, that a tribe not be blotted out from Israel. However we may not give them wives of our daughters, for the children of Israel had sworn, saying, ‘Cursed is he who gives a wife to Benjamin.’” They say, “Look, there is a feast of YHWH from year to year in Shiloh, which is on the north of Bethel, on the east side of the highway that goes up from Bethel to Shechem, and on the south of Lebonah.” They command the children of Benjamin, saying, “Go and lie in wait in the vineyards, and see, and look, if the daughters of Shiloh come out to dance in the dances, then come out of the vineyards, and each man catch his wife of the daughters of Shiloh, and go to the land of Benjamin. It will be, when their fathers or their brothers come to complain to us, that we will say to them, ‘Grant them graciously to us, because we didn’t take for each man his wife in battle, neither did you give them to them, otherwise you would now be guilty.’”

The children of Benjamin do so, and take wives for themselves, according to their number, of those who dance, whom they carry off. They go and return to their inheritance, build the cities, and live in them.
The Last Line · 21:24–25

The children of Israel depart from there at that time, every man to his tribe and to his family, and they each go out from there to his own inheritance. In those days there is no king in Israel. Everyone does that which is right in his own eyes.
Famine, Loss, and the Road Home · 1:1–7

Back in the days when the judges rule, a famine strikes the land. So a man from Bethlehem in Judah sets out to live for a while in the country of Moab — he, his wife, and their two sons. The man's name is Elimelech, and his wife's name is Naomi. Their two sons are Mahlon and Chilion, Ephrathites from Bethlehem in Judah. They come into Moab and settle there.

Then Elimelech, Naomi's husband, dies, and she is left with her two sons. The sons marry Moabite women. One is named Orpah, and the other Ruth. They live there about ten years. Then Mahlon and Chilion die too, and Naomi is left alone, without her two boys and without her husband.

Then word reaches her in Moab that YHWH has taken notice of his people and given them bread again. So she gets up with her daughters-in-law to go back home. She leaves the place where she has been living, her two daughters-in-law with her, and they take the road back toward the land of Judah.
Naomi Urges Them to Return · 1:8–14

But Naomi says to her two daughters-in-law, “Go back. Each of you, go home to your mother's house. May YHWH show you steadfast love, as you have shown it to the dead and to me. May YHWH give each of you rest in the home of a new husband.” Then she kisses them goodbye, and they burst into tears. “No,” they tell her. “We are going back with you, to your people.”

But Naomi says, “Turn back, my daughters. Why come with me? Do I have more sons in my womb to become your husbands? Turn back, my daughters. Go on your way. I am too old to have a husband. Even if I said, ‘There is still hope for me’ — even if I had a husband tonight and bore sons — would you wait for them to grow up? Would you shut yourselves away and never marry? No, my daughters. This is far more bitter for me than for you, because the hand of YHWH has come out against me.”
Again they weep out loud. Then Orpah kisses her mother-in-law goodbye, but Ruth clings to her.
Ruth's Declaration · 1:15–18

“Look,” says Naomi, “your sister-in-law is going back to her people and her gods. Go back with her.” But Ruth says, “Don't press me to leave you, or to turn back from following you. Where you go, I will go. Where you spend the night, I will spend the night. Your people will be my people, and your God will be my God. Where you die, I will die, and there I will be buried. May YHWH deal with me, and worse, if anything but death comes between you and me.” When Naomi sees how set Ruth is on going with her, she says nothing more.
Arrival in Bethlehem · 1:19–22

So the two of them walk on until they come to Bethlehem. When they arrive, the whole town is buzzing about them. The women say, “Can this be Naomi?” “Don't call me Naomi,” she tells them. “Call me Mara — call me Bitter — because the Almighty has made my life very bitter. I went away full, and YHWH has brought me back empty. Why call me Naomi, Pleasant, when YHWH has testified against me and the Almighty has brought me harm?”
So Naomi comes home, and with her comes Ruth the Moabite, her daughter-in-law, back from the country of Moab. They arrive in Bethlehem just as the barley harvest is beginning.
Ruth Goes to Glean · 2:1–3

Now Naomi has a kinsman through her husband: Boaz, a strong and well-to-do man from Elimelech's family. Ruth the Moabite says to Naomi, “Let me go out to the fields. I'll gather the stray grain behind whoever is kind to me.” “Go, my daughter,” Naomi tells her. So Ruth goes out and gleans behind the reapers — and as luck would have it, she lands in the very strip of field that belongs to Boaz, from Elimelech's family.
Boaz Notices Ruth · 2:4–17

And look, here comes Boaz out from Bethlehem! “YHWH be with you!” he calls to the reapers. “YHWH bless you!” they call back. Boaz asks the young man in charge of the reapers, “Who does this young woman belong to?” The foreman answers, “She is the Moabite girl who came back with Naomi from the country of Moab. She asked, ‘Please let me glean and gather among the bundles behind the reapers.’ So she came, and she has been on her feet from morning until now, except for a short rest in the shelter.”

Then Boaz says to Ruth, “Listen, my daughter. Don't go glean in any other field. Don't leave this one. Stay right here with my young women. Keep your eyes on the field they are reaping and follow along behind them. I have told the young men not to lay a hand on you. And when you are thirsty, go to the jars and drink what the young men have drawn.” Ruth drops to the ground, face down, and says, “Why have I found such favor with you, that you would take notice of me, when I am only a stranger here?” Boaz answers, “I have heard everything — all you have done for your mother-in-law since your husband died. You left your father and your mother and the land where you were born, and you came to a people you had never known before. May YHWH repay what you have done. May you be paid in full by YHWH, the God of Israel, under whose wings you have come to find shelter.” “May I keep finding favor with you, my lord,” she says, “for you have comforted me and spoken to my heart, though I am not even one of your servant girls.”

At mealtime Boaz says to her, “Come over here. Have some bread, and dip your piece in the sour wine.” So she sits down beside the reapers, and he hands her roasted grain. She eats until she is full, and she has some left over. When she gets up to glean again, Boaz gives orders to his young men: “Let her glean even among the bundles, and don't shame her. And pull some stalks out of the bundles for her on purpose, and leave them for her to pick up. Don't scold her.”
So Ruth gleans in the field until evening. Then she beats out what she has gathered, and it comes to about an ephah of barley — more than half a bushel.
Ruth Returns to Naomi · 2:18–23

She picks it up and carries it into town, and her mother-in-law sees how much she has gleaned. Then Ruth brings out the food she saved after eating her fill and gives it to her. Her mother-in-law says, “Where did you glean today? Where did you work? Bless the man who took notice of you!” So Ruth tells her whose field she worked in. “The man I worked with today,” she says, “is named Boaz.” “May YHWH bless him!” Naomi says to her daughter-in-law. “His steadfast love has not let go of the living or the dead!” And Naomi tells her, “That man is close kin to us. He is one of our family redeemers.” Then Ruth the Moabite says, “He even told me, ‘Stay close to my young workers until they have finished my whole harvest.’” Naomi says to Ruth her daughter-in-law, “It is good, my daughter, for you to go out with his young women. In some other field you might be harmed.” So Ruth stays close to Boaz's young women and gleans until the barley harvest and the wheat harvest are finished. And she lives with her mother-in-law.
Naomi's Plan · 3:1–5

One day Naomi, her mother-in-law, says to her, “My daughter, isn't it time I looked for a place of rest for you, where life will go well for you? Now Boaz, whose young women you have been working with — isn't he our kinsman? Listen: tonight he is winnowing barley on the threshing floor. So wash, put on perfume, and dress in your best. Then go down to the threshing floor. But don't let the man know you are there until he has finished eating and drinking. When he lies down, mark the spot where he is lying. Then go in, uncover his feet, and lie down. He will tell you what to do.” “I will do everything you say,” Ruth answers.
At the Threshing Floor · 3:6–13

So she goes down to the threshing floor and does exactly what her mother-in-law told her. When Boaz has eaten and drunk and is in good spirits, he goes to lie down at the far end of the grain pile. Then she slips in quietly, uncovers his feet, and lies down.

In the middle of the night the man gives a start and rolls over — and look! There is a woman lying at his feet! “Who are you?” he says. “I am Ruth, your servant,” she answers. “Spread the wing of your cloak over your servant, for you are a family redeemer.” “YHWH bless you, my daughter!” he says. “This last act of steadfast love is even greater than the first. You have not gone running after young men, poor or rich. And now, my daughter, don't be afraid. I will do for you everything you ask. The whole town knows you are a woman of worth. It is true that I am a family redeemer. But there is another redeemer more closely related than I am. Stay here tonight. In the morning, if he will redeem you, good — let him redeem. But if he is not willing to redeem you, then as surely as YHWH lives, I will redeem you myself. Lie down until morning.”
Ruth Returns to Naomi · 3:14–18

So she lies at his feet until morning and gets up before it is light enough for anyone to recognize anyone, for he says, “No one must know that the woman came to the threshing floor.” Then he says, “Bring the shawl you are wearing and hold it out.” She holds it out, and he pours in six measures of barley and lifts it onto her. Then he goes into town.

When Ruth comes to her mother-in-law, Naomi asks, “How did it go, my daughter?” And Ruth tells her everything the man has done for her. “He gave me these six measures of barley,” she says, “because he told me, ‘Don't go back to your mother-in-law empty-handed.’” Naomi says, “Sit tight, my daughter, until you see how this turns out. That man will not rest until he has settled the matter today.”
The Gate · 4:1–12

Meanwhile Boaz goes up to the town gate and sits down there. And look, here comes the very redeemer Boaz spoke about! Boaz calls to him (the storyteller never tells us his name), “Come over here, friend, and sit down.” So he comes over and sits down. Then Boaz takes ten of the town's elders and says, “Sit down here,” and they sit. He says to the redeemer, “Naomi, who has come back from the country of Moab, is selling the plot of land that belonged to our brother Elimelech. I thought I should bring it to your attention and say, ‘Buy it, in front of these men sitting here and in front of the elders of my people.’ If you will redeem it, redeem it. If you won't, tell me, so I know. No one has the right to redeem it but you, and I am next in line after you.” “I will redeem it,” he says. Then Boaz says, “On the day you buy the field from Naomi, you also take on Ruth the Moabite, the dead man's widow, to keep the dead man's name alive on his inheritance.” At that the redeemer says, “Then I can't redeem it for myself, or I will ruin my own inheritance. You take my right of redemption. I can't redeem it.”

Now in those earlier days in Israel, this was how people settled a redemption or a trade: one man would pull off his sandal and hand it to the other. That was how a deal was made binding in Israel. So the redeemer says to Boaz, “Buy it yourself,” and he pulls off his sandal.

Then Boaz says to the elders and to all the people, “Today you are witnesses that I am buying from Naomi everything that belonged to Elimelech, Chilion, and Mahlon. And I am also taking Ruth the Moabite, Mahlon's widow, to be my wife, to keep the dead man's name alive on his inheritance, so that his name will not be cut off from among his relatives or from the gate of his hometown. Today you are witnesses!” Then all the people at the gate and the elders say, “We are witnesses! May YHWH make the woman who is coming into your home like Rachel and Leah, the two who built up the house of Israel. May you do great things in Ephrathah and make a name for yourself in Bethlehem. Through the children YHWH gives you by this young woman, may your house be like the house of Perez, whom Tamar bore to Judah.”
A Son Is Born · 4:13–17

So Boaz takes Ruth, and she becomes his wife. He goes in to her, YHWH lets her conceive, and she gives birth to a son. Then the women say to Naomi, “Blessed be YHWH, who has not left you today without a redeemer! May his name be famous in Israel! He will bring your life back to you and take care of you in your old age. For your daughter-in-law who loves you has given birth to him — and she is better to you than seven sons.” Then Naomi takes the child, holds him close against her, and cares for him. The neighbor women give him a name. “A son is born to Naomi!” they say. They name him Obed. He becomes the father of Jesse, the father of David.
The Genealogy · 4:18–22

This is the family line of Perez: Perez is the father of Hezron, Hezron the father of Ram, Ram the father of Amminadab, Amminadab the father of Nahshon, Nahshon the father of Salmon, Salmon the father of Boaz, Boaz the father of Obed, Obed the father of Jesse, and Jesse the father of David.
Elkanah and His Household · 1:1–8

Now there is a certain man of Ramathaim Zophim, of the hill country of Ephraim, and his name is Elkanah, the son of Jeroham, the son of Elihu, the son of Tohu, the son of Zuph, an Ephraimite. He has two wives. The name of one is Hannah, and the name of other Peninnah. Peninnah has children, but Hannah has no children. This man goes up out of his city from year to year to worship and to sacrifice to YHWH of hosts in Shiloh. The two sons of Eli, Hophni and Phinehas, priests to YHWH, are there. When the day comes that Elkanah sacrifices, he gives to Peninnah his wife, and to all her sons and her daughters, portions; but to Hannah he gives a double portion, for he loves Hannah, but YHWH has shut up her womb. Her rival provokes her severely, to irritate her, because YHWH has shut up her womb. As he does so year by year, when she goes up to YHWH’s house. Her rival provokes her; therefore she weeps, and doesn’t eat. Elkanah her husband says to her, “Hannah, why do you weep? Why don’t you eat? Why is your heart grieved? Am I not better to you than ten sons?”
Hannah’s Prayer at Shiloh · 1:9–18

So Hannah rises up after they have finished eating and drinking in Shiloh. Now Eli the priest is sitting on his seat by the doorpost of YHWH’s temple. She is in bitterness of soul, and prays to YHWH, weeping bitterly. She vows a vow, and says, “YHWH of hosts, if you will indeed look at the affliction of your servant, and remember me, and not forget your servant, but will give to your servant a boy, then I will give him to YHWH all the days of his life, and no razor will come on his head.”

As she continues praying before YHWH, Eli sees her mouth. Now Hannah speaks in her heart. Only her lips move, but her voice is not heard. Therefore Eli thinks she is drunk. Eli says to her, “How long will you be drunk? Get rid of your wine!”

Hannah answers, “No, my lord, I am a woman of a sorrowful spirit. I have not been drinking wine or strong drink, but I poured out my soul before YHWH. Don’t consider your servant a wicked woman; for I have been speaking out of the abundance of my complaint and my provocation.”
Then Eli answers, “Go in peace; and may the God of Israel grant your petition that you have asked of him.”
She says, “Let your servant find favor in your sight.” So the woman goes her way, and eats; and her facial expression isn’t sad any more.
The Birth of Samuel · 1:19–20
They rise up in the morning early, and worship before YHWH, and return, and come to their house to Ramah. Then Elkanah knows Hannah his wife; and YHWH remembers her.
When the time has come, Hannah conceives, and bears a son; and she names him Samuel, saying, “Because I have asked him of YHWH.”
Hannah Presents Samuel · 1:21–28

The man Elkanah, and all his house, go up to offer to YHWH the yearly sacrifice, and his vow. But Hannah doesn’t go up; for she says to her husband, “Not until the child is weaned; then I will bring him, that he may appear before YHWH, and stay there forever.”
Elkanah her husband says to her, “Do what seems good to you. Wait until you have weaned him; only may YHWH establish his word.”

So the woman waits and nurses her son, until she weans him. When she has weaned him, she takes him up with her, with three bulls, and one ephah of meal, and a bottle of wine, and brings him to YHWH’s house in Shiloh. The child is young. They kill the bull, and bring the child to Eli. She says, “Oh, my lord, as your soul lives, my lord, I am the woman who stood by you here, praying to YHWH. I prayed for this child; and YHWH has given me my petition which I asked of him. Therefore I have also given him to YHWH. As long as he lives he is given to YHWH.” He worships YHWH there.
Hannah’s Song · 2:1–10
Hannah prays, and says:
“My heart exults in YHWH!
My horn is exalted in YHWH.
My mouth is enlarged over my enemies,
because I rejoice in your salvation.
There is no one as holy as YHWH,
For there is no one besides you,
nor is there any rock like our God.
“Don’t keep talking so exceedingly proudly.
Don’t let arrogance come out of your mouth,
For YHWH is a God of knowledge.
By him actions are weighed.
“The bows of the mighty men are broken.
Those who stumbled are armed with strength.
Those who were full have hired themselves out for bread.
Those who were hungry are satisfied.
Yes, the barren has borne seven.
She who has many children languishes.
“YHWH kills, and makes alive.
He brings down to Sheol, and brings up.
YHWH makes poor, and makes rich.
He brings low, he also lifts up.
He raises up the poor out of the dust.
He lifts up the needy from the dunghill,
To make them sit with princes,
and inherit the throne of glory.
For the pillars of the earth are YHWH’s.
He has set the world on them.
He will keep the feet of his holy ones,
but the wicked will be put to silence in darkness;
for no man will prevail by strength.
Those who strive with YHWH will be broken to pieces.
He will thunder against them in the sky.
“YHWH will judge the ends of the earth.
He will give strength to his king,
and exalt the horn of his anointed.”
The Wickedness of Eli’s Sons · 2:11–17

Elkanah goes to Ramah to his house. The child serves YHWH before Eli the priest. Now the sons of Eli are wicked men. They don’t know YHWH. The custom of the priests with the people is that when anyone offers a sacrifice, the priest’s servant comes while the meat is boiling, with a fork of three teeth in his hand; and he stabs it into the pan, or kettle, or cauldron, or pot. The priest takes all that the fork brings up for himself. So they do in Shiloh to all the Israelites who come there. Yes, before they burn the fat, the priest’s servant comes, and says to the man who sacrifices, “Give meat to roast for the priest; for he will not accept boiled meat from you, but raw.”

If the man says to him, “Let the fat be burned first, and then take as much as your soul desires”; then he would say, “No, but you will give it to me now; and if not, I will take it by force.” The sin of the young men is very great before YHWH; for the men despise the offering of YHWH.
Samuel Grows Before YHWH · 2:18–26

But Samuel ministers before YHWH, being a child, clothed with a linen ephod. Moreover his mother makes him a little robe, and brings it to him from year to year, when she comes up with her husband to offer the yearly sacrifice. Eli blesses Elkanah and his wife, and says, “May YHWH give you offspring from this woman for the petition which was asked of YHWH.” Then they go to their own home. YHWH visits Hannah, and she conceives, and bears three sons and two daughters. The child Samuel grows before YHWH. Now Eli is very old; and he hears all that his sons do to all Israel, and how that they sleep with the women who serve at the door of the Tent of Meeting. He says to them, “Why do you do such things? for I hear of your evil dealings from all this people. No, my sons; for it is no good report that I hear! You make YHWH’s people disobey. If one man sins against another, God will judge him; but if a man sins against YHWH, who will intercede for him?” Notwithstanding, they don’t listen to the voice of their father, because YHWH intends to kill them. The child Samuel grows on, and increases in favor both with YHWH, and also with men.
The Prophecy against Eli’s House · 2:27–36

A man of God comes to Eli, and says to him, “YHWH says, ‘Did I reveal myself to the house of your father, when they were in Egypt in bondage to Pharaoh’s house? Didn’t I choose him out of all the tribes of Israel to be my priest, to go up to my altar, to burn incense, to wear an ephod before me? Didn’t I give to the house of your father all the offerings of the children of Israel made by fire? Why do you kick at my sacrifice and at my offering, which I have commanded in my habitation, and honor your sons above me, to make yourselves fat with the best of all the offerings of Israel my people?’

“Therefore YHWH, the God of Israel, says, ‘I said indeed that your house, and the house of your father, should walk before me forever.’ But now YHWH says, ‘Far be it from me; for those who honor me I will honor, and those who despise me will be cursed. Look, the days come, that I will cut off your arm, and the arm of your father’s house, that there will not be an old man in your house. You will see the affliction of my habitation, in all the wealth which I will give Israel; and there will not be an old man in your house forever. The man of yours, whom I don’t cut off from my altar, will consume your eyes and grieve your heart; and all the increase of your house will die in the flower of their age.

“‘This will be the sign to you, that will come on your two sons, on Hophni and Phinehas: in one day they will both die. I will raise me up a faithful priest, that will do according to that which is in my heart and in my mind. I will build him a sure house; and he will walk before my anointed forever. It will happen, that everyone who is left in your house will come and bow down to him for a piece of silver and a loaf of bread, and will say, “Please put me into one of the priests’ offices, that I may eat a morsel of bread.”’”
YHWH Calls Samuel · 3:1–10

The child Samuel ministers to YHWH before Eli. YHWH’s word is precious in those days. There are not many visions, then. At that time, when Eli is laid down in his place (now his eyes have begun to grow dim, so that he can not see), and God’s lamp hasn’t yet gone out, and Samuel has laid down in YHWH’s temple, where God’s ark is; YHWH calls Samuel; and he says, “Here I am.” He runs to Eli, and says, “Here I am; for you called me.”
He says, “I didn’t call. Lie down again.”
He goes and lies down. YHWH called yet again, “Samuel!”
Samuel arises and goes to Eli, and says, “Here I am; for you called me.”

He answers, “I didn’t call, my son. Lie down again.” Now Samuel doesn’t yet know YHWH, neither is YHWH’s word yet revealed to him. YHWH calls Samuel again the third time. He arises and goes to Eli, and says, “Here I am; for you called me.”

Eli perceives that YHWH has called the child. Therefore Eli says to Samuel, “Go, lie down. It will be, if he calls you, that you will say, ‘Speak, YHWH; for your servant hears.’” So Samuel goes and lies down in his place. YHWH comes, and stands, and calls as at other times, “Samuel! Samuel!”
Then Samuel says, “Speak; for your servant hears.”
The Word Given to Samuel · 3:11–18

YHWH says to Samuel, “Look, I will do a thing in Israel, at which both the ears of everyone who hears it will tingle. In that day I will perform against Eli all that I have spoken concerning his house, from the beginning even to the end. For I have told him that I will judge his house forever, for the iniquity which he knew, because his sons brought a curse on themselves, and he didn’t restrain them. Therefore I have sworn to the house of Eli, that the iniquity of Eli’s house will not be removed with sacrifice or offering forever.”
Samuel lies until the morning, and opens the doors of YHWH’s house. Samuel fears to show Eli the vision. Then Eli calls Samuel, and says, “Samuel, my son!”
He says, “Here I am.”
He says, “What is the thing that he has spoken to you? Please don’t hide it from me. God do so to you, and more also, if you hide anything from me of all the things that he spoke to you.”
Samuel tells him every bit, and hides nothing from him.
He says, “It is YHWH. Let him do what seems good to him.”
Samuel Established as Prophet · 3:19–21

Samuel grows, and YHWH is with him, and let none of his words fall to the ground. All Israel from Dan even to Beersheba knows that Samuel is established to be a prophet of YHWH. YHWH appears again in Shiloh; for YHWH reveals himself to Samuel in Shiloh by YHWH’s word.
The Ark Brought to Battle · 4:1–9
The word of Samuel comes to all Israel.

Now Israel goes out against the Philistines to battle, and encamps beside Ebenezer; and the Philistines encamps in Aphek. The Philistines puts themselves in array against Israel. When they join battle, Israel is defeated by the Philistines, who kills about four thousand men of the army in the field. When the people have come into the camp, the elders of Israel say, “Why has YHWH defeated us today before the Philistines? Let us get the ark of YHWH’s covenant out of Shiloh and bring it to us, that it may come among us, and save us out of the hand of our enemies.”

So the people send to Shiloh; and they bring from there the ark of the covenant of YHWH of hosts, who sits above the cherubim: and the two sons of Eli, Hophni and Phinehas, are there with the ark of the covenant of God. When the ark of YHWH’s covenant comes into the camp, all Israel shouts with a great shout, so that the earth rings again. When the Philistines hears the noise of the shout, they say, “What does the noise of this great shout in the camp of the Hebrews mean?” They understand that YHWH’s ark has come into the camp. The Philistines are afraid, for they say, “God has come into the camp.” They say, “Woe to us! For there has not been such a thing before. Woe to us! Who will deliver us out of the hand of these mighty gods? These are the gods that struck the Egyptians with all kinds of plagues in the wilderness. Be strong, and behave like men, O you Philistines, that you not be servants to the Hebrews, as they have been to you. Strengthen yourselves like men, and fight!”
Israel Defeated; the Ark Captured · 4:10–11

The Philistines fights, and Israel is defeated, and each man flees to his tent. There is a very great slaughter; for thirty thousand footmen of Israel fall. God’s ark is taken; and the two sons of Eli, Hophni and Phinehas, are slain.
The Death of Eli · 4:12–18

A man of Benjamin runs out of the army, and comes to Shiloh the same day, with his clothes torn, and with dirt on his head. When he comes, look, Eli is sitting on his seat by the road watching; for his heart trembles for God’s ark. When the man comes into the city and tells about it, all the city cries out. When Eli hears the noise of the crying, he says, “What does the noise of this tumult mean?”

The man hurries, and comes and tells Eli. Now Eli is ninety-eight years old. His eyes are set, so that he can not see. The man says to Eli, “I am he who came out of the army, and I fled today out of the army.”
He says, “How did the matter go, my son?”

He who brings the news answers, “Israel has fled before the Philistines, and there has been also a great slaughter among the people. Your two sons also, Hophni and Phinehas, are dead, and God’s ark has been captured.”
When he makes mention of God’s ark, Eli falls from off his seat backward by the side of the gate; and his neck breaks, and he dies; for he is an old man, and heavy. He has judged Israel forty years.
Ichabod · 4:19–22

His daughter-in-law, Phinehas’ wife, is with child, near to be delivered. When she hears the news that God’s ark is taken, and that her father-in-law and her husband are dead, she bows herself and gives birth; for her pains come on her. About the time of her death the women who stand by her say to her, “Don’t be afraid; for you have given birth to a son.” But she doesn’t answer, neither does she regard it. She names the child Ichabod, saying, “The glory has departed from Israel”; because God’s ark is taken, and because of her father-in-law and her husband. She says, “The glory has departed from Israel; for God’s ark has been taken.”
Dagon Falls Before the Ark · 5:1–5

Now the Philistines has taken God’s ark, and they bring it from Ebenezer to Ashdod. The Philistines takes God’s ark, and brings it into the house of Dagon, and sets it by Dagon. When the people of Ashdod arise early on the next day, look, Dagon has fallen on his face to the ground before YHWH’s ark. They take Dagon, and set him in his place again. When they arise early on the following morning, look, Dagon has fallen on his face to the ground before YHWH’s ark; and the head of Dagon and both the palms of his hands are cut off on the threshold. Only Dagon’s torso is intact. Therefore neither the priests of Dagon, nor any who come into Dagon’s house, step on the threshold of Dagon in Ashdod, to this day.
The Hand of YHWH on the Philistines · 5:6–12
But YHWH’s hand is heavy on the people of Ashdod, and he destroys them, and strikes them with tumors, even Ashdod and its borders.

When the men of Ashdod see that it is so, they say, “The ark of the God of Israel will not stay with us; for his hand is severe on us, and on Dagon our god.” They send therefore and gather together all the lords of the Philistines, and say, “What should we do with the ark of the God of Israel?”

They answer, “Let the ark of the God of Israel be carried over to Gath.” They carry the ark of the God of Israel there. It is so, that after they have carried it there, YHWH’s hand is against the city with a very great confusion; and he strikes the men of the city, both small and great so that tumors break out on them. So they send God’s ark to Ekron.

As God’s ark comes to Ekron, the Ekronites cry out, saying, “They have brought the ark of the God of Israel here to us, to kill us and our people.” They send therefore and gather together all the lords of the Philistines, and they say, “Send the ark of the God of Israel away, and let it go again to its own place, that it not kill us and our people.” For there is a deadly confusion throughout all the city. The hand of God is very heavy there. The men who don’t die are struck with the tumors; and the cry of the city goes up to heaven.
The Philistines Send the Ark Home · 6:1–9

YHWH’s ark is in the country of the Philistines seven months. The Philistines calls for the priests and the diviners, saying, “What should we do with YHWH’s ark? Show us how we should send it to its place.”

They say, “If you send away the ark of the God of Israel, don’t send it empty; but by all means return a trespass offering to him. Then you will be healed, and it will be known to you why his hand is not removed from you.”
Then they say, “What should the trespass offering be which we will return to him?”

They say, “Five golden tumors, and five golden mice, for the number of the lords of the Philistines; for one plague was on you all, and on your lords. Therefore you will make images of your tumors, and images of your mice that mar the land; and you will give glory to the God of Israel. Perhaps he will release his hand from you, from your gods, and from your land. Why then do you harden your hearts, as the Egyptians and Pharaoh hardened their hearts? When he had worked wonderfully among them, didn’t they let the people go, and they departed?

“Now therefore take and prepare yourselves a new cart, and two milk cows, on which there has come no yoke; and tie the cows to the cart, and bring their calves home from them; and take YHWH’s ark, and lay it on the cart. Put the jewels of gold, which you return him for a trespass offering, in a coffer by its side; and send it away, that it may go. Look; if it goes up by the way of its own border to Beth Shemesh, then he has done us this great evil; but if not, then we will know that it is not his hand that struck us. It was a chance that happened to us.”
The Ark Arrives at Beth-shemesh · 6:10–18

The men do so, and take two milk cows, and tie them to the cart, and shut up their calves at home. They put YHWH’s ark on the cart, and the coffer with the golden mice and the images of their tumors. The cows take the straight way by the way to Beth Shemesh. They go along the highway, lowing as they go, and don’t turn away to the right hand or to the left; and the lords of the Philistines go after them to the border of Beth Shemesh. The people of Beth Shemesh are reaping their wheat harvest in the valley; and they lift up their eyes, and see the ark, and rejoice to see it. The cart comes into the field of Joshua of Beth Shemesh, and stands there, where there is a great stone. Then they split the wood of the cart, and offer up the cows for a burnt offering to YHWH. The Levites take down YHWH’s ark, and the coffer that is with it, in which the jewels of gold are, and put them on the great stone; and the men of Beth Shemesh offer burnt offerings and sacrifice sacrifices the same day to YHWH. When the five lords of the Philistines have seen it, they return to Ekron the same day. These are the golden tumors which the Philistines return for a trespass offering to YHWH: for Ashdod one, for Gaza one, for Ashkelon one, for Gath one, for Ekron one; and the golden mice, according to the number of all the cities of the Philistines belonging to the five lords, both of fortified cities and of country villages, even to the great stone, on which they set down YHWH’s ark. That stone remains to this day in the field of Joshua of Beth Shemesh.
The Men of Beth-shemesh Struck Down · 6:19–21

He strikes of the men of Beth Shemesh, because they have looked into YHWH’s ark, he strikes fifty thousand seventy of the men. Then the people mourn, because YHWH has struck the people with a great slaughter. The men of Beth Shemesh say, “Who is able to stand before YHWH, this holy God? To whom will he go up from us?”
They send messengers to the inhabitants of Kiriath Jearim, saying, “The Philistines have brought back YHWH’s ark. Come down, and bring it up to yourselves.”
The Ark at Kiriath-jearim · 7:1–2

The men of Kiriath Jearim come, and take YHWH’s ark, and bring it into Abinadab’s house on the hill, and consecrate Eleazar his son to keep YHWH’s ark. From the day that the ark stays in Kiriath Jearim, the time is long; for it is twenty years; and all the house of Israel laments after YHWH.
Samuel Calls Israel to Repentance · 7:3–6

Samuel speaks to all the house of Israel, saying, “If you are returning to YHWH with all your heart, then put away the foreign gods and the Ashtaroth from among you, and direct your hearts to YHWH, and serve him only; and he will deliver you out of the hand of the Philistines.” Then the children of Israel remove the Baals and the Ashtaroth, and serve YHWH only. Samuel says, “Gather all Israel to Mizpah, and I will pray to YHWH for you.” They gather together to Mizpah, and draw water, and pour it out before YHWH, and fast on that day, and say there, “We have sinned against YHWH.” Samuel judges the children of Israel in Mizpah.
Victory at Mizpah · 7:7–12

When the Philistines hears that the children of Israel are gathered together at Mizpah, the lords of the Philistines go up against Israel. When the children of Israel hear it, they are afraid of the Philistines. The children of Israel say to Samuel, “Don’t stop crying to YHWH our God for us, that he will save us out of the hand of the Philistines.” Samuel takes a suckling lamb, and offers it for a whole burnt offering to YHWH. Samuel cries to YHWH for Israel; and YHWH answers him. As Samuel is offering up the burnt offering, the Philistines comes near to battle against Israel; but YHWH thunders with a great thunder on that day on the Philistines, and confuses them; and they are struck down before Israel. The men of Israel go out of Mizpah, and pursue the Philistines, and strike them, until they come under Beth Kar.
Then Samuel takes a stone, and sets it between Mizpah and Shen, and calls its name Ebenezer, saying, “YHWH helped us until now.”
Samuel as Judge · 7:13–17
So the Philistines are subdued, and they stop coming within the border of Israel. YHWH’s hand is against the Philistines all the days of Samuel.

The cities which the Philistines has taken from Israel are restored to Israel, from Ekron even to Gath; and Israel recovers its border out of the hand of the Philistines. There is peace between Israel and the Amorites.

Samuel judges Israel all the days of his life. He goes from year to year in a circuit to Bethel, Gilgal, and Mizpah; and he judges Israel in all those places. His return is to Ramah, for his house is there; and he judges Israel there; and he builds an altar to YHWH there.
Israel Demands a King · 8:1–9

When Samuel is old, he makes his sons judges over Israel. Now the name of his firstborn is Joel; and the name of his second, Abijah. They are judges in Beersheba. His sons don’t walk in his ways, but turn away after dishonest gain, take bribes, and pervert justice. Then all the elders of Israel gather themselves together and come to Samuel to Ramah. They say to him, “Look, you are old, and your sons don’t walk in your ways. Now make us a king to judge us like all the nations.” But the thing displeases Samuel, when they say, “Give us a king to judge us.”

Samuel prays to YHWH. YHWH says to Samuel, “Listen to the voice of the people in all that they tell you; for they have not rejected you, but they have rejected me as the king over them. According to all the works which they have done since the day that I brought them up out of Egypt even to this day, in that they have forsaken me, and served other gods, so they also do to you. Now therefore listen to their voice. However you will protest solemnly to them, and will show them the way of the king who will reign over them.”
Samuel Warns About Kings · 8:10–18

Samuel tells all YHWH’s words to the people who ask him for a king. He says, “This will be the way of the king who will reign over you: he will take your sons, and appoint them as his servants, for his chariots, and to be his horsemen; and they will run before his chariots. He will appoint them to him for captains of thousands, and captains of fifties; and he will assign some to plow his ground, and to reap his harvest, and to make his instruments of war, and the instruments of his chariots. He will take your daughters to be perfumers, to be cooks, and to be bakers. He will take your fields, your vineyards, and your olive groves, even their best, and give them to his servants. He will take one tenth of your seed, and of your vineyards, and give it to his officers, and to his servants. He will take your male servants, your female servants, your best young men, and your donkeys, and assign them to his own work. He will take one tenth of your flocks; and you will be his servants. You will cry out in that day because of your king whom you will have chosen for yourselves; and YHWH will not answer you in that day.”
YHWH Grants the Request · 8:19–22

But the people refuse to listen to the voice of Samuel; and they say, “No; but we will have a king over us, that we also may be like all the nations, and that our king may judge us, and go out before us, and fight our battles.”
Samuel hears all the words of the people, and he rehearses them in the ears of YHWH. YHWH says to Samuel, “Listen to their voice, and make them a king.”
Samuel says to the men of Israel, “Everyone go to your own city.”
Saul Son of Kish · 9:1–2

Now there is a man of Benjamin, whose name is Kish, the son of Abiel, the son of Zeror, the son of Becorath, the son of Aphiah, the son of a Benjamite, a mighty man of valor. He has a son, whose name is Saul, an impressive young man; and there is not among the children of Israel a better person than he. From his shoulders and upward he is taller than any of the people.
The Search for the Donkeys · 9:3–14

The donkeys of Kish, Saul’s father, are lost. Kish says to Saul his son, “Take now one of the servants with you, and arise, go look for the donkeys.” He passes through the hill country of Ephraim, and passes through the land of Shalishah, but they don’t find them. Then they pass through the land of Shaalim, and there they aren’t there. Then he passes through the land of the Benjamites, but they don’t find them.
When they have come to the land of Zuph, Saul says to his servant who is with him, “Come, and let us return, lest my father stop caring about the donkeys, and be anxious for us.”

The servant says to him, “Look now, there is in this city a man of God, and he is a man who is held in honor. All that he says surely happens. Now let us go there. Perhaps he can tell us which way to go.”
Then Saul says to his servant, “But, look, if we go, what should we bring the man? For the bread is spent in our sacks, and there is not a present to bring to the man of God. What do we have?”

The servant answers Saul again, and says, “Look, I have in my hand the fourth part of a shekel of silver. I will give that to the man of God, to tell us our way.” (In earlier times in Israel, when a man goes to inquire of God, he says, “Come, and let us go to the seer”; for he who is now called a prophet is before called a seer.)

Then Saul says to his servant, “Well said. Come, let us go.” So they go to the city where the man of God is. As they go up the ascent to the city, they find young maidens going out to draw water, and say to them, “Is the seer here?”

They answer them, and say, “He is. Look, he is before you. Hurry now, for he has come today into the city; for the people have a sacrifice today in the high place. As soon as you have come into the city, you will immediately find him, before he goes up to the high place to eat; for the people will not eat until he come, because he blesses the sacrifice. Afterwards those who are invited eat. Now therefore go up; for at this time you will find him.”
They go up to the city. As they come within the city, look, Samuel comes out toward them, to go up to the high place.
Samuel and Saul Meet · 9:15–21

Now YHWH has revealed to Samuel a day before Saul comes, saying, “Tomorrow about this time I will send you a man out of the land of Benjamin, and you will anoint him to be prince over my people Israel. He will save my people out of the hand of the Philistines; for I have looked upon my people, because their cry has come to me.”
When Samuel sees Saul, YHWH says to him, “Look, the man of whom I spoke to you! He will have authority over my people.”
Then Saul approaches Samuel in the gateway, and says, “Please tell me where the seer’s house is.”

Samuel answers Saul, and says, “I am the seer. Go up before me to the high place, for you are to eat with me today. In the morning I will let you go, and will tell you all that is in your heart. As for your donkeys who were lost three days ago, don’t set your mind on them; for they have been found. For whom is all that is desirable in Israel? Is it not for you, and for all your father’s house?”
Saul answers, “Am I not a Benjamite, of the smallest of the tribes of Israel? And my family the least of all the families of the tribe of Benjamin? Why then do you speak to me like this?”
Saul Honored at the Feast · 9:22–27

Samuel takes Saul and his servant, and brings them into the guest room, and makes them sit in the best place among those who are invited, who are about thirty persons. Samuel says to the cook, “Bring the portion which I gave you, of which I said to you, ‘Set it aside.’” The cook takes up the thigh, and that which is on it, and sets it before Saul. Samuel says, “Look, that which has been reserved!
