Set it before yourself and eat; because for the appointed time has it been kept for you, for I said, ‘I have invited the people.’” So Saul eats with Samuel that day.

When they have come down from the high place into the city, he talks with Saul on the housetop. They arise early; and about daybreak, Samuel calls to Saul on the housetop, saying, “Get up, that I may send you away.” Saul arises, and they both go outside, he and Samuel, together. As they are going down at the end of the city, Samuel says to Saul, “Tell the servant to go on ahead of us.” He goes ahead, then Samuel says, “But stand still first, that I may cause you to hear God’s message.”
Samuel Anoints Saul · 10:1
Then Samuel takes the vial of oil, and pours it on his head, and kisses him, and says, “Hasn’t YHWH anointed you to be prince over his inheritance?
The Three Signs · 10:2–8

When you have departed from me today, then you will find two men by Rachel’s tomb, on the border of Benjamin at Zelzah. They will tell you, ‘The donkeys which you went to look for have been found; and look, your father has stopped caring about the donkeys, and is anxious for you, saying, “What should I do for my son?”’

“Then you will go on forward from there, and you will come to the oak of Tabor. Three men will meet you there going up to God to Bethel, one carrying three young goats, and another carrying three loaves of bread, and another carrying a bottle of wine. They will greet you, and give you two loaves of bread, which you will receive from their hand.

“After that you will come to the hill of God, where the garrison of the Philistines is; and it will happen, when you have come there to the city, that you will meet a band of prophets coming down from the high place with a lute, a tambourine, a pipe, and a harp before them; and they will be prophesying. Then YHWH’s Spirit will come mightily on you, and you will prophesy with them, and will be turned into another man. Let it be, when these signs have come to you, that you do what is appropriate for the occasion; for God is with you.

“Go down ahead of me to Gilgal; and look, I will come down to you, to offer burnt offerings, and to sacrifice sacrifices of peace offerings. Wait seven days, until I come to you, and show you what you are to do.”
Saul Among the Prophets · 10:9–13

It is so, that when he has turned his back to go from Samuel, God gives him another heart; and all those signs happen that day. When they come there to the hill, look, a band of prophets meets him; and the Spirit of God comes mightily on him, and he prophesies among them. When all who know him before see that, look, he prophesies with the prophets, then the people say to one another, “What is this that has come to the son of Kish? Is Saul also among the prophets?”
One of the same place answers, “Who is their father?” Therefore it becomes a proverb, “Is Saul also among the prophets?” When he has finished prophesying, he comes to the high place.
Saul Chosen at Mizpah · 10:14–27
Saul’s uncle says to him and to his servant, “Where did you go?”
He says, “To seek the donkeys. When we saw that they were not found, we came to Samuel.”
Saul’s uncle says, “Please tell me what Samuel said to you.”
Saul says to his uncle, “He told us plainly that the donkeys were found.” But concerning the matter of the kingdom, of which Samuel speaks, he doesn’t tell him.

Samuel calls the people together to YHWH to Mizpah; and he says to the children of Israel, “YHWH, the God of Israel, says ‘I brought Israel up out of Egypt, and I delivered you out of the hand of the Egyptians, and out of the hand of all the kingdoms that oppressed you.’ But you have today rejected your God, who himself saves you out of all your calamities and your distresses; and you have said to him, ‘No! Set a king over us.’ Now therefore present yourselves before YHWH by your tribes, and by your thousands.”

So Samuel brings all the tribes of Israel near, and the tribe of Benjamin is chosen. He brings the tribe of Benjamin near by their families; and the family of the Matrites is chosen. Then Saul the son of Kish is chosen; but when they look for him, he can not be found. Therefore they ask of YHWH further, “Is there yet a man to come here?”
YHWH answers, “Look, he has hidden himself among the baggage.”

They run and get him there. When he stands among the people, he is higher than any of the people from his shoulders and upward. Samuel says to all the people, “Do you see him whom YHWH has chosen, that there is no one like him among all the people?”
All the people shout, and say, “Long live the king!”

Then Samuel tells the people the regulations of the kingdom, and writes it in a book, and lays it up before YHWH. Samuel sends all the people away, every man to his house. Saul also goes to his house to Gibeah; and the army goes with him, whose hearts God has touched. But certain worthless fellows say, “How could this man save us?” They despise him, and bring him no present. But he holds his peace.
The Ammonite Threat · 11:1–4

Then Nahash the Ammonite comes up, and encamps against Jabesh Gilead: and all the men of Jabesh say to Nahash, “Make a covenant with us, and we will serve you.” Nahash the Ammonite says to them, “On this condition I will make it with you, that all your right eyes be gouged out. I will make this dishonor all Israel.”

The elders of Jabesh say to him, “Give us seven days, that we may send messengers to all the borders of Israel; and then, if there is no one to save us, we will come out to you.” Then the messengers come to Gibeah of Saul, and speak these words in the ears of the people, then all the people lift up their voice, and wept.
Saul Summons Israel · 11:5–11

Look, Saul comes following the oxen out of the field; and Saul says, “What ails the people that they weep?” They tell him the words of the men of Jabesh. God’s Spirit comes mightily on Saul when he hears those words, and his anger burns hot. He takes a yoke of oxen, and cuts them in pieces, and sends them throughout all the borders of Israel by the hand of messengers, saying, “Whoever doesn’t come out after Saul and after Samuel, so will it be done to his oxen.” The dread of YHWH falls on the people, and they come out as one man. He counts them in Bezek; and the children of Israel are three hundred thousand, and the men of Judah thirty thousand. They say to the messengers who come, “Tell the men of Jabesh Gilead, ‘Tomorrow, by the time the sun is hot, you will be rescued.’” The messengers come and tell the men of Jabesh; and they are glad. Therefore the men of Jabesh say, “Tomorrow we will come out to you, and you will do with us all that seems good to you.” On the next day, Saul puts the people in three companies; and they come into the middle of the camp in the morning watch, and strike the Ammonites until the heat of the day. Those who remain are scattered, so that no two of them are left together.
Saul Confirmed as King · 11:12–15
The people say to Samuel, “Who is he who said, ‘Will Saul reign over us?’ Bring those men, that we may put them to death!”

Saul says, “No man will be put to death today; for today YHWH has rescued Israel.” Then Samuel says to the people, “Come, and let us go to Gilgal, and renew the kingdom there.” All the people go to Gilgal; and there they make Saul king before YHWH in Gilgal. There they offer sacrifices of peace offerings before YHWH; and there Saul and all the men of Israel rejoice greatly.
Samuel’s Integrity Before Israel · 12:1–5

Samuel says to all Israel, “Look, I have listened to your voice in all that you said to me, and have made a king over you. Now, look, the king walks before you. I am old and gray-headed. Look, my sons are with you. I have walked before you from my youth to this day. Here I am. Witness against me before YHWH, and before his anointed. Whose ox have I taken? Whose donkey have I taken? Whom have I defrauded? Whom have I oppressed? Of whose hand have I taken a ransom to make me blind my eyes? I will restore it to you.”
They say, “You have not defrauded us, nor oppressed us, neither have you taken anything from anyone’s hand.”
He says to them, “YHWH is witness against you, and his anointed is witness today, that you have not found anything in my hand.”
They say, “He is witness.”
YHWH’s Faithfulness in History · 12:6–13

Samuel says to the people, “It is YHWH who appointed Moses and Aaron, and that brought your fathers up out of the land of Egypt. Now therefore stand still, that I may plead with you before YHWH concerning all the righteous acts of YHWH, which he did to you and to your fathers.
“When Jacob had come into Egypt, and your fathers cried to YHWH, then YHWH sent Moses and Aaron, who brought your fathers out of Egypt, and made them to dwell in this place.

“But they forgot YHWH their God; and he sold them into the hand of Sisera, captain of the army of Hazor, and into the hand of the Philistines, and into the hand of the king of Moab; and they fought against them. They cried to YHWH, and said, ‘We have sinned, because we have forsaken YHWH, and have served the Baals and the Ashtaroth: but now deliver us out of the hand of our enemies, and we will serve you.’ YHWH sent Jerubbaal, Bedan, Jephthah, and Samuel, and delivered you out of the hand of your enemies on every side; and you lived in safety.

“When you saw that Nahash the king of the children of Ammon came against you, you said to me, ‘No, but a king will reign over us;’ when YHWH your God was your king. Now therefore see the king whom you have chosen, and whom you have asked for. Look, YHWH has set a king over you.
Warning and Sign · 12:14–19

If you will fear YHWH, and serve him, and listen to his voice, and not rebel against the commandment of YHWH, then both you and also the king who reigns over you are followers of YHWH your God. But if you will not listen to YHWH’s voice, but rebel against the commandment of YHWH, then YHWH’s hand will be against you, as it was against your fathers.

“Now therefore stand still and see this great thing, which YHWH will do before your eyes. Isn’t it wheat harvest today? I will call to YHWH, that he may send thunder and rain; and you will know and see that your wickedness is great, which you have done in YHWH’s sight, in asking for a king.”
So Samuel calls to YHWH; and YHWH sends thunder and rain that day. Then all the people greatly fear YHWH and Samuel.
All the people say to Samuel, “Pray for your servants to YHWH your God, that we not die; for we have added to all our sins this evil, to ask for a king.”
Samuel’s Final Word · 12:20–25

Samuel says to the people, “Don’t be afraid. You have indeed done all this evil; yet don’t turn away from following YHWH, but serve YHWH with all your heart. Don’t turn away to go after vain things which can’t profit or deliver, for they are vain. For YHWH will not forsake his people for his great name’s sake, because it has pleased YHWH to make you a people for himself. Moreover as for me, far be it from me that I should sin against YHWH in ceasing to pray for you: but I will instruct you in the good and the right way. Only fear YHWH, and serve him in truth with all your heart; for consider what great things he has done for you. But if you keep doing evil, you will be consumed, both you and your king.”
Saul’s Army and the Philistine Threat · 13:1–7

Saul is thirty years old when he becomes king, and he reigns over Israel forty-two years. Saul chooses for himself three thousand men of Israel, of which two thousand are with Saul in Michmash and in the Mount of Bethel, and one thousand are with Jonathan in Gibeah of Benjamin. He sends the rest of the people to their own tents. Jonathan strikes the garrison of the Philistines that is in Geba, and the Philistines hears of it. Saul blows the trumpet throughout all the land, saying, “Let the Hebrews hear!” All Israel hears that Saul has struck the garrison of the Philistines, and also that Israel is considered an abomination to the Philistines. The people are gathered together after Saul to Gilgal. The Philistines assembles themselves together to fight with Israel, thirty thousand chariots, and six thousand horsemen, and people as the sand which is on the seashore in multitude. They come up and encamp in Michmash, eastward of Beth Aven. When the men of Israel see that they are in trouble (for the people are distressed), then the people hide themselves in caves, in thickets, in rocks, in tombs, and in pits. Now some of the Hebrews has gone over the Jordan to the land of Gad and Gilead; but as for Saul, he is yet in Gilgal, and all the people follow him trembling.
Saul’s Unlawful Sacrifice · 13:8–14

He stays seven days, according to the time set by Samuel; but Samuel doesn’t come to Gilgal, and the people are scattering from him. Saul says, “Bring the burnt offering to me here, and the peace offerings.” He offers the burnt offering.
It comes to pass that as soon as he has finished offering the burnt offering, look, Samuel comes; and Saul goes out to meet him, that he might greet him. Samuel says, “What have you done?”

Saul says, “Because I saw that the people were scattered from me, and that you didn’t come within the days appointed, and that the Philistines assembled themselves together at Michmash; therefore I said, ‘Now the Philistines will come down on me to Gilgal, and I haven’t entreated the favor of YHWH.’ I forced myself therefore, and offered the burnt offering.”

Samuel says to Saul, “You have done foolishly. You have not kept the commandment of YHWH your God, which he commanded you; for now YHWH would have established your kingdom on Israel forever. But now your kingdom will not continue. YHWH has sought for himself a man after his own heart, and YHWH has appointed him to be prince over his people, because you have not kept that which YHWH commanded you.”
The Philistine Advantage · 13:15–23

Samuel arises, and goes from Gilgal to Gibeah of Benjamin. Saul counts the people who are present with him, about six hundred men. Saul, and Jonathan his son, and the people who are present with them, stay in Geba of Benjamin; but the Philistines encamps in Michmash. The raiders come out of the camp of the Philistines in three companies: one company turns to the way that leads to Ophrah, to the land of Shual; another company turns the way to Beth Horon; and another company turns the way of the border that looks down on the valley of Zeboim toward the wilderness. Now there is no blacksmith found throughout all the land of Israel; for the Philistines says, “Lest the Hebrews make themselves swords or spears”; but all the Israelites go down to the Philistines, each man to sharpen his own plowshare, mattock, ax, and sickle. The price is one payim each to sharpen mattocks, plowshares, pitchforks, axes, and goads. So it comes to pass in the day of battle, that neither sword nor spear are found in the hand of any of the people who are with Saul and Jonathan; but Saul and Jonathan his son have them. The garrison of the Philistines goes out to the pass of Michmash.
Jonathan’s Bold Venture · 14:1–15

Now it falls on a day, that Jonathan the son of Saul says to the young man who bears his armor, “Come, and let us go over to the Philistines’ garrison, that is on the other side.” But he doesn’t tell his father. Saul stays in the uttermost part of Gibeah under the pomegranate tree which is in Migron: and the people who are with him are about six hundred men; including Ahijah, the son of Ahitub, Ichabod’s brother, the son of Phinehas, the son of Eli, the priest of YHWH in Shiloh, wearing an ephod. The people don’t know that Jonathan are gone. Between the passes, by which Jonathan seeks to go over to the Philistines’ garrison, there is a rocky crag on the one side, and a rocky crag on the other side: and the name of the one is Bozez, and the name of the other Seneh. The one crag rises up on the north in front of Michmash, and the other on the south in front of Geba. Jonathan says to the young man who bears his armor, “Come, let us go over to the garrison of these uncircumcised. It may be that YHWH will work for us; for there is no restraint on YHWH to save by many or by few.” His armor bearer says to him, “Do all that is in your heart. Turn and, look, I am with you according to your heart.” Then Jonathan says, “Look, we will pass over to the men, and we will reveal ourselves to them. If they say thus to us, ‘Wait until we come to you!’ then we will stand still in our place, and will not go up to them. But if they say this, ‘Come up to us!’ then we will go up; for YHWH has delivered them into our hand. This will be the sign to us.”

Both of them reveal themselves to the garrison of the Philistines: and the Philistines says, “Look, the Hebrews are coming out of the holes where they had hidden themselves!” The men of the garrison answer Jonathan and his armor bearer, and say, “Come up to us, and we will show you something!”

Jonathan says to his armor bearer, “Come up after me; for YHWH has delivered them into the hand of Israel.” Jonathan climbs up on his hands and on his feet, and his armor bearer after him: and they fall before Jonathan; and his armor bearer kills them after him. That first slaughter, which Jonathan and his armor bearer make, is about twenty men, within as it were half a furrow’s length in an acre of land. There is a trembling in the camp, in the field, and among all the people; the garrison, and the raiders, also trembled; and the earth quakes, so there is an exceedingly great trembling.
The Rout of the Philistines · 14:16–23

The watchmen of Saul in Gibeah of Benjamin look; and look, the multitude melted away and scattered. Then Saul says to the people who are with him, “Count now, and see who is missing from us.” When they have counted, look, Jonathan and his armor bearer are not there.

Saul says to Ahijah, “Bring God’s ark here.” For God’s ark is with the children of Israel at that time. While Saul talks to the priest, the tumult that is in the camp of the Philistines goes on and increases; and Saul says to the priest, “Withdraw your hand!”

Saul and all the people who are with him are gathered together, and come to the battle; and look, they are all striking each other with their swords in very great confusion. Now the Hebrews who are with the Philistines before, and who goes up with them into the camp, from all around, even they also turn to be with the Israelites who are with Saul and Jonathan. Likewise all the men of Israel who have hidden themselves in the hill country of Ephraim, when they hear that the Philistines flees, even they also follow hard after them in the battle. So YHWH saves Israel that day; and the battle passed over by Beth Aven.
Saul’s Rash Oath · 14:24–35

The men of Israel are distressed that day; for Saul has adjured the people, saying, “Cursed is the man who eats any food until it is evening, and I am avenged of my enemies.” So none of the people tastes food.

All the people come into the forest; and there is honey on the ground. When the people have come to the forest, look, honey is dripping, but no one puts his hand to his mouth; for the people fear the oath. But Jonathan doesn’t hear when his father commands the people with the oath. Therefore he puts out the end of the rod that is in his hand, and dips it in the honeycomb, and puts his hand to his mouth; and his eyes brighten. Then one of the people answers, and says, “Your father directly commanded the people with an oath, saying, ‘Cursed is the man who eats food today.’” The people are faint.

Then Jonathan says, “My father has troubled the land. Please look how my eyes have brightened, because I tasted a little of this honey. How much more, if perhaps the people had eaten freely today of the plunder of their enemies which they found? For now has there been no great slaughter among the Philistines.” They strike the Philistines that day from Michmash to Aijalon. The people are very faint; and the people pounced on the plunder, and take sheep, cattle, and calves, and kill them on the ground; and the people eat them with the blood. Then they tell Saul, saying, “Look, the people are sinning against YHWH, in that they eat meat with the blood.”

He says, “You have dealt treacherously. Roll a large stone to me today!” Saul says, “Disperse yourselves among the people, and tell them, ‘Every man bring me here his ox, and every man his sheep, and kill them here, and eat; and don’t sin against YHWH in eating meat with the blood.’” All the people bring every man his ox with him that night, and kill them there.
Saul builds an altar to YHWH. This is the first altar that he builds to YHWH.
Jonathan Nearly Executed · 14:36–46
Saul says, “Let us go down after the Philistines by night, and take plunder among them until the morning light, and let us not leave a man of them.”
They say, “Do whatever seems good to you.”
Then the priest says, “Let us draw near here to God.”

Saul asks counsel of God, “Should I go down after the Philistines? Will you deliver them into the hand of Israel?” But he doesn’t answer him that day. Saul says, “Draw near here, all you chiefs of the people; and know and see in which this sin has been today. For, as YHWH lives, who saves Israel, though it is in Jonathan my son, he will surely die.” But there is not a man among all the people who answer him. Then he says to all Israel, “You be on one side, and I and Jonathan my son will be on the other side.”
The people say to Saul, “Do what seems good to you.”
Therefore Saul says to YHWH, the God of Israel, “Show the right.”
Jonathan and Saul are chosen, but the people escape.
Saul says, “Cast lots between me and Jonathan my son.”
Jonathan is selected.
Then Saul says to Jonathan, “Tell me what you have done!”
Jonathan tells him, and says, “I certainly did taste a little honey with the end of the rod that was in my hand; and look, I must die.”
Saul says, “God do so and more also; for you will surely die, Jonathan.”

The people say to Saul, “Will Jonathan die, who has worked this great salvation in Israel? Far from it! As YHWH lives, there will not one hair of his head fall to the ground; for he has worked with God today!” So the people rescue Jonathan, that he doesn’t die. Then Saul goes up from following the Philistines; and the Philistines goes to their own place.
Saul’s Reign and Wars · 14:47–52

Now when Saul has taken the kingdom over Israel, he fights against all his enemies on every side, against Moab, and against the children of Ammon, and against Edom, and against the kings of Zobah, and against the Philistines. Wherever he turns himself, he defeats them. He does valiantly, and strikes the Amalekites, and delivers Israel out of the hands of those who plunder them. Now the sons of Saul are Jonathan, Ishvi, and Malchishua; and the names of his two daughters are these: the name of the firstborn Merab, and the name of the younger Michal. The name of Saul’s wife is Ahinoam the daughter of Ahimaaz. The name of the captain of his army is Abner the son of Ner, Saul’s uncle. Kish is the father of Saul; and Ner the father of Abner is the son of Abiel. There is severe war against the Philistines all the days of Saul; and when Saul sees any mighty man, or any valiant man, he takes him into his service.
The Command against Amalek · 15:1–9

Samuel says to Saul, “YHWH sent me to anoint you to be king over his people, over Israel. Now therefore listen to the voice of YHWH’s words. YHWH of hosts says, ‘I remember what Amalek did to Israel, how he set himself against him on the way, when he came up out of Egypt. Now go and strike Amalek, and utterly destroy all that they have, and don’t spare them; but kill both man and woman, infant and nursing baby, ox and sheep, camel and donkey.’”

Saul summons the people, and counts them in Telaim, two hundred thousand footmen, and ten thousand men of Judah. Saul comes to the city of Amalek, and sets an ambush in the valley. Saul says to the Kenites, “Go, depart, go down from among the Amalekites, lest I destroy you with them; for you showed kindness to all the children of Israel, when they came up out of Egypt.” So the Kenites depart from among the Amalekites.

Saul strikes the Amalekites, from Havilah as you go to Shur, that is before Egypt. He takes Agag the king of the Amalekites alive, and utterly destroys all the people with the edge of the sword. But Saul and the people spar Agag, and the best of the sheep, of the cattle, and of the fat calves, and the lambs, and all that are good, and are not willing to utterly destroy them; but everything that is vile and refuse, that they destroy utterly.
Saul’s Disobedience Exposed · 15:10–21

Then YHWH’s word comes to Samuel, saying, “It grieves me that I have set up Saul to be king; for he has turned back from following me, and has not performed my commandments.” Samuel is angry; and he cries to YHWH all night.
Samuel rises early to meet Saul in the morning; and Samuel is told, saying, “Saul came to Carmel, and look, he set up a monument for himself, and turned, and passed on, and went down to Gilgal.”
Samuel comes to Saul; and Saul says to him, “You are blessed by YHWH! I have performed the commandment of YHWH.”
Samuel says, “Then what does this bleating of the sheep in my ears, and the lowing of the cattle which I hear mean?”
Saul says, “They have brought them from the Amalekites; for the people spared the best of the sheep and of the cattle, to sacrifice to YHWH your God. We have utterly destroyed the rest.”
Then Samuel says to Saul, “Stay, and I will tell you what YHWH said to me last night.”
He says to him, “Say on.”

Samuel says, “Though you were little in your own sight, weren’t you made the head of the tribes of Israel? YHWH anointed you king over Israel; and YHWH sent you on a journey, and said, ‘Go, and utterly destroy the sinners the Amalekites, and fight against them until they are consumed.’ Why then didn’t you obey YHWH’s voice, but took the plunder, and did that which was evil in YHWH’s sight?”

Saul says to Samuel, “But I have obeyed YHWH’s voice, and have gone the way which YHWH sent me, and have brought Agag the king of Amalek, and have utterly destroyed the Amalekites. But the people took of the plunder, sheep and cattle, the chief of the devoted things, to sacrifice to YHWH your God in Gilgal.”
To Obey is Better Than Sacrifice · 15:22–31

Samuel says, “Has YHWH as great delight in burnt offerings and sacrifices, as in obeying YHWH’s voice? Look, to obey is better than sacrifice, and to listen than the fat of rams. For rebellion is as the sin of witchcraft, and stubbornness is as idolatry and teraphim. Because you have rejected YHWH’s word, he has also rejected you from being king.”

Saul says to Samuel, “I have sinned; for I have transgressed the commandment of YHWH, and your words, because I feared the people, and obeyed their voice. Now therefore, please pardon my sin, and turn again with me, that I may worship YHWH.”

Samuel says to Saul, “I will not return with you; for you have rejected YHWH’s word, and YHWH has rejected you from being king over Israel.” As Samuel turns around to go away, Saul grabs the skirt of his robe, and it tore. Samuel says to him, “YHWH has torn the kingdom of Israel from you today, and has given it to a neighbor of yours who is better than you. Also the Strength of Israel will not lie nor repent; for he is not a man, that he should repent.”
Then he says, “I have sinned; yet please honor me now before the elders of my people, and before Israel, and come back with me, that I may worship YHWH your God.”
So Samuel goes back with Saul; and Saul worships YHWH.
Agag is Killed · 15:32–35
Then Samuel says, “Bring Agag the king of the Amalekites here to me!”
Agag comes to him cheerfully. Agag says, “Surely the bitterness of death is past.”
Samuel says, “As your sword has made women childless, so your mother will be childless among women!” Then Samuel cuts Agag in pieces before YHWH in Gilgal.

Then Samuel goes to Ramah; and Saul goes up to his house to Gibeah of Saul. Samuel comes no more to see Saul until the day of his death; for Samuel mourns for Saul: and YHWH grieves that he has made Saul king over Israel.
The Anointing of David · 16:1–13

YHWH says to Samuel, “How long will you mourn for Saul, since I have rejected him from being king over Israel? Fill your horn with oil, and go. I will send you to Jesse the Bethlehemite; for I have provided a king for myself among his sons.”
Samuel says, “How can I go? If Saul hears it, he will kill me.”
YHWH says, “Take a heifer with you, and say, I have come to sacrifice to YHWH. Call Jesse to the sacrifice, and I will show you what you will do. You will anoint to me him whom I name to you.”
Samuel does that which YHWH speaks, and comes to Bethlehem. The elders of the city come to meet him trembling, and say, “Do you come peaceably?”

He says, “Peaceably; I have come to sacrifice to YHWH. Sanctify yourselves, and come with me to the sacrifice.” He sanctifies Jesse and his sons, and calls them to the sacrifice. When they have come, he looks at Eliab, and says, “Surely YHWH’s anointed is before him.”

But YHWH says to Samuel, “Don’t look on his face, or on the height of his stature, because I have rejected him; for I don’t see as man sees. For man looks at the outward appearance, but YHWH looks at the heart.” Then Jesse calls Abinadab, and makes him pass before Samuel. He says, “YHWH has not chosen this one, either.” Then Jesse makes Shammah to pass by. He says, “YHWH has not chosen this one, either.” Jesse makes seven of his sons to pass before Samuel. Samuel says to Jesse, “YHWH has not chosen these.” Samuel says to Jesse, “Are all your children here?”
He says, “There remains yet the youngest. Look, he is keeping the sheep.”
Samuel says to Jesse, “Send and get him, for we will not sit down until he comes here.”
He sends, and brings him in. Now he is ruddy, with a handsome face and good appearance. YHWH says, “Arise! Anoint him, for this is he.”
Then Samuel takes the horn of oil, and anoints him in the middle of his brothers. Then YHWH’s Spirit comes mightily on David from that day forward. So Samuel rises up and goes to Ramah.
David Enters Saul’s Service · 16:14–23

Now YHWH’s Spirit departs from Saul, and an evil spirit from YHWH troubles him. Saul’s servants say to him, “See now, an evil spirit from God troubles you. Let our lord now command your servants who are in front of you to seek out a man who is a skillful player on the harp. Then when the evil spirit from God is on you, he will play with his hand, and you will be well.”
Saul says to his servants, “Provide me now a man who can play well, and bring him to me.”

Then one of the young men answers, and says, “Look, I have seen a son of Jesse the Bethlehemite who is skillful in playing, a mighty man of valor, a man of war, prudent in speech, and a handsome person; and YHWH is with him.”
Therefore Saul sends messengers to Jesse, and says, “Send me David your son, who is with the sheep.”

Jesse takes a donkey loaded with bread, and a bottle of wine, and a young goat, and sends them by David his son to Saul. David comes to Saul, and stands before him. He loves him greatly; and he becomes his armor bearer. Saul sends to Jesse, saying, “Please let David stand before me; for he has found favor in my sight.” When the spirit from God is on Saul, David takes the harp, and plays with his hand; so Saul is refreshed, and is well, and the evil spirit departs from him.
The Philistine Champion · 17:1–11

Now the Philistines gathers together their armies to battle; and they are gathered together at Socoh, which belongs to Judah, and encamp between Socoh and Azekah, in Ephesdammim. Saul and the men of Israel are gathered together, and encamp in the valley of Elah, and set the battle in array against the Philistines. The Philistines stand on the mountain on the one side, and Israel stands on the mountain on the other side: and there is a valley between them. A champion out of the camp of the Philistines named Goliath, of Gath, whose height is six cubits and a span goes out. He has a helmet of brass on his head, and he wears a coat of mail; and the weight of the coat is five thousand shekels of brass. He has brass shin armor on his legs, and a brass javelin between his shoulders. The staff of his spear is like a weaver’s beam; and his spear’s head weighs six hundred shekels of iron. His shield bearer goes before him. He stands and cries to the armies of Israel, and says to them, “Why have you come out to set your battle in array? Am I not a Philistine, and you servants to Saul? Choose a man for yourselves, and let him come down to me. If he is able to fight with me and kill me, then will we be your servants; but if I prevail against him and kill him, then you will be our servants and serve us.” The Philistine says, “I defy the armies of Israel today! Give me a man, that we may fight together!”
When Saul and all Israel hear those words of the Philistine, they are dismayed, and greatly afraid.
David Arrives at the Battlefield · 17:12–30

Now David is the son of that Ephrathite of Bethlehem Judah, whose name is Jesse; and he has eight sons. The man is an elderly old man in the days of Saul. The three oldest sons of Jesse have gone after Saul to the battle: and the names of his three sons who go to the battle are Eliab the firstborn, and next to him Abinadab, and the third Shammah. David is the youngest; and the three oldest follows Saul. Now David goes back and forth from Saul to feed his father’s sheep at Bethlehem. The Philistine comes near morning and evening, and presents himself forty days. Jesse says to David his son, “Now take for your brothers an ephah of this parched grain, and these ten loaves, and carry them quickly to the camp to your brothers; and bring these ten cheeses to the captain of their thousand, and see how your brothers are doing, and bring back news.” Now Saul, and they, and all the men of Israel, are in the valley of Elah, fighting with the Philistines. David rises up early in the morning, and leaves the sheep with a keeper, and takes and goes, as Jesse has commanded him. He comes to the place of the wagons, as the army which is going out to the fight shouts for the battle. Israel and the Philistines put the battle in array, army against army. David leaves his baggage in the hand of the keeper of the baggage, and runs to the army, and comes and greets his brothers. As he talks with them, look, the champion, the Philistine of Gath, Goliath by name, comes up out of the ranks of the Philistines, and says the same words; and David hears them. All the men of Israel, when they see the man, flee from him, and are terrified. The men of Israel say, “Have you seen this man who has come up? He has surely come up to defy Israel. The king will give great riches to the man who kills him, and will give him his daughter, and make his father’s house free in Israel.”

David speaks to the men who stand by him, saying, “What will be done to the man who kills this Philistine, and takes away the reproach from Israel? For who is this uncircumcised Philistine, that he should defy the armies of the living God?”
The people answer him in this way, saying, “So will it be done to the man who kills him.”

Eliab his oldest brother hears when he speaks to the men; and Eliab’s anger burns against David, and he says, “Why have you come down? With whom have you left those few sheep in the wilderness? I know your pride, and the naughtiness of your heart; for you have come down that you might see the battle.”
David says, “What have I now done? Is there not a cause?” He turns away from him toward another, and speaks like that again; and the people answer him again the same way.
David Before Saul · 17:31–40

When the words are heard which David speaks, they rehearse them before Saul; and he sends for him. David says to Saul, “Let no man’s heart fail because of him. Your servant will go and fight with this Philistine.”
Saul says to David, “You are not able to go against this Philistine to fight with him; for you are but a youth, and he a man of war from his youth.”

David says to Saul, “Your servant was keeping his father’s sheep; and when a lion or a bear came, and took a lamb out of the flock, I went out after him, and struck him, and rescued it out of his mouth. When he arose against me, I caught him by his beard, and struck him, and killed him. Your servant struck both the lion and the bear. This uncircumcised Philistine will be as one of them, since he has defied the armies of the living God.” David says, “YHWH who delivered me out of the paw of the lion, and out of the paw of the bear, he will deliver me out of the hand of this Philistine.”

Saul says to David, “Go! YHWH will be with you.” Saul dresses David with his clothing. He puts a helmet of brass on his head, and he clothes him with a coat of mail. David straps his sword on his clothing, and he tries to move; for he has not tested it. David says to Saul, “I can’t go with these; for I have not tested them.” Then David takes them off.

He takes his staff in his hand, and chooses for himself five smooth stones out of the brook, and puts them in the pouch of his shepherd’s bag which he has. His sling is in his hand; and he comes near to the Philistine.
The Battle · 17:41–54

The Philistine walks and comes near to David; and the man who bears the shield goes before him. When the Philistine looks around, and sees David, he disdains him; for he is but a youth, and ruddy, and has a good looking face. The Philistine says to David, “Am I a dog, that you come to me with sticks?” The Philistine curses David by his gods. The Philistine says to David, “Come to me, and I will give your flesh to the birds of the sky, and to the animals of the field.”

Then David says to the Philistine, “You come to me with a sword, with a spear, and with a javelin; but I come to you in the name of YHWH of hosts, the God of the armies of Israel, whom you have defied. Today, YHWH will deliver you into my hand. I will strike you, and take your head from off you. I will give the dead bodies of the army of the Philistines today to the birds of the sky, and to the wild animals of the earth; that all the earth may know that there is a God in Israel, and that all this assembly may know that YHWH doesn’t save with sword and spear; for the battle is YHWH’s, and he will give you into our hand.”

When the Philistine arises, and walks and comes near to meet David, David hurries, and runs toward the army to meet the Philistine. David puts his hand in his bag, takes a stone, and slings it, and strikes the Philistine in his forehead. The stone sinks into his forehead, and he falls on his face to the earth. So David prevails over the Philistine with a sling and with a stone, and strikes the Philistine, and kills him; but there is no sword in the hand of David. Then David runs, stands over the Philistine, takes his sword, draws it out of its sheath, kills him, and cuts off his head with it. When the Philistines see that their champion is dead, they flee. The men of Israel and of Judah arise and shout, and pursue the Philistines as far as Gai and to the gates of Ekron. The wounded of the Philistines falls down by the way to Shaaraim, even to Gath and to Ekron. The children of Israel return from chasing after the Philistines and they plunder their camp. David takes the head of the Philistine, and brings it to Jerusalem; but he puts his armor in his tent.
David Brought to Saul · 17:55–58
When Saul sees David go out against the Philistine, he says to Abner, the captain of the army, “Abner, whose son is this youth?”
Abner says, “As your soul lives, O king, I can’t tell.”
The king says, “Inquire whose son the young man is!”
As David returns from the slaughter of the Philistine, Abner takes him and brings him before Saul with the head of the Philistine in his hand. Saul says to him, “Whose son are you, you young man?”
David answers, “I am the son of your servant Jesse the Bethlehemite.”
Jonathan’s Covenant with David · 18:1–5

When he has finished speaking to Saul, the soul of Jonathan is knit with the soul of David, and Jonathan loves him as his own soul. Saul takes him that day, and would let him go no more home to his father’s house. Then Jonathan and David make a covenant, because he loves him as his own soul. Jonathan strips himself of the robe that is on him, and gives it to David, and his clothing, even including his sword, his bow, and his sash. David goes out wherever Saul sends him, and behaves himself wisely; and Saul sets him over the men of war. It is good in the sight of all the people, and also in the sight of Saul’s servants.
Saul’s Jealousy Awakens · 18:6–16

As they come, when David returns from the slaughter of the Philistine, the women come out of all the cities of Israel, singing and dancing, to meet king Saul, with tambourines, with joy, and with instruments of music. The women sing to one another as they play, and say,
“Saul has slain his thousands,
and David his ten thousands.”

Saul is very angry, and this saying displeases him. He says, “They have ascribed to David ten thousands, and to me they have ascribed only thousands. What can he have more but the kingdom?” Saul watches David from that day and forward. On the next day, an evil spirit from God comes mightily on Saul, and he prophesies in the middle of the house. David plays with his hand, as he does day by day. Saul has his spear in his hand; and Saul throws the spear, for he says, “I will pin David even to the wall!” David escapes from his presence twice. Saul is afraid of David, because YHWH is with him, and has departed from Saul. Therefore Saul removes him from his presence, and makes him his captain over a thousand; and he goes out and comes in before the people.

David behaves himself wisely in all his ways; and YHWH is with him. When Saul sees that he behaves himself very wisely, he stands in awe of him. But all Israel and Judah love David; for he goes out and comes in before them.
David and Michal · 18:17–30

Saul says to David, “Look, my elder daughter Merab, I will give her to you as wife. Only be valiant for me, and fight YHWH’s battles.” For Saul says, “Don’t let my hand be on him, but let the hand of the Philistines be on him.” David says to Saul, “Who am I, and what is my life, or my father’s family in Israel, that I should be son-in-law to the king?”

But at the time when Merab, Saul’s daughter, should have been given to David, she is given to Adriel the Meholathite as wife. Michal, Saul’s daughter, loves David; and they tell Saul, and the thing pleases him. Saul says, I will give her to him, that she may be a snare to him, and that the hand of the Philistines may be against him. Therefore Saul says to David, “You will today be my son-in-law a second time.” Saul commands his servants, “Talk with David secretly, and say, ‘Look, the king has delight in you, and all his servants love you. Now therefore be the king’s son-in-law.’”
Saul’s servants speak those words in the ears of David. David says, “Does it seem to you a light thing to be the king’s son-in-law, since I am a poor man, and little known?”
The servants of Saul tell him, saying, “David spoke like this.”

Saul says, “Tell David, ‘The king desires no dowry except one hundred foreskins of the Philistines, to be avenged of the king’s enemies.’” Now Saul thinks he would make David fall by the hand of the Philistines. When his servants tell David these words, it pleases David well to be the king’s son-in-law. Before the deadline, David arises and goes, he and his men, and kills two hundred men of the Philistines. Then David brings their foreskins, and they give them in full number to the king, that he might be the king’s son-in-law. Then Saul gives him Michal his daughter as wife. Saul sees and knows that YHWH is with David; and Michal, Saul’s daughter, loves him. Saul is even more afraid of David; and Saul is David’s enemy continually. Then the princes of the Philistines go out; and as often as they go out, David behaves himself more wisely than all the servants of Saul, so that his name is highly esteemed.
Jonathan Intercedes for David · 19:1–7

Saul speaks to Jonathan his son, and to all his servants, that they should kill David. But Jonathan, Saul’s son, greatly delighted in David. Jonathan tells David, saying, “Saul my father seeks to kill you. Now therefore, please take care of yourself in the morning, and live in a secret place, and hide yourself. I will go out and stand beside my father in the field where you are, and I will talk with my father about you; and if I see anything, I will tell you.”

Jonathan speaks good of David to Saul his father, and says to him, “Don’t let the king sin against his servant, against David; because he has not sinned against you, and because his works have been very good toward you; for he put his life in his hand, and struck the Philistine, and YHWH worked a great victory for all Israel. You saw it, and rejoiced. Why then will you sin against innocent blood, to kill David without a cause?”
Saul listens to the voice of Jonathan: and Saul swears, “As YHWH lives, he will not be put to death.”
Jonathan calls David, and Jonathan shows him all those things. Then Jonathan brings David to Saul, and he is in his presence, as before.
Saul’s Renewed Attempts · 19:8–17
There is war again. David goes out, and fights with the Philistines, and kills them with a great slaughter; and they flee before him.

An evil spirit from YHWH is on Saul, as he sits in his house with his spear in his hand; and David is playing with his hand. Saul seeks to pin David to the wall with the spear; but he slips away out of Saul’s presence, and he sticks the spear into the wall. David flees, and escapes that night. Saul sends messengers to David’s house, to watch him, and to kill him in the morning. Michal, David’s wife, tells him, saying, “If you don’t save your life tonight, tomorrow you will be killed.” So Michal lets David down through the window. He goes away, flees, and escapes. Michal takes the teraphim, and lays it in the bed, and puts a pillow of goats’ hair at its head, and covers it with clothes. When Saul sends messengers to take David, she says, “He is sick.”

Saul sends the messengers to see David, saying, “Bring him up to me in the bed, that I may kill him.” When the messengers come in, look, the teraphim is in the bed, with the pillow of goats’ hair at its head.
Saul says to Michal, “Why have you deceived me thus, and let my enemy go, so that he is escaped?”
Michal answers Saul, “He said to me, ‘Let me go! Why should I kill you?’”
David at Ramah with Samuel · 19:18–24

Now David flees and escapes, and comes to Samuel at Ramah, and tells him all that Saul has done to him. He and Samuel goes and lives in Naioth. Saul is told, saying, “Look, David is at Naioth in Ramah.”

Saul sends messengers to seize David: and when they see the company of the prophets prophesying, and Samuel standing as head over them, God’s Spirit comes on Saul’s messengers, and they also prophesy. When Saul is told, he sends other messengers, and they also prophesy. Saul sends messengers again the third time, and they also prophesy. Then he also goes to Ramah, and comes to the great well that is in Secu: and he asks, “Where are Samuel and David?”
One says, “Look, they are at Naioth in Ramah.”

He goes there to Naioth in Ramah. Then God’s Spirit comes on him also, and he goes on, and prophesies, until he comes to Naioth in Ramah. He also strips off his clothes, and he also prophesies before Samuel, and lies down naked all that day and all that night. Therefore they say, “Is Saul also among the prophets?”
David and Jonathan’s Covenant · 20:1–17
David flees from Naioth in Ramah, and comes and says before Jonathan, “What have I done? What is my iniquity? What is my sin before your father, that he seeks my life?”
He says to him, “Far from it; you will not die. Look, my father does nothing either great or small, but that he discloses it to me. Why would my father hide this thing from me? It is not so.”

David swears moreover, and says, “Your father knows well that I have found favor in your eyes; and he says, ‘Don’t let Jonathan know this, lest he be grieved:’ but truly as YHWH lives, and as your soul lives, there is but a step between me and death.”
Then Jonathan says to David, “Whatever your soul desires, I will even do it for you.”

David says to Jonathan, “Look, tomorrow is the new moon, and I should not fail to dine with the king; but let me go, that I may hide myself in the field to the third day at evening. If your father misses me at all, then say, ‘David earnestly asked leave of me that he might run to Bethlehem his city; for it is the yearly sacrifice there for all the family.’ If he says, ‘It is well;’ your servant will have peace: but if he is angry, then know that evil is determined by him. Therefore deal kindly with your servant; for you have brought your servant into a covenant of YHWH with you; but if there is iniquity in me, kill me yourself; for why should you bring me to your father?”
Jonathan says, “Far be it from you; for if I should at all know that evil were determined by my father to come on you, then wouldn’t I tell you that?”
Then David says to Jonathan, “Who will tell me if your father answers you roughly?”

Jonathan says to David, “Come, and let us go out into the field.” They both go out into the field. Jonathan says to David, “By YHWH, the God of Israel, when I have sounded my father about this time tomorrow, or the third day, look, if there is good toward David, won’t I then send to you, and disclose it to you? YHWH do so to Jonathan, and more also, should it please my father to do you evil, if I don’t disclose it to you, and send you away, that you may go in peace. May YHWH be with you, as he has been with my father. You will not only while yet I live show me the steadfast love of YHWH, that I not die; but you will also not cut off your kindness from my house forever; no, not when YHWH has cut off every one of the enemies of David from the surface of the earth.” So Jonathan makes a covenant with David’s house, saying, “YHWH will require it at the hand of David’s enemies.” Jonathan causes David to swear again, for the love that he has to him; for he loves him as he loves his own soul.
The Test at the New Moon Feast · 20:18–34

Then Jonathan says to him, “Tomorrow is the new moon, and you will be missed, because your seat will be empty. When you have stayed three days, go down quickly, and come to the place where you hid yourself when this started, and remain by the stone Ezel. I will shoot three arrows on its side, as though I shot at a mark. Look, I will send the boy, saying, ‘Go, find the arrows!’ If I tell the boy, ‘Look, the arrows are on this side of you. Take them;’ then come; for there is peace to you and no danger, as YHWH lives. But if I say this to the boy, ‘Look, the arrows are beyond you;’ then go your way; for YHWH has sent you away. Concerning the matter which you and I have spoken of, look, YHWH is between you and me forever.”

So David hides himself in the field. When the new moon has come, the king sits himself down to eat food. The king sits on his seat, as at other times, even on the seat by the wall; and Jonathan stands up, and Abner sits by Saul’s side, but David’s place is empty. Nevertheless Saul doesn’t say anything that day, for he thinks, “Something has happened to him. He is not clean. Surely he is not clean.”
On the next day after the new moon, the second day, David’s place is empty. Saul says to Jonathan his son, “Why doesn’t the son of Jesse come to eat, either yesterday, or today?”

Jonathan answers Saul, “David earnestly asked permission of me to go to Bethlehem. He said, ‘Please let me go, for our family has a sacrifice in the city. My brother has commanded me to be there. Now, if I have found favor in your eyes, please let me go away and see my brothers.’ Therefore he has not come to the king’s table.”

Then Saul’s anger burns against Jonathan, and he says to him, “You son of a perverse rebellious woman, don’t I know that you have chosen the son of Jesse to your own shame, and to the shame of your mother’s nakedness? For as long as the son of Jesse lives on the earth, you will not be established, nor will your kingdom. Therefore now send and bring him to me, for he will surely die!”
Jonathan answers Saul his father, and says to him, “Why should he be put to death? What has he done?”

Saul casts his spear at him to strike him. By this Jonathan knows that his father is determined to put David to death. So Jonathan arises from the table in fierce anger, and eats no food the second day of the month; for he is grieved for David, because his father has treated him shamefully.
Jonathan’s Warning and Farewell · 20:35–42

In the morning, Jonathan goes out into the field at the time appointed with David, and a little boy with him. He says to his boy, “Run, find now the arrows which I shoot.” As the boy runs, he shoots an arrow beyond him. When the boy has come to the place of the arrow which Jonathan has shot, Jonathan cries after the boy, and says, “Isn’t the arrow beyond you?” Jonathan cries after the boy, “Go fast! Hurry! Don’t delay!” Jonathan’s boy gathers up the arrows, and comes to his master. But the boy doesn’t know anything. Only Jonathan and David know the matter. Jonathan gives his weapons to his boy, and says to him, “Go, carry them to the city.”

As soon as the boy is gone, David arises out of the south, and falls on his face to the ground, and bows himself three times. They kiss one another, and weep one with another, and David weeps the most. Jonathan says to David, “Go in peace, because we have both sworn in YHWH’s name, saying, ‘YHWH is between me and you, and between my offspring and your offspring, forever.’” He arises and departs; and Jonathan goes into the city.
David at Nob · 21:1–9

Then David comes to Nob to Ahimelech the priest. Ahimelech comes to meet David trembling, and says to him, “Why are you alone, and no man with you?” David says to Ahimelech the priest, “The king has commanded me to do something, and has said to me, ‘Let no one know anything about the business about which I send you, and what I have commanded you. I have sent the young men to a certain place.’ Now therefore what is under your hand? Please give me five loaves of bread in my hand, or whatever is available.”
The priest answers David, and says, “I have no common bread, but there is holy bread; if only the young men have kept themselves from women.”

David answers the priest, and says to him, “Truly, women have been kept from us as usual these three days. When I came out, the vessels of the young men were holy, though it was only a common journey. How much more then today will their vessels be holy?” So the priest gives him holy bread; for there is no bread there but the show bread that is taken from before YHWH, to put hot bread in the day when it is taken away.

Now a certain man of the servants of Saul is there that day, detained before YHWH; and his name is Doeg the Edomite, the best of the herdsmen who belong to Saul. David says to Ahimelech, “Isn’t there here under your hand spear or sword? For I have neither brought my sword nor my weapons with me, because the king’s business required haste.”

The priest says, “Look, the sword of Goliath the Philistine, whom you killed in the valley of Elah, is here wrapped in a cloth behind the ephod. If you would like to take that, take it; for there is no other except that here.”
David says, “There is none like that. Give it to me.”
David at Gath · 21:10–15

David arises, and flees that day for fear of Saul, and goes to Achish the king of Gath. The servants of Achish say to him, “Isn’t this David the king of the land? Didn’t they sing to one another about him in dances, saying,
‘Saul has slain his thousands,
and David his ten thousands?’”

David lays up these words in his heart, and is very afraid of Achish the king of Gath. He changes his behavior before them, and pretends to be insane in their hands, and scribbles on the doors of the gate, and let his spittle fall down on his beard. Then Achish says to his servants, “Look, you see the man is insane. Why then have you brought him to me? Do I lack madmen, that you have brought this fellow to play the madman in my presence? Should this fellow come into my house?”
The Cave of Adullam · 22:1–5

David therefore departs from there, and escapes to the cave of Adullam. When his brothers and all his father’s house hear it, they go down there to him. Everyone who is in distress, everyone who is in debt, and everyone who is discontented, gathers themselves to him; and he becomes captain over them. There are with him about four hundred men. David goes from there to Mizpeh of Moab, and he says to the king of Moab, “Please let my father and my mother come out with you, until I know what God will do for me.” He brings them before the king of Moab; and they live with him all the time that David is in the stronghold. The prophet Gad says to David, “Don’t stay in the stronghold. Depart, and go into the land of Judah.”
Then David departs, and comes into the forest of Hereth.
Saul’s Paranoid Court · 22:6–10

Saul hears that David is discovered, with the men who are with him. Now Saul is sitting in Gibeah, under the tamarisk tree in Ramah, with his spear in his hand, and all his servants are standing around him. Saul says to his servants who stand around him, “Hear now, you Benjamites! Will the son of Jesse give everyone of you fields and vineyards? Will he make you all captains of thousands and captains of hundreds, that all of you have conspired against me, and there is no one who discloses to me when my son makes a treaty with the son of Jesse, and there is none of you who is sorry for me, or discloses to me that my son has stirred up my servant against me, to lie in wait, as it is today?”

Then Doeg the Edomite, who stands by the servants of Saul, answers and says, “I saw the son of Jesse coming to Nob, to Ahimelech the son of Ahitub. He inquired of YHWH for him, gave him food, and gave him the sword of Goliath the Philistine.”
The Massacre at Nob · 22:11–23
Then the king sends to call Ahimelech the priest, the son of Ahitub, and all his father’s house, the priests who are in Nob; and they all come to the king. Saul says, “Hear now, you son of Ahitub.”
He answers, “Here I am, my lord.”

Saul says to him, “Why have you conspired against me, you and the son of Jesse, in that you have given him bread, and a sword, and have inquired of God for him, that he should rise against me, to lie in wait, as it is today?”

Then Ahimelech answers the king, and says, “Who among all your servants is so faithful as David, who is the king’s son-in-law, and is taken into your council, and is honorable in your house? Have I today begun to inquire of God for him? Be it far from me! Don’t let the king impute anything to his servant, nor to all the house of my father; for your servant knows nothing of all this, less or more.”

The king says, “You will surely die, Ahimelech, you, and all your father’s house.” The king says to the guard who stands about him, “Turn, and kill the priests of YHWH; because their hand also is with David, and because they knew that he fled, and didn’t disclose it to me.” But the servants of the king wouldn’t put out their hand to fall on the priests of YHWH.
The king says to Doeg, “Turn and attack the priests!”

Doeg the Edomite turns, and he attacks the priests, and he kills on that day eighty-five people who wear a linen ephod. He strikes Nob, the city of the priests, with the edge of the sword, both men and women, children and nursing babies, and cattle and donkeys and sheep, with the edge of the sword. One of the sons of Ahimelech, the son of Ahitub, named Abiathar, escapes, and flees after David. Abiathar tells David that Saul has slain YHWH’s priests.

David says to Abiathar, “I knew on that day, when Doeg the Edomite was there, that he would surely tell Saul. I am responsible for the death of all the persons of your father’s house. Stay with me. Don’t be afraid, for he who seeks my life seeks your life. For you will be safe with me.”
David Saves Keilah · 23:1–13
David is told, “Look, the Philistines are fighting against Keilah, and are robbing the threshing floors.”
Therefore David inquires of YHWH, saying, “Should I go and strike these Philistines?”
YHWH says to David, “Go strike the Philistines, and save Keilah.”
David’s men say to him, “Look, we are afraid here in Judah. How much more then if we go to Keilah against the armies of the Philistines?”
Then David inquires of YHWH yet again. YHWH answers him, and says, “Arise, go down to Keilah; for I will deliver the Philistines into your hand.”

David and his men go to Keilah, and fight with the Philistines, and bring away their livestock, and kill them with a great slaughter. So David saves the inhabitants of Keilah. When Abiathar the son of Ahimelech flees to David to Keilah, he comes down with an ephod in his hand.

Saul is told that David has come to Keilah. Saul says, “God has delivered him into my hand; for he is shut in by entering into a town that has gates and bars.” Saul summons all the people to war, to go down to Keilah, to besiege David and his men. David knows that Saul is devising mischief against him; and he says to Abiathar the priest, “Bring the ephod here.” Then David says, “O YHWH, the God of Israel, your servant has surely heard that Saul seeks to come to Keilah, to destroy the city for my sake. Will the men of Keilah deliver me up into his hand? Will Saul come down, as your servant has heard? YHWH, the God of Israel, I beg you, tell your servant.”
YHWH says, “He will come down.”
Then David says, “Will the men of Keilah deliver me and my men into the hand of Saul?”
YHWH says, “They will deliver you up.”
Then David and his men, who are about six hundred, arise and depart out of Keilah, and go wherever they can go. Saul is told that David is escaped from Keilah; and he gives up going there.
Jonathan’s Last Visit · 23:14–18

David stays in the wilderness in the strongholds, and remains in the hill country in the wilderness of Ziph. Saul seeks him every day, but God doesn’t deliver him into his hand. David sees that Saul has come out to seek his life. David is in the wilderness of Ziph in the wood.

Jonathan, Saul’s son, arises, and goes to David into the woods, and strengthens his hand in God. He says to him, “Don’t be afraid; for the hand of Saul my father won’t find you; and you will be king over Israel, and I will be next to you; and Saul my father knows that also.” They both make a covenant before YHWH. Then David stays in the woods, and Jonathan goes to his house.
The Ziphites, the Maonites, and the Rock of Escape · 23:19–29

Then the Ziphites come up to Saul to Gibeah, saying, “Doesn’t David hide himself with us in the strongholds in the woods, in the hill of Hachilah, which is on the south of the desert? Now therefore, O king, come down. According to all the desire of your soul to come down; and our part will be to deliver him up into the king’s hand.”

Saul says, “You are blessed by YHWH; for you have had compassion on me. Please go make yet more sure, and know and see his place where his haunt is, and who has seen him there; for I have been told that he deals very crafty. See therefore, and take knowledge of all the lurking places where he hides himself, and come again to me with certainty, and I will go with you. It will happen, if he is in the land, that I will search him out among all the thousands of Judah.”

They arise, and go to Ziph before Saul: but David and his men are in the wilderness of Maon, in the Arabah on the south of the desert. Saul and his men go to seek him. When David is told, he goes down to the rock, and stays in the wilderness of Maon. When Saul hears that, he pursues David in the wilderness of Maon. Saul goes on this side of the mountain, and David and his men on that side of the mountain; and David hurry to get away for fear of Saul; for Saul and his men surround David and his men to take them. But a messenger comes to Saul, saying, “Hurry and come; for the Philistines have made a raid on the land!” So Saul returns from pursuing David, and goes against the Philistines. Therefore they call that place Sela Hammahlekoth.
David goes up from there, and lives in the strongholds of En Gedi.
David Spares Saul in the Cave · 24:1–7

When Saul has returned from following the Philistines, he is told, “Look, David is in the wilderness of En Gedi.” Then Saul takes three thousand chosen men out of all Israel, and goes to seek David and his men on the rocks of the wild goats. He comes to the sheep pens by the way, where there is a cave; and Saul goes in to relieve himself. Now David and his men are staying in the innermost parts of the cave. David’s men say to him, “Look, the day of which YHWH said to you, ‘Look, I will deliver your enemy into your hand, and you will do to him as it will seem good to you.’” Then David arises, and cuts off the skirt of Saul’s robe secretly. Afterward, David’s heart strikes him, because he has cut off Saul’s skirt. He says to his men, “YHWH forbid that I should do this thing to my lord, YHWH’s anointed, to stretch out my hand against him, since he is YHWH’s anointed.” So David checks his men with these words, and doesn’t allow them to rise against Saul. Saul rises up out of the cave, and goes on his way.
David’s Appeal to Saul · 24:8–15
David also arises afterward, and goes out of the cave, and cries after Saul, saying, “My lord the king!”

When Saul looks behind him, David bows with his face to the earth, and shows respect. David says to Saul, “Why do you listen to men’s words, saying, ‘Look, David seeks to harm you?’ Look, today your eyes have seen how YHWH had delivered you today into my hand in the cave. Some urged me to kill you; but I spared you; and I said, I will not stretch out my hand against my lord; for he is YHWH’s anointed. Moreover, my father, look, yes, see the skirt of your robe in my hand; for in that I cut off the skirt of your robe, and didn’t kill you, know and see that there is neither evil nor disobedience in my hand, and I have not sinned against you, though you hunt for my life to take it. May YHWH judge between me and you, and may YHWH avenge me of you; but my hand will not be on you. As the proverb of the ancients says, ‘Out of the wicked comes wickedness;’ but my hand will not be on you. Against whom has the king of Israel come out? Whom do you pursue? A dead dog? A flea? May YHWH therefore be judge, and give sentence between me and you, and see, and plead my cause, and deliver me out of your hand.”
Saul’s Response · 24:16–22

It comes to pass, when David has finished speaking these words to Saul, that Saul says, “Is that your voice, my son David?” Saul lifts up his voice, and wept. He says to David, “You are more righteous than I; for you have done good to me, whereas I have done evil to you. You have declared today how you have dealt well with me, because when YHWH had delivered me up into your hand, you didn’t kill me. For if a man finds his enemy, will he let him go away unharmed? Therefore may YHWH reward you good for that which you have done to me today. Now, look, I know that you will surely be king, and that the kingdom of Israel will be established in your hand. Swear now therefore to me by YHWH, that you will not cut off my offspring after me, and that you will not destroy my name out of my father’s house.”
David swears to Saul. Saul goes home, but David and his men go up to the stronghold.
The Death of Samuel · 25:1
Samuel dies; and all Israel gathers themselves together, and mourns for him, and buries him at his house at Ramah.
Then David arises, and goes down to the wilderness of Paran.
Nabal and Abigail · 25:2–13

There is a man in Maon, whose possessions are in Carmel; and the man is very great. He has three thousand sheep and a thousand goats; and he is shearing his sheep in Carmel. Now the name of the man is Nabal; and the name of his wife Abigail. This woman is intelligent and has a beautiful face; but the man is surly and evil in his doings. He is of the house of Caleb. David hears in the wilderness that Nabal is shearing his sheep. David sends ten young men, and David says to the young men, “Go up to Carmel, and go to Nabal, and greet him in my name. Tell him, ‘Long life to you! Peace be to you, and peace be to your house, and peace be to all that you have. Now I have heard that you have shearers. Your shepherds have now been with us, and we didn’t harm them, neither was there anything missing from them, all the while they were in Carmel. Ask your young men, and they will tell you. Therefore let the young men find favor in your eyes; for we come on a good day. Please give whatever comes to your hand, to your servants, and to your son David.’”
When David’s young men come, they speak to Nabal all those words in the name of David, and wait.

Nabal answers David’s servants, and says, “Who is David? Who is the son of Jesse? There are many servants who break away from their masters these days. Should I then take my bread, my water, and my meat that I have killed for my shearers, and give it to men who I don’t know where they come from?”
So David’s young men turn on their way, and go back, and come and tell him all these words.
David says to his men, “Every man put on his sword!”
Every man puts on his sword. David also puts on his sword. About four hundred men follow David, and two hundred stays by the baggage.
Abigail’s Intervention · 25:14–35

But one of the young men tells Abigail, Nabal’s wife, saying, “Look, David sent messengers out of the wilderness to Greet our master; and he insulted them. But the men were very good to us, and we were not harmed, and we didn’t miss anything, as long as we went with them, when we were in the fields. They were a wall to us both by night and by day, all the while we were with them keeping the sheep. Now therefore know and consider what you will do; for evil is determined against our master, and against all his house; for he is such a worthless fellow that one can’t speak to him.”

Then Abigail hurries and takes two hundred loaves of bread, two bottles of wine, five sheep ready dressed, five seahs of parched grain, one hundred clusters of raisins, and two hundred cakes of figs, and lays them on donkeys. She says to her young men, “Go on before me. Look, I am coming after you.” But she doesn’t tell her husband, Nabal. As she rides on her donkey, and comes down by the covert of the mountain, that look, David and his men come down toward her, and she meets them.

Now David has said, “Surely in vain I have kept all that this fellow has in the wilderness, so that nothing was missed of all that pertained to him. He has returned me evil for good. God do so to the enemies of David, and more also, if I leave of all that belongs to him by the morning light so much as one who urinates on a wall.”

When Abigail sees David, she hurries and gets off her donkey, and falls before David on her face, and bows herself to the ground. She falls at his feet, and says, “On me, my lord, on me be the blame! Please let your servant speak in your ears. Hear the words of your servant. Please don’t let my lord pay attention to this worthless fellow, Nabal; for as his name is, so is he. Nabal is his name, and folly is with him; but I, your servant, didn’t see my lord’s young men, whom you sent. Now therefore, my lord, as YHWH lives, and as your soul lives, since YHWH has withheld you from blood guiltiness, and from avenging yourself with your own hand, now therefore let your enemies, and those who seek evil to my lord, be as Nabal. Now this present which your servant has brought to my lord, let it be given to the young men who follow my lord. Please forgive the trespass of your servant. For YHWH will certainly make my lord a sure house, because my lord fights YHWH’s battles. Evil will not be found in you all your days. Though men may rise up to pursue you, and to seek your soul, yet the soul of my lord will be bound in the bundle of life with YHWH your God. He will sling out the souls of your enemies, as from the hollow of a sling. It will come to pass, when YHWH has done to my lord according to all the good that he has spoken concerning you, and has appointed you prince over Israel, that this will be no grief to you, nor offense of heart to my lord, either that you have shed blood without cause, or that my lord has avenged himself. When YHWH has dealt well with my lord, then remember your servant.”

David says to Abigail, “Blessed is YHWH, the God of Israel, who sent you today to meet me! Blessed is your discretion, and blessed are you, who have kept me today from blood guiltiness, and from avenging myself with my own hand. For indeed, as YHWH, the God of Israel, lives, who has withheld me from harming you, unless you had hurried and come to meet me, surely there wouldn’t have been left to Nabal by the morning light so much as one who urinates on a wall.”
So David receives from her hand that which she has brought him. Then he says to her, “Go up in peace to your house. Look, I have listened to your voice, and have granted your request.”
Nabal’s Death and David’s Marriages · 25:36–44

Abigail comes to Nabal; and look, he holds a feast in his house, like the feast of a king. Nabal’s heart is merry within him, for he is very drunk. Therefore she tells him nothing, until the morning light. In the morning, when the wine has gone out of Nabal, his wife tells him these things, and his heart dies within him, and he becomes as a stone. About ten days later, YHWH strikes Nabal, so that he dies. When David hears that Nabal is dead, he says, “Blessed is YHWH, who has pleaded the cause of my reproach from the hand of Nabal, and has kept back his servant from evil. YHWH has returned the evildoing of Nabal on his own head.” David sends and speaks concerning Abigail, to take her to himself as wife. When David’s servants have come to Abigail to Carmel, they speak to her, saying, “David has sent us to you, to take you to him as wife.”

She arises, and bows herself with her face to the earth, and says, “Look, your servant is a servant to wash the feet of the servants of my lord.” Abigail hurries, and arises, and rides on a donkey, with five ladies of hers who follow her; and she goes after the messengers of David, and becomes his wife. David also takes Ahinoam of Jezreel; and they both become his wives. Now Saul has given Michal his daughter, David’s wife, to Palti the son of Laish, who is of Gallim.
David Enters Saul’s Camp · 26:1–12

The Ziphites come to Saul to Gibeah, saying, “Doesn’t David hide himself in the hill of Hachilah, which is before the desert?” Then Saul arises, and goes down to the wilderness of Ziph, having three thousand chosen men of Israel with him, to seek David in the wilderness of Ziph. Saul encamps in the hill of Hachilah, which is before the desert, by the way. But David stays in the wilderness, and he sees that Saul comes after him into the wilderness. David therefore sends out spies, and understands that Saul has certainly come. Then David arises, and comes to the place where Saul has encamped; and David sees the place where Saul lay, with Abner the son of Ner, the captain of his army. Saul lies within the place of the wagons, and the people are encamped around him.
Then David answers and says to Ahimelech the Hittite, and to Abishai the son of Zeruiah, brother of Joab, saying, “Who will go down with me to Saul to the camp?”

Abishai says, “I will go down with you.” So David and Abishai come to the people by night: and, look, Saul lies sleeping within the place of the wagons, with his spear sticks in the ground at his head; and Abner and the people lay around him. Then Abishai says to David, “God has delivered up your enemy into your hand today. Now therefore please let me strike him with the spear to the earth at one stroke, and I will not strike him the second time.”

David says to Abishai, “Don’t destroy him; for who can stretch out his hand against YHWH’s anointed, and be guiltless?” David says, “As YHWH lives, YHWH will strike him; or his day will come to die; or he will go down into battle and perish. YHWH forbid that I should stretch out my hand against YHWH’s anointed; but now please take the spear that is at his head, and the jar of water, and let us go.”

So David takes the spear and the jar of water from Saul’s head; and they go away: and no man sees it, or knows it, nor does any awake; for they are all asleep, because a deep sleep from YHWH are fallen on them.
David’s Challenge from the Hillside · 26:13–20

Then David goes over to the other side, and stands on the top of the mountain afar off; a great space being between them; and David cries to the people, and to Abner the son of Ner, saying, “Don’t you answer, Abner?”
Then Abner answers, “Who are you who cries to the king?”

David says to Abner, “Aren’t you a man? Who is like you in Israel? Why then have you not kept watch over your lord, the king? For one of the people came in to destroy the king your lord. This thing isn’t good that you have done. As YHWH lives, you are worthy to die, because you have not kept watch over your lord, YHWH’s anointed. Now see where the king’s spear is, and the jar of water that was at his head.”
Saul knows David’s voice, and says, “Is this your voice, my son David?”

David says, “It is my voice, my lord, O king.” He says, “Why does my lord pursue his servant? For what have I done? What evil is in my hand? Now therefore, please let my lord the king hear the words of his servant. If it is so that YHWH has stirred you up against me, let him accept an offering. But if it is the children of men, they are cursed before YHWH; for they have driven me out today that I shouldn’t cling to YHWH’s inheritance, saying, ‘Go, serve other gods!’ Now therefore, don’t let my blood fall to the earth away from the presence of YHWH; for the king of Israel has come out to seek a flea, as when one hunts a partridge in the mountains.”
Saul’s Second Confession · 26:21–25
Then Saul says, “I have sinned. Return, my son David; for I will no more do you harm, because my life was precious in your eyes today. Look, I have played the fool, and have erred exceedingly.”

David answers, “Look the spear, O king! Then let one of the young men come over and get it. YHWH will render to every man his righteousness and his faithfulness; because YHWH delivered you into my hand today, and I wouldn’t stretch out my hand against YHWH’s anointed. Look, as your life was respected today in my eyes, so let my life be respected in YHWH’s eyes, and let him deliver me out of all oppression.”
Then Saul says to David, “You are blessed, my son David. You will both do mightily, and will surely prevail.” So David goes his way, and Saul returns to his place.
David Defects to Gath · 27:1–4

David says in his heart, “I will now perish one day by the hand of Saul. There is nothing better for me than that I should escape into the land of the Philistines; and Saul will despair of me, to seek me any more in all the borders of Israel. So should I escape out of his hand.” David arises, and passes over, he and the six hundred men who are with him, to Achish the son of Maoch, king of Gath. David lives with Achish at Gath, he and his men, every man with his household, even David with his two wives, Ahinoam the Jezreelitess, and Abigail the Carmelitess, Nabal’s wife. Saul is told that David has fled to Gath: and he seeks no more again for him.
David at Ziklag · 27:5–12
