David says to Achish, “If now I have found favor in your eyes, let them give me a place in one of the cities in the country, that I may dwell there. For why should your servant dwell in the royal city with you?” Then Achish gives him Ziklag that day: therefore Ziklag belongs to the kings of Judah to this day. The number of the days that David lives in the country of the Philistines is a full year and four months. David and his men go up and raid the Geshurites, the Girzites, and the Amalekites; for those are the inhabitants of the land, who are of old, on the way to Shur, even to the land of Egypt. David strikes the land, and saves no man or woman alive, and takes away the sheep, the cattle, the donkeys, the camels, and the clothing. Then he returns, and comes to Achish.
Achish says, “Against whom have you made a raid today?”

David says, “Against the South of Judah, against the South of the Jerahmeelites, and against the South of the Kenites.” David saves neither man nor woman alive, to bring them to Gath, saying, “Lest they should tell about us, saying, ‘David did this, and this has been his way all the time he has lived in the country of the Philistines.’”
Achish believes David, saying, “He has made his people Israel utterly to abhor him. Therefore he will be my servant forever.”
The Philistine Muster and Saul’s Fear · 28:1–7
In those days, the Philistines gathers their armies together for warfare, to fight with Israel. Achish says to David, “Know assuredly that you will go out with me in the army, you and your men.”
David says to Achish, “Therefore you will know what your servant can do.”
Achish says to David, “Therefore I will make you my bodyguard forever.”

Now Samuel is dead, and all Israel has mourned for him, and buries him in Ramah, even in his own city. Saul has sent away those who have familiar spirits and the wizards out of the land. The Philistines gathers themselves together, and comes and encamps in Shunem; and Saul gathers all Israel together, and they encamp in Gilboa. When Saul sees the army of the Philistines, he is afraid, and his heart trembles greatly. When Saul inquires of YHWH, YHWH doesn’t answer him by dreams, by Urim, or by prophets. Then Saul says to his servants, “Seek for me a woman who has a familiar spirit, that I may go to her, and inquire of her.”
His servants say to him, “Look, there is a woman who has a familiar spirit at Endor.”
The Medium at En-dor · 28:8–19

Saul disguises himself and puts on other clothing, and goes, he and two men with him, and they come to the woman by night. Then he says, “Please consult for me by the familiar spirit, and bring me up whomever I will name to you.”

The woman says to him, “Look, you know what Saul has done, how he has cut off those who have familiar spirits, and the wizards, out of the land. Why then do you lay a snare for my life, to cause me to die?”
Saul swears to her by YHWH, saying, “As YHWH lives, no punishment will happen to you for this thing.”
Then the woman says, “Whom should I bring up to you?”
He says, “Bring Samuel up for me.”
When the woman sees Samuel, she cries with a loud voice; and the woman speaks to Saul, saying, “Why have you deceived me? For you are Saul!”
The king says to her, “Don’t be afraid! What do you see?”
The woman says to Saul, “I see a god coming up out of the earth.”
He says to her, “What does he look like?”
She says, “An old man comes up. He is covered with a robe.” Saul perceives that it is Samuel, and he bows with his face to the ground, and shows respect.
Samuel says to Saul, “Why have you disturbed me, to bring me up?”

Saul answers, “I am very distressed; for the Philistines make war against me, and God has departed from me, and answers me no more, by prophets, or by dreams. Therefore I have called you, that you may make known to me what I will do.”

Samuel says, “Why then do you ask me, since YHWH has departed from you and has become your adversary? YHWH has done to you as he spoke by me. YHWH has torn the kingdom out of your hand, and given it to your neighbor, even to David. Because you didn’t obey YHWH’s voice, and didn’t execute his fierce wrath on Amalek, therefore YHWH has done this thing to you today. Moreover YHWH will deliver Israel also with you into the hand of the Philistines; and tomorrow you and your sons will be with me. YHWH will deliver the army of Israel also into the hand of the Philistines.”
Saul’s Collapse and Restoration · 28:20–25
Then Saul falls immediately his full length on the earth, and is terrified, because of Samuel’s words. There is no strength in him; for he has eaten no bread all day long or all night long.

The woman comes to Saul, and sees that he is very troubled, and says to him, “Look, your servant has listened to your voice, and I have put my life in my hand, and have listened to your words which you spoke to me. Now therefore, please listen also to the voice of your servant, and let me set a morsel of bread before you. Eat, that you may have strength, when you go on your way.”

But he refuses, and says, “I will not eat.” But his servants, together with the woman, constrain him; and he listens to their voice. So he arises from the earth and sits on the bed. The woman has a fattened calf in the house. She hurries and kills it; and she takes flour, and kneads it, and bakes unleavened bread of it. She brings it before Saul, and before his servants; and they eat. Then they rise up, and go away that night.
David Dismissed from the Philistine Army · 29:1–11

Now the Philistines gathers together all their armies to Aphek; and the Israelites encamp by the spring which is in Jezreel. The lords of the Philistines pass on by hundreds and by thousands; and David and his men pass on in the rear with Achish.
Then the princes of the Philistines say, “What about these Hebrews?”

Achish says to the princes of the Philistines, “Isn’t this David, the servant of Saul the king of Israel, who has been with me these days, or rather these years, and I have found no fault in him since he fell away to today?”

But the princes of the Philistines are angry with him; and the princes of the Philistines say to him, “Make the man return, that he may go back to his place where you have appointed him, and let him not go down with us to battle, lest in the battle he become an adversary to us. For with what should this fellow reconcile himself to his lord? Should it not be with the heads of these men? Isn’t this David, of whom people sang to one another in dances, saying,
‘Saul has slain his thousands,
and David his ten thousands?’”

Then Achish calls David, and says to him, “As YHWH lives, you have been upright, and your going out and your coming in with me in the army is good in my sight; for I have not found evil in you since the day of your coming to me to this day. Nevertheless, the lords don’t favor you. Therefore now return, and go in peace, that you not displease the lords of the Philistines.”
David says to Achish, “But what have I done? What have you found in your servant so long as I have been before you to this day, that I may not go and fight against the enemies of my lord the king?”

Achish answers David, “I know that you are good in my sight, as an angel of God. Notwithstanding the princes of the Philistines have said, ‘He will not go up with us to the battle.’ Therefore now rise up early in the morning with the servants of your lord who have come with you; and as soon as you are up early in the morning, and have light, depart.”
So David rises up early, he and his men, to depart in the morning, to return into the land of the Philistines, and the Philistines goes up to Jezreel.
The Destruction of Ziklag · 30:1–6

When David and his men have come to Ziklag on the third day, the Amalekites have made a raid on the South, and on Ziklag, and have struck Ziklag, and burn it with fire, and have taken captive the women and all who are in it, both small and great. They don’t kill any, but carry them off, and go their way. When David and his men come to the city, look, it is burned with fire; and their wives, their sons, and their daughters are taken captive. Then David and the people who are with him lift up their voice and weep until they have no more power to weep. David’s two wives are taken captive, Ahinoam the Jezreelitess, and Abigail the wife of Nabal the Carmelite. David is greatly distressed; for the people speak of stoning him, because the souls of all the people are grieved, every man for his sons and for his daughters; but David strengthens himself in YHWH his God.
David Pursues the Amalekites · 30:7–20
David says to Abiathar the priest, the son of Ahimelech, “Please bring the ephod here to me.”
Abiathar brings the ephod to David. David inquires of YHWH, saying, “If I pursue after this troop, will I overtake them?”
He answers him, “Pursue; for you will surely overtake them, and will without fail recover all.”

So David goes, he and the six hundred men who are with him, and comes to the brook Besor, where those who are left behind stayed. But David pursues, he and four hundred men; for two hundred stays behind, who are so faint that they can’t go over the brook Besor. They find an Egyptian in the field, and bring him to David, and give him bread, and he eats; and they give him water to drink. They give him a piece of a cake of figs, and two clusters of raisins. When he has eaten, his spirit comes again to him; for he has eaten no bread, and drinks no water for three days and three nights. David asks him, “To whom do you belong? Where are you from?”

He says, “I am a young man of Egypt, servant to an Amalekite; and my master left me, because three days ago I got sick. We made a raid on the South of the Cherethites, and on that which belongs to Judah, and on the South of Caleb; and we burned Ziklag with fire.”
David says to him, “Will you bring me down to this troop?”
He says, “Swear to me by God that you will not kill me and not deliver me up into the hands of my master, and I will bring you down to this troop.”

When he has brought him down, look, they are spread around over all the ground, eating, drinking, and dancing, because of all the great plunder that they have taken out of the land of the Philistines, and out of the land of Judah. David strikes them from the twilight even to the evening of the next day. Not a man of them escapes from there, except four hundred young men, who ride on camels and flee. David recovers all that the Amalekites have taken; and David rescues his two wives. There is nothing lacking to them, neither small nor great, neither sons nor daughters, neither plunder, nor anything that they have taken to them. David brings back all. David takes all the flocks and the herds, which they drive before those other livestock, and says, “This is David’s plunder.”
The Division of Spoil · 30:21–31

David comes to the two hundred men, who are so faint that they can not follow David, whom also they have made to stay at the brook Besor; and they go out to meet David, and to meet the people who are with him. When David comes near to the people, he greets them. Then all the wicked men and worthless fellows, of those who go with David, answer and say, “Because they didn’t go with us, we will not give them anything of the plunder that we have recovered, except to every man his wife and his children, that he may lead them away, and depart.”

Then David says, “Do not do so, my brothers, with that which YHWH has given to us, who has preserved us, and delivered the troop that came against us into our hand. Who will listen to you in this matter? For as his share is who goes down to the battle, so will his share be who stays with the baggage. They will share alike.” It is so from that day forward, that he makes it a statute and an ordinance for Israel to this day. When David comes to Ziklag, he sends some of the plunder to the elders of Judah, even to his friends, saying, “Look, a present for you from the plunder of YHWH’s enemies.” He sends it to those who are in Bethel, to those who are in Ramoth of the South, to those who are in Jattir, to those who are in Aroer, to those who are in Siphmoth, to those who are in Eshtemoa, to those who are in Racal, to those who are in the cities of the Jerahmeelites, to those who are in the cities of the Kenites, to those who are in Hormah, to those who are in Borashan, to those who are in Athach, to those who are in Hebron, and to all the places where David himself and his men use to stay.
The Death of Saul · 31:1–7

Now the Philistines fights against Israel; and the men of Israel flee from before the Philistines, and fall down slain on Mount Gilboa. The Philistines overtakes Saul and on his sons; and the Philistines kills Jonathan, Abinadab, and Malchishua, the sons of Saul. The battle goes hard against Saul, and the archers overtake him; and he is greatly distressed by reason of the archers. Then Saul says to his armor bearer, “Draw your sword, and thrust me through with it, lest these uncircumcised come and thrust me through, and abuse me!” But his armor bearer would not; for he is terrified. Therefore Saul takes his sword, and falls on it. When his armor bearer sees that Saul is dead, he likewise falls on his sword, and dies with him. So Saul dies, and his three sons, and his armor bearer, and all his men, that same day together.

When the men of Israel who are on the other side of the valley, and those who are beyond the Jordan, see that the men of Israel flee, and that Saul and his sons are dead, they abandon the cities and flee; and the Philistines comes and lives in them.
The Philistines Dishonor Saul · 31:8–10

On the next day, when the Philistines comes to strip the slain, they find Saul and his three sons fallen on Mount Gilboa. They cut off his head, strip off his armor, and send into the land of the Philistines all around, to carry the news to the house of their idols, and to the people. They put his armor in the house of the Ashtaroth, and they fasten his body to the wall of Beth Shan.
The Men of Jabesh-gilead Honor Saul · 31:11–13

When the inhabitants of Jabesh Gilead hear what the Philistines has done to Saul, all the valiant men arise, go all night, and take the body of Saul and the bodies of his sons from the wall of Beth Shan; and they come to Jabesh, and burn them there. They take their bones and bury them under the tamarisk tree in Jabesh, and fast seven days.
The Messenger from Jezreel · 1:1–16

After the death of Saul, when David has returned from the slaughter of the Amalekites, and David has stayed two days in Ziklag; on the third day, look, a man comes out of the camp from Saul, with his clothes torn, and earth on his head. When he comes to David, he falls to the earth, and shows respect.
David says to him, “Where do you come from?”
He says to him, “I have escaped out of the camp of Israel.”
David says to him, “How did it go? Please tell me.”
He answers, “The people have fled from the battle, and many of the people also have fallen and are dead. Saul and Jonathan his son are dead also.”
David says to the young man who tells him, “How do you know that Saul and Jonathan his son are dead?”

The young man who tells him says, “As I happened by chance on Mount Gilboa, look, Saul was leaning on his spear; and look, the chariots and the horsemen followed close behind him. When he looked behind him, he saw me, and called to me. I answered, ‘Here I am.’ He said to me, ‘Who are you?’ I answered him, ‘I am an Amalekite.’ He said to me, ‘Please stand beside me, and kill me; for anguish has taken hold of me, because my life lingers in me.’ So I stood beside him and killed him, because I was sure that he could not live after that he had fallen. I took the crown that was on his head and the bracelet that was on his arm, and have brought them here to my lord.”

Then David takes hold on his clothes, and tears them; and all the men who are with him do likewise. They mourn, wept, and fast until evening, for Saul, and for Jonathan his son, and for the people of YHWH, and for the house of Israel; because they have fallen by the sword. David says to the young man who tells him, “Where are you from?”
He answers, “I am the son of a foreigner, an Amalekite.”

David says to him, “Why were you not afraid to stretch out your hand to destroy YHWH’s anointed?” David calls one of the young men, and says, “Go near, and cut him down!” He strikes him so that he dies. David says to him, “Your blood be on your head; for your mouth has testified against you, saying, ‘I have slain YHWH’s anointed.’”
The Song of the Bow · 1:17–27
David laments with this lamentation over Saul and over Jonathan his son (and he commands them to teach the children of Judah the song of the bow; look, it is written in the book of Jashar):
“Your glory, Israel, was slain on your high places!
How the mighty have fallen!
Don’t tell it in Gath.
Don’t publish it in the streets of Ashkelon,
lest the daughters of the Philistines rejoice,
lest the daughters of the uncircumcised triumph.
You mountains of Gilboa,
let there be no dew or rain on you, and no fields of offerings;
For there the shield of the mighty was defiled and cast away,
The shield of Saul was not anointed with oil.
From the blood of the slain,
from the fat of the mighty,
Jonathan’s bow didn’t turn back.
Saul’s sword didn’t return empty.
Saul and Jonathan were lovely and pleasant in their lives.
In their death, they were not divided.
They were swifter than eagles.
They were stronger than lions.
You daughters of Israel, weep over Saul,
who clothed you delicately in scarlet,
who put ornaments of gold on your clothing.
How the mighty have fallen in the middle of the battle!
Jonathan was slain on your high places.
I am distressed for you, my brother Jonathan.
You have been very pleasant to me.
Your love to me was wonderful,
passing the love of women.
How the mighty have fallen,
and the weapons of war have perished!”
David Anointed at Hebron · 2:1–7
After this, David inquires of YHWH, saying, “Should I go up into any of the cities of Judah?”
YHWH says to him, “Go up.”
David says, “Where should I go up?”
He says, “To Hebron.”

So David goes up there with his two wives, Ahinoam the Jezreelitess, and Abigail the wife of Nabal the Carmelite. David brings up his men who are with him, every man with his household. They live in the cities of Hebron. The men of Judah come, and there they anoint David king over the house of Judah. They tell David, “The men of Jabesh Gilead were those who buried Saul.” David sends messengers to the men of Jabesh Gilead, and says to them, “Blessed are you by YHWH, that you have shown this kindness to your lord, even to Saul, and have buried him. Now may YHWH show steadfast love and truth to you. I also will reward you for this kindness, because you have done this thing. Now therefore let your hands be strong, and be valiant; for Saul your lord is dead, and also the house of Judah have anointed me king over them.”
Two Kings · 2:8–11

Now Abner the son of Ner, captain of Saul’s army, has taken Ishbosheth the son of Saul, and brings him over to Mahanaim; and he makes him king over Gilead, and over the Ashurites, and over Jezreel, and over Ephraim, and over Benjamin, and over all Israel. Ishbosheth, Saul’s son, is forty years old when he begins to reign over Israel, and he reigns two years. But the house of Judah follows David. The time that David is king in Hebron over the house of Judah is seven years and six months.
The Pool of Gibeon · 2:12–17

Abner the son of Ner, and the servants of Ishbosheth the son of Saul, go out from Mahanaim to Gibeon. Joab the son of Zeruiah and David’s servants go out, and meet them by the pool of Gibeon; and they sit down, the one on the one side of the pool, and the other on the other side of the pool. Abner says to Joab, “Please let the young men arise and play before us!”

Joab says, “Let them arise!” Then they arise and go over by number: twelve for Benjamin and for Ishbosheth the son of Saul, and twelve of David’s servants. They each catch his opponent by the head, and thrust his sword in his fellow’s side; so they fall down together: therefore that place in Gibeon is called Helkath Hazzurim. The battle is very severe that day; and Abner is beaten, and the men of Israel, before David’s servants.
The Death of Asahel · 2:18–23

The three sons of Zeruiah are there, Joab, and Abishai, and Asahel: and Asahel is as light of foot as a wild gazelle. Asahel pursues Abner; and in going he doesn’t turn to the right hand or to the left from following Abner. Then Abner looks behind him, and says, “Is that you, Asahel?”
He answers, “It is.”

Abner says to him, “Turn away to your right hand or to your left, and grab one of the young men, and take his armor.” But Asahel would not turn away from following him. Abner says again to Asahel, “Turn away from following me. Why should I strike you to the ground? How then could I look Joab your brother in the face?” However he refuses to turn away. Therefore Abner with the back end of the spear strikes him in the body, so that the spear comes out behind him; and he falls down there, and dies in the same place. As many as come to the place where Asahel falls down and dies stand still.
The Pursuit Ends · 2:24–32

But Joab and Abishai pursue Abner. The sun goes down when they have come to the hill of Ammah, that lies before Giah by the way of the wilderness of Gibeon. The children of Benjamin gather themselves together after Abner, and become one band, and stand on the top of a hill. Then Abner calls to Joab, and says, “Will the sword devour forever? Don’t you know that it will be bitterness in the latter end? How long will it be then, before you ask the people to return from following their brothers?”

Joab says, “As God lives, if you had not spoken, surely then in the morning the people would have gone away, and not each followed his brother.” So Joab blows the trumpet; and all the people stand still, and pursue Israel no more, and they fight no more. Abner and his men go all that night through the Arabah; and they pass over the Jordan, and go through all Bithron, and come to Mahanaim. Joab returns from following Abner; and when he has gathered all the people together, nineteen men of David’s and Asahel are missing. But David’s servants have struck Benjamin and of Abner’s men so that three hundred sixty men die. They take up Asahel, and bury him in the tomb of his father, which is in Bethlehem. Joab and his men go all night, and the day breaks on them at Hebron.
The Long War · 3:1–6

Now there is long war between Saul’s house and David’s house. David grows stronger and stronger, but Saul’s house grows weaker and weaker. Sons are born to David in Hebron. His firstborn is Amnon, of Ahinoam the Jezreelitess; and his second, Chileab, of Abigail the wife of Nabal the Carmelite; and the third, Absalom the son of Maacah the daughter of Talmai king of Geshur; and the fourth, Adonijah the son of Haggith; and the fifth, Shephatiah the son of Abital; and the sixth, Ithream, of Eglah, David’s wife. These are born to David in Hebron.
While there is war between Saul’s house and David’s house, Abner makes himself strong in Saul’s house.
Abner's Anger · 3:7–11
Now Saul has a concubine, whose name is Rizpah, the daughter of Aiah; and Ishbosheth says to Abner, “Why have you gone in to my father’s concubine?”

Then Abner is very angry about Ishbosheth’s words, and says, “Am I a dog’s head that belongs to Judah? Today I show kindness to Saul’s house your father, to his brothers, and to his friends, and have not delivered you into the hand of David; and yet you charge me today with a fault concerning this woman! God do so to Abner, and more also, if, as YHWH has sworn to David, I don’t do even so to him; to transfer the kingdom from Saul’s house, and to set up David’s throne over Israel and over Judah, from Dan even to Beersheba.”
He can not answer Abner another word, because he is afraid of him.
Abner Makes an Offer · 3:12–21
Abner sends messengers to David on his behalf, saying, “Whose is the land?” and saying, “Make your alliance with me, and look, my hand will be with you, to bring all Israel around to you.”
He says, “Good. I will make a treaty with you, but one thing I require of you. That is, you will not see my face unless you first bring Michal, Saul’s daughter, when you come to see my face.”
David sends messengers to Ishbosheth, Saul’s son, saying, “Deliver me my wife Michal, whom I was given to marry for one hundred foreskins of the Philistines.”

Ishbosheth sends and takes her from her husband, even from Paltiel the son of Laish. Her husband goes with her, weeping as he goes, and follows her to Bahurim. Then Abner says to him, “Go! Return!” and he returns. Abner has communication with the elders of Israel, saying, “In times past, you sought for David to be king over you. Now then do it; for YHWH has spoken of David, saying, ‘By the hand of my servant David, I will save my people Israel out of the hand of the Philistines, and out of the hand of all their enemies.’”

Abner also speaks in the ears of Benjamin: and Abner goes also to speak in the ears of David in Hebron all that seem good to Israel, and to the whole house of Benjamin. So Abner comes to David to Hebron, and twenty men with him. David makes Abner and the men who are with him a feast. Abner says to David, “I will arise and go, and will gather all Israel to my lord the king, that they may make a covenant with you, and that you may reign over all that your soul desires.” David sends Abner away; and he goes in peace.
Joab's Ambush · 3:22–30

Look, David’s servants and Joab come from a raid, and bring in a great plunder with them; but Abner is not with David in Hebron; for he has sent him away, and he has gone in peace. When Joab and all the army who is with him have come, they tell Joab, “Abner the son of Ner came to the king, and he has sent him away, and he has gone in peace.”

Then Joab comes to the king, and says, “What have you done? Look, Abner came to you. Why is it that you have sent him away, and he is already gone? You know Abner the son of Ner. He came to deceive you, and to know your going out and your coming in, and to know all that you do.”

When Joab has come out from David, he sends messengers after Abner, and they bring him back from the well of Sirah; but David doesn’t know it. When Abner is returned to Hebron, Joab takes him aside into the middle of the gate to speak with him quietly, and strikes him there in the body, so that he dies, for the blood of Asahel his brother. Afterward, when David hears it, he says, “I and my kingdom are guiltless before YHWH forever of the blood of Abner the son of Ner. Let it fall on the head of Joab, and on all his father’s house. Let there not fail from the house of Joab one who has an issue, or who is a leper, or who leans on a staff, or who falls by the sword, or who lacks bread.” So Joab and Abishai his brother kill Abner, because he has killed their brother Asahel at Gibeon in the battle.
David Mourns Abner · 3:31–39

David says to Joab, and to all the people who are with him, “Tear your clothes, and clothe yourselves with sackcloth, and mourn in front of Abner.” King David follows the bier. They bury Abner in Hebron; and the king lifts up his voice, and weeps at Abner’s grave; and all the people weep. The king laments for Abner, and says, “Should Abner die as a fool dies? Your hands weren’t bound, and your feet weren’t put into fetters. As a man falls before the children of iniquity, so you fell.”

All the people weep again over him. All the people come to urge David to eat bread while it is yet day; but David swears, saying, “God do so to me, and more also, if I taste bread, or anything else, until the sun goes down.”

All the people take notice of it, and it pleases them; as whatever the king does pleases all the people. So all the people and all Israel understand that day that it is not of the king to kill Abner the son of Ner. The king says to his servants, “Don’t you know that there a prince and a great man has fallen today in Israel? I am weak today, though anointed king. These men, the sons of Zeruiah are too hard for me. May YHWH reward the evildoer according to his wickedness.”
The Killing of Ish-bosheth · 4:1–8

When Saul’s son hears that Abner is dead in Hebron, his hands become feeble, and all the Israelites are troubled. Saul’s son has two men who are captains of raiding bands. The name of one is Baanah, and the name of the other Rechab, the sons of Rimmon the Beerothite, of the children of Benjamin (for Beeroth also is considered a part of Benjamin: and the Beerothites flee to Gittaim, and have lived as foreigners there until today). Now Jonathan, Saul’s son, has a son who is lame in his feet. He is five years old when the news comes about Saul and Jonathan out of Jezreel; and his nurse picks him up and flees. As she hurries to flee, he falls and becomes lame. His name is Mephibosheth. The sons of Rimmon the Beerothite, Rechab and Baanah, go and come at about the heat of the day to the house of Ishbosheth, as he takes his rest at noon. They come there into the middle of the house, as though they would have fetched wheat; and they strike him in the body: and Rechab and Baanah his brother escape. Now when they come into the house, as he lies on his bed in his bedroom, they strike him, kill him, behead him, and take his head, and go by the way of the Arabah all night. They bring the head of Ishbosheth to David to Hebron, and say to the king, “Look, the head of Ishbosheth, the son of Saul, your enemy, who sought your life! YHWH has avenged my lord the king today of Saul, and of his offspring.”
David's Justice · 4:9–12

David answers Rechab and Baanah his brother, the sons of Rimmon the Beerothite, and says to them, “As YHWH lives, who has redeemed my soul out of all adversity, when someone told me, ‘Look, Saul is dead,’ thinking that he brought good news, I seized him and killed him in Ziklag, which was the reward I gave him for his news. How much more, when wicked men have slain a righteous person in his own house on his bed, should I not now require his blood from your hand, and rid the earth of you?” David commands his young men, and they kill them, cut off their hands and their feet, and hang them up beside the pool in Hebron. But they take the head of Ishbosheth, and bury it in Abner’s grave in Hebron.
King over All Israel · 5:1–5

Then all the tribes of Israel come to David at Hebron, and speak, saying, “Look, we are your bone and your flesh. In times past, when Saul was king over us, it was you who led Israel out and in. YHWH said to you, ‘You will be shepherd of my people Israel, and you will be prince over Israel.’” So all the elders of Israel come to the king to Hebron, and king David makes a covenant with them in Hebron before YHWH; and they anoint David king over Israel.

David is thirty years old when he begins to reign, and he reigns forty years. In Hebron he reigns over Judah seven years and six months; and in Jerusalem he reigns thirty-three years over all Israel and Judah.
The Capture of Jerusalem · 5:6–12

The king and his men go to Jerusalem against the Jebusites, the inhabitants of the land, who speaks to David, saying, “The blind and the lame will keep you out of here”; thinking, “David can’t come in here.” Nevertheless David takes the stronghold of Zion. This is David’s city. David says on that day, “Whoever strikes the Jebusites, let him go up to the watercourse and strike those lame and blind, who are hated by David’s soul.” Therefore they say, “The blind and the lame can’t come into the house.”

David lives in the stronghold, and calls it David’s city. David builds around from Millo and inward. David grows greater and greater; for YHWH, the God of Armies, is with him. Hiram king of Tyre sends messengers to David, with cedar trees, carpenters, and masons; and they build David a house. David perceives that YHWH has established him king over Israel, and that he has exalted his kingdom for his people Israel’s sake.
Sons Born in Jerusalem · 5:13–16

David takes more concubines and wives for himself out of Jerusalem, after he has come from Hebron; and more sons and daughters are born to David. These are the names of those who are born to him in Jerusalem: Shammua, Shobab, Nathan, Solomon, Ibhar, Elishua, Nepheg, Japhia, Elishama, Eliada, and Eliphelet.
Two Victories over the Philistines · 5:17–25

When the Philistines hears that they have anointed David king over Israel, all the Philistines goes up to seek David, but David hears about it and goes down to the stronghold. Now the Philistines has come and spread themselves in the valley of Rephaim. David inquires of YHWH, saying, “Should I go up against the Philistines? Will you deliver them into my hand?”
YHWH says to David, “Go up; for I will certainly deliver the Philistines into your hand.”

David comes to Baal Perazim, and David strikes them there. Then he says, “YHWH has broken my enemies before me, like the breach of waters.” Therefore he calls the name of that place Baal Perazim. They leave their images there; and David and his men take them away.

The Philistines comes up yet again, and spreads themselves in the valley of Rephaim. When David inquires of YHWH, he says, “You will not go up. Circle around behind them, and attack them in front of the mulberry trees. When you hear the sound of marching in the tops of the mulberry trees, then stir yourself up; for then YHWH has gone out before you to strike the army of the Philistines.”
David does so, as YHWH commands him, and strikes the Philistines all the way from Geba to Gezer.
The Ark Set Out · 6:1–5

David again gathers together all the chosen men of Israel, thirty thousand. David arises, and goes with all the people who are with him, from Baale Judah, to bring up from there God’s ark, which is called by the Name, even the name of YHWH of hosts who sits above the cherubim. They set God’s ark on a new cart, and bring it out of Abinadab’s house that is on the hill; and Uzzah and Ahio, the sons of Abinadab, drive the new cart. They bring it out of Abinadab’s house, which is in the hill, with God’s ark; and Ahio goes before the ark. David and all the house of Israel play before YHWH with all kinds of instruments made of cypress wood, with harps, with stringed instruments, with tambourines, with castanets, and with cymbals.
The Death of Uzzah · 6:6–12

When they come to the threshing floor of Nacon, Uzzah reaches for God’s ark, and takes hold of it; for the cattle stumble. YHWH’s anger burned against Uzzah; and God strikes him there for his error; and he dies there by God’s ark. David is displeased, because YHWH has broken out against Uzzah; and he calls that place Perez Uzzah, to this day. David is afraid of YHWH that day; and he says, “How could YHWH’s ark come to me?” So David would not move YHWH’s ark to be with him in David’s city; but David carries it aside into Obed-Edom the Gittite’s house. YHWH’s ark remains in Obed-Edom the Gittite’s house three months; and YHWH blesses Obed-Edom and all his house. King David is told, “YHWH has blessed the house of Obed-Edom, and all that belongs to him, because of God’s ark.”
So David goes and brings up God’s ark from the house of Obed-Edom into David’s city with joy.
David Dances Before YHWH · 6:13–19

When those who bear YHWH’s ark have gone six paces, he sacrifices an ox and a fattened calf. David dances before YHWH with all his might; and David is clothed in a linen ephod. So David and all the house of Israel bring up YHWH’s ark with shouting, and with the sound of the trumpet.

As YHWH’s ark comes into David’s city, Michal the daughter of Saul looks out through the window, and sees king David leaping and dancing before YHWH; and she despises him in her heart. They bring in YHWH’s ark, and set it in its place, in the middle of the tent that David has pitched for it; and David offers burnt offerings and peace offerings before YHWH. When David has finished offering the burnt offering and the peace offerings, he blesses the people in the name of YHWH of hosts. He gives to all the people, even among the whole multitude of Israel, both to men and women, to everyone a portion of bread, dates, and raisins. So all the people depart, each to his own house.
Michal's Contempt · 6:20–23

Then David returns to bless his household. Michal the daughter of Saul comes out to meet David, and says, “How glorious the king of Israel was today, who uncovered himself today in the eyes of the servants of his servants, as one of the vain fellows shamelessly uncovers himself!”

David says to Michal, “It was before YHWH, who chose me above your father, and above all his house, to appoint me prince over the people of YHWH, over Israel. Therefore I will celebrate before YHWH. I will be yet more vile than this, and will be worthless in my own sight. But of the servants of whom you have spoken, they will honor me.”
Michal the daughter of Saul has no child to the day of her death.
David's Desire · 7:1–3

When the king lives in his house, and YHWH has given him rest from all his enemies all around, the king says to Nathan the prophet, “See now, I dwell in a house of cedar, but God’s ark dwells within curtains.”
Nathan says to the king, “Go, do all that is in your heart; for YHWH is with you.”
YHWH's Answer · 7:4–17

That same night, YHWH’s word comes to Nathan, saying, “Go and tell my servant David, ‘YHWH says, “Should you build me a house for me to dwell in? For I have not lived in a house since the day that I brought the children of Israel up out of Egypt, even to this day, but have moved around in a tent and in a tabernacle. In all places in which I have walked with all the children of Israel, did I say a word to any of the tribes of Israel, whom I commanded to be shepherd of my people Israel, saying, ‘Why have you not built me a house of cedar?’”’ Now therefore tell my servant David this, ‘YHWH of hosts says, “I took you from the sheep pen, from following the sheep, to be prince over my people, over Israel. I have been with you wherever you went, and have cut off all your enemies from before you. I will make you a great name, like the name of the great ones who are in the earth. I will appoint a place for my people Israel, and will plant them, that they may dwell in their own place, and be moved no more. The children of wickedness will not afflict them any more, as at the first, and as from the day that I commanded judges to be over my people Israel. I will cause you to rest from all your enemies. Moreover YHWH tells you that YHWH will make you a house. When your days are fulfilled, and you sleep with your fathers, I will set up your offspring after you, who will proceed out of your body, and I will establish his kingdom. He will build a house for my name, and I will establish the throne of his kingdom forever. I will be his father, and he will be my son. If he commits iniquity, I will chasten him with the rod of men, and with the stripes of the children of men; but my steadfast love will not depart from him, as I took it from Saul, whom I put away before you. Your house and your kingdom will be made sure forever before you. Your throne will be established forever.”’” Nathan speaks to David all these words, and according to all this vision.
David's Prayer · 7:18–29

Then David the king goes in, and sits before YHWH; and he says, “Who am I, Lord YHWH, and what is my house, that you have brought me this far? This was yet a small thing in your eyes, Lord YHWH; but you have spoken also of your servant’s house for a great while to come; and this among men, Lord YHWH! What more can David say to you? For you know your servant, Lord YHWH. For your word’s sake, and according to your own heart, you have worked all this greatness, to make your servant know it. Therefore you are great, YHWH God. For there is no one like you, neither is there any God besides you, according to all that we have heard with our ears. What one nation in the earth is like your people, even like Israel, whom God went to redeem to himself for a people, and to make himself a name, and to do great things for you, and awesome things for your land, before your people, whom you redeemed to yourself out of Egypt, from the nations and their gods? You established for yourself your people Israel to be your people forever; and you, YHWH, became their God. Now, YHWH God, the word that you have spoken concerning your servant, and concerning his house, confirm it forever, and do as you have spoken. Let your name be magnified forever, saying, ‘YHWH of hosts is God over Israel; and the house of your servant David will be established before you.’ For you, YHWH of hosts, the God of Israel, have revealed to your servant, saying, ‘I will build you a house.’ Therefore your servant has found in his heart to pray this prayer to you.

“Now, O Lord YHWH, you are God, and your words are truth, and you have promised this good thing to your servant. Now therefore let it please you to bless the house of your servant, that it may continue forever before you; for you, Lord YHWH, have spoken it. Let the house of your servant be blessed forever with your blessing.”
David's Campaigns · 8:1–14

After this, David strikes the Philistines and subdues them; and David takes the bridle of the mother city out of the hand of the Philistines. He strikes Moab, and measures them with the line, making them to lie down on the ground; and he measures two lines to put to death, and one full line to keep alive. The Moabites become servants to David, and bring tribute. David strikes also Hadadezer the son of Rehob, king of Zobah, as he goes to recover his dominion at the River. David takes from him one thousand seven hundred horsemen and twenty thousand footmen. David hamstrings all the chariot horses, but reserved of them for one hundred chariots. When the Syrians of Damascus come to help Hadadezer king of Zobah, David strikes twenty two thousand men of the Syrians. Then David puts garrisons in Syria of Damascus; and the Syrians become servants to David, and bring tribute. YHWH gives victory to David wherever he goes. David takes the shields of gold that are on the servants of Hadadezer, and brings them to Jerusalem. From Betah and from Berothai, cities of Hadadezer, king David takes a great quantity of brass. When Toi king of Hamath hears that David has struck all the army of Hadadezer, then Toi sends Joram his son to king David, to greet him, and to bless him, because he has fought against Hadadezer and strikes him; for Hadadezer has wars with Toi. Joram brings with him vessels of silver, vessels of gold, and vessels of brass: King David also dedicates these to YHWH, with the silver and gold that he dedicates of all the nations which he subdues; of Syria, of Moab, of the children of Ammon, of the Philistines, of Amalek, and of the plunder of Hadadezer, son of Rehob, king of Zobah.

David earns a reputation when he returns from striking down eighteen thousand men of the Syrians in the Valley of Salt. He puts garrisons in Edom. Throughout all Edom puts he garrisons, and all the Edomites become servants to David. YHWH gives victory to David wherever he goes.
David's Administration · 8:15–18

David reigns over all Israel; and David executes justice and righteousness for all his people. Joab the son of Zeruiah is over the army, Jehoshaphat the son of Ahilud is recorder, Zadok the son of Ahitub and Ahimelech the son of Abiathar are priests, Seraiah is scribe, Benaiah the son of Jehoiada is over the Cherethites and the Pelethites, David’s sons are chief ministers.
David Seeks Jonathan's Son · 9:1–8

David says, “Is there yet any who is left of Saul’s house, that I may show him kindness for Jonathan’s sake?” There is of Saul’s house a servant whose name is Ziba, and they call him to David; and the king says to him, “Are you Ziba?”
He says, “I am your servant.”
The king says, “Is there not yet any of Saul’s house, that I may show the kindness of God to him?”
Ziba says to the king, “Jonathan still has a son, who is lame in his feet.”
The king says to him, “Where is he?”
Ziba says to the king, “Look, he is in the house of Machir the son of Ammiel, in Lo Debar.”

Then king David sends, and brings him out of the house of Machir the son of Ammiel, from Lo Debar. Mephibosheth, the son of Jonathan, the son of Saul, comes to David, and falls on his face, and shows respect. David says, “Mephibosheth.”
He answers, “Look, your servant!”

David says to him, “Don’t be afraid; for I will surely show you kindness for Jonathan your father’s sake, and will restore to you all the land of Saul your father. You will eat bread at my table continually.”
He bows down, and says, “What is your servant, that you should look at such a dead dog as I am?”
Mephibosheth Restored · 9:9–13

Then the king calls to Ziba, Saul’s servant, and says to him, “All that belonged to Saul and to all his house I have given to your master’s son. Till the land for him, you, your sons, and your servants. Bring in the harvest, that your master’s son may have bread to eat; but Mephibosheth your master’s son will always eat bread at my table.”

Now Ziba has fifteen sons and twenty servants. Then Ziba says to the king, “According to all that my lord the king commands his servant, so your servant will do.” So Mephibosheth eats at the king’s table, like one of the king’s sons. Mephibosheth has a young son, whose name is Mica. All that live in Ziba’s house are servants to Mephibosheth. So Mephibosheth lives in Jerusalem; for he eats continually at the king’s table. He is lame in both his feet.
The Insult to David's Envoys · 10:1–5

After this, the king of the children of Ammon dies, and Hanun his son reigns in his place. David says, “I will show kindness to Hanun the son of Nahash, as his father showed kindness to me.” So David sends by his servants to comfort him concerning his father. David’s servants come into the land of the children of Ammon.

But the princes of the children of Ammon say to Hanun their lord, “Do you think that David honors your father, in that he has sent comforters to you? Hasn’t David sent his servants to you to search the city, to spy it out, and to overthrow it?”

So Hanun takes David’s servants, shaves off one half of their beards, and cuts off their garments in the middle, even to their buttocks, and sends them away. When they tell David this, he sends to meet them, for the men are greatly ashamed. The king says, “Wait at Jericho until your beards have grown, and then return.”
The Ammonite-syrian Coalition · 10:6–14

When the children of Ammon see that they have become odious to David, the children of Ammon send and hire the Syrians of Beth Rehob, and the Syrians of Zobah, twenty thousand footmen, and the king of Maacah with one thousand men, and the men of Tob twelve thousand men. When David hears of it, he sends Joab, and all the army of the mighty men. The children of Ammon come out, and put the battle in array at the entrance of the gate. The Syrians of Zobah and of Rehob, and the men of Tob and Maacah, are by themselves in the field. Now when Joab sees that the battle is set against him before and behind, he chooses of all the choice men of Israel, and puts them in array against the Syrians. The rest of the people he commits into the hand of Abishai his brother; and he puts them in array against the children of Ammon. He says, “If the Syrians are too strong for me, then you will help me; but if the children of Ammon are too strong for you, then I will come and help you. Be courageous, and let us be strong for our people, and for the cities of our God; and may YHWH do what seems good to him.” So Joab and the people who are with him come near to the battle against the Syrians, and they flee before him. When the children of Ammon see that the Syrians have fled, they likewise flee before Abishai, and enter into the city. Then Joab returns from the children of Ammon, and comes to Jerusalem.
David Defeats the Syrians · 10:15–19

When the Syrians see that they are defeated by Israel, they gather themselves together. Hadadezer sends, and brings out the Syrians who are beyond the River: and they come to Helam, with Shobach the captain of the army of Hadadezer at their head. David is told that; and he gathers all Israel together, passes over the Jordan, and comes to Helam. The Syrians set themselves in array against David, and fight with him. The Syrians flee before Israel; and David kills seven hundred charioteers of the Syrians, and forty thousand horsemen, and strikes Shobach the captain of their army, so that he dies there. When all the kings who are servants to Hadadezer see that they are defeated before Israel, they make peace with Israel, and serve them. So the Syrians are afraid to help the children of Ammon any more.
The King Who Stays Home · 11:1–5

At the return of the year, at the time when kings go out, David sends Joab, and his servants with him, and all Israel; and they destroy the children of Ammon, and besieged Rabbah. But David stays at Jerusalem. At evening, David arises from his bed and walks on the roof of the king’s house. From the roof, he sees a woman bathing, and the woman is very beautiful to look at. David sends and inquires after the woman. One says, “Isn’t this Bathsheba, the daughter of Eliam, Uriah the Hittite’s wife?”

David sends messengers, and takes her; and she comes in to him, and he lies with her (for she is purified from her uncleanness); and she returns to her house. The woman conceives; and she sends and tells David, and says, “I am with child.”
The Schemes · 11:6–13

David sends to Joab, “Send me Uriah the Hittite.” Joab sends Uriah to David. When Uriah has come to him, David asks him how Joab does, and how the people fare, and how the war prospers. David says to Uriah, “Go down to your house and wash your feet.” Uriah departs out of the king’s house, and a gift from the king is sent after him. But Uriah sleeps at the door of the king’s house with all the servants of his lord, and doesn’t go down to his house. When they have told David, saying, “Uriah didn’t go down to his house,” David says to Uriah, “Haven’t you come from a journey? Why didn’t you go down to your house?”

Uriah says to David, “The ark, Israel, and Judah, are staying in tents; and my lord Joab and the servants of my lord, are encamped in the open field. Should I then go into my house to eat and to drink, and to lie with my wife? As you live, and as your soul lives, I will not do this thing!”

David says to Uriah, “Stay here today also, and tomorrow I will let you depart.” So Uriah stays in Jerusalem that day, and the next day. When David has called him, he eats and drink before him; and he makes him drunk. At evening, he goes out to lie on his bed with the servants of his lord, but doesn’t go down to his house.
The Letter · 11:14–25

In the morning, David writes a letter to Joab, and sends it by the hand of Uriah. He writes in the letter, saying, “Send Uriah to the forefront of the hottest battle, and retreat from him, that he may be struck, and die.”

When Joab keeps watch on the city, he assigns Uriah to the place where he knows that valiant men are. The men of the city go out, and fight with Joab. Some of the people falls, even of David’s servants; and Uriah the Hittite dies also. Then Joab sends and tells David all the things concerning the war; and he commands the messenger, saying, “When you have finished telling all the things concerning the war to the king, it will be that, if the king’s wrath arise, and he asks you, ‘Why did you go so near to the city to fight? Didn’t you know that they would shoot from the wall? Who struck Abimelech the son of Jerubbesheth? Didn’t a woman cast an upper millstone on him from the wall, so that he died at Thebez? Why did you go so near the wall?’ then you will say, ‘Your servant Uriah the Hittite is also dead.’”

So the messenger goes, and comes and shows David all that Joab has sent him for. The messenger says to David, “The men prevailed against us, and came out to us into the field, and we were on them even to the entrance of the gate. The shooters shot at your servants from off the wall; and some of the king’s servants are dead, and your servant Uriah the Hittite is also dead.”

Then David says to the messenger, “Tell Joab, ‘Don’t let this thing displease you, for the sword devours one as well as another. Make your battle stronger against the city, and overthrow it.’ Encourage him.”
The Thing That Was Evil · 11:26–27

When Uriah’s wife hears that Uriah her husband is dead, she mourns for her husband. When the mourning is past, David sends and takes her home to his house, and she becomes his wife, and bears him a son. But the thing that David has done displeased YHWH.
Nathan's Parable · 12:1–6

YHWH sends Nathan to David. He comes to him, and says to him, “There were two men in one city; the one rich, and the other poor. The rich man had very many flocks and herds, but the poor man had nothing, except one little ewe lamb, which he had bought and raised. It grew up together with him, and with his children. It ate of his own food, drank of his own cup, and lay in his bosom, and was like a daughter to him. A traveler came to the rich man, and he spared to take of his own flock and of his own herd, to prepare for the wayfaring man who had come to him, but took the poor man’s lamb, and prepared it for the man who had come to him.”

David’s anger burns hot against the man, and he says to Nathan, “As YHWH lives, the man who has done this deserves to die! He must restore the lamb fourfold, because he did this thing, and because he had no pity!”
You are the Man · 12:7–15

Nathan says to David, “You are the man. This is what YHWH, the God of Israel, says: ‘I anointed you king over Israel, and I delivered you out of the hand of Saul. I gave you your master’s house, and your master’s wives into your bosom, and gave you the house of Israel and of Judah; and if that would have been too little, I would have added to you many more such things. Why have you despised YHWH’s word, to do that which is evil in his sight? You have struck Uriah the Hittite with the sword, and have taken his wife to be your wife, and have slain him with the sword of the children of Ammon. Now therefore the sword will never depart from your house, because you have despised me, and have taken Uriah the Hittite’s wife to be your wife.’

“This is what YHWH says: ‘Look, I will raise up evil against you out of your own house; and I will take your wives before your eyes, and give them to your neighbor, and he will lie with your wives in the sight of this sun. For you did this secretly, but I will do this thing before all Israel, and before the sun.’”
David says to Nathan, “I have sinned against YHWH.”

Nathan says to David, “YHWH also has put away your sin. You will not die. However, because by this deed you have given great occasion to YHWH’s enemies to blaspheme, the child also who is born to you will surely die.” Nathan departs to his house.
YHWH strikes the child that Uriah’s wife bears to David, and it is very sick.
The Child's Death · 12:16–23

David therefore begs God for the child; and David fasts, and goes in, and lies all night on the ground. The elders of his house arise beside him, to raise him up from the earth: but he would not, and he doesn’t eat bread with them. On the seventh day, the child dies. David’s servants are afraid to tell him that the child is dead, for they say, “Look, while the child was yet alive, we spoke to him, and he didn’t listen to our voice. How will he then harm himself, if we tell him that the child is dead?”
But when David sees that his servants are whispering together, David perceives that the child is dead; and David says to his servants, “Is the child dead?”
They say, “He is dead.”

Then David arises from the earth, and washes, and anoints himself, and changes his clothing; and he comes into YHWH’s house, and worships. Then he comes to his own house; and when he requests, they set bread before him, and he eats. Then his servants say to him, “What is this that you have done? You fasted and wept for the child while he was alive, but when the child was dead, you rose up and ate bread.”

He says, “While the child was yet alive, I fasted and wept; for I said, ‘Who knows whether YHWH will not be gracious to me, that the child may live?’ But now he is dead, why should I fast? Can I bring him back again? I will go to him, but he will not return to me.”
Solomon and Rabbah · 12:24–31

David comforts Bathsheba his wife, and goes in to her, and lies with her. She bears a son, and he calls his name Solomon. YHWH loves him; and he sends by the hand of Nathan the prophet, and he names him Jedidiah, for YHWH’s sake.

Now Joab fights against Rabbah of the children of Ammon, and takes the royal city. Joab sends messengers to David, and says, “I have fought against Rabbah. Yes, I have taken the city of waters. Now therefore gather the rest of the people together, and encamp against the city, and take it; lest I take the city, and it be called by my name.”

David gathers all the people together, and goes to Rabbah, and fights against it, and takes it. He takes the crown of their king from off his head; and its weight is a talent of gold, and in it are precious stones; and it is set on David’s head. He brings a great quantity of plunder out of the city. He brings out the people who are in it, and puts them under saws, under iron picks, under axes of iron, and makes them pass through the brick kiln; and he does so to all the cities of the children of Ammon. Then David and all the people return to Jerusalem.
Amnon and Tamar · 13:1–22

Some time later this happens. Absalom son of David has a beautiful sister named Tamar, and Amnon son of David falls in love with her. Amnon is so tormented over his sister Tamar that he makes himself sick, for she is a virgin, and it seems impossible to Amnon to do anything to her.

But Amnon has a friend named Jonadab, son of Shimeah, David’s brother, and Jonadab is a very shrewd man. “Why are you so pale and thin, son of the king, morning after morning?” he asks him. “Won’t you tell me?”
“I love Tamar,” Amnon tells him, “my brother Absalom’s sister.”

Jonadab says to him, “Lie down on your bed and pretend to be sick. When your father comes to see you, say to him, ‘Please let my sister Tamar come and give me something to eat. Let her prepare the food here where I can watch, so I can eat it from her hand.’”

So Amnon lies down and pretends to be sick. When the king comes to see him, Amnon says to the king, “Please let my sister Tamar come and make a couple of cakes here where I can watch, so I can eat from her hand.”

David sends word home to Tamar: “Please go to your brother Amnon’s house and prepare some food for him.” So Tamar goes to her brother Amnon’s house, where he is lying down. She takes dough, kneads it, shapes cakes while he watches, and bakes them. Then she takes the pan and sets them out before him — but he refuses to eat.
“Send everyone out from me,” Amnon says. And everyone goes out.

Then Amnon says to Tamar, “Bring the food into the bedroom, so I can eat from your hand.” So Tamar takes the cakes she has made and brings them to her brother Amnon in the bedroom. But when she brings them near for him to eat, he grabs hold of her and says, “Come, lie with me, my sister.”

“No, my brother!” she says to him. “Do not force me! Such a thing is not done in Israel. Do not do this outrageous thing! And I — where could I carry my shame? And you — you would be like one of the outrageous fools in Israel. Now please, speak to the king; he will not keep me from you.” But he will not listen to her. Being stronger than she, he forces her and lies with her.
Then Amnon hates her with a very great hatred. The hatred he hates her with is greater than the love he loved her with. “Get up! Go!” Amnon tells her.

“No,” she says to him, “sending me away is a greater wrong than the other you have done to me.” But he will not listen to her. He calls the young man who serves him and says, “Get this woman out of my sight and bolt the door behind her.”

She is wearing a long robe with sleeves, for that is how the king’s virgin daughters dress. His servant puts her out and bolts the door behind her. And Tamar puts ashes on her head and tears the long robe she is wearing. She puts her hand on her head and goes away, crying aloud as she goes.

Her brother Absalom says to her, “Has Amnon your brother been with you? Now, my sister, keep quiet. He is your brother. Do not take this thing to heart.” So Tamar lives, a desolate woman, in the house of her brother Absalom.
When King David hears of all these things, he is very angry. But Absalom says nothing to Amnon, neither bad nor good, for Absalom hates Amnon because he forced his sister Tamar.
Absalom Avenges Tamar · 13:23–39

Two full years later Absalom has sheepshearers at Baal-hazor near Ephraim, and he invites all the king’s sons. Absalom comes to the king and says, “Your servant has sheepshearers. Please let the king and his servants come with your servant.”
“No, my son,” the king tells Absalom. “We should not all go, or we would be a burden to you.” Absalom presses him, but he will not go, though he gives him his blessing.
“If not,” Absalom says, “then please let my brother Amnon go with us.”
“Why should he go with you?” the king asks him. But Absalom keeps pressing him until he lets Amnon and all the king’s sons go with him.

Then Absalom gives orders to his young men: “Watch closely. When Amnon’s heart is merry with wine and I say to you, ‘Strike Amnon,’ then put him to death. Do not be afraid. Is it not I who am giving you the order? Be courageous and be valiant.” So Absalom’s young men do to Amnon just as Absalom has ordered. Then all the king’s sons get up, each one mounts his mule, and they flee.

While they are still on the road, the report reaches David: “Absalom has struck down all the king’s sons, and not one of them is left!” The king gets up, tears his clothes, and lies down on the ground, and all his servants stand by with their clothes torn.

But Jonadab son of Shimeah, David’s brother, speaks up: “Do not let my lord think they have killed all the young men, the king’s sons. Only Amnon is dead. This has been settled on Absalom’s face ever since the day Amnon forced his sister Tamar. So now let my lord the king not take it to heart, thinking that all the king’s sons are dead. Only Amnon is dead.”

Absalom has fled. Meanwhile the young man keeping watch looks up — and there are many people coming down the road behind him, along the side of the hill. “Look,” Jonadab says to the king, “the king’s sons have come! It is just as your servant said.” And just as he finishes speaking, the king’s sons arrive. They lift up their voices and weep, and the king too and all his servants weep very bitterly.

But Absalom flees and goes to Talmai son of Ammihud, king of Geshur. And David mourns for his son day after day. So Absalom flees and goes to Geshur, and he stays there three years. And the spirit of King David longs to go out to Absalom, for he has been comforted over Amnon’s death.
Joab’s Stratagem · 14:1–20

Now Joab son of Zeruiah can see that the king’s heart is set on Absalom. So Joab sends to Tekoa and brings back a wise woman from there. “Pretend you are in mourning,” he tells her. “Put on mourning clothes and do not anoint yourself with oil. Be like a woman who has been grieving a long time for someone dead. Then go to the king and speak to him like this.” And Joab puts the words in her mouth.
The woman of Tekoa goes in to the king. She falls with her face to the ground, bows low, and says, “Help, O king!”
“What is troubling you?” the king asks her.

“Alas,” she says, “I am a widow; my husband is dead. Your servant had two sons. The two of them fought out in the field, and there was no one to pull them apart. One struck the other and killed him. And now the whole clan has risen up against your servant. They say, ‘Hand over the one who struck down his brother, so we can put him to death for the life of the brother he killed’ — and so they would destroy the heir too. They would quench my coal, the only one I have left, and leave my husband neither name nor remnant on the face of the earth.”
“Go home,” the king tells the woman. “I myself will give orders concerning you.”
But the woman of Tekoa says to the king, “My lord the king, let the guilt be on me and on my father’s house, and let the king and his throne be clear of it.”
The king says, “If anyone says anything to you, bring him to me, and he will never touch you again.”
“Please,” she says, “let the king remember YHWH your God, so that the avenger of blood does not go on destroying, and my son is not wiped out.”
“As YHWH lives,” he says, “not one hair of your son will fall to the ground.”
Then the woman says, “Please let your servant speak one more word to my lord the king.”
“Speak,” he says.

“Why then,” the woman says, “have you planned this very thing against the people of God? In saying this, the king has convicted himself — for the king does not bring his own banished one home. We all must die. We are like water spilled on the ground, which cannot be gathered up again. But God does not take away life; he devises means so that the banished one will not stay banished from him.

“Now I have come to say this to my lord the king because the people frightened me. Your servant thought, ‘Let me speak to the king. Perhaps the king will do what his servant asks. Surely the king will listen and rescue his servant from the hand of the man who would cut off both me and my son from God’s inheritance.’ And your servant thought, ‘Let the word of my lord the king bring me rest’ — for my lord the king is like the angel of God, able to discern good and evil. May YHWH your God be with you!”
Then the king answers the woman, “Do not hide from me anything I ask you.”
“Let my lord the king speak,” the woman says.
“Is the hand of Joab with you in all this?” the king asks.

The woman answers, “As surely as you live, my lord the king, no one can turn to the right or to the left from anything my lord the king says. Yes — it was your servant Joab who commanded me. He is the one who put all these words in your servant’s mouth. Your servant Joab did this to change the face of things. But my lord is wise, with the wisdom of the angel of God, to know everything that happens in the land.”
Absalom Returns to Jerusalem · 14:21–33
Then the king says to Joab, “Very well — I am doing this thing. Go, bring back the young man Absalom.”

Joab falls with his face to the ground, bows low, and blesses the king. “Today your servant knows that I have found favor in your eyes, my lord the king,” Joab says, “because the king has done what his servant asked.” So Joab gets up, goes to Geshur, and brings Absalom to Jerusalem.
But the king says, “Let him go to his own house. He is not to see my face.” So Absalom goes to his own house and does not see the king’s face.

Now in all Israel there is no one so handsome as Absalom, no one so praised. From the sole of his foot to the crown of his head there is not a flaw in him. When he cuts his hair — he cuts it at the end of every year, because it grows heavy on him — he weighs the hair of his head: two hundred shekels by the king’s weight. Three sons are born to Absalom, and one daughter, whose name is Tamar. She is a beautiful woman.

Absalom lives two full years in Jerusalem without seeing the king’s face. Then Absalom sends for Joab, to send him to the king, but Joab will not come to him. He sends a second time, and still Joab will not come.
So Absalom says to his servants, “Look — Joab’s field is next to mine, and he has barley there. Go and set it on fire.” And Absalom’s servants set the field on fire.
Then Joab gets up and comes to Absalom at his house. “Why have your servants set my field on fire?” he demands.

“Look,” Absalom says to Joab, “I sent word to you: ‘Come here, so I can send you to the king to ask, “Why did I come back from Geshur? It would be better for me if I were still there.”’ So now — let me see the king’s face. And if there is guilt in me, let him put me to death.”
So Joab goes to the king and tells him. And the king calls for Absalom. He comes to the king and bows down before him with his face to the ground. And the king kisses Absalom.
Absalom Steals the Hearts of Israel · 15:1–12

Some time after this, Absalom gets himself a chariot and horses, with fifty men to run ahead of him. He rises early and takes his stand beside the road that leads to the city gate. Whenever someone comes with a dispute to bring before the king for judgment, Absalom calls out to him: “What town are you from?”
And the man says, “Your servant is from one of the tribes of Israel.”

Then Absalom says to him, “Look — your case is good and right. But there is no one from the king to hear you.” And Absalom adds, “If only someone would make me judge in the land! Then anyone with a dispute or a case could come to me, and I would see that he gets justice.”

And whenever anyone comes near to bow down to him, Absalom reaches out his hand, takes hold of him, and kisses him. This is how Absalom treats every Israelite who comes to the king for judgment. And so Absalom steals the hearts of the men of Israel.

At the end of forty years Absalom says to the king, “Please let me go to Hebron and fulfill the vow I made to YHWH. For your servant made a vow while I was living at Geshur in Aram: ‘If YHWH really brings me back to Jerusalem, then I will worship YHWH.’”
“Go in peace,” the king tells him. So he gets up and goes to Hebron.

But Absalom sends secret messengers through all the tribes of Israel: “As soon as you hear the sound of the shofar, shout, ‘Absalom is king in Hebron!’” Two hundred men go with Absalom from Jerusalem. They have been invited as guests and go in all innocence, knowing nothing of the matter. And while he is offering the sacrifices, Absalom sends for Ahithophel the Gilonite, David’s counselor, from his town of Giloh. The conspiracy grows strong, and the people with Absalom keep growing in number.
David Flees Jerusalem · 15:13–29
A messenger comes to David: “The hearts of the men of Israel have gone after Absalom.”

Then David says to all his servants who are with him in Jerusalem, “Get up! We must flee, or none of us will escape from Absalom. Go quickly, or he will overtake us fast, bring disaster down on us, and put the city to the sword.”
“Whatever my lord the king chooses,” the king’s servants say, “here are your servants.”

So the king goes out with his whole household following on foot. But the king leaves ten concubines behind to keep the house. The king goes out with all the people following on foot, and they stop at the last house. All his servants pass by beside him — all the Cherethites and all the Pelethites, and all the Gittites, six hundred men who have followed him from Gath — marching on past the king.

Then the king says to Ittai the Gittite, “Why should you come with us too? Go back and stay with the king, for you are a foreigner — an exile from your own home as well. You only arrived yesterday. Should I make you wander with us today, when I go wherever I can? Go back, and take your brothers with you. May steadfast love and faithfulness go with you.”
But Ittai answers the king, “As YHWH lives, and as my lord the king lives — wherever my lord the king is, whether for death or for life, there your servant will be.”
“Then go on ahead,” David tells Ittai. So Ittai the Gittite passes on with all his men and all the little ones who are with him.
The whole countryside is weeping aloud as all the people pass by. The king crosses the Kidron Valley, and all the people move on toward the wilderness road.

And there is Zadok too, and all the Levites with him, carrying the ark of the covenant of God. They set down the ark of God, and Abiathar offers sacrifices until all the people have finished passing out of the city.

Then the king says to Zadok, “Take the ark of God back into the city. If I find favor in YHWH’s eyes, he will bring me back and let me see both it and his dwelling place. But if he says, ‘I take no pleasure in you,’ then here I am — let him do to me whatever seems good to him.”

The king also says to Zadok the priest, “Are you not a seer? Go back to the city in peace, you and Abiathar, with your two sons — Ahimaaz your son and Jonathan son of Abiathar. Look, I will wait at the fords of the wilderness until word comes from you to tell me.” So Zadok and Abiathar carry the ark of God back to Jerusalem, and they stay there.
David on the Mount of Olives · 15:30–37
But David goes up the ascent of the Mount of Olives, weeping as he goes, his head covered and his feet bare. And all the people with him cover their heads, and they go up weeping as they climb.
Then David is told, “Ahithophel is among the conspirators with Absalom.” And David says, “YHWH, please make the counsel of Ahithophel foolishness.”
As David comes to the summit, where God is worshiped, Hushai the Archite is there to meet him, his robe torn and dirt on his head.

David says to him, “If you go on with me, you will only be a burden to me. But if you go back to the city and say to Absalom, ‘I will be your servant, O king; as I was your father’s servant in the past, so now I will be your servant,’ then you can defeat the counsel of Ahithophel for me. Will not Zadok and Abiathar the priests be there with you? Whatever you hear from the king’s house, tell it to Zadok and Abiathar the priests. Their two sons are there with them — Ahimaaz son of Zadok and Jonathan son of Abiathar. By them you can send me everything you hear.”
So Hushai, David’s friend, comes into the city, just as Absalom is entering Jerusalem.
Ziba Meets the King · 16:1–4

When David is a little past the top, look, Ziba the servant of Mephibosheth meets him with a couple of donkeys saddled, and on them two hundred loaves of bread, and one hundred clusters of raisins, and one hundred summer fruits, and a bottle of wine. The king says to Ziba, “What do you mean by these?”
Ziba says, “The donkeys are for the king’s household to ride on; and the bread and summer fruit for the young men to eat; and the wine, that those who are faint in the wilderness may drink.”
The king says, “Where is your master’s son?”
Ziba says to the king, “Look, he is staying in Jerusalem; for he said, ‘Today the house of Israel will restore me the kingdom of my father.’”
Then the king says to Ziba, “Look, all that belongs to Mephibosheth is yours.”
Ziba says, “I bow down. Let me find favor in your sight, my lord, O king.”
Shimei Curses the King · 16:5–14

When king David comes to Bahurim, look, a man of the family of Saul’s house comes out, whose name is Shimei, the son of Gera. He comes out and curses as he comes. He casts stones at David, and at all the servants of king David, and all the people and all the mighty men are on his right hand and on his left. Shimei says when he curses, “Be gone, be gone, you man of blood, and wicked fellow! YHWH has returned on you all the blood of Saul’s house, in whose place you have reigned! YHWH has delivered the kingdom into the hand of Absalom your son! Look, you are caught by your own mischief, because you are a man of blood!”

Then Abishai the son of Zeruiah says to the king, “Why should this dead dog curse my lord the king? Please let me go over and take off his head.” The king says, “What have I to do with you, you sons of Zeruiah? Because he curses, and because YHWH has said to him, ‘Curse David;’ who then will say, ‘Why have you done so?’”

David says to Abishai, and to all his servants, “Look, my son, who came out of my bowels, seeks my life. How much more this Benjamite, now? Leave him alone, and let him curse; for YHWH has invited him. It may be that YHWH will look on the wrong done to me, and that YHWH will repay me good for the cursing of me today.” So David and his men go by the way; and Shimei goes along on the hillside opposite him, and curses as he goes, throws stones at him, and throws dust. The king, and all the people who are with him, come weary; and he refreshes himself there.
Absalom Enters Jerusalem · 16:15–23

Absalom and all the people, the men of Israel, come to Jerusalem, and Ahithophel with him. When Hushai the Archite, David’s friend, has come to Absalom, Hushai says to Absalom, “Long live the king! Long live the king!”
Absalom says to Hushai, “Is this your kindness to your friend? Why didn’t you go with your friend?”

Hushai says to Absalom, “No; but whomever YHWH, and this people, and all the men of Israel have chosen, his will I be, and with him I will stay. Again, whom should I serve? Shouldn’t I serve in the presence of his son? As I have served in your father’s presence, so will I be in your presence.”
Then Absalom says to Ahithophel, “Give your counsel what we will do.”

Ahithophel says to Absalom, “Go in to your father’s concubines that he has left to keep the house. Then all Israel will hear that you are abhorred by your father. Then the hands of all who are with you will be strong.”

So they spread a tent for Absalom on the top of the house, and Absalom goes in to his father’s concubines in the sight of all Israel. The counsel of Ahithophel, which he gives in those days, is as if a man inquires at the inner sanctuary of God. So is all the counsel of Ahithophel both with David and with Absalom.
Ahithophel's Counsel · 17:1–4

Moreover Ahithophel says to Absalom, “Let me now choose twelve thousand men, and I will arise and pursue after David tonight. I will come on him while he is weary and exhausted, and will make him afraid. All the people who are with him will flee. I will strike the king only, and I will bring back all the people to you. The man whom you seek is as if all returned. All the people will be in peace.”
The saying pleases Absalom well, and all the elders of Israel.
Hushai Defeats Ahithophel · 17:5–14
Then Absalom says, “Now call Hushai the Archite also, and let us hear likewise what he says.”
When Hushai has come to Absalom, Absalom speaks to him, saying, “Ahithophel has spoken like this. Should we do what he says? If not, speak up.”

Hushai says to Absalom, “The counsel that Ahithophel has given this time is not good.” Hushai says moreover, “You know your father and his men, that they are mighty men, and they are fierce in their minds, like a bear robbed of her cubs in the field. Your father is a man of war, and will not lodge with the people. Look, he is now hidden in some pit, or in some other place. It will happen, when some of them have fallen at the first, that whoever hears it will say, ‘There is a slaughter among the people who follow Absalom!’ Even he who is valiant, whose heart is as the heart of a lion, will utterly melt; for all Israel knows that your father is a mighty man, and those who are with him are valiant men. But I counsel that all Israel be gathered together to you, from Dan even to Beersheba, as the sand that is by the sea for multitude; and that you go to battle in your own person. So should we come on him in some place where he will be found, and we will light on him as the dew falls on the ground; and of him and of all the men who are with him we will not leave so much as one. Moreover, if he has gone into a city, then will all Israel bring ropes to that city, and we will draw it into the river, until there isn’t one small stone found there.”
