Absalom and all the men of Israel say, “The counsel of Hushai the Archite is better than the counsel of Ahithophel.” For YHWH have ordained to defeat the good counsel of Ahithophel, to the intent that YHWH might bring evil on Absalom.
The Message Carried to David · 17:15–22

Then Hushai says to Zadok and to Abiathar the priests, “Ahithophel counseled Absalom and the elders of Israel that way; and I have counseled this way. Now therefore send quickly, and tell David, saying, ‘Don’t lodge tonight at the fords of the wilderness, but by all means pass over; lest the king be swallowed up, and all the people who are with him.’”

Now Jonathan and Ahimaaz are staying by En Rogel; and a female servant uses to go and tell them; and they go and tell king David. For they might not be seen to come into the city. But a boy sees them, and tells Absalom. Then they both go away quickly, and come to the house of a man in Bahurim, who has a well in his court; and they go down there. The woman takes and spreads the covering over the well’s mouth, and spreads out bruised grain on it; and nothing is known. Absalom’s servants come to the woman to the house; and they say, “Where are Ahimaaz and Jonathan?”
The woman says to them, “They have gone over the brook of water.”

When they have sought and can not find them, they return to Jerusalem. After they have departed, they come up out of the well, and go and tell king David; and they say to David, “Arise and pass quickly over the water; for thus has Ahithophel counseled against you.”
Then David arises, and all the people who are with him, and they pass over the Jordan. By the morning light there lacks not one of them who has not gone over the Jordan.
Ahithophel's End · 17:23

When Ahithophel sees that his counsel is not followed, he saddles his donkey, arises, and goes home, to his city, and set his house in order, and hangs himself; and he dies, and is buried in the tomb of his father.
Absalom Crosses the Jordan · 17:24–29

Then David comes to Mahanaim. Absalom passes over the Jordan, he and all the men of Israel with him. Absalom sets Amasa over the army instead of Joab. Now Amasa is the son of a man whose name is Ithra the Israelite, who goes in to Abigail the daughter of Nahash, sister to Zeruiah, Joab’s mother. Israel and Absalom encamp in the land of Gilead. When David has come to Mahanaim, Shobi the son of Nahash of Rabbah of the children of Ammon, and Machir the son of Ammiel of Lodebar, and Barzillai the Gileadite of Rogelim, brings beds, basins, earthen vessels, wheat, barley, meal, parches grain, beans, lentils, roasted grain, honey, butter, sheep, and cheese of the herd, for David, and for the people who are with him, to eat; for they say, “The people are hungry, and weary, and thirsty in the wilderness.”
The Battle in the Forest · 18:1–8

David counts the people who are with him, and sets captains of thousands and captains of hundreds over them. David sends the people out, a third part under the hand of Joab, and a third part under the hand of Abishai the son of Zeruiah, Joab’s brother, and a third part under the hand of Ittai the Gittite. The king says to the people, “I will also surely go out with you myself.”

But the people say, “You will not go out; for if we flee away, they will not care for us; neither if half of us die, will they care for us. But you are worth ten thousand of us. Therefore now it is better that you are ready to help us out of the city.”
The king says to them, “I will do what seems best to you.”

The king stands beside the gate, and all the people go out by hundreds and by thousands. The king commands Joab and Abishai and Ittai, saying, “Deal gently for my sake with the young man, even with Absalom.” All the people hear when the king commands all the captains concerning Absalom.

So the people go out into the field against Israel; and the battle is in the forest of Ephraim. The people of Israel are struck there before David’s servants, and there is a great slaughter there that day of twenty thousand men. For the battle are there spread over the surface of all the country, and the forest devours more people that day than the sword devours.
The Death of Absalom · 18:9–18

Absalom happens to meet David’s servants. Absalom is riding on his mule, and the mule goes under the thick boughs of a great oak, and his head catches hold of the oak, and he is taken up between the sky and earth; and the mule that is under him goes on. A certain man sees it, and tells Joab, and says, “Look, I saw Absalom hanging in an oak.”
Joab says to the man who tells him, “Look, you saw it, and why didn’t you strike him there to the ground? I would have given you ten pieces of silver, and a sash.”

The man says to Joab, “Though I should receive a thousand pieces of silver in my hand, I still wouldn’t stretch out my hand against the king’s son; for in our hearing the king commanded you and Abishai and Ittai, saying, ‘Beware that no one touch the young man Absalom.’ Otherwise if I had dealt falsely against his life (and there is no matter hidden from the king), then you yourself would have set yourself against me.”

Then Joab says, “I’m not going to wait like this with you.” He takes three darts in his hand, and thrusts them through the heart of Absalom, while he is yet alive in the middle of the oak. Ten young men who bear Joab’s armor surround and strike Absalom, and kill him. Joab blows the trumpet, and the people return from pursuing after Israel; for Joab holds the people back. They take Absalom and cast him into the great pit in the forest, and raise over him a very great heap of stones. Then all Israel flees, each to his own tent. Now Absalom in his lifetime has taken and reared up for himself the pillar which is in the king’s valley, for he says, “I have no son to keep my name in memory.” He calls the pillar after his own name. It is called Absalom’s monument, to this day.
The News Comes to David · 18:19–33
Then Ahimaaz the son of Zadok says, “Let me now run, and carry the king news, how YHWH has avenged him of his enemies.”
Joab says to him, “You must not be the bearer of news today, but you must carry news another day. But today you must carry no news, because the king’s son is dead.”
Then Joab says to the Cushite, “Go, tell the king what you have seen!” The Cushite bows himself to Joab, and runs.
Then Ahimaaz the son of Zadok says yet again to Joab, “But come what may, please let me also run after the Cushite.”
Joab says, “Why do you want to run, my son, since that you will have no reward for the news?”
“But come what may,” he says, “I will run.”
He says to him, “Run!” Then Ahimaaz runs by the way of the Plain, and outruns the Cushite.

Now David is sitting between the two gates; and the watchman goes up to the roof of the gate to the wall, and lifts up his eyes, and looks, and, look, a man running alone. The watchman cries, and tells the king. The king says, “If he is alone, there is news in his mouth.” He comes closer and closer.
The watchman sees another man running; and the watchman calls to the gatekeeper, and says, “Look, a man running alone!”
The king says, “He also brings news.”
The watchman says, “I think the running of the first one is like the running of Ahimaaz the son of Zadok.”
The king says, “He is a good man, and comes with good news.”

Ahimaaz calls, and says to the king, “All is well.” He bows himself before the king with his face to the earth, and says, “Blessed is YHWH your God, who has delivered up the men who lifted up their hand against my lord the king!”
The king says, “Is it well with the young man Absalom?”
Ahimaaz answers, “When Joab sent the king’s servant, even me your servant, I saw a great tumult, but I don’t know what it was.”
The king says, “Come and stand here.” He comes, and stands still.
Look, the Cushite comes. The Cushite says, “News for my lord the king, for YHWH has avenged you today of all those who rose up against you.”
The king says to the Cushite, “Is it well with the young man Absalom?”
The Cushite answers, “May the enemies of my lord the king, and all who rise up against you to do you harm, be as that young man is.”
The king is much moved, and goes up to the room over the gate, and wept. As he goes, he says, “My son Absalom! My son, my son Absalom! I wish I had died for you, Absalom, my son, my son!”
Joab Rebukes the King · 19:1–8
Joab is told, “Look, the king weeps and mourns for Absalom.” The victory that day is turned into mourning among all the people; for the people hear it says that day, “The king grieves for his son.”

The people sneak into the city that day, as people who are ashamed steal away when they flee in battle. The king covers his face, and the king cries with a loud voice, “My son Absalom, Absalom, my son, my son!”

Joab comes into the house to the king, and says, “Today you have shamed the faces of all your servants, who today have saved your life, and the lives of your sons and of your daughters, and the lives of your wives, and the lives of your concubines; in that you love those who hate you, and hate those who love you. For you have declared today, that princes and servants are nothing to you. For today I perceive that if Absalom had lived, and all we had died today, then it would have pleased you well. Now therefore arise, go out, and speak to comfort your servants; for I swear by YHWH, if you don’t go out, not a man will stay with you this night. That would be worse to you than all the evil that has happened to you from your youth until now.”

Then the king arises, and sits in the gate. They tell to all the people, saying, “Look, the king is sitting in the gate.” All the people come before the king. Now Israel has fled every man to his tent.
Israel Debates David's Return · 19:9–15

All the people are at strife throughout all the tribes of Israel, saying, “The king delivered us out of the hand of our enemies, and he saved us out of the hand of the Philistines; and now he has fled out of the land from Absalom. Absalom, whom we anointed over us, is dead in battle. Now therefore why don’t you speak a word of bringing the king back?”

King David sends to Zadok and to Abiathar the priests, saying, “Speak to the elders of Judah, saying, ‘Why are you the last to bring the king back to his house? Since the speech of all Israel has come to the king, to return him to his house. You are my brothers. You are my bone and my flesh. Why then are you the last to bring back the king?’ Say to Amasa, ‘Aren’t you my bone and my flesh? God do so to me, and more also, if you aren’t captain of the army before me continually instead of Joab.’” He bows the heart of all the men of Judah, even as one man; so that they send to the king, saying, “Return, you and all your servants.”
So the king returns, and comes to the Jordan. Judah comes to Gilgal, to go to meet the king, to bring the king over the Jordan.
Shimei, Mephibosheth, and Barzillai · 19:16–40

Shimei the son of Gera, the Benjamite, who is of Bahurim, hurried and comes down with the men of Judah to meet king David. There are a thousand men of Benjamin with him, and Ziba the servant of Saul’s house, and his fifteen sons and his twenty servants with him; and they go through the Jordan in the presence of the king. A ferry boat goes to bring over the king’s household, and to do what he thinks good. Shimei the son of Gera falls down before the king, when he has come over the Jordan. He says to the king, “Don’t let my lord impute iniquity to me, or remember that which your servant did perversely the day that my lord the king went out of Jerusalem, that the king should take it to his heart. For your servant knows that I have sinned. Therefore look, I have come today as the first of all the house of Joseph to go down to meet my lord the king.”
But Abishai the son of Zeruiah answers, “Shouldn’t Shimei be put to death for this, because he cursed YHWH’s anointed?”

David says, “What have I to do with you, you sons of Zeruiah, that you should be adversaries to me today? Will any man be put to death today in Israel? For don’t I know that I am king over Israel today?” The king says to Shimei, “You will not die.” The king swears to him.

Mephibosheth the son of Saul comes down to meet the king; and he has neither groomed his feet, nor trims his beard, nor washes his clothes, from the day the king departs until the day he comes home in peace. When he has come to Jerusalem to meet the king, the king says to him, “Why didn’t you go with me, Mephibosheth?”

He answers, “My lord, O king, my servant deceived me. For your servant said, I will saddle me a donkey, that I may ride on it, and go with the king; because your servant is lame. He has slandered your servant to my lord the king, but my lord the king is as an angel of God. Do therefore what is good in your eyes. For all my father’s house were but dead men before my lord the king; yet you set your servant among those who ate at your own table. What right therefore have I yet that I should cry any more to the king?”
The king says to him, “Why do you speak any more of your matters? I say, you and Ziba divide the land.”

Mephibosheth says to the king, “Yes, let him take all, because my lord the king has come in peace to his own house.” Barzillai the Gileadite comes down from Rogelim; and he goes over the Jordan with the king, to conduct him over the Jordan. Now Barzillai is a very aged man, even eighty years old. He has provided the king with sustenance while he stays at Mahanaim; for he is a very great man. The king says to Barzillai, “Come over with me, and I will sustain you with me in Jerusalem.” Barzillai says to the king, “How many are the days of the years of my life, that I should go up with the king to Jerusalem? I am eighty years old, today. Can I discern between good and bad? Can your servant taste what I eat or what I drink? Can I hear the voice of singing men and singing women any more? Why then should your servant be a burden to my lord the king? Your servant would but just go over the Jordan with the king. Why should the king repay me with such a reward? Please let your servant turn back again, that I may die in my own city, by the grave of my father and my mother. But look, your servant Chimham; let him go over with my lord the king; and do to him what will seem good to you.”
The king answers, “Chimham will go over with me, and I will do to him that which will seem good to you. Whatever you request of me, that I will do for you.”

All the people go over the Jordan, and the king goes over. Then the king kisses Barzillai, and blesses him; and he returns to his own place. So the king goes over to Gilgal, and Chimham goes over with him. All the people of Judah bring the king over, and also half the people of Israel.
The Quarrel Between Judah and Israel · 19:41–43

Look, all the men of Israel come to the king, and say to the king, “Why have our brothers the men of Judah stolen you away, and brought the king, and his household, over the Jordan, and all David’s men with him?”

All the men of Judah answer the men of Israel, “Because the king is a close relative to us. Why then are you angry about this matter? Have we eaten at all at the king’s cost? Or has he given us any gift?”

The men of Israel answer the men of Judah, and say, “We have ten parts in the king, and we have also more claim to David than you. Why then did you despise us, that our advice should not be first had in bringing back our king?” The words of the men of Judah are fiercer than the words of the men of Israel.
Sheba's Revolt · 20:1–7

There happens to be there a wicked fellow, whose name is Sheba, the son of Bichri, a Benjamite; and he blows the trumpet, and says, “We have no portion in David, neither have we inheritance in the son of Jesse. Every man to his tents, Israel!”

So all the men of Israel go up from following David, and follow Sheba the son of Bichri; but the men of Judah join with their king, from the Jordan even to Jerusalem. David comes to his house at Jerusalem; and the king takes the ten women his concubines, whom he has left to keep the house, and puts them in custody, and provides them with sustenance, but doesn’t go in to them. So they are shut up to the day of their death, living in widowhood.
Then the king says to Amasa, “Call me the men of Judah together within three days, and be here present.”

So Amasa goes to call the men of Judah together; but he stays longer than the set time which he has appointed him. David says to Abishai, “Now Sheba the son of Bichri will do us more harm than Absalom did. Take your lord’s servants, and pursue after him, lest he get himself fortified cities, and escape out of our sight.”
Joab’s men go out after him, and the Cherethites and the Pelethites, and all the mighty men; and they go out of Jerusalem, to pursue Sheba the son of Bichri.
Joab Kills Amasa · 20:8–13

When they are at the great stone which is in Gibeon, Amasa comes to meet them. Joab is clothed in his apparel of war that he has put on, and on it is a sash with a sword fastens on his waist in its sheath; and as he goes along it falls out. Joab says to Amasa, “Is it well with you, my brother?” Joab takes Amasa by the beard with his right hand to kiss him. But Amasa takes no heed to the sword that is in Joab’s hand. So he strikes him with it in the body, and sheds out his bowels to the ground, and doesn’t strike him again; and he dies. Joab and Abishai his brother pursue Sheba the son of Bichri. One of Joab’s young men stands by him, and says, “He who favors Joab, and he who is for David, let him follow Joab!”

Amasa lies wallowing in his blood in the middle of the highway. When the man sees that all the people stand still, he carries Amasa out of the highway into the field, and casts a garment over him, when he sees that everyone who comes by him stands still. When he is removed out of the highway, all the people go on after Joab, to pursue Sheba the son of Bichri.
The Wise Woman of Abel · 20:14–22

He goes through all the tribes of Israel to Abel, and to Beth Maacah, and all the Berites. They are gathered together, and go also after him. They come and besiege him in Abel of Beth Maacah, and they cast up a mound against the city, and it stands against the rampart; and all the people who are with Joab batter the wall, to throw it down. Then a wise woman cries out of the city, “Hear, hear! Please say to Joab, ‘Come near here, that I may speak with you.’” He comes near to her; and the woman says, “Are you Joab?”
He answers, “I am.”
Then she says to him, “Hear the words of your servant.”
He answers, “I’m listening.”

Then she speaks, saying, “They used to say in old times, ‘They will surely ask counsel at Abel;’ and so they settled a matter. I am among those who are peaceable and faithful in Israel. You seek to destroy a city and a mother in Israel. Why will you swallow up YHWH’s inheritance?”

Joab answers, “Far be it, far be it from me, that I should swallow up or destroy. The matter is not so. But a man of the hill country of Ephraim, Sheba the son of Bichri by name, has lifted up his hand against the king, even against David. Just deliver him, and I will depart from the city.”
The woman says to Joab, “Look, his head will be thrown to you over the wall.”

Then the woman goes to all the people in her wisdom. They cut off the head of Sheba the son of Bichri, and throw it out to Joab. He blows the trumpet, and they are dispersed from the city, every man to his tent. Then Joab returns to Jerusalem to the king.
David's Officers · 20:23–26

Now Joab is over all the army of Israel, Benaiah the son of Jehoiada is over the Cherethites and over the Pelethites, Adoram is over the men subject to forced labor, Jehoshaphat the son of Ahilud is the recorder, Sheva is scribe, and Zadok and Abiathar are priests, and Ira the Jairite is chief minister to David.
The Famine and the Gibeonites · 21:1–14

There is a famine in the days of David for three years, year after year; and David seeks the face of YHWH. YHWH says, “It is for Saul, and for his bloody house, because he put the Gibeonites to death.”

The king calls the Gibeonites, and says to them (now the Gibeonites are not of the children of Israel, but of the remnant of the Amorites, and the children of Israel have sworn to them; and Saul seeks to kill them in his zeal for the children of Israel and Judah); and David says to the Gibeonites, “What should I do for you? And with what should I make atonement, that you may bless YHWH’s inheritance?”
The Gibeonites say to him, “It is no matter of silver or gold between us and Saul, or his house; neither is it for us to put any man to death in Israel.”
He says, “Whatever you say, that I will do for you.”

They say to the king, “The man who consumed us, and who devised against us, that we should be destroyed from remaining in any of the borders of Israel, let seven men of his sons be delivered to us, and we will hang them up to YHWH in Gibeah of Saul, the chosen of YHWH.”
The king says, “I will give them.”

But the king spars Mephibosheth, the son of Jonathan the son of Saul, because of YHWH’s oath that is between them, between David and Jonathan the son of Saul. But the king takes the two sons of Rizpah the daughter of Aiah, whom she bears to Saul, Armoni and Mephibosheth; and the five sons of Michal the daughter of Saul, whom she bears to Adriel the son of Barzillai the Meholathite. He delivers them into the hands of the Gibeonites, and they hang them on the mountain before YHWH, and all seven of them falls together. They are put to death in the days of harvest, in the first days, at the beginning of barley harvest. Rizpah the daughter of Aiah takes sackcloth, and spread it for herself on the rock, from the beginning of harvest until water pours on them from the sky. She allows neither the birds of the sky to rest on them by day, nor the animals of the field by night. David is told what Rizpah the daughter of Aiah, the concubine of Saul, has done. So David goes and takes the bones of Saul and the bones of Jonathan his son from the men of Jabesh Gilead, who has stolen them from the street of Beth Shan, where the Philistines has hanged them, in the day that the Philistines kills Saul in Gilboa; and he brings up from there the bones of Saul and the bones of Jonathan his son. They also gather the bones of those who are hanged. They bury the bones of Saul and Jonathan his son in the country of Benjamin in Zela, in the tomb of Kish his father: and they perform all that the king commands. After that, God answers prayer for the land.
Wars against the Philistines · 21:15–22

The Philistines has war again with Israel; and David goes down, and his servants with him, and fights against the Philistines. David grows faint; and Ishbibenob, who is of the sons of the giant, the weight of whose spear is three hundred shekels of brass in weight, he being armed with a new sword, thinks he would kill David. But Abishai the son of Zeruiah helps him, and strikes the Philistine, and kills him. Then the men of David swear to him, saying, “Don’t go out with us to battle any more, so that you don’t quench the lamp of Israel.”

After this, that there is again war with the Philistines at Gob. Then Sibbecai the Hushathite kills Saph, who is of the sons of the giant. There is again war with the Philistines at Gob; and Elhanan the son of Jaare-Oregim the Bethlehemite kills Goliath the Gittite’s brother, the staff of whose spear is like a weaver’s beam. There is again war at Gath, where there is a man of great stature, who has six fingers on every hand, and six toes on every foot, twenty four in count; and he also is born to the giant. When he defies Israel, Jonathan the son of Shimei, David’s brother, kills him. These four are born to the giant in Gath; and they fall by the hand of David, and by the hand of his servants.
David's Song of Deliverance · 22:1–51
David speaks to YHWH the words of this song in the day that YHWH delivers him out of the hand of all his enemies, and out of the hand of Saul, and he says:
“YHWH is my rock,
my fortress,
and my deliverer, even mine;
God is my rock in whom I take refuge;
my shield, and the horn of my salvation,
my high tower, and my refuge.
My savior, you save me from violence.
I call on YHWH, who is worthy to be praised;
So should I be saved from my enemies.
For the waves of death surrounded me.
The floods of ungodliness made me afraid.
The cords of Sheol were around me.
The snares of death caught me.
In my distress, I called on YHWH.
Yes, I called to my God.
He heard my voice out of his temple.
My cry came into his ears.
Then the earth shook and trembled.
The foundations of heaven quaked and were shaken,
because he was angry.
Smoke went up out of his nostrils.
Consuming fire came out of his mouth.
Coals were kindled by it.
He bowed the heavens also, and came down.
Thick darkness was under his feet.
He rode on a cherub, and flew.
Yes, he was seen on the wings of the wind.
He made darkness a shelter around himself:
gathering of waters, and thick clouds of the skies.
At the brightness before him,
coals of fire were kindled.
YHWH thundered from heaven.
The Most High uttered his voice.
He sent out arrows, and scattered them;
lightning, and confused them.
Then the channels of the sea appeared.
The foundations of the world were laid bare by YHWH’s rebuke,
at the blast of the breath of his nostrils.
He sent from on high and he took me.
He drew me out of many waters.
He delivered me from my strong enemy,
from those who hated me, for they were too mighty for me.
They came on me in the day of my calamity,
but YHWH was my support.
He also brought me out into a large place.
He delivered me, because he delighted in me.
YHWH rewarded me according to my righteousness.
He rewarded me according to the cleanness of my hands.
For I have kept YHWH’s ways,
and have not wickedly departed from my God.
For all his ordinances were before me.
As for his statutes, I did not depart from them.
I was also perfect toward him.
I kept myself from my iniquity.
Therefore YHWH has rewarded me according to my righteousness,
According to my cleanness in his eyesight.
With the merciful you will show yourself merciful.
With the perfect man you will show yourself perfect.
With the pure you will show yourself pure.
With the crooked you will show yourself shrewd.
You will save the afflicted people,
But your eyes are on the haughty, that you may bring them down.
For you are my lamp, YHWH.
YHWH will light up my darkness.
For by you, I run against a troop.
By my God, I leap over a wall.
As for God, his way is perfect.
YHWH’s word is tested.
He is a shield to all those who take refuge in him.
For who is God, besides YHWH?
Who is a rock, besides our God?
God is my strong fortress.
He makes my way perfect.
He makes his feet like hinds’ feet,
and sets me on my high places.
He teaches my hands to war,
so that my arms bend a bow of brass.
You have also given me the shield of your salvation.
Your gentleness has made me great.
You have enlarged my steps under me.
My feet have not slipped.
I have pursued my enemies and destroyed them.
I didn’t turn again until they were consumed.
I have consumed them,
and struck them through,
so that they can’t arise.
Yes, they have fallen under my feet.
For you have armed me with strength for the battle.
You have subdued under me those who rose up against me.
You have also made my enemies turn their backs to me,
that I might cut off those who hate me.
They looked, but there was no one to save;
even to YHWH, but he didn’t answer them.
Then I beat them as small as the dust of the earth.
I crushed them as the mire of the streets, and spread them abroad.
You also have delivered me from the strivings of my people.
You have kept me to be the head of the nations.
A people whom I have not known will serve me.
The foreigners will submit themselves to me.
As soon as they hear of me, they will obey me.
The foreigners will fade away,
and will come trembling out of their close places.
YHWH lives!
Blessed be my rock!
Exalted be God, the rock of my salvation,
even the God who executes vengeance for me,
who brings down peoples under me,
who brings me away from my enemies.
Yes, you lift me up above those who rise up against me.
You deliver me from the violent man.
Therefore I will give thanks to you, YHWH, among the nations,
and will sing praises to your name.
He gives great deliverance to his king,
and shows steadfast love to his anointed,
to David and to his offspring, forever more.”
The Last Words of David · 23:1–7
Now these are the last words of David.
David the son of Jesse says,
the man who was raised on high says,
the anointed of the God of Jacob,
the sweet psalmist of Israel:
“YHWH’s Spirit spoke by me.
His word was on my tongue.
The God of Israel said,
the Rock of Israel spoke to me,
‘One who rules over men righteously,
who rules in the fear of God,
will be as the light of the morning, when the sun rises,
a morning without clouds,
when the tender grass springs out of the earth,
through clear shining after rain.’
Isn’t my house so with God?
Yet he has made with me an everlasting covenant,
ordered in all things, and sure,
for it is all my salvation, and all my desire,
although he doesn’t make it grow.
But all the ungodly will be as thorns to be thrust away,
because they can’t be taken with the hand,
But the man who touches them must be armed with iron and the staff of a spear.
They will be utterly burned with fire in their place.”
David's Mighty Men · 23:8–39

These are the names of the mighty men whom David has: Josheb Basshebeth a Tahchemonite, chief of the captains; the same is Adino the Eznite, against eight hundred slain at one time. After him is Eleazar the son of Dodai the son of an Ahohite, one of the three mighty men with David, when they defy the Philistines who are there gathered together to battle, and the men of Israel have gone away. He arises and strikes the Philistines until his hand is weary, and his hand freezes to the sword; and YHWH works a great victory that day; and the people return after him only to take plunder. After him is Shammah the son of Agee a Hararite. The Philistines has gathered together into a troop, where there is a plot of ground full of lentils; and the people flee from the Philistines. But he stands in the middle of the plot and defends it, and kills the Philistines; and YHWH works a great victory. Three of the thirty chief men goes down, and comes to David in the harvest time to the cave of Adullam; and the troop of the Philistines is encamped in the valley of Rephaim. David is then in the stronghold; and the garrison of the Philistines is then in Bethlehem. David longs, and says, “Oh that someone would give me water to drink from the well of Bethlehem, which is by the gate!”

The three mighty men break through the army of the Philistines, and draw water out of the well of Bethlehem that is by the gate, and take it and bring it to David; but he would not drink of it, but pours it out to YHWH. He says, “Be it far from me, YHWH, that I should do this! Isn’t this the blood of the men who risked their lives to go?” Therefore he would not drink it. The three mighty men do these things.

Abishai, the brother of Joab, the son of Zeruiah, is chief of the three. He lifts up his spear against three hundred and kills them, and has a name among the three. Isn’t he most honorable of the three? therefore he is made their captain. However he isn’t included as one of the three. Benaiah the son of Jehoiada, the son of a valiant man of Kabzeel, who has done mighty deeds, kills the two sons of Ariel of Moab. He also goes down and kills a lion in the middle of a pit in a time of snow. He kills a huge Egyptian, and the Egyptian has a spear in his hand; but he goes down to him with a staff, and plucks the spear out of the Egyptian’s hand, and kills him with his own spear. Benaiah the son of Jehoiada does these things, and has a name among the three mighty men. He is more honorable than the thirty, but he doesn’t attain to the three. David sets him over his guard. Asahel the brother of Joab is one of the thirty: Elhanan the son of Dodo of Bethlehem, Shammah the Harodite, Elika the Harodite, Helez the Paltite, Ira the son of Ikkesh the Tekoite, Abiezer the Anathothite, Mebunnai the Hushathite, Zalmon the Ahohite, Maharai the Netophathite, Heleb the son of Baanah the Netophathite, Ittai the son of Ribai of Gibeah of the children of Benjamin, Benaiah a Pirathonite, Hiddai of the brooks of Gaash. Abialbon the Arbathite, Azmaveth the Barhumite, Eliahba the Shaalbonite, the sons of Jashen, Jonathan, Shammah the Hararite, Ahiam the son of Sharar the Ararite, Eliphelet the son of Ahasbai, the son of the Maacathite, Eliam the son of Ahithophel the Gilonite, Hezro the Carmelite, Paarai the Arbite, Igal the son of Nathan of Zobah, Bani the Gadite, Zelek the Ammonite, Naharai the Beerothite, armor bearers to Joab the son of Zeruiah, Ira the Ithrite, Gareb the Ithrite, and Uriah the Hittite: thirty-seven in all.
The Census · 24:1–9

Again YHWH’s anger burns against Israel, and he moves David against them, saying, “Go, count Israel and Judah.” The king says to Joab the captain of the army, who is with him, “Now go back and forth through all the tribes of Israel, from Dan even to Beersheba, and count the people, that I may know the sum of the people.”

Joab says to the king, “Now may YHWH your God add to the people, however many they may be, one hundred times; and may the eyes of my lord the king see it. But why does my lord the king delight in this thing?”

Notwithstanding, the king’s word prevails against Joab, and against the captains of the army. Joab and the captains of the army go out from the presence of the king to count the people of Israel. They pass over the Jordan, and encamp in Aroer, on the right side of the city that is in the middle of the valley of Gad, and to Jazer; then they come to Gilead, and to the land of Tahtim Hodshi; and they come to Dan Jaan, and around to Sidon, and come to the stronghold of Tyre, and to all the cities of the Hivites, and of the Canaanites; and they go out to the south of Judah, at Beersheba. So when they have gone back and forth through all the land, they come to Jerusalem at the end of nine months and twenty days. Joab gives up the sum of the counting of the people to the king: and there are in Israel eight hundred thousand valiant men who draw the sword; and the men of Judah are five hundred thousand men.
David's Conscience and God's Judgment · 24:10–17

David’s heart strikes him after he has counted the people. David says to YHWH, “I have sinned greatly in that which I have done. But now, YHWH, put away, I beg you, the iniquity of your servant; for I have done very foolishly.”

When David rises up in the morning, YHWH’s word comes to the prophet Gad, David’s seer, saying, “Go and speak to David, ‘YHWH says, “I offer you three things. Choose one of them, that I may do it to you.”’”

So Gad comes to David, and tells him, and says to him, “Will seven years of famine come to you in your land? Or will you flee three months before your foes while they pursue you? Or will there be three days’ pestilence in your land? Now answer, and consider what answer I will return to him who sent me.”
David says to Gad, “I am in distress. Let us fall now into YHWH’s hand; for his mercies are great. Let me not fall into man’s hand.”

So YHWH sends a pestilence on Israel from the morning even to the appointed time; and seventy thousand men die of the people from Dan even to Beersheba. When the angel stretches out his hand toward Jerusalem to destroy it, YHWH relents of the disaster, and says to the angel who destroys the people, “It is enough. Now withdraw your hand.” YHWH’s angel is by the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite.

David speaks to YHWH when he sees the angel who strikes the people, and says, “Look, I have sinned, and I have done perversely; but these sheep, what have they done? Please let your hand be against me, and against my father’s house.”
The Threshing Floor of Araunah · 24:18–25
Gad comes that day to David, and says to him, “Go up, build an altar to YHWH on the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite.”

David goes up according to the saying of Gad, as YHWH commands. Araunah looks out, and sees the king and his servants coming on toward him. Then Araunah goes out, and bows himself before the king with his face to the ground. Araunah says, “Why has my lord the king come to his servant?”
David says, “To buy your threshing floor, to build an altar to YHWH, that the plague may be stopped from afflicting the people.”

Araunah says to David, “Let my lord the king take and offer up what seems good to him. Look, the cattle for the burnt offering, and the threshing instruments and the yokes of the oxen for the wood. All this, O king, does Araunah give to the king.” Araunah says to the king, “May YHWH your God accept you.”

The king says to Araunah, “No; but I will most certainly buy it from you for a price. I will not offer burnt offerings to YHWH my God which cost me nothing.” So David buys the threshing floor and the oxen for fifty shekels of silver. David builds an altar to YHWH there, and offers burnt offerings and peace offerings. So YHWH is entreated for the land, and the plague is removed from Israel.
The Old King and the Shunammite · 1:1–4

Now king David is old and advanced in years; and they cover him with clothes, but he can’t keep warm. Therefore his servants say to him, “Let a young virgin be sought for my lord the king. Let her stand before the king, and cherish him; and let her lie in your bosom, that my lord the king may keep warm.” So they seek for a beautiful young lady throughout all the borders of Israel, and find Abishag the Shunammite, and bring her to the king. The young lady is very beautiful; and she cherishes the king, and serves him; but the king doesn’t know her intimately.
Adonijah Seizes His Chance · 1:5–10

Then Adonijah the son of Haggith exalts himself, saying, “I will be king.” Then he prepares him chariots and horsemen, and fifty men to run before him. His father has not displeased him at any time in saying, “Why have you done so?” and he is also a very handsome man; and he is born after Absalom. He confers with Joab the son of Zeruiah, and with Abiathar the priest; and they follow Adonijah and help him. But Zadok the priest, Benaiah the son of Jehoiada, Nathan the prophet, Shimei, Rei, and the mighty men who belong to David, are not with Adonijah. Adonijah kills sheep, cattle, and fatlings by the stone of Zoheleth, which is beside En Rogel; and he calls all his brothers, the king’s sons, and all the men of Judah, the king’s servants; but he doesn’t call Nathan the prophet, and Benaiah, and the mighty men, and Solomon his brother.
Bathsheba and Nathan Move · 1:11–27

Then Nathan speaks to Bathsheba the mother of Solomon, saying, “Haven’t you heard that Adonijah the son of Haggith reigns, and David our lord doesn’t know it? Now therefore come, please let me give you counsel, that you may save your own life, and your son Solomon’s life. Go in to king David, and tell him, ‘Didn’t you, my lord, king, swear to your servant, saying, “Assuredly Solomon your son will reign after me, and he will sit on my throne?” Why then does Adonijah reign?’ Look, while you are still talking there with the king, I will also come in after you and confirm your words.”
Bathsheba goes in to the king in his room. The king is very old; and Abishag the Shunammite is serving the king. Bathsheba bows, and shows respect to the king. The king says, “What would you like?”

She says to him, “My lord, you swore by YHWH your God to your servant, ‘Assuredly Solomon your son will reign after me, and he will sit on my throne.’ Now, look, Adonijah reigns; and you, my lord the king, don’t know it. He has slain cattle and fatlings and sheep in abundance, and has called all the sons of the king, Abiathar the priest, and Joab the captain of the army; but he hasn’t called Solomon your servant. You, my lord the king, the eyes of all Israel are on you, that you should tell them who will sit on the throne of my lord the king after him. Otherwise it will happen, when my lord the king sleeps with his fathers, that I and my son Solomon will be considered criminals.”
Look, while she is still talking with the king, Nathan the prophet comes in. They tell the king, saying, “Look, Nathan the prophet!”

When he has come in before the king, he bows himself before the king with his face to the ground. Nathan says, “My lord, king, have you said, ‘Adonijah will reign after me, and he will sit on my throne?’ For he has gone down today, and has slain cattle, fatlings, and sheep in abundance, and has called all the king’s sons, the captains of the army, and Abiathar the priest. Look, they are eating and drinking before him, and saying, ‘Long live king Adonijah!’ But he hasn’t called me, even me your servant, Zadok the priest, Benaiah the son of Jehoiada, and your servant Solomon. Was this thing done by my lord the king, and you haven’t shown to your servants who should sit on the throne of my lord the king after him?”
David Commands Solomon's Anointing · 1:28–40

Then king David answers, “Call Bathsheba in to me.” She comes into the king’s presence and stands before the king. The king swears, and says, “As YHWH lives, who has redeemed my soul out of all adversity, most certainly as I swore to you by YHWH, the God of Israel, saying, ‘Assuredly Solomon your son will reign after me, and he will sit on my throne in my place;’ I will most certainly do this today.”
Then Bathsheba bows with her face to the earth, and shows respect to the king, and says, “Let my lord king David live forever!”

King David says, “Call to me Zadok the priest, Nathan the prophet, and Benaiah the son of Jehoiada.” They come before the king. The king says to them, “Take with you the servants of your lord, and cause Solomon my son to ride on my own mule, and bring him down to Gihon. Let Zadok the priest and Nathan the prophet anoint him there king over Israel. Blow the trumpet, and say, ‘Long live king Solomon!’ Then come up after him, and he will come and sit on my throne; for he will be king in my place. I have appointed him to be prince over Israel and over Judah.”

Benaiah the son of Jehoiada answers the king, and says, “Amen. May YHWH, the God of my lord the king, say so. As YHWH has been with my lord the king, even so may he be with Solomon, and make his throne greater than the throne of my lord king David.”

So Zadok the priest, Nathan the prophet, Benaiah the son of Jehoiada, and the Cherethites and the Pelethites go down and have Solomon ride on king David’s mule, and bring him to Gihon. Zadok the priest takes the horn of oil from the Tent, and anoints Solomon. They blow the trumpet; and all the people say, “Long live king Solomon!”
All the people come up after him, and the people pip with pipes, and rejoice with great joy, so that the earth shakes with their sound.
Solomon is King · 1:41–53
Adonijah and all the guests who are with him hear it as they have finished eating. When Joab hears the sound of the trumpet, he says, “Why is this noise of the city being in an uproar?”
While he yet speaks, look, Jonathan the son of Abiathar the priest comes; and Adonijah says, “Come in; for you are a worthy man, and bring good news.”

Jonathan answers Adonijah, “Most certainly our lord king David has made Solomon king. The king has sent with him Zadok the priest, Nathan the prophet, Benaiah the son of Jehoiada, and the Cherethites and the Pelethites; and they have caused him to ride on the king’s mule. Zadok the priest and Nathan the prophet have anointed him king in Gihon. They have come up from there rejoicing, so that the city rang again. This is the noise that you have heard. Also, Solomon sits on the throne of the kingdom. Moreover the king’s servants came to bless our lord king David, saying, ‘May your God make the name of Solomon better than your name, and make his throne greater than your throne;’ and the king bowed himself on the bed. Also thus said the king, ‘Blessed be YHWH, the God of Israel, who has given one to sit on my throne today, my eyes even seeing it.’”

All the guests of Adonijah are afraid, and rise up, and each man goes his way. Adonijah is afraid because of Solomon; and he arises, and goes, and hangs onto the horns of the altar. Solomon is told, “Look, Adonijah fears king Solomon; for, look, he is hanging onto the horns of the altar, saying, ‘Let king Solomon swear to me first that he will not kill his servant with the sword.’”
Solomon says, “If he shows himself a worthy man, not a hair of his will fall to the earth; but if wickedness is found in him, he will die.”
So king Solomon sends, and they bring him down from the altar. He comes and bows down to king Solomon; and Solomon says to him, “Go to your house.”
David's Last Charge to Solomon · 2:1–9

Now the days of David come near that he should die; and he commands Solomon his son, saying, “I am going the way of all the earth. You be strong therefore, and show yourself a man; and keep the instruction of YHWH your God, to walk in his ways, to keep his statutes, his commandments, his ordinances, and his testimonies, according to that which is written in the law of Moses, that you may prosper in all that you do, and wherever you turn yourself. Then YHWH may establish his word which he spoke concerning me, saying, ‘If your children are careful of their way, to walk before me in truth with all their heart and with all their soul, there will not fail you,’ he said, ‘a man on the throne of Israel.’

“Moreover you know also what Joab the son of Zeruiah did to me, even what he did to the two captains of the armies of Israel, to Abner the son of Ner, and to Amasa the son of Jether, whom he killed, and shed the blood of war in peace, and put the blood of war on his sash that was around his waist, and in his shoes that were on his feet. Do therefore according to your wisdom, and don’t let his gray head go down to Sheol in peace. But show kindness to the sons of Barzillai the Gileadite, and let them be among those who eat at your table; for so they came to me when I fled from Absalom your brother.

“Look, there is with you Shimei the son of Gera, the Benjamite, of Bahurim, who cursed me with a grievous curse in the day when I went to Mahanaim; but he came down to meet me at the Jordan, and I swore to him by YHWH, saying, ‘I will not put you to death with the sword.’ Now therefore don’t hold him guiltless, for you are a wise man; and you will know what you ought to do to him, and you will bring his gray head down to Sheol with blood.”
David Dies · 2:10–12

David sleeps with his fathers, and is buried in David’s city. The days that David reigns over Israel are forty years; he reigns seven years in Hebron, and he reigns thirty-three years in Jerusalem. Solomon sits on David his father’s throne; and his kingdom is firmly established.
Adonijah's Fatal Request · 2:13–25
Then Adonijah the son of Haggith comes to Bathsheba the mother of Solomon. She says, “Do you come peaceably?”
He says, “Peaceably. He said moreover, I have something to tell you.”
She says, “Say on.”

He says, “You know that the kingdom was mine, and that all Israel set their faces on me, that I should reign. However the kingdom is turned around, and has become my brother’s; for it was his from YHWH. Now I ask one petition of you. Don’t deny me.”
She says to him, “Say on.” He says, “Please speak to Solomon the king (for he will not tell you ‘no’), that he give me Abishag the Shunammite as wife.”
Bathsheba says, “Alright. I will speak for you to the king.”

Bathsheba therefore goes to king Solomon, to speak to him for Adonijah. The king rises up to meet her, and bows himself to her, and sits down on his throne, and causes a throne to be set for the king’s mother; and she sits on his right hand. Then she says, “I ask one small petition of you; don’t deny me.”
The king says to her, “Ask on, my mother; for I will not deny you.”
She says, “Let Abishag the Shunammite be given to Adonijah your brother as wife.”

King Solomon answers his mother, “Why do you ask Abishag the Shunammite for Adonijah? Ask for him the kingdom also; for he is my elder brother; even for him, and for Abiathar the priest, and for Joab the son of Zeruiah.” Then king Solomon swears by YHWH, saying, “God do so to me, and more also, if Adonijah has not spoken this word against his own life. Now therefore as YHWH lives, who has established me, and set me on my father David’s throne, and who has made me a house as he promised, surely Adonijah will be put to death today.”
King Solomon sends Benaiah the son of Jehoiada; and he falls on him, so that he dies.
Abiathar Exiled, Joab Executed · 2:26–35

To Abiathar the priest the king says, “Go to Anathoth, to your own fields; for you are worthy of death. But I will not at this time put you to death, because you bore the Lord YHWH’s ark before David my father, and because you were afflicted in all in which my father was afflicted.” So Solomon thrusts Abiathar out from being priest to YHWH, that he might fulfill YHWH’s word, which he speaks concerning the house of Eli in Shiloh.

This news comes to Joab; for Joab has followed Adonijah, although he doesn’t follow Absalom. Joab flees to YHWH’s Tent, and holds onto the horns of the altar. King Solomon is told, “Joab has fled to YHWH’s Tent, and look, he is by the altar.” Then Solomon sends Benaiah the son of Jehoiada, saying, “Go, fall on him.”
Benaiah comes to YHWH’s Tent, and says to him, “Thus says the king, ‘Come out!’”
He says, “No; but I will die here.”
Benaiah brings the king word again, saying, “Thus said Joab, and thus he answered me.”

The king says to him, “Do as he has said, and fall on him, and bury him; that you may take away the blood, which Joab shed without cause, from me and from my father’s house. YHWH will return his blood on his own head, because he fell on two men more righteous and better than he, and killed them with the sword, and my father David didn’t know it: Abner the son of Ner, captain of the army of Israel, and Amasa the son of Jether, captain of the army of Judah. So their blood will return on the head of Joab, and on the head of his offspring forever. But for David, for his offspring, for his house, and for his throne, there will be peace forever from YHWH.”

Then Benaiah the son of Jehoiada goes up and falls on him, and kills him; and he is buried in his own house in the wilderness. The king puts Benaiah the son of Jehoiada in his place over the army; and the king puts Zadok the priest in the place of Abiathar.
Shimei's Reckless Journey · 2:36–46

The king sends and calls for Shimei, and says to him, “Build yourself a house in Jerusalem, and live there, and don’t go anywhere else. For on the day you go out and pass over the brook Kidron, know for certain that you will surely die. Your blood will be on your own head.”
Shimei says to the king, “What you say is good. As my lord the king has said, so will your servant do.” Shimei lives in Jerusalem many days.
At the end of three years, two of Shimei’s slaves runs away to Achish, son of Maacah, king of Gath. They tell Shimei, saying, “Look, your slaves are in Gath.”

Shimei arises, saddles his donkey, and goes to Gath to Achish, to seek his slaves; and Shimei goes, and brings his slaves from Gath. Solomon is told that Shimei has gone from Jerusalem to Gath, and has come again.

The king sends and calls for Shimei, and says to him, “Didn’t I adjure you by YHWH, and warn you, saying, ‘Know for certain, that on the day you go out, and walk anywhere else, you will surely die?’ You said to me, ‘The saying that I have heard is good.’ Why then have you not kept the oath of YHWH, and the commandment that I have instructed you with?” The king says moreover to Shimei, “You know in your heart all the wickedness that you did to David my father. Therefore YHWH will return your wickedness on your own head. But king Solomon will be blessed, and David’s throne will be established before YHWH forever.” So the king commands Benaiah the son of Jehoiada; and he goes out, and falls on him, so that he dies. The kingdom is established in the hand of Solomon.
Alliance and Ambivalence · 3:1–3

Solomon makes an alliance with Pharaoh king of Egypt, and takes Pharaoh’s daughter, and brings her into David’s city, until he has finished building his own house, YHWH’s house, and the wall around Jerusalem. However the people sacrifices in the high places, because there is not yet a house built for YHWH’s name. Solomon loves YHWH, walking in the statutes of David his father; except that he sacrifices and burns incense in the high places.
The Dream at Gibeon · 3:4–15

The king goes to Gibeon to sacrifice there; for that is the great high place. Solomon offers a thousand burnt offerings on that altar. In Gibeon, YHWH appears to Solomon in a dream by night; and God says, “Ask for what I should give you.”

Solomon says, “You have shown to your servant David my father great steadfast love, because he walked before you in truth, in righteousness, and in uprightness of heart with you. You have kept for him this great steadfast love, that you have given him a son to sit on his throne, as it is today. Now, YHWH my God, you have made your servant king instead of David my father. I am just a little child. I don’t know how to go out or come in. Your servant is among your people which you have chosen, a great people, that can’t be numbered or counted for multitude. Give your servant therefore an understanding heart to judge your people, that I may discern between good and evil; for who is able to judge this great people of yours?”

This request pleases the Lord, that Solomon has asked this thing. God says to him, “Because you have asked this thing, and have not asked for yourself long life, nor have you asked for riches for yourself, nor have you asked for the life of your enemies, but have asked for yourself understanding to discern justice; look, I have done according to your word. Look, I have given you a wise and understanding heart; so that there has been no one like you before you, and after you none will arise like you. I have also given you that which you have not asked, both riches and honor, so that there will not be any among the kings like you for all your days. If you will walk in my ways, to keep my statutes and my commandments, as your father David walked, then I will lengthen your days.”

Solomon awakes; and look, it is a dream. Then he comes to Jerusalem, and stands before the ark of YHWH’s covenant, and offers up burnt offerings, offers peace offerings, and makes a feast for all his servants.
The Two Mothers · 3:16–28

Then two women who are prostitutes come to the king, and stand before him. The one woman says, “Oh, my lord, I and this woman dwell in one house. I delivered a child with her in the house. The third day after I delivered, this woman delivered also. We were together. There was no stranger with us in the house, just us two in the house. This woman’s child died in the night, because she lay on it. She arose at midnight, and took my son from beside me, while your servant slept, and laid it in her bosom, and laid her dead child in my bosom. When I rose in the morning to nurse my child, look, it was dead; but when I had looked at it in the morning, look, it was not my son, whom I bore.”
The other woman says, “No; but the living one is my son, and the dead one is your son.”
The first one says, “No; but the dead one is your son, and the living one is my son.” Thus they speak before the king.
Then the king says, “One says, ‘This is my son who lives, and your son is the dead;’ and the other says, ‘No; but your son is the dead one, and my son is the living one.’”
The king says, “Get me a sword.” So they bring a sword before the king.
The king says, “Divide the living child in two, and give half to the one, and half to the other.”
Then the woman whose the living child is spoke to the king, for her heart yearned over her son, and she says, “Oh, my lord, give her the living child, and in no way kill him!”
But the other says, “He will be neither mine nor yours. Divide him.”
Then the king answers, “Give her the living child, and definitely do not kill him. She is his mother.”
All Israel hears of the judgment which the king has judged; and they fear the king; for they see that the wisdom of God is in him, to do justice.
Solomon's Royal Officials · 4:1–6

King Solomon is king over all Israel. These are the princes whom he has: Azariah the son of Zadok, the priest; Elihoreph and Ahijah, the sons of Shisha, scribes; Jehoshaphat the son of Ahilud, the recorder; Benaiah the son of Jehoiada is over the army; Zadok and Abiathar are priests; Azariah the son of Nathan is over the officers; Zabud the son of Nathan is chief minister, the king’s friend; Ahishar is over the household; and Adoniram the son of Abda is over the men subject to forced labor.
The Twelve District Governors · 4:7–19

Solomon has twelve officers over all Israel, who provides food for the king and his household. Each man has to make provision for a month in the year. These are their names: Ben Hur, in the hill country of Ephraim; Ben Deker, in Makaz, in Shaalbim, Beth Shemesh, and Elon Beth Hanan; Ben Hesed, in Arubboth (Socoh and all the land of Hepher belongs to him); Ben Abinadab, in all the height of Dor (he has Taphath, Solomon’s daughter, as wife); Baana the son of Ahilud, in Taanach and Megiddo, and all Beth Shean which is beside Zarethan, beneath Jezreel, from Beth Shean to Abel Meholah, as far as beyond Jokmeam; Ben Geber, in Ramoth Gilead (the towns of Jair the son of Manasseh, which are in Gilead, belongs to him; and the region of Argob, which is in Bashan, sixty great cities with walls and bronze bars, belongs to him); Ahinadab the son of Iddo, in Mahanaim; Ahimaaz, in Naphtali (he also takes Basemath the daughter of Solomon as wife); Baana the son of Hushai, in Asher and Bealoth; Jehoshaphat the son of Paruah, in Issachar; Shimei the son of Ela, in Benjamin; Geber the son of Uri, in the land of Gilead, the country of Sihon king of the Amorites and of Og king of Bashan; and he is the only officer who is in the land.
Prosperity and Peace · 4:20–25

Judah and Israel are numerous as the sand which is by the sea in multitude, eating and drinking and making merry. Solomon rules over all the kingdoms from the River to the land of the Philistines, and to the border of Egypt. They bring tribute and serve Solomon all the days of his life. Solomon’s provision for one day is thirty cors of fine flour, sixty measures of meal, ten head of fat cattle, twenty head of cattle out of the pastures, and one hundred sheep, besides deer, and gazelles, and roebucks, and fattened fowl. For he has dominion over all on this side the River, from Tiphsah even to Gaza, over all the kings on this side the River: and he has peace on all sides around him. Judah and Israel live safely, every man under his vine and under his fig tree, from Dan even to Beersheba, all the days of Solomon.
Provision, Horses, and the Reach of Wisdom · 4:26–34

Solomon has forty thousand stalls of horses for his chariots, and twelve thousand horsemen. Those officers provide food for king Solomon, and for all who come to king Solomon’s table, every man in his month. They let nothing be lacking. They also bring Barley and straw for the horses and swift steeds to the place where the officers are, each man according to his duty. God gives Solomon abundant wisdom and understanding, and very great understanding, even as the sand that is on the seashore. Solomon’s wisdom excels the wisdom of all the children of the east and all the wisdom of Egypt. For he is wiser than all men; than Ethan the Ezrahite, Heman, Calcol, and Darda, the sons of Mahol: and his fame is in all the nations all around. He speaks three thousand proverbs; and his songs number one thousand five. He speaks of trees, from the cedar that is in Lebanon even to the hyssop that grows out of the wall; he also speaks of animals, of birds, of creeping things, and of fish. People of all nations come to hear the wisdom of Solomon, sent by all kings of the earth, who has heard of his wisdom.
Solomon and Hiram · 5:1–12

Hiram king of Tyre sends his servants to Solomon; for he has heard that they have anointed him king in the place of his father, and Hiram has always loved David. Solomon sends to Hiram, saying, “You know that David my father could not build a house for the name of YHWH his God because of the wars which were around him on every side, until YHWH put his enemies under the soles of his feet. But now YHWH my God has given me rest on every side. There is no enemy and no evil occurrence. Look, I intend to build a house for the name of YHWH my God, as YHWH spoke to David my father, saying, ‘Your son, whom I will set on your throne in your place will build the house for my name.’ Now therefore command that cedar trees be cut for me out of Lebanon. My servants will be with your servants; and I will give you wages for your servants according to all that you say. For you know that there is nobody among us who knows how to cut timber like the Sidonians.”

When Hiram hears the words of Solomon, he rejoices greatly, and says, “Blessed is YHWH today, who has given to David a wise son to rule over this great people.” Hiram sends to Solomon, saying, “I have heard the message which you have sent to me. I will do all your desire concerning timber of cedar, and concerning cypress timber. My servants will bring them down from Lebanon to the sea. I will make them into rafts to go by sea to the place that you specify to me, and will cause them to be broken up there, and you will receive them. You will accomplish my desire, in giving food for my household.”

So Hiram gives Solomon cedar timber and cypress timber according to all his desire. Solomon gives Hiram twenty thousand cors of wheat for food to his household, and twenty cors of pure oil. Solomon gives this to Hiram year by year. YHWH gives Solomon wisdom, as he promises him. There is peace between Hiram and Solomon, and the two of them makes a treaty together.
The Levy of Labor · 5:13–18

King Solomon raises a levy out of all Israel; and the levy is thirty thousand men. He sends them to Lebanon, ten thousand a month by courses; for a month they are in Lebanon, and two months at home; and Adoniram is over the men subject to forced labor. Solomon has seventy thousand who bears burdens, and eighty thousand who are stone cutters in the mountains; besides Solomon’s chief officers who are over the work, three thousand and three hundred, who rule over the people who labor in the work. The king commands, and they cut out large stones, costly stones, to lay the foundation of the house with worked stone. Solomon’s builders and Hiram’s builders and the Gebalites cut them, and prepare the timber and the stones to build the house.
The Temple is Begun · 6:1–10

In the four hundred and eightieth year after the children of Israel has come out of the land of Egypt, in the fourth year of Solomon’s reign over Israel, in the month Ziv, which is the second month, he begins to build YHWH’s house. The house which king Solomon builds for YHWH has a length of sixty cubits, and its width twenty, and its height thirty cubits. The porch in front of the temple of the house has a length of twenty cubits, which are along the width of the house. Ten cubits are its width in front of the house. He makes windows of fixed lattice work for the house. Against the wall of the house, he builds floors all around, against the walls of the house all around, both of the temple and of the inner sanctuary; and he makes side rooms all around. The lowest floor is five cubits wide, and the middle is six cubits wide, and the third is seven cubits wide; for on the outside he makes offsets in the wall of the house all around, that the beams should not be inserted into the walls of the house. The house, when it is under construction, is built of stone prepared at the quarry; and no hammer or ax or any tool of iron are heard in the house while it is under construction. The door for the middle side rooms is in the right side of the house. They go up by winding stairs into the middle floor, and out of the middle into the third. So he builds the house, and finishes it; and he covers the house with beams and planks of cedar. He builds the floors all along the house, each five cubits high; and they rest on the house with timber of cedar.
The Word of YHWH in the Building · 6:11–13

YHWH’s word comes to Solomon, saying, “Concerning this house which you are building, if you will walk in my statutes, and execute my ordinances, and keep all my commandments to walk in them; then I will establish my word with you, which I spoke to David your father. I will dwell among the children of Israel, and will not forsake my people Israel.”
The Interior: Cedar and Gold · 6:14–36

So Solomon builds the house, and finishes it. He builds the walls of the house within with boards of cedar: from the floor of the house to the walls of the ceiling, he covers them on the inside with wood; and he covers the floor of the house with cypress boards. He builds twenty cubits on the back part of the house with boards of cedar from the floor to the ceiling. He builds them for it within, for an inner sanctuary, even for the most holy place. In front of the temple sanctuary is forty cubits. There is cedar on the house within, carved with buds and open flowers. All are cedar. No stone is visible. He prepares an inner sanctuary in the middle of the house within, to set the ark of YHWH’s covenant there. Within the inner sanctuary is twenty cubits in length, and twenty cubits in width, and twenty cubits in its height; and he overlays it with pure gold; and he covers the altar with cedar. So Solomon overlays the house within with pure gold. He draws chains of gold across before the inner sanctuary, and he overlays it with gold. He overlays the whole house with gold, until all the house is finished. He also overlays the whole altar that belongs to the inner sanctuary with gold. In the inner sanctuary he makes two cherubim of olive wood, each ten cubits high. Five cubits are the one wing of the cherub, and five cubits the other wing of the cherub. From the tip of one wing to the tip of the other are ten cubits. The other cherub is ten cubits. Both the cherubim are of one measure and one form. One cherub is ten cubits high, and so is the other cherub. He sets the cherubim within the inner house. The wings of the cherubim are stretched out, so that the wing of the one touches the one wall, and the wing of the other cherub touches the other wall; and their wings touch one another in the middle of the house. He overlays the cherubim with gold. He carves all the walls of the house around with carved figures of cherubim, palm trees, and open flowers, inside and outside. He overlays the floor of the house with gold, inside and outside. For the entrance of the inner sanctuary, he makes doors of olive wood. The lintel and door posts are a fifth part of the wall. So he makes two doors of olive wood; and he carves on them carvings of cherubim, palm trees, and open flowers, and overlays them with gold. He spreads the gold on the cherubim and on the palm trees. He also does so for the entrance of the temple door posts of olive wood, out of a fourth part of the wall; and two doors of cypress wood. The two leaves of the one door are folding, and the two leaves of the other door are folding. He carves cherubim, palm trees, and open flowers; and he overlays them with gold fitted on the engraved work. He builds the inner court with three courses of cut stone and a course of cedar beams.
The Temple Completed · 6:37–38

The foundation of YHWH’s house is laid in the fourth year, in the month Ziv. In the eleventh year, in the month Bul, which is the eighth month, the house is finished throughout all its parts, and according to all its specifications. So he spends seven years building it.
Solomon's Palace Complex · 7:1–12

Solomon is building his own house thirteen years, and he finishes all his house. For he builds the House of the Forest of Lebanon. Its length is one hundred cubits, its width fifty cubits, and its height thirty cubits, on four rows of cedar pillars, with cedar beams on the pillars. It is covered with cedar above over the forty-five beams, that are on the pillars, fifteen in a row. There are beams in three rows, and window is facing window in three ranks. All the doors and posts are made square with beams: and window is facing window in three ranks. He makes the porch of pillars. Its length is fifty cubits and its width thirty cubits; with a porch before them, and pillars and a threshold before them. He makes the porch of the throne where he is to judge, even the porch of judgment; and it is covered with cedar from floor to floor. His house where he is to dwell, the other court within the porch, is of the like work. He makes also a house for Pharaoh’s daughter (whom Solomon has taken as wife), like this porch. All these are of costly stones, even of cut stone, according to measure, sawed with saws, inside and outside, even from the foundation to the coping, and so on the outside to the great court. The foundation is of costly stones, even great stones, stones of ten cubits, and stones of eight cubits. Above are costly stones, even cut stone, according to measure, and cedar wood. The great court around has three courses of cut stone, and a course of cedar beams; like the inner court of YHWH’s house and the porch of the house.
Hiram the Craftsman · 7:13–22

King Solomon sends and brings Hiram out of Tyre. He is the son of a widow of the tribe of Naphtali, and his father is a man of Tyre, a worker in brass; and he is filled with wisdom and understanding and skill, to work all works in brass. He comes to king Solomon, and performs all his work. For he fashions the two pillars of brass, eighteen cubits high apiece; and a line of twelve cubits encircled either of them. He makes two capitals of molten brass, to set on the tops of the pillars. The height of the one capital is five cubits, and the height of the other capital is five cubits. There are nets of checker work, and wreaths of chain work, for the capitals which are on the top of the pillars; seven for the one capital, and seven for the other capital. So he makes the pillars; and there are two rows around on the one network, to cover the capitals that are on the top of the pillars: and he does so for the other capital. The capitals that are on the top of the pillars in the porch are of lily work, four cubits. There are capitals above also on the two pillars, close by the belly which is beside the network. There are two hundred pomegranates in rows around the other capital. He sets up the pillars at the porch of the temple. He sets up the right pillar, and calls its name Jachin; and he sets up the left pillar, and calls its name Boaz. On the top of the pillars is lily work: so the work of the pillars is finished.
The Molten Sea and the Carts · 7:23–39

He makes the molten sea of ten cubits from brim to brim, round in shape. Its height is five cubits; and a line of thirty cubits encircles it. Under its brim around there are buds which encircle it for ten cubits, encircling the sea. The buds are in two rows, cast when it is cast. It stands on twelve oxen, three looking toward the north, and three looking toward the west, and three looking toward the south, and three looking toward the east; and the sea is set on them above, and all their hindquarters are inward. It is a hand width thick. Its brim is worked like the brim of a cup, like the flower of a lily. It holds two thousand baths. He makes the ten bases of brass. The length of one base is four cubits, four cubits its width, and three cubits its height. The work of the bases is like this: they have panels; and there are panels between the ledges; and on the panels that are between the ledges are lions, oxen, and cherubim; and on the ledges there is a pedestal above; and beneath the lions and oxen are wreaths of hanging work. Every base has four bronze wheels, and axles of brass; and the four feet of it has supports. The supports are cast beneath the basin, with wreaths at the side of each. Its mouth within the capital and above is a cubit. Its mouth is round after the work of a pedestal, a cubit and a half; and also on its mouth are engravings, and their panels are square, not round. The four wheels are underneath the panels; and the axles of the wheels are in the base. The height of a wheel is a cubit and half a cubit. The work of the wheels is like the work of a chariot wheel. Their axles, and their rims, and their spokes, and their naves, are all of cast metal. There are four supports at the four corners of each base. Its supports are of the base itself. In the top of the base there is a round band half a cubit high; and on the top of the base its supports and its panels are of the same. On the plates of its supports, and on its panels, he engraves cherubim, lions, and palm trees, each in its space, with wreaths all around. He makes the ten bases in this way: all of them have one casting, one measure, and one form. He makes ten basins of brass. One basin contains forty baths; and every basin is four cubits; and on every one of the ten bases one basin. He sets the bases, five on the right side of the house, and five on the left side of the house. He sets the sea on the right side of the house eastward and toward the south.
The Temple Furnishings Completed · 7:40–51

Hiram makes the basins, the shovels, and the basins. So Hiram finishes doing all the work that he works for king Solomon in YHWH’s house: the two pillars; the two bowls of the capitals that are on the top of the pillars; the two networks to cover the two bowls of the capitals that are on the top of the pillars; the four hundred pomegranates for the two networks; two rows of pomegranates for each network, to cover the two bowls of the capitals that are on the pillars; the ten bases; the ten basins on the bases; the one sea; the twelve oxen under the sea; the pots; the shovels; and the basins: even all these vessels, which Hiram makes for king Solomon, in YHWH’s house, are of burnished brass. The king casts them in the plain of the Jordan, in the clay ground between Succoth and Zarethan. Solomon leaves all the vessels unweighes, because there are so many of them. The weight of the brass can not be determined. Solomon makes all the vessels that are in YHWH’s house: the golden altar and the table that the show bread is on, of gold; and the lamp stands, five on the right side, and five on the left, before the inner sanctuary, of pure gold; and the flowers, the lamps, and the tongs, of gold; the cups, the snuffers, the basins, the spoons, and the fire pans, of pure gold; and the hinges, both for the doors of the inner house, the most holy place, and for the doors of the house, of the temple, of gold. Thus all the work that king Solomon does in YHWH’s house is finished. Solomon brings in the things which David his father has dedicated, the silver, the gold, and the vessels, and puts them in the treasuries of YHWH’s house.
The Ark is Brought to the Temple · 8:1–13

Then Solomon assembles the elders of Israel, with all the heads of the tribes, the princes of the fathers’ households of the children of Israel, to king Solomon in Jerusalem, to bring up the ark of YHWH’s covenant out of David’s city, which is Zion. All the men of Israel assemble themselves to king Solomon at the feast, in the month Ethanim, which is the seventh month. All the elders of Israel come, and the priests pick up the ark. They bring up YHWH’s ark, the Tent of Meeting, and all the holy vessels that are in the Tent. The priests and the Levites bring these up. King Solomon and all the congregation of Israel, who are assembled to him, are with him before the ark, sacrificing sheep and cattle, that can not be counted or numbered for multitude. The priests bring in the ark of YHWH’s covenant to its place, into the inner sanctuary of the house, to the most holy place, even under the cherubim’s wings. For the cherubim spread their wings out over the place of the ark, and the cherubim covers the ark and its poles above. The poles are so long that the ends of the poles are seen from the holy place before the inner sanctuary; but they are not seen outside. They are there to this day. There is nothing in the ark except the two stone tablets which Moses puts there at Horeb, when YHWH makes a covenant with the children of Israel, when they come out of the land of Egypt. It comes to pass, when the priests have come out of the holy place, that the cloud fills YHWH’s house, so that the priests can not stand to minister by reason of the cloud; for YHWH’s glory filled YHWH’s house. Then Solomon says, “YHWH has said that he would dwell in the thick darkness. I have surely built you a house of habitation, a place for you to dwell in forever.”
Solomon Addresses the Assembly · 8:14–21

The king turns his face around, and blesses all the assembly of Israel; and all the assembly of Israel stands. He says, “Blessed is YHWH, the God of Israel, who spoke with his mouth to David your father, and has with his hand fulfilled it, saying, ‘Since the day that I brought my people Israel out of Egypt, I chose no city out of all the tribes of Israel to build a house, that my name might be there; but I chose David to be over my people Israel.’

“Now it was in the heart of David my father to build a house for the name of YHWH, the God of Israel. But YHWH said to David my father, ‘Whereas it was in your heart to build a house for my name, you did well that it was in your heart. Nevertheless, you will not build the house; but your son who will come out of your body, he will build the house for my name.’ YHWH has established his word that he spoke; for I have risen up in the place of David my father, and I sit on the throne of Israel, as YHWH promised, and have built the house for the name of YHWH, the God of Israel. There I have set a place for the ark, in which is YHWH’s covenant, which he made with our fathers, when he brought them out of the land of Egypt.”
Solomon's Prayer of Dedication · 8:22–53

Solomon stands before YHWH’s altar in the presence of all the assembly of Israel, and spreads out his hands toward heaven; and he says, “YHWH, the God of Israel, there is no God like you, in heaven above, or on earth beneath; who keeps covenant and steadfast love with your servants, who walk before you with all their heart; who has kept with your servant David my father that which you promised him. Yes, you spoke with your mouth, and have fulfilled it with your hand, as it is today. Now therefore, may YHWH, the God of Israel, keep with your servant David my father that which you have promised him, saying, ‘There will not fail from you a man in my sight to sit on the throne of Israel, if only your children take heed to their way, to walk before me as you have walked before me.’

“Now therefore, God of Israel, please let your word be verified, which you spoke to your servant David my father. But will God in very deed dwell on the earth? Look, heaven and the heaven of heavens can’t contain you; how much less this house that I have built!
