Sir!’ they cry. ‘Let us in!’ But he calls back, ‘Truly I tell you, I do not know you.’ So keep watch. Neither the day nor the hour is known to you.
Money Put to Work · 25:14–30

It is like a man who is about to go on a journey. He calls in his servants and hands his wealth over to them. To one he gives five talents, to another two talents, and to another one, to each according to what he can handle. (A single talent is about twenty years’ wages for a working man.) Then he leaves on his journey. Right away the one with five talents starts trading with them, and he earns five more. In the same way, the one with the two talents makes two more. But the one who got a single talent goes and scoops out a hole in the dirt and buries his master’s money there.

A long while later the master comes home and calls his servants to account. The one who was given the five talents comes forward and brings five more. ‘Master,’ he says, ‘you put five talents in my hands. Look, here are five more that I’ve earned.’
‘Well done!’ his master tells him. ‘You are a good servant, and a faithful one. You have been faithful with a little, so I’ll trust you with much more. Come in, into your master’s joy!’
The one with the two talents comes forward too. ‘Master,’ he says, ‘you put two talents in my hands. Look, here are two more that I’ve earned.’
‘Well done!’ his master tells him. ‘You are a good servant, and a faithful one. You have been faithful with a little, so I’ll trust you with much more. Come in, into your master’s joy!’

Then the one who was given one talent comes forward. ‘Master,’ he says, ‘I knew you were a hard man. You reap fields you never sowed, and you gather grain where you never scattered any. I was scared, so I went and buried your talent in the ground. Here, take it. It’s yours.’

But his master answers him, ‘You wicked, lazy servant! You knew, did you, that I reap where I never sowed and gather where I never scattered? Then you should have put my money in the bank, and when I came home, I would have gotten it back with interest. Take that talent off him and hand it to the man with ten. Everyone who has will be given more, and he will have plenty. But the one who has nothing will lose even what he has. As for this useless servant, throw him out into the dark. There they will weep and grind their teeth.’
The Sheep and the Goats · 25:31–46

When the Son of Man comes in all his glory, with every angel at his side, he will sit down on the throne of his glory. Every nation will be brought together in front of him, and he will sort the people into two groups, the way a shepherd sorts the sheep from the goats. The sheep he will set at his right hand, and the goats at his left. Then the King will turn to those at his right. ‘Come here, you whom my Father has blessed,’ he will say. ‘Come into the kingdom that has been waiting for you since the world was made. It is yours. When I was hungry, you fed me. When I was thirsty, you gave me a drink. When I was a stranger, you took me in. When I had nothing to wear, you clothed me. When I was sick, you cared for me. When I was in prison, you came to see me.’

And the righteous will say to him, ‘Lord, when was it that we saw you hungry and fed you, or saw you thirsty and gave you a drink? When did we find you a stranger and take you in, or with nothing to wear and clothe you? When did we come to you sick, or visit you in prison?’

And the King will answer them, ‘Truly I tell you, every time you did it for one of these brothers and sisters of mine, even the smallest, you were doing it for me.’ Then he will say to the ones on his left, ‘Get away from me, you who are under the curse, into the fire that never ends, the fire made ready for the devil and his angels. When I was hungry, you didn’t feed me. When I was thirsty, you didn’t give me a drink. When I was a stranger, you didn’t take me in. When I had nothing to wear, you didn’t clothe me. When I was sick and in prison, you never came to me.’
And they too will say, ‘Lord, when did we ever find you hungry, or thirsty, or a stranger, or with nothing to wear, or sick, or in prison, and not take care of you?’

And he will answer them, ‘Truly I tell you, every time you turned away from one of these, even the smallest, you turned away from me.’ These will go away to be punished forever, but the righteous will go into eternal life.”
The Plot and the Perfume · 26:1–13
When Jesus has finished all this teaching, he turns to his disciples. “In two days, as you know, it will be Passover,” he says, “and the Son of Man is going to be betrayed and crucified.”

At that very time the chief priests and the elders of the people are meeting in the courtyard of the high priest, a man named Caiaphas. Together they work out a scheme to take Jesus by stealth and put him to death. “But not at the feast,” they say, “or the people will riot.”

Jesus is in Bethany, staying at the house of Simon, a man who once had leprosy. While he is reclining at the table, a woman comes up to him carrying an alabaster jar of perfume, very costly. And she pours it over his head. The disciples are outraged when they see it. “What a waste!” they say. “That could have fetched a lot of money, and it could have gone to the poor.”

Jesus knows what they are saying. “Why are you giving this woman a hard time?” he asks them. “What she has done for me is lovely. You will always have poor people among you. You won’t always have me. By pouring this perfume over my body, she has made me ready to be buried. Truly I tell you, wherever this good news is told, anywhere in the whole world, what she has done will be told too, and she will be remembered.”
Thirty Pieces of Silver · 26:14–16

Then Judas Iscariot, one of the Twelve, goes off to see the chief priests. “What will you give me,” he asks, “if I hand him over to you?” And they weigh out thirty pieces of silver for him. From that moment he is on the lookout for a chance to betray him.
The Last Passover · 26:17–30
On the first day of the Feast of Unleavened Bread, the disciples ask Jesus, “Where would you like us to prepare the Passover meal for you?”
“Go into the city and find a certain man,” he tells them. “Say to him, ‘The Teacher says his hour has come close. He will eat the Passover at your house with his disciples.’”

The disciples do exactly as Jesus has told them, and they get the Passover meal ready. That evening he takes his place at the table with the Twelve. In the middle of the meal he says, “Truly I tell you, one of you is going to betray me.”
They are deeply hurt, and one after another they start asking him, “Lord, it isn’t me, is it?”

He answers, “It’s someone who has dipped his bread into the same bowl as me. He’s the one who will betray me. The Son of Man is going the way the Scriptures say he will. But how terrible for the man who betrays the Son of Man! It would have been better for that man if he had never been born.”
Then Judas, the one who is betraying him, speaks up. “Rabbi, it isn’t me, is it?” Jesus says to him, “You’ve said it yourself.”

As the meal goes on, Jesus picks up a loaf of bread and speaks a blessing over it. Then he breaks it and hands it around to the disciples. “Take this and eat it,” he says. “This is my body.” Then he lifts a cup, gives thanks, and passes it to them. “Drink from this, every one of you,” he says. “This is my blood, the blood of the covenant, which is being poured out for many people so that their sins can be forgiven. I tell you, from now on I won’t taste the fruit of the vine again until that day when I drink it new with you in my Father’s kingdom.” Then they sing the Hallel, the psalms of Passover, and go out to the Mount of Olives.
Peter’s Promise · 26:31–35

Then Jesus tells them, “Tonight every one of you will stumble and fall away because of me. It is written: ‘I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock will scatter.’ But after I am raised, I will lead the way ahead of you into Galilee.”
Peter answers, “Everyone else may fall away because of you, but I won’t. Not ever.”
Jesus says to him, “Truly I tell you, before the rooster crows tonight, you will have denied me three times.”
“Even if it means dying with you,” Peter tells him, “I will not deny you!” And every one of the disciples says it too.
Gethsemane · 26:36–46

Then Jesus comes with them to a place called Gethsemane, which means Oil Press. “Wait here,” he tells the disciples, “while I go on a little way to pray.” He takes Peter and the two sons of Zebedee with him, and he begins to be filled with sorrow and anguish. “My soul is crushed with grief, to the point of death,” he tells them. “Stay here, and stay awake with me.”
He goes on a little farther and falls face down on the ground and prays. “My Father, if it can be done, let this cup pass me by. Yet not the way I want, but the way you want.”

When he comes back, the disciples are asleep. “So you couldn’t stay awake with me for one hour?” he says to Peter. “Keep awake, and pray, so you won’t give way when the test comes. The spirit is eager, but the flesh is weak.”

Once more he goes off and prays, “My Father, if this cup can’t pass me by unless I drink it, then let your will be done.” He returns, and again they’re asleep. They can’t keep their eyes open. He leaves them there and goes off to pray a third time, using the same words. Then he comes back to the disciples. “Still sleeping? Still resting?” he says. “Look, the hour is here. The Son of Man is being handed over into the hands of sinners. Get up! Let’s go. Look, here comes the man who is betraying me.”
The Kiss · 26:47–56

He is still speaking when, look, Judas arrives, one of the Twelve. A mob comes with him, carrying swords and clubs. The chief priests and the people’s elders have sent them. The traitor has told them how they’ll know: “Whoever I kiss, that’s him. Take him.” Judas goes right up to Jesus. “Hello, Rabbi,” he says, and kisses him.

“Friend,” Jesus says to him, “get on with what you came here for.” Then they step forward, lay hands on Jesus, and seize him. And look, one of Jesus’ companions pulls out his sword, swings at the high priest’s slave, and slices off his ear. “Put that sword away,” Jesus tells him. “Everyone who lives by the sword dies by the sword. Don’t you think I could call on my Father, and he would send me more than twelve legions of angels this very moment? But then how would the Scriptures come true, which say it has to happen this way?”
Then Jesus says to the crowd, “Have you come out with swords and clubs to arrest me, as if I were some bandit? Day after day I sat in the temple teaching, and you never laid a hand on me.
But all this has happened so that the writings of the prophets will come true.” And every one of the disciples abandons him and runs.
Before the High Priest · 26:57–68

The men who have seized Jesus take him to Caiaphas the high priest, where the scribes and the elders have gathered. Peter trails along behind, keeping his distance, all the way into the high priest’s courtyard. He slips inside and sits with the guards to see how it will all turn out. Meanwhile the chief priests and the whole council are searching for false evidence, anything that will let them have Jesus executed. They come up with nothing, though plenty of lying witnesses step forward. Finally two men come up. “This man said, ‘I can destroy the temple of God and build it again in three days.’”

The high priest rises to his feet. “Have you nothing to say?” he asks Jesus. “What about all this these men are testifying against you?” But Jesus says nothing. Then the high priest says to him, “I put you under oath by the living God: tell us, are you the Messiah, the Son of God?”
Jesus answers, “You have said it. But I tell you all: from this moment on, you will see the Son of Man enthroned at the right hand of the Power, and coming on the clouds of heaven.”
Then the high priest tears his robes. “Blasphemy!” he says. “What more do we need witnesses for? You’ve just heard him blaspheme.
What is your verdict?” “He deserves to die!” they answer. Then they spit in his face and punch him. Some slap him across the face and say, “Come on, Messiah, prophesy! Which one of us hit you?”
Peter’s Denial · 26:69–75
All this time Peter has been sitting out in the courtyard. A slave girl walks up to him. “You were with Jesus the Galilean too,” she says.
But Peter denies it, loud enough for everyone to hear. “I have no idea what you mean,” he says.
He moves away toward the gate, and another girl spots him. “That man was with Jesus the Nazarene,” she tells the people standing around.
Again he denies it, this time with an oath: “I don’t know the man!”
A little while later the people standing around come up to Peter. “You must be one of them,” they say. “The way you talk gives you away.”

Then he begins calling down curses on himself and swearing, “I don’t know the man!” And just then a rooster crows. And Peter remembers what Jesus said: “Before the rooster crows, you will deny me three times.” And he goes outside and weeps bitterly.
Handed Over to Pilate · 27:1–2

When morning comes, all the chief priests and the elders of the people make their decision against Jesus, to have him put to death. They put him in chains, march him off, and turn him over to Pilate, the governor.
The Death of Judas · 27:3–10
Judas, who betrayed him, sees that Jesus has been condemned, and he is sick with regret. He takes the thirty pieces of silver back to the chief priests and elders.
“I’ve sinned,” he tells them. “The blood I betrayed was innocent.” “What do we care?” they say. “That’s your affair.”

Judas flings the silver into the sanctuary and walks out. Then he goes away and hangs himself. The chief priests pick up the silver. “We can’t put this in the temple treasury,” they say. “It’s been paid for blood.” So after talking it over, they use the money to buy the Potter’s Field, to bury strangers in. And that is why people call that piece of land the Field of Blood even now. So what Jeremiah the prophet spoke comes true: “They took the thirty silver coins, the value placed on the one whom some of the people of Israel had valued, and they paid them out for the potter’s field, just as the Lord instructed me.”
The King of the Jews · 27:11–26
Now Jesus stands before the governor, and the governor questions him. “Are you the king of the Jews?” “You say so,” Jesus answers.
But when the chief priests and the elders bring their charges against him, he gives no answer. Then Pilate says to him, “Don’t you hear all the things they are testifying against you?”

He won’t say a word in reply to any of it, and the governor is astonished. Now at the festival it is the governor’s custom to set free one prisoner for the crowd, whoever they choose. And they are holding a prisoner then who is famous for all the wrong reasons, a man called Jesus Barabbas. When the people have gathered, Pilate puts it to them: “Who should I let go for you? Jesus Barabbas? Or Jesus, the one they call the Messiah?” He knows they’ve handed Jesus over because they’re jealous of him.

And while Pilate is seated on the judgment bench, his wife sends word to him: “Leave that righteous man alone. I’ve been through agony today in a dream because of him.” But the chief priests and the elders talk the crowds into asking for Barabbas and having Jesus put to death.
So the governor asks them again, “Which of these two should I give back to you?” “Barabbas!” they say.
“Then what am I to do with Jesus, the one they call Messiah?” Pilate asks. “Crucify him!” they all shout.
“Why? What wrong has he done?” he asks. But they only scream louder, “Crucify him!”
Pilate can see it’s useless. If anything, a riot is brewing. So he calls for water and washes his hands where the crowd can see. “This man’s blood is not on my hands,” he says. “It’s on yours.”
And all the people answer, “His blood be on us and on our children!”
So he gives them Barabbas. But Jesus he has whipped, and then he hands him over for crucifixion.
Mocked by the Soldiers · 27:27–31

The governor’s soldiers drag Jesus into the Praetorium, the governor’s palace, and call the whole troop together around him. They strip off his clothes and wrap him in a scarlet cloak. They twist some thorny branches into a crown and push it onto his head. They put a reed in his right hand, and then they kneel in front of him and make fun of him. “Hail, king of the Jews!” they say. They spit on him. They take the reed and beat him over the head with it again and again. When they’ve had their fun, they strip the cloak off him and dress him in his own clothes again, and they march him out to crucify him.
The Crucifixion · 27:32–44

On the way out they run into a man from Cyrene, Simon by name, and they make him carry the cross. They come to a place called Golgotha, which means Skull Place. They hold out wine mixed with bitter gall for him. He tastes it and won’t drink any more. They crucify him. Then they share out his clothes among themselves, rolling dice to see who gets what. And they settle down there to guard him. Over his head they nail up the charge against him. It reads: THIS IS JESUS, THE KING OF THE JEWS.

They crucify two bandits with him, one at his right hand and one at his left. People passing by shout insults at him, wagging their heads. “You were going to tear down the temple and build it again in three days!” they say. “Save yourself! If you are the Son of God, come down off that cross!”

The chief priests, the scribes, and the elders mock him the same way. “Other people he saved,” they say. “Himself he can’t save! The king of Israel, is he? Then let him climb down from that cross, here and now, and we’ll put our faith in him. He relies on God. Well, let God come and get him out of this, if he wants him. Didn’t he say, ‘I am God’s Son’?” Even the bandits crucified with him heap the same insults on him.
The Death of Jesus · 27:45–56

From noon on, darkness covers the whole land until three in the afternoon. And about three o’clock Jesus shouts with a great voice, “Eli, Eli, lema sabachthani?” which means, “My God, my God, why have you abandoned me?”
Some of the bystanders hear it. “Listen, he’s calling Elijah,” they say.

Right away one of them dashes off for a sponge, soaks it in sour wine, sticks it on the end of a reed, and holds it up for him to drink. But the others say, “Wait! Let’s see whether Elijah comes to rescue him.”

Then Jesus gives one more great cry and lets go of his spirit. And look, the curtain in the temple rips in two, from the top all the way to the bottom. The ground quakes. Rocks crack open. Graves are opened, and many of God’s holy people who had fallen asleep in death are raised. Once Jesus has risen, they come out of their graves, walk into the holy city, and show themselves to many. The centurion and the soldiers guarding Jesus with him feel the earthquake and see everything that is happening, and terror grips them. “This man really was God’s Son!” they say.

A number of women are there too, looking on from far off. They are the ones who came with Jesus from Galilee and looked after him. Mary Magdalene is among them, and Mary the mother of James and Joseph, and Zebedee’s wife, the mother of his sons.
The Burial · 27:57–61

Evening is coming on when a wealthy man arrives from Arimathea. His name is Joseph, and he too has become a follower of Jesus. He goes in to Pilate and asks him for Jesus’ body, and Pilate gives orders to release it. Joseph takes the body and winds it in fresh, clean linen. He lays it in a new tomb of his own, carved out of the rock face. Then he rolls a great stone over the opening and leaves. But Mary Magdalene and the other Mary stay there, sitting across from the tomb.
The Guard at the Tomb · 27:62–66

On the following day, the day after Preparation Day, a group of chief priests and Pharisees comes to see Pilate. “Sir,” they say, “it has come back to us that this impostor, while he was still living, said, ‘After three days I’ll rise again.’ So order the tomb sealed tight until the third day. If you don’t, his disciples might come and steal him away and then tell everyone, ‘He has been raised from the dead.’ And that last lie would be worse than the first.”
“You have your guard,” Pilate says. “Go and seal it up as tight as you can.” So off they go and secure the tomb, setting a seal on the stone and leaving the guard on watch.
He Is Risen · 28:1–10

The Sabbath is over, and the first day of the week is just beginning to dawn, when Mary Magdalene and the other Mary come to see the tomb. And look, the earth heaves in a great quake, because an angel of the Lord has come down out of heaven. He walks up to the stone, rolls it back, and sits down on top of it. His face flashes like lightning, and his clothes are white as snow. The guards are so terrified of him that they tremble and go rigid, like dead men. “As for you, don’t be afraid,” the angel says to the women. “I know you’ve come looking for Jesus, the one they crucified. He isn’t here. He has been raised, exactly as he told you. Come, look at the place where he lay. And then hurry and tell his disciples, ‘He has been raised from the dead! Look, he’s going ahead of you to Galilee, and that’s where you’ll see him.’ There. That’s my message for you.”
They leave the tomb in a rush, half afraid and half bursting with joy, and they run to bring the news to his disciples.
And look, there is Jesus, coming to meet them. “Rejoice!” he says. They come close, take hold of his feet, and worship him.
“Don’t be afraid,” Jesus tells them. “Go and tell my brothers to head for Galilee. That is where they’ll see me.”
The Guards’ Story · 28:11–15

While the women are still on their way, look, some of the guards go into the city and tell the chief priests all that has taken place. The chief priests and the elders meet and decide what to do. Then they hand the soldiers a great deal of silver with these instructions: “Here’s what you say: ‘His disciples came in the night while we were sleeping, and they stole him.’ And if the governor hears about this, we’ll talk him around and keep you out of trouble.” The soldiers pocket the money and do as they’ve been told. And that’s the story still being passed around among the Jewish people even now.
With You Always · 28:16–20

The eleven disciples make their way to Galilee, to the mountain Jesus had named for them. When they see him, they bow down and worship him, but some are of two minds. Jesus comes up to them and speaks. “I have been given all authority, in heaven and on the earth,” he says. “So go, and make disciples of all the nations. Baptize them into the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. Teach them to keep everything I have commanded you. And look, I myself am with you, every single day, right up to the end of the age.”
The Opening Claim · 1:1
This is where it all begins — the good news of Jesus the Messiah, the Son of God.
The Herald in the Wilderness · 1:2–8
Just as the prophet Isaiah wrote:

“Look — I am sending my messenger ahead of you, to prepare your road. A voice cries out in the wilderness: Prepare the road for the Lord! Make his paths straight.” That voice is John — who appears in the wilderness, proclaiming a baptism of repentance for the release of sins. And the whole Judean countryside goes out to him — all the people of Jerusalem. They are baptized by him in the Jordan River, openly naming what they have done.

John is clothed in camel hair with a leather belt around his waist. He eats locusts and wild honey. And he keeps proclaiming: “The one stronger than I am is coming after me. I am not fit to bend down and untie the strap of his sandals. I baptized you in water. He will baptize you in the Holy Spirit.”
The Baptism of Jesus · 1:9–11

In those days Jesus comes from Nazareth in Galilee and is baptized by John in the Jordan. And immediately — as he comes up out of the water — the heavens are ripped open, and the Spirit descends on him like a dove.
And a voice comes from the heavens: “You are my Son — the Beloved. In you I delight.”
Into the Wilderness · 1:12–13
And immediately the Spirit drives him out into the wilderness. He is in the wilderness forty days, being tested by Satan. He is with the wild animals. And the angels attend to him.
The Kingdom Has Come Near · 1:14–15
After John is handed over, Jesus comes into Galilee proclaiming the good news of God.
“The moment has come,” he says. “The kingdom of God has drawn near — and it’s staying near. Turn around. Trust this good news.”
Four Fishermen · 1:16–20
Walking along the Sea of Galilee, he sees Simon and his brother Andrew casting a net into the sea — they are fishermen.

“Come after me,” Jesus says. “I will make you become fishers of people.” And immediately they leave their nets and follow him. Going on a little further, he sees James and John, the sons of Zebedee, in their boat mending the nets. And immediately he calls them. They leave their father Zebedee in the boat with the hired crew and go after him.
Authority in the Synagogue · 1:21–27
They go into Capernaum. And immediately, on the Sabbath, he enters the synagogue and teaches.
They are astonished at his teaching — because he teaches as one who has authority, and not like the scribes. And immediately there is a man in their synagogue with an unclean spirit. He cries out:

“What do you want with us, Jesus of Nazareth? Have you come to destroy us? I know who you are — the Holy One of God!” Jesus rebukes him: “Be muzzled — and come out of him.” The unclean spirit convulses him, cries out with a loud voice, and comes out. Everyone is astonished, and they ask one another: “What is this? A new kind of teaching — with authority! He commands even the unclean spirits and they obey him.” And immediately the report about him spreads everywhere — throughout the whole surrounding region of Galilee.
Healings and Withdrawal · 1:28–39

And immediately, leaving the synagogue, they go into the house of Simon and Andrew, with James and John. Simon’s mother-in-law is lying there, gripped by a fever. And immediately they tell him about her. He goes to her, takes her by the hand, and raises her up. The fever releases her. And she begins to serve them. When evening comes — when the sun sets — they bring to him all who are sick and all who are dominated by demons.

The whole city is gathered at the door. And he heals many who are sick with various diseases and drives out many demons. He does not allow the demons to speak — because they know him. Very early — while it is still deep dark — he gets up and goes out to a deserted place and prays there. Simon and those with him hunt for him. They find him and say: “Everyone is looking for you.”

“Let’s go on,” he says, “to the nearby towns — so I can proclaim there too. That is what I came out for.” And he goes throughout all of Galilee, proclaiming in their synagogues and driving out demons.
The Man with Leprosy · 1:40–45

A man with leprosy comes to him, begging him and falling on his knees: “If you are willing — you can make me clean.” Moved in his very gut, he reaches out his hand and touches him. “I am willing,” he says. “Be clean.”

And immediately the leprosy leaves him, and he is made clean. And warning him sternly, he sends him away at once, saying: “See that you say nothing to anyone. But go — show yourself to the priest and offer what Moses commanded for your cleansing, as a testimony to them.” But he goes out and begins to proclaim it freely and to spread the word — so that Jesus can no longer openly enter a town. He stays out in deserted places. And people keep coming to him from everywhere.
The Paralyzed Man · 2:1–12

After some days he comes back into Capernaum. Word gets out that he is home. And so many gather that there is no room left — not even at the door. And he speaks the word to them. They come bringing a paralyzed man to him, carried by four. And not being able to bring him in because of the crowd, they unroof the roof above him. Having dug through it, they lower the mat on which the paralyzed man is lying.
Seeing their faith, Jesus says to the paralyzed man: “Child — your sins are released.” But some of the scribes are sitting there, reasoning in their hearts:

“Why does this man speak like this? He is blaspheming. Who can release sins except God — God alone?” And immediately Jesus, knowing in his spirit that they are reasoning this way within themselves, says to them: “Why are you reasoning these things in your hearts? Which is easier — to say to the paralyzed man, “Your sins are released,” or to say, “Get up, take your mat, and walk”? But so that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to release sins —”

he says to the paralyzed man — “I say to you: get up, take your mat, and go home.” And he gets up. Immediately. He takes the mat and goes out in front of everyone. They are all amazed and glorify God, saying: “We have never seen anything like this.”
The Call of Levi · 2:13–17

He goes out again beside the sea. The whole crowd comes to him, and he teaches them. And passing by, he sees Levi the son of Alphaeus sitting at the tax booth. “Follow me,” he says to him. And he gets up and follows him.

And it happens — he is reclining at table in Levi’s house, and many tax collectors and sinners are reclining with Jesus and his disciples. For there are many of them, and they are following him. The scribes of the Pharisees, seeing that he is eating with sinners and tax collectors, say to his disciples: “Why does he eat with tax collectors and sinners?” Hearing this, Jesus says to them: “The healthy have no need of a doctor — but those who are sick. I did not come to call the righteous — but sinners.”
The Question about Fasting · 2:18–22

John’s disciples and the Pharisees are fasting. And they come and say to him: “Why do John’s disciples and the disciples of the Pharisees fast — but your disciples do not fast?” Jesus says to them: “Can the wedding guests fast while the bridegroom is with them? As long as they have the bridegroom with them, they cannot fast. But days are coming when the bridegroom is taken away from them — and then they will fast in that day.

No one sews a patch of unshrunk cloth onto an old garment. If they do, the new patch tears away from the old — and a worse tear is made. And no one puts new wine into old wineskins. If they do, the wine bursts the skins — and the wine is destroyed, and the skins as well. New wine goes into fresh skins.”
Lord of the Sabbath · 2:23–28
And it happens — on the Sabbath he is going through the grain fields. And his disciples begin to make their way, plucking heads of grain.

The Pharisees say to him: “Look — why are they doing what is not lawful on the Sabbath?” And he says to them: “Have you never read what David did when he had need and was hungry — he and those with him? How he entered the house of God in the time of Abiathar the high priest, and ate the bread of the Presence — which is not lawful for anyone to eat except the priests — and also gave it to those with him?” And he says to them: “The Sabbath came into being for the sake of the human. Not the human for the sake of the Sabbath.
So the Son of Man is Lord even of the Sabbath.”
The Man with the Withered Hand · 3:1–6

He enters a synagogue again. There is a man there with a withered hand. And they watch him closely — will he heal on the Sabbath? — so that they might accuse him. He says to the man with the withered hand: “Stand up in the middle.” And he says to them: “Is it lawful on the Sabbath to do good or to do harm? To save a life — or to kill?” They are silent. And looking around at them with anger — grieved at the hardness of their hearts — he says to the man: “Stretch out your hand.” He stretches it out. And his hand is restored.
And the Pharisees go out immediately and begin plotting with the Herodians against him — how they might destroy him.
The Crowd by the Sea · 3:7–12

Jesus withdraws with his disciples to the sea. A large crowd follows from Galilee — and from Judea, and from Jerusalem, and from Idumea, and from beyond the Jordan, and from around Tyre and Sidon. A great multitude, hearing all that he is doing, comes to him. And he tells his disciples to have a small boat ready for him because of the crowd — so they will not crush him.

For he heals many, so that all who have afflictions press in on him to touch him. And whenever the unclean spirits see him, they throw themselves down before him and cry out: “You are the Son of God!” And he warns them strongly not to make him known.
The Twelve Appointed · 3:13–18
And he goes up on the mountain and calls to him those he himself wants. And they come to him. And he appoints twelve — so that they might be with him, and so that he might send them out to proclaim,

and to have authority to drive out demons. He appoints the twelve: Simon — to whom he gives the name Peter; James the son of Zebedee, and John the brother of James — to whom he gives the name Boanerges, which means Sons of Thunder; Andrew; Philip; Bartholomew; Matthew; Thomas; James the son of Alphaeus; Thaddaeus; Simon the Zealot; and Judas Iscariot — who also hands him over.
A House Divided · 3:19–30
And he comes into a house. The crowd gathers again — so that they cannot even eat bread.

And when his own people hear about it, they go out to seize him. For they are saying: “He is out of his mind.” And the scribes who have come down from Jerusalem are saying: “He has Beelzebul — and by the ruler of the demons he drives out demons.” And calling them to him, he speaks to them in parables: “How can Satan drive out Satan? If a kingdom is divided against itself, that kingdom cannot stand. And if a house is divided against itself, that house will not be able to stand.

And if Satan has risen against himself and is divided — he cannot stand, but has come to an end. But no one can enter the house of the strong man and plunder his goods unless he first binds the strong man. Then he will plunder his house. Truly I tell you — all sins will be released to the children of men, and whatever blasphemies they may speak. But whoever blasphemes against the Holy Spirit does not have release into the age — but is held in an eternal sin.”
This because they are saying: “He has an unclean spirit.”
The True Family · 3:31–35

And his mother and his brothers arrive. Standing outside, they send to him and call him. A crowd is sitting around him, and they say to him: “Look — your mother and your brothers are outside, looking for you.” And answering them, he says: “Who is my mother? And my brothers?” And looking around at those sitting in a circle around him, he says: “Look — my mother and my brothers.
Whoever does the will of God — this is my brother and sister and mother.”
The Parable of the Sower · 4:1–9

He begins to teach again beside the sea. An enormous crowd gathers around him — so he gets into a boat and sits there, out on the water. And the whole crowd is along the shore, facing the sea. And he teaches them many things in parables. And in his teaching he says to them:

“Listen. Look — the sower goes out to sow. And as he sows, some falls along the path — and the birds come and devour it. Some falls on rocky ground where there is not much soil. And immediately it springs up — because it has no depth of soil. But when the sun rises, it is scorched. And because it has no root, it withers. Some falls among thorns. The thorns grow up and choke it — and it produces no fruit. And some falls into good soil and produces fruit — coming up and growing, yielding thirty, and sixty, and a hundredfold.”
And he says: “Whoever has ears to hear — let them hear.”
Why Parables · 4:10–12

And when he is alone, those around him — with the Twelve — begin asking him about the parables. And he says to them: “To you the mystery of the kingdom of God has been given. But for those outside — everything comes in parables, so that looking they may look and not see, and hearing they may hear and not understand, lest they turn — and be released.”
The Parable Explained · 4:13–20

And he says to them: “Do you not understand this parable? Then how will you understand any of the parables? The sower sows the word. And these are the ones along the path where the word is sown: when they hear, Satan comes immediately and takes away the word that was sown in them. And these are the ones sown on rocky ground: when they hear the word, they receive it immediately with joy. But they have no root in themselves — they are temporary. When affliction or persecution comes because of the word, they immediately fall away.

And others are the ones sown among thorns: they are those who hear the word, but the cares of the age and the seduction of wealth and desires for other things come in and choke the word — and it produces no fruit. And these are the ones sown on good soil: they hear the word and receive it and bear fruit — thirty, and sixty, and a hundredfold.”
The Lamp · 4:21–25
And he says to them: “Does the lamp come in order to be put under a basket or under a bed? Does it not come to be placed on the stand?

For there is nothing hidden except to be revealed — and nothing concealed except to come into the open. If anyone has ears to hear — let them hear.” And he says to them: “Pay attention to what you hear. The measure you use will be the measure used for you — and more will be added. For to the one who has, more will be given. And from the one who has nothing — even what they have will be taken.”
The Seed Growing · 4:26–29
And he says: “The kingdom of God is like this — as when a man scatters seed on the ground.

He sleeps and rises, night and day. And the seed sprouts and grows — he does not know how. The earth produces by itself: first the blade, then the head, then the full grain in the head. And when the grain delivers itself up, he immediately puts in the sickle — because the harvest has come.”
The Mustard Seed · 4:30–32
And he says: “How shall we liken the kingdom of God? Or with what parable shall we present it? It is like a mustard seed — which, when sown in the ground, is the smallest of all seeds on earth.
Yet when it is sown, it comes up and becomes greater than all the garden plants and puts out large branches — so that the birds of the sky can nest in its shade.”
Parables and the Crowd · 4:33–34

And with many parables like these he speaks the word to them — as much as they are able to hear. He says nothing to them without a parable. But privately, to his own disciples, he explains everything.
The Storm · 4:35–41
And on that day, when evening comes, he says to them: “Let us cross to the other side.”

And leaving the crowd, they take him with them in the boat — just as he is. And other boats are with him. And a great squall of wind arises. The waves beat into the boat so that it is already filling. And he is in the stern, asleep on the cushion. And they wake him and say to him: “Teacher — don’t you care that we are perishing?” And waking up, he rebukes the wind and says to the sea: “Silence. Be muzzled.” And the wind dies down. And there is a great calm.
And he says to them: “Why are you afraid? Do you still have no faith?” And they fear a great fear and say to one another: “Who then is this — that even the wind and the sea obey him?”
The Gerasene Demoniac · 5:1–20

They come to the other side of the sea — to the region of the Gerasenes. And immediately, as he steps out of the boat, a man with an unclean spirit comes out of the tombs and meets him. He lives among the tombs. And no one can bind him anymore — not even with a chain. For he has often been bound with shackles and chains — and the chains have been wrenched apart by him, and the shackles smashed. No one has the strength to subdue him.

And continually — night and day — among the tombs and on the mountains, he is crying out and cutting himself with stones. And seeing Jesus from a distance, he runs and prostrates himself before him. And crying out with a loud voice he says: “What do you want with me, Jesus — Son of the Most High God? I adjure you by God: do not torment me!” For Jesus has been saying to him: “Come out of the man, you unclean spirit.” And he asks him: “What is your name?” “My name is Legion,” he says — “for we are many.”

And he begs him urgently not to send them out of the region. Now there is a large herd of pigs on the hillside, feeding. And they beg him: “Send us into the pigs — let us enter them.” And he gives them permission. And the unclean spirits come out and enter the pigs. And the herd rushes down the steep bank into the sea — about two thousand of them. And they are choked in the sea. The herdsmen flee and report it in the town and in the countryside. And people come out to see what has happened.

And they come to Jesus and see the man who had been possessed by the legion — sitting, clothed, in his right mind. And they are afraid. And those who had seen it tell them what happened to the demon-possessed man — and about the pigs. And they begin to beg Jesus to leave their region. And as he is getting into the boat, the man who had been possessed begs him — that he might be with him. And Jesus does not allow him, but says to him: “Go home to your own people. And tell them how much the Lord has done for you — and how he had mercy on you.”
And he goes away and begins to proclaim in the Decapolis how much Jesus has done for him. And everyone is astonished.
Jairus, and the Woman with the Hemorrhage · 5:21–43

When Jesus has crossed again in the boat to the other side, a large crowd gathers around him. And he is beside the sea. And one of the synagogue rulers comes — Jairus by name. And seeing him, he falls at his feet and begs him urgently: “My little daughter is at the point of death. Come and lay your hands on her — so that she may be saved and live.”

And he goes with him. And a large crowd follows and presses in on him. And a woman who has had a discharge of blood for twelve years — and who has suffered much under many doctors, and has spent everything she had, and is not better but rather has grown worse — hears about Jesus. She comes through the crowd from behind and touches his garment. For she has been saying to herself: “If I touch even his garments, I will be saved.”

And immediately the source of her blood dries up. And she knows in her body that she is healed of her affliction. And immediately Jesus, knowing in himself that power has gone out from him, turns around in the crowd and says: “Who touched my garments?” And his disciples say to him: “You see the crowd pressing in on you — and you say, ‘Who touched me?’” And he looks around to see who has done this. And the woman — knowing what has happened to her — comes in fear and trembling. She falls before him and tells him the whole truth.

And he says to her: “Daughter — your faith has saved you. Go in peace. Be well from your affliction.” While he is still speaking, people come from the house of the synagogue ruler: “Your daughter has died. Why trouble the teacher any further?” But overhearing what is said, Jesus says to the synagogue ruler: “Don’t be afraid. Only believe.” And he allows no one to follow with him except Peter and James and John the brother of James.

They come to the house of the synagogue ruler. And he sees the commotion — people weeping and wailing loudly. And going in he says to them: “Why this commotion and weeping? The child has not died — she is sleeping.” And they laugh at him. But putting them all outside, he takes the father and the mother of the child and those with him — and goes in where the child is. And taking the child by the hand, he says to her: “Talitha koum” — which means: “Little girl, I say to you — get up.”

And immediately the little girl gets up and walks about. She is twelve years old. And immediately they are overcome with great astonishment. And he gives them strict orders that no one should know about this. And he tells them to give her something to eat.
The Rejection at Nazareth · 6:1–6

He leaves there and comes to his hometown. And his disciples follow him. When the Sabbath comes, he begins to teach in the synagogue. And many who hear him are astonished: “Where does this man get these things? What is this wisdom given to him? What mighty works are done by his hands? Is this not the craftsman — the son of Mary and brother of James and Joses and Judas and Simon? And are not his sisters here with us?” And they are tripped up by him.

And Jesus says to them: “A prophet is not without honor except in his hometown and among his relatives and in his own house.” And he is not able to do any mighty work there — except that he lays his hands on a few sick people and heals them. And he marvels at their unbelief. And he goes around among the villages teaching.
The Sending of the Twelve · 6:7–13
And he calls the Twelve and begins to send them out two by two. And he gives them authority over unclean spirits.

And he charges them to take nothing for the road except a staff — no bread, no bag, no money in their belt. But to wear sandals. And not to put on two tunics. And he says to them: “Wherever you enter a house, stay there until you leave the place. And wherever they do not receive you and they do not listen to you — when you leave, shake off the dust from under your feet as a testimony against them.” And going out, they proclaim that people should repent.
And they drive out many demons. And they anoint many sick people with oil and heal them.
Herod and the Death of John · 6:14–29

King Herod hears of it — for Jesus’ name has become known. And people are saying: “John the Baptist has been raised from the dead. That is why these powers are at work in him.” But others say: “He is Elijah.” And others: “He is a prophet — like one of the prophets of old.” But when Herod hears, he says: “John — whom I beheaded — he has been raised.”

For Herod himself had sent and seized John and bound him in prison — on account of Herodias, his brother Philip’s wife, whom he had married. For John had been saying to Herod: “It is not lawful for you to have your brother’s wife.” And Herodias had it in for him and wanted to kill him. But she could not — for Herod feared John, knowing him to be a righteous and holy man, and kept him safe. And when he heard him he was deeply perplexed — and yet he heard him gladly.

But an opportune day comes — when Herod on his birthday gives a banquet for his nobles and his military commanders and the leading men of Galilee. And the daughter of Herodias comes in and dances. She pleases Herod and his guests. And the king says to the girl: “Ask me for whatever you want and I will give it to you.” And he swears to her: “Whatever you ask I will give you — up to half my kingdom.” And she goes out and says to her mother: “What should I ask for?” “The head of John the Baptist,” she says.

And coming back immediately — with urgency — she asks the king: “I want you to give me right now the head of John the Baptist on a platter.” And the king is deeply grieved. But because of his oaths and because of his guests, he does not want to refuse her. And immediately the king sends an executioner with orders to bring his head. And he goes and beheads him in the prison and brings his head on a platter and gives it to the girl. And the girl gives it to her mother.
When his disciples hear of it, they come and take his body and lay it in a tomb.
The Return and the Feeding · 6:30–44

The apostles gather around Jesus and report to him everything they have done and everything they have taught. And he says to them: “Come away by yourselves to a deserted place and rest a little.” For many are coming and going, and they have no opportunity even to eat. And they go away in the boat to a deserted place by themselves.

And many see them going and recognize them. And from all the towns they run there on foot and arrive ahead of them. And stepping out of the boat, he sees a large crowd. And his heart breaks for them — because they are like sheep without a shepherd. And he begins to teach them many things. And when the hour is already late, his disciples come to him and say: “This is a deserted place and the hour is already late. Send them away — so they can go into the surrounding countryside and villages and buy themselves something to eat.”
But he answers them: “You give them something to eat.” “Are we to go and spend two hundred denarii on bread,” they say, “and give it to them to eat?”

“How many loaves do you have?” he says. “Go and see.” And when they find out, they say: “Five. And two fish.” And he orders them to have everyone recline in groups on the green grass. And they recline — group by group — in hundreds and in fifties. And taking the five loaves and the two fish, he looks up to heaven and blesses and breaks the loaves and gives them to the disciples to set before the people. And he divides the two fish among them all.
And they all eat and are satisfied. And they gather up twelve baskets full of broken pieces — and pieces of the fish. And those who ate the loaves are five thousand men.
Walking on the Water · 6:45–52

And immediately he makes his disciples get into the boat and go ahead to the other side — to Bethsaida — while he dismisses the crowd. And after taking leave of them, he goes up on the mountain to pray. When evening comes, the boat is in the middle of the sea, and he is alone on the land.

And seeing them straining at the oars — for the wind is against them — sometime between three and six in the morning he comes toward them, walking on the sea. And he intends to pass by them. But when they see him walking on the sea, they think it is a ghost and cry out. For they all see him and are terrified. But immediately he speaks with them: “Take courage — it is I. Do not be afraid.” And he gets into the boat with them, and the wind dies down. And they are utterly astounded within themselves —
for they had not understood about the loaves. Their hearts were hardened.
Healings at Gennesaret · 6:53–56

And when they have crossed over, they come to land at Gennesaret and moor the boat. And when they get out of the boat, immediately the people recognize him. They run through that whole region and begin to carry around on mats those who are sick — to wherever they hear he is. And wherever he enters — into villages or cities or countryside — they lay the sick in the marketplaces and beg him that they might touch even the hem of his garment. And as many as touch it are saved.
The Tradition of the Elders · 7:1–13

The Pharisees gather around him — along with some of the scribes who have come from Jerusalem. And they see that some of his disciples are eating bread with unclean hands — that is, unwashed. For the Pharisees — and all the Jews — do not eat unless they wash their hands with the fist, holding to the tradition of the elders. And when they come from the marketplace, they do not eat unless they wash. And there are many other things they hold to — the washing of cups and pitchers and copper vessels and dining couches.

And the Pharisees and scribes ask him: “Why do your disciples not walk according to the tradition of the elders? Why do they eat bread with unclean hands?” And he says to them: “Isaiah prophesied rightly about you hypocrites — as it is written: ‘This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me. They worship me in vain, teaching as doctrines the commandments of men.’ Leaving aside the commandment of God, you hold to the tradition of men.”

And he says to them: “How well you set aside the commandment of God — in order to keep your tradition. For Moses said: ‘Honor your father and your mother’ — and: ‘Whoever speaks evil of father or mother must surely die.’ But you say: if a man says to his father or his mother, ‘Whatever I might have given you is Korban’ — that is, a gift dedicated to God — you no longer allow him to do anything for his father or mother.
You are nullifying the word of God by your tradition that you have handed down. And many such things you do.”
What Defiles · 7:14–23

And calling the crowd to him again, he says to them: “Hear me — all of you — and understand. There is nothing outside a person that by going into them can defile them. But the things that come out of a person — those are what defile.” And when he has gone into a house away from the crowd, his disciples ask him about the parable.

And he says to them: “Are you also so without understanding? Do you not see that whatever goes into a person from outside cannot defile them — since it does not enter the heart but the stomach, and passes out into the sewer?” — declaring all foods clean. And he says: “What comes out of a person — that is what defiles a person. For from within — out of the human heart — come evil intentions: sexual immorality, theft, murder,
adultery, greed, wickedness, deceit, lewdness, envy, slander, pride, foolishness. All these evil things come from within — and they defile a person.”
The Syrophoenician Woman · 7:24–29

Rising from there, he goes into the region of Tyre. And going into a house, he wants no one to know — but he cannot escape notice. For immediately a woman whose little daughter has an unclean spirit hears about him and comes and falls at his feet.

The woman is a Greek — Syrophoenician by race. And she begs him to drive the demon out of her daughter. And he says to her: “Let the children first be satisfied — for it is not good to take the children’s bread and throw it to the little dogs.” But she answers him: “Lord — even the little dogs under the table eat the children’s crumbs.” And he says to her: “Because of this word — go. The demon has gone out of your daughter.”
And going home, she finds the child lying on the bed — and the demon gone.
The Deaf Man · 7:30–37

And going out again from the region of Tyre, he comes through Sidon to the Sea of Galilee — through the region of the Decapolis. And they bring to him a man who is deaf and speaks with difficulty. And they beg him to lay his hand on him. And taking him aside privately from the crowd, he puts his fingers into his ears — and having spat, he touches his tongue.

And looking up to heaven, he sighs deeply and says to him: “Ephphatha” — which means: “Be opened.” And immediately his ears are opened. And the bond of his tongue is released. And he speaks correctly. And Jesus charges them to tell no one. But the more he charges them, the more they proclaim it. And they are astonished beyond all measure: “He has done all things well,” they say. “He even makes the deaf hear and the mute speak.”
The Feeding of the Four Thousand · 8:1–10
In those days, when again a great crowd has gathered and they have nothing to eat, he calls his disciples and says to them:

“My heart breaks for this crowd — they have been with me now for three days and have nothing to eat. And if I send them away hungry to their homes, they will faint on the road — and some of them have come from far away.” And his disciples answer him: “How can anyone satisfy these people with bread here in this deserted place?” And he asks them: “How many loaves do you have?” “Seven,” they say. And he directs the crowd to sit down on the ground. And taking the seven loaves, he gives thanks and breaks them and gives them to his disciples to set before the people. And they set them before the crowd.

And they have a few small fish. And having blessed them, he says to distribute these also. And they eat and are satisfied. And they gather up seven baskets of broken pieces left over. There are about four thousand people. And he sends them away. And immediately getting into the boat with his disciples, he comes to the region of Dalmanutha.
The Demand for a Sign · 8:11–13
And the Pharisees come out and begin to debate with him, seeking from him a sign from heaven — testing him.

And sighing deeply in his spirit, he says: “Why does this generation seek a sign? Truly I tell you — no sign will be given to this generation.” And leaving them, he gets into the boat again and goes to the other side.
The Leaven of the Pharisees · 8:14–21
And they have forgotten to bring bread — and they have only one loaf with them in the boat. And he charges them: “Watch out — be on guard against the leaven of the Pharisees and the leaven of Herod.”

And they begin talking with one another about the fact that they have no bread. And knowing this, he says to them: “Why are you talking about having no bread? Do you not yet see or understand? Do you have hardened hearts? Having eyes — do you not see? And having ears — do you not hear? And do you not remember? When I broke the five loaves for the five thousand — how many baskets full of broken pieces did you gather?” “Twelve,” they say.
“And the seven for the four thousand — how many baskets full of broken pieces did you gather?” “Seven,” they say. And he says to them: “Do you not yet understand?”
The Blind Man of Bethsaida · 8:22–26

And they come to Bethsaida. And they bring to him a blind man and beg him to touch him. And taking the blind man by the hand, he leads him outside the village. And spitting into his eyes and laying his hands on him, he asks him: “Do you see anything?”

And looking up he says: “I see people — but I see them as trees, walking.” Then he lays his hands on his eyes again. And he looks intently — and is restored and sees everything clearly. And Jesus sends him home, saying: “Do not even enter the village.”
Peter’s Confession · 8:27–30

And Jesus goes out with his disciples to the villages of Caesarea Philippi. And on the road he asks his disciples: “Who do people say that I am?” And they tell him: “John the Baptist. And others: Elijah. And others: one of the prophets.”
And he asks them: “But you — who do you say that I am?” Peter answers him: “You are the Messiah.” And he sternly charges them to say nothing about him to anyone.
The First Passion Prediction · 8:31–33

And he begins to teach them that the Son of Man must suffer many things and be rejected by the elders and the chief priests and the scribes — and be killed — and after three days rise. And he speaks this word openly. And Peter takes him aside and begins to rebuke him.
But turning and seeing his disciples, he rebukes Peter and says: “Get behind me, Satan. For you are not thinking the things of God — but the things of men.”
The Cost of Following · 8:34–38

And calling the crowd to him with his disciples, he says to them: “If anyone wants to come after me — let them deny themselves and take up their cross and follow me. For whoever wants to save their life will lose it. But whoever loses their life for my sake and the gospel’s will save it.

For what does it profit a person to gain the whole world and forfeit their life? For what can a person give in exchange for their life? For whoever is ashamed of me and of my words in this adulterous and sinful generation — the Son of Man will also be ashamed of them when he comes in the glory of his Father with the holy angels.”
The Transfiguration · 9:1–8

And he says to them: “Truly I tell you — there are some standing here who will not taste death before they see the kingdom of God having come in power.” And after six days Jesus takes Peter and James and John and brings them up a high mountain privately — just themselves. And he is transfigured before them. And his garments become dazzling — intensely white, as no launderer on earth can whiten them.

And Elijah appears to them with Moses. And they are talking with Jesus. And Peter answers and says to Jesus: “Rabbi — it is good for us to be here. Let us make three shelters: one for you and one for Moses and one for Elijah.” For he does not know what to say — for they are terrified. And a cloud comes, overshadowing them. And a voice comes out of the cloud: “This is my Son — the Beloved. Listen to him.” And suddenly, looking around, they no longer see anyone — only Jesus with them.
The Question about Elijah · 9:9–13

And as they are coming down from the mountain, he charges them to say nothing about what they have seen to anyone — until the Son of Man rises from the dead. And they keep the word to themselves, debating with one another what “rising from the dead” means. And they ask him: “Why do the scribes say that Elijah must come first?” And he says to them: “Elijah does come first and restores all things. And how is it written of the Son of Man — that he should suffer many things and be treated with contempt?
But I tell you that Elijah has come — and they did to him whatever they wanted, just as it is written of him.”
The Boy with the Convulsing Spirit · 9:14–29

And coming to the disciples, they see a large crowd around them and scribes arguing with them. And immediately all the crowd, when they see him, are greatly amazed and run to greet him. And he asks them: “What are you arguing about with them?” And one from the crowd answers him: “Teacher — I brought my son to you. He has a spirit that makes him mute.

And wherever it seizes him, it throws him down. And he foams and grinds his teeth and becomes rigid. And I asked your disciples to drive it out — and they were not able.” And he answers them: “O faithless generation — how long am I to be with you? How long am I to bear with you? Bring him to me.” And they bring the boy to him. And when the spirit sees him, immediately it convulses the boy. And falling on the ground, he rolls about, foaming.
And Jesus asks his father: “How long has this been happening to him?” “From childhood,” he says.

“And it has often thrown him into fire and into water to destroy him. But if you are able to do anything — have compassion on us and help us.” And Jesus says to him: “‘If you are able’ — all things are possible for the one who believes.” Immediately the father of the boy cries out: “I believe — help my unbelief!” And seeing that a crowd is running together, Jesus rebukes the unclean spirit: “You mute and deaf spirit — I command you: come out of him and never enter him again.”

And crying out and convulsing him terribly, it comes out. And the boy becomes like a corpse — so that most say: “He has died.” But Jesus takes him by the hand and raises him up. And he stands. And when he has gone into a house, his disciples ask him privately: “Why could we not drive it out?” And he says to them: “This kind cannot be driven out by anything except prayer.”
The Second Passion Prediction · 9:30–32
Going out from there, they pass through Galilee. And he does not want anyone to know —

for he is teaching his disciples and saying to them: “The Son of Man is being handed over into the hands of men. And they will kill him. And when he is killed, after three days he will rise.” But they do not understand the saying. And they are afraid to ask him.
Who is the Greatest · 9:33–37

And they come to Capernaum. And when he is in the house he asks them: “What were you discussing on the road?” But they are silent — for on the road they had discussed with one another who was the greatest.

And sitting down, he calls the Twelve and says to them: “If anyone wants to be first — they shall be last of all and servant of all.” And taking a child, he sets it in the middle of them. And taking it in his arms, he says to them:
“Whoever receives one such child in my name receives me. And whoever receives me — receives not me but the one who sent me.”
The One who is not Against us · 9:38–41

John says to him: “Teacher — we saw someone driving out demons in your name. And we tried to stop him, because he was not following us.” But Jesus says: “Do not stop him — for there is no one who will do a mighty work in my name and be able soon after to speak evil of me.
For whoever is not against us is for us. For truly I tell you — whoever gives you a cup of water to drink because you bear the name of Christ will by no means lose their reward.”
Warnings about Stumbling · 9:42–50

“And whoever causes one of these little ones who believe to stumble — it would be better for them if a great millstone were hung around their neck and they were thrown into the sea. And if your hand causes you to stumble — cut it off. It is better for you to enter life crippled than to go with two hands into Gehenna — into the unquenchable fire. And if your foot causes you to stumble — cut it off. It is better for you to enter life lame than to be thrown with two feet into Gehenna.

And if your eye causes you to stumble — tear it out. It is better for you to enter the kingdom of God with one eye than to be thrown with two eyes into Gehenna — where their worm does not die and the fire is not quenched. For everyone will be salted with fire. Salt is good — but if the salt has lost its saltiness, how will you make it salty again? Have salt in yourselves — and be at peace with one another.”
On Divorce · 10:1–12

And rising from there, he comes into the region of Judea and beyond the Jordan. And crowds gather to him again. And again, as was his custom, he teaches them. And Pharisees come to him and ask: “Is it lawful for a man to divorce his wife?” — testing him. He answers them: “What did Moses command you?” They say: “Moses permitted a man to write a certificate of divorce and to send her away.” And Jesus says to them: “Because of the hardness of your hearts he wrote you this commandment.

But from the beginning of creation — ‘Male and female he made them. ‘For this reason a man will leave his father and mother and the two will become one flesh.’ What therefore God has joined together — let no human being separate.” And in the house the disciples ask him again about this. And he says to them: “Whoever divorces his wife and marries another commits adultery against her. And if she divorces her husband and marries another — she commits adultery.”
Let the Children Come · 10:13–16

And they are bringing children to him so that he might touch them. But the disciples rebuke them. And seeing this, Jesus is indignant. And he says to them: “Let the children come to me — do not stop them. For the kingdom of God belongs to such as these. Truly I tell you — whoever does not receive the kingdom of God like a child will never enter it.” And taking them in his arms, he blesses them, laying his hands on them.
The Rich Man · 10:17–22

And as he is setting out on the road, a man runs up and kneels before him and asks him: “Good Teacher — what must I do to inherit eternal life?” And Jesus says to him: “Why do you call me good? No one is good except God alone. You know the commandments: ‘Do not murder. Do not commit adultery. Do not steal. Do not bear false witness. Do not defraud. Honor your father and mother.’” And he says to him: “Teacher — all these I have kept from my youth.”

And looking at him, Jesus loves him. And he says to him: “You lack one thing. Go — sell everything you have and give to the poor. And you will have treasure in heaven. Then come — follow me.” But his face falls at this word. And he goes away grieving — for he has great possessions.
The Danger of Wealth · 10:23–31
And looking around, Jesus says to his disciples: “How hard it will be for those who have wealth to enter the kingdom of God!”

And the disciples are astonished at his words. But Jesus answers again: “Children — how hard it is to enter the kingdom of God! It is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich person to enter the kingdom of God.” And they are utterly astonished, saying to one another: “Then who can be saved?” Looking at them, Jesus says: “With human beings it is impossible — but not with God. For all things are possible with God.”

Peter begins to say to him: “Look — we have left everything and followed you.” Jesus says: “Truly I tell you — there is no one who has left house or brothers or sisters or mother or father or children or fields for my sake and for the gospel’s sake who will not receive a hundredfold now in this age — houses and brothers and sisters and mothers and children and fields, with persecutions — and in the age to come eternal life.
But many who are first will be last — and the last first.”
The Third Passion Prediction · 10:32–34

And they are on the road going up to Jerusalem. And Jesus is going ahead of them. And they are astonished. And those following are afraid. And taking the Twelve aside again, he begins to tell them what is going to happen to him:

“Look — we are going up to Jerusalem. And the Son of Man will be handed over to the chief priests and the scribes. And they will condemn him to death and hand him over to the Gentiles. And they will mock him and spit on him and flog him and kill him. And after three days he will rise.”
The Request of James and John · 10:35–45
And James and John, the sons of Zebedee, come forward to him and say: “Teacher — we want you to do for us whatever we ask of you.”

And he says to them: “What do you want me to do for you?” They say to him: “Grant us to sit — one at your right hand and one at your left — in your glory.” But Jesus says to them: “You do not know what you are asking. Are you able to drink the cup that I drink — or to be baptized with the baptism with which I am baptized?” And they say to him: “We are able.” And Jesus says to them: “The cup that I drink you will drink — and with the baptism with which I am baptized, you will be baptized.

But to sit at my right hand or at my left — this is not mine to grant. It is for those for whom it has been prepared.” And when the ten hear it, they begin to be indignant at James and John. And calling them to him, Jesus says to them: “You know that those who are considered rulers of the Gentiles lord it over them — and their great ones exercise authority over them. But it shall not be so among you. But whoever wants to become great among you must be your servant.
And whoever wants to be first among you must be slave of all. For even the Son of Man did not come to be served — but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.”
Blind Bartimaeus · 10:46–52

And they come to Jericho. And as he is leaving Jericho with his disciples and a large crowd, the son of Timaeus — Bartimaeus, a blind beggar — is sitting by the road. And hearing that it is Jesus of Nazareth, he begins to cry out: “Son of David — Jesus — have mercy on me!”

And many rebuke him, telling him to be quiet. But he cries out all the more: “Son of David — have mercy on me!” And Jesus stops and says: “Call him.” And they call the blind man, saying to him: “Take courage — get up. He is calling you.” And throwing off his cloak, he springs up and comes to Jesus. And Jesus answers him: “What do you want me to do for you?” The blind man says to him: “Rabbouni — let me see again.” And Jesus says to him: “Go — your faith has saved you.” And immediately he receives his sight. And he follows him on the road.
The Triumphal Entry · 11:1–11

And when they draw near to Jerusalem — to Bethphage and Bethany, at the Mount of Olives — he sends two of his disciples and says to them: “Go into the village ahead of you. And immediately as you enter it you will find a colt tied — one on which no one has ever sat. Untie it and bring it. And if anyone says to you, ‘Why are you doing this?’ — say: ‘The Lord has need of it.’” And they go and find a colt tied at a door outside in the street. And they untie it.

And some of those standing there say to them: “What are you doing, untying the colt?” And they say to them just as Jesus had told them. And they let them go. And they bring the colt to Jesus and throw their cloaks on it. And he sits on it. And many spread their cloaks on the road. And others spread leafy branches they have cut from the fields. And those going ahead and those following are crying out:

“Hosanna! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord! Blessed is the coming kingdom of our father David! Hosanna in the highest!” And he enters Jerusalem — into the temple. And looking around at everything, since the hour is already late, he goes out to Bethany with the Twelve.
The Fig Tree · 11:12–14

Prologue · 1:1–4

Since many have taken in hand to draw up a narrative of the events that have been brought to completion among us — 2 just as they were handed down to us by those who from the beginning were eyewitnesses and attendants of the word — 3 it seemed good to me as well, having followed everything carefully from the very beginning, to write an orderly account for you, most excellent Theophilus, 4 so that you may know the certainty of the things in which you have been instructed.

In the days of Herod, king of Judea, there is a priest named Zechariah, from the priestly division of Abijah. His wife Elizabeth is a descendant of Aaron. Both of them are righteous before God — walking blamelessly in all the commandments and requirements of the Lord. But they have no child. Elizabeth is barren, and both of them are well along in years. One day Zechariah’s division is on duty and he is serving as priest before God.

The sacred lot falls to him — as it sometimes did in a priest’s lifetime, and sometimes never did — to enter the sanctuary of the Lord and burn incense. And the whole crowd of people is outside, praying during the hour of incense. Then an angel of the Lord appears to him, standing on the right side of the altar of incense. Zechariah sees him and is shaken to his core. Fear falls on him.

“Don’t be afraid, Zechariah,” the angel says. “Your petition has been heard. Your wife Elizabeth will bear you a son, and you are to name him John. He will be your joy and delight — and many will rejoice at his birth. He will be great before the Lord. He must drink no wine or strong drink. And he will be filled with the Holy Spirit even from his mother’s womb. He will turn many of the children of Israel back to the Lord their God.

He will go before him in the spirit and power of Elijah — turning the hearts of fathers toward their children, and the disobedient toward the wisdom of the righteous — to make ready a people prepared for the Lord.”
“How am I supposed to know this is true?” Zechariah says to the angel. “I’m an old man. My wife is well along in years.”

“I am Gabriel,” the angel answers. “I stand in the presence of God. He sent me to speak to you — to bring you this good news. And now, because you didn’t believe my words — which will be fulfilled at their appointed time — you will be silent and unable to speak until the day these things happen.” The people are waiting for Zechariah outside. They are puzzled — he’s taking so long in the sanctuary. When he finally comes out, he can’t speak to them. They realize he’s seen a vision inside. He keeps motioning to them, but he stays mute.

When his days of service are done, he goes home. And after those days his wife Elizabeth conceives. She keeps herself in seclusion for five months and says, “This is what the Lord has done for me — in the days when he looked on me and took away my disgrace among people.”
