And coming to her, he says, “Rejoice, you who have been graced! The Lord is with you.” She is deeply troubled by his word. She turns it over in her mind — what kind of greeting is this?

“Don’t be afraid, Mary,” the angel says. “You have found favor with God. Listen — you will conceive in your womb and give birth to a son, and you are to call his name Jesus. He will be great. He will be called Son of the Most High. And the Lord God will give him the throne of his ancestor David. He will reign over the house of Jacob forever, and his kingdom will have no end.”
“But how?” Mary asks the angel. “I haven’t known a man.”

“The Holy Spirit will come upon you,” the angel answers her. “And the power of the Most High will overshadow you. And for this reason the holy one being born will be called Son of God. And listen — your relative Elizabeth has also conceived a son in her old age. This is the sixth month for her who was called barren. No word from God will be impossible.”
“Here I am,” Mary says. “The Lord’s servant. Let it happen to me according to your word.” And the angel departs from her.
Mary Visits Elizabeth · 1:39–45

In those days Mary sets out and travels quickly into the hill country, to a town in Judah. She enters the house of Zechariah and greets Elizabeth. And when Elizabeth hears Mary’s greeting, the baby leaps in her womb. Elizabeth is filled with the Holy Spirit and cries out with a great cry: “Blessed are you among women — and blessed is the fruit of your womb! Why has this been granted to me — that the mother of my Lord should come to me?
For look — when the sound of your greeting reached my ears, the baby in my womb leaped for joy! Blessed is she who believed — that what was spoken to her from the Lord would be fulfilled.”
The Magnificat · 1:46–56
And Mary says:
“My soul makes the Lord great;
my spirit exults in God my Savior,
for he has looked upon the lowliness of his servant.
From now on, every generation will call me blessed —
because the Mighty One has done great things for me.
Holy is his name.
And his mercy reaches from generation to generation
to those who fear him.
He has acted with the strength of his arm.
He has scattered the arrogant in the schemes of their hearts.
He has brought down the powerful from their thrones
and lifted up the lowly.
He has filled the hungry with good things
and sent the rich away empty.
He has come to the aid of his servant Israel,
remembering mercy —
just as he spoke to our ancestors,
to Abraham and his descendants forever.”
Mary stays with her about three months, and then returns home.
The Birth of John · 1:57–66

When the time is fulfilled, Elizabeth gives birth to a son. And her neighbors and relatives hear that the Lord has shown her great mercy. They rejoice with her. On the eighth day they come to circumcise the child, and they are going to name him Zechariah — after his father. But his mother speaks up. “No,” she says. “He is to be called John.”

“There’s no one in your family with that name,” they tell her. So they make signs to his father to find out what he wants the child called. He asks for a writing tablet and writes: “His name is John.” And everyone is amazed. At once his mouth opens and his tongue is freed. And he speaks — blessing God. Fear comes on all their neighbors. And all through the hill country of Judea, people are talking about these things.
Everyone who hears lays it up in their heart. “What then will this child become?” they ask. And the hand of the Lord is with him.
The Benedictus · 1:67–79
And his father Zechariah is filled with the Holy Spirit and prophesies:
“Blessed be the Lord, the God of Israel —
for he has visited and accomplished redemption for his people.
He has raised up a horn of salvation for us
in the house of his servant David —
as he spoke through the mouth of his holy prophets from of old —
salvation from our enemies,
and from the hand of all who hate us;
to show mercy to our ancestors
and to remember his holy covenant,
the oath he swore to Abraham our ancestor,
to grant us that we, rescued from the hand of our enemies,
might serve him without fear,
in holiness and righteousness before him
all our days.
And you, child — you will be called prophet of the Most High,
for you will go before the Lord to prepare his ways,
to give his people the knowledge of salvation
in the forgiveness of their sins —
through the tender mercy of our God,
by which the rising sun will visit us from on high,
to shine on those who sit in darkness and in the shadow of death,
to guide our feet into the way of peace.”
John in the Wilderness · 1:80
And the child grows and becomes strong in spirit. And he is in the wilderness until the day of his appearing to Israel.
The Birth of Jesus · 2:1–7

In those days a decree goes out from Caesar Augustus — all the inhabited world is to be registered. This first registration takes place while Quirinius is governing Syria. And everyone makes their way to their own town to be registered. Joseph too goes up from Galilee, from the town of Nazareth, into Judea — to the city of David called Bethlehem — because he belongs to the house and lineage of David. He goes to be registered with Mary, his betrothed, who is carrying a child.

While they are there, the days for her to give birth are completed. She gives birth to her firstborn son, wraps him in swaddling bands, and lays him in a feeding trough — because there is no room for them in the guest room.
The Shepherds and The Angels · 2:8–20

In the same region there are shepherds out in the fields, keeping the night watch over their flock. An angel of the Lord suddenly stands before them, and the glory of the Lord blazes around them. They are seized with terror.

“Do not be afraid,” the angel says to them. “I bring you good news — great joy, for all the people. Today, in the city of David, a Savior is born to you: he is the Messiah, the Lord. And here is the sign for you: you will find a baby wrapped in swaddling bands, lying in a feeding trough.” Then suddenly with the angel there is a vast multitude of the heavenly army, praising God and saying:

“Glory to God in the highest heaven, and on earth — peace among the people of his favor.” When the angels leave them and return to heaven, the shepherds say to one another, “Let’s go straight to Bethlehem and see this thing that has happened — the thing the Lord has made known to us.” They hurry off and find Mary and Joseph, and the baby lying in the feeding trough. When they see him, they spread the word about what they were told concerning this child.

Everyone who hears it is amazed at what the shepherds say. But Mary treasures all these things, turning them over and over in her heart. The shepherds return, glorifying and praising God for everything they heard and saw — exactly as it had been told to them.
The Circumcision and Naming · 2:21
Eight days later, when the time comes to circumcise him, he is named Jesus — the name the angel gave before he was conceived in the womb.
The Presentation at The Temple · 2:22–38

When the days of their purification are complete according to the Law of Moses, they bring him up to Jerusalem to present him to the Lord — as it is written in the Law of the Lord: “Every firstborn male who opens the womb is to be consecrated to the Lord” — and to offer the sacrifice the Law of the Lord requires: a pair of turtledoves, or two young pigeons. Now there is a man in Jerusalem named Simeon. He is righteous and devout, waiting for the consolation of Israel, and the Holy Spirit is upon him.

The Spirit had revealed to him that he would not see death before he had seen the Lord’s Messiah. Led by the Spirit, he comes into the temple courts. When the parents bring in the child Jesus to do for him what the Law requires, Simeon takes him in his arms and blesses God:

“Sovereign Lord, now you are releasing your servant — as you have promised — in peace. For my eyes have seen your salvation, which you have prepared in the sight of all peoples: a light of revelation for the Gentiles, and the glory of your people Israel.” His father and mother are astonished at what is being said about him. Simeon blesses them and says to Mary his mother, “This child is appointed for the fall and rising of many in Israel — and as a sign that will be spoken against.

A sword will pass through your own soul too — so that the thoughts of many hearts may be laid bare.” There is also a prophetess named Anna, daughter of Phanuel, from the tribe of Asher. She is very old, having lived with her husband seven years after her marriage, and then as a widow until she is eighty-four. She never leaves the temple, serving God night and day with fasting and prayer. Coming up to them at that very moment, she gives thanks to God and speaks about the child to everyone who is waiting for the redemption of Jerusalem.
The Return to Nazareth · 2:39–40

When they have completed everything required by the Law of the Lord, they return to Galilee — to their own town of Nazareth. The child grows and becomes strong, filled with wisdom. The favor of God is on him.
The Boy Jesus at The Temple · 2:41–52

Every year his parents make the journey to Jerusalem for the Passover festival. When he is twelve, they go up as usual for the feast. When the festival days are over and they set out for home, the boy Jesus stays behind in Jerusalem. His parents don’t know it. Assuming he is somewhere in their traveling party, they go a full day’s journey before they begin searching for him among their relatives and friends. When they don’t find him, they turn back to Jerusalem to search.
After three days they find him in the temple courts, sitting among the teachers, listening to them and asking questions. Everyone who hears him is astounded at his understanding and his answers.
“Child,” his mother says to him, when they see him, “why have you done this to us? Your father and I have been searching for you in anguish.”

“Why were you searching for me?” he says to them. “Didn’t you know that I had to be about my Father’s affairs?” But they don’t understand what he means. He goes back down to Nazareth with them and submits to them. His mother holds all these things carefully in her heart. And Jesus advances in wisdom and in stature, and in favor with God and with people.
The Word Comes to John · 3:1–6

In the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar — when Pontius Pilate is governor of Judea, Herod tetrarch of Galilee, his brother Philip tetrarch of the region of Iturea and Trachonitis, and Lysanias tetrarch of Abilene — 2 during the high priesthood of Annas and Caiaphas — a word from God comes to John, son of Zechariah, in the wilderness.
And he goes into all the country around the Jordan, proclaiming a baptism of repentance for the release of sins —
as it is written in the scroll of the words of Isaiah the prophet:
“A voice cries out in the wilderness:
Prepare the way of the Lord,
make his paths straight.
Every ravine will be filled,
every mountain and hill brought low.
The crooked will become straight,
the rough ways made smooth.
And all flesh will see the salvation of God.”
John’s Preaching · 3:7–14

So John says to the crowds coming out to be baptized by him: “You offspring of vipers — who tipped you off to flee from the coming wrath? Produce fruit that shows your repentance is real. And don’t start telling yourselves, ‘We have Abraham as our father.’ I’m telling you — God can raise up children for Abraham from these stones. Even now the axe is lying at the root of the trees. Every tree that doesn’t produce good fruit is cut down and thrown into the fire.”
“What should we do, then?” the crowds ask him.

“The one who has two shirts,” he answers, “let him share with the one who has none. And the one who has food — let him do the same.” Tax collectors also come to be baptized. “Teacher,” they ask, “what should we do?”
“Don’t collect more than you’re authorized to,” he tells them. Soldiers also ask him: “And what about us — what should we do?”
“Don’t shake anyone down,” he says. “Don’t make false accusations. And be content with your wages.”
The One Who is Coming · 3:15–18

The people are full of expectation. And everyone is turning it over in their hearts about John — wondering whether he might be the Messiah. John answers them all: “I baptize you in water. But the one who is stronger than me is coming — I am not fit to untie the strap of his sandals. He will baptize you in the Holy Spirit and in fire. His winnowing fork is in his hand, ready to clear his threshing floor. He will gather the wheat into his barn — but the chaff he will burn with fire that can’t be put out.”
And with many other words like these he urges the people on, proclaiming the good news to them.
Herod Imprisons John · 3:19–20
But Herod the tetrarch — being called out by John over Herodias, his brother’s wife, and over all the other evil things Herod has done — adds this to everything else: he locks John up in prison.
The Baptism of Jesus · 3:21–22

Now when all the people are being baptized, Jesus is baptized too. And while he is praying, heaven opens — and the Holy Spirit descends on him in bodily form, like a dove. And a voice comes out of heaven:
“You are my Son — the Beloved. In you I am well pleased.”
The Genealogy of Jesus · 3:23–38
Jesus himself is about thirty years old when he begins. He is the son — or so it was thought — of Joseph.
Joseph, son of Heli, son of Matthat, son of Levi, son of Melchi, son of Jannai, son of Joseph,
son of Mattathias, son of Amos, son of Nahum, son of Esli, son of Naggai,
son of Maath, son of Mattathias, son of Semein, son of Josech, son of Joda,
son of Joanan, son of Rhesa, son of Zerubbabel, son of Shealtiel, son of Neri,
son of Melchi, son of Addi, son of Cosam, son of Elmadam, son of Er,
son of Joshua, son of Eliezer, son of Jorim, son of Matthat, son of Levi,
son of Simeon, son of Judah, son of Joseph, son of Jonam, son of Eliakim,
son of Melea, son of Menna, son of Mattatha, son of Nathan, son of David,
son of Jesse, son of Obed, son of Boaz, son of Salmon, son of Nahshon,
son of Amminadab, son of Admin, son of Arni, son of Hezron, son of Perez, son of Judah,
son of Jacob, son of Isaac, son of Abraham, son of Terah, son of Nahor,
son of Serug, son of Reu, son of Peleg, son of Eber, son of Shelah,
son of Cainan, son of Arphaxad, son of Shem, son of Noah, son of Lamech,
son of Methuselah, son of Enoch, son of Jared, son of Mahalaleel, son of Cainan,
son of Enosh, son of Seth, son of Adam — son of God.
The Temptation in The Wilderness · 4:1–13

Jesus returns from the Jordan full of the Holy Spirit. And the Spirit leads him into the wilderness, where he is tested by the devil for forty days. He eats nothing during those days, and when they are over he is starving.

“If you are the Son of God,” the devil says to him, “tell this stone to become bread.” Jesus answers him: “It is written: ‘A person does not live on bread alone.’” And leading him up, the devil shows him all the kingdoms of the inhabited world in a single instant.

“I will give you all this authority,” he says, “and all their glory — for it has been handed over to me, and I give it to whoever I want. So if you will bow down before me, all of it will be yours.” Jesus answers him: “It is written: ‘You shall bow down before the Lord your God, and serve him alone.’” And he brings him to Jerusalem and stands him on the highest point of the temple. “If you are the Son of God,” he says, “throw yourself down from here.
For it is written: ‘He will command his angels concerning you, to guard you’ — and: ‘On their hands they will lift you up, so that you won’t strike your foot against a stone.’”
“It has been said,” Jesus answers him, “‘You shall not put the Lord your God to the test.’” And when the devil has finished every test, he withdraws from him — until an opportune time.
Return to Galilee · 4:14–15
And Jesus returns to Galilee in the power of the Spirit. Word about him spreads through the whole surrounding region. He teaches in their synagogues, and everyone praises him.
The Synagogue at Nazareth · 4:16–30

He comes to Nazareth, where he had been raised. On the Sabbath day he goes into the synagogue, as was his custom. And he stands up to read. The scroll of the prophet Isaiah is handed to him. He unrolls it and finds the place where it is written:

“The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me to proclaim good news to the poor. He has sent me to proclaim release to the captives, and recovery of sight to the blind, to send away the crushed in release, to proclaim the year of the Lord’s favor.” He rolls up the scroll, gives it back to the attendant, and sits down. Every eye in the synagogue is fixed on him. And he begins to speak: “Today — this scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing.”
And they all speak well of him. They are astonished at the gracious words coming out of his mouth. “Isn’t this Joseph’s son?” they ask.

“I know what you’re going to say,” he tells them. “‘Physician, heal yourself. Do here in your hometown what we’ve heard you did in Capernaum.’ But the truth is — no prophet is welcomed in his hometown. I tell you truthfully: there were many widows in Israel in the days of Elijah, when the sky was shut for three and a half years and a great famine came over all the land. And Elijah was sent to none of them — only to a widow at Zarephath, in the region of Sidon.

And there were many lepers in Israel in the time of the prophet Elisha. And none of them were cleansed — only Naaman the Syrian.” When they hear this, everyone in the synagogue is filled with fury. They rise up and drive him out of the town. They take him to the edge of the hill their town is built on, intending to throw him off the cliff. But he walks straight through the middle of them and goes on his way.
An Unclean Spirit in the Synagogue · 4:31–37

And he goes down to Capernaum, a town in Galilee. He teaches them on the Sabbath, and they are astonished at his teaching — because his word carries authority. In the synagogue there is a man who has a spirit of an unclean demon. And he cries out with a loud voice:

“Ha! What do you want with us, Jesus of Nazareth? Have you come to destroy us? I know who you are — the Holy One of God!” Jesus rebukes him: “Be silent — and come out of him!” The demon throws the man down in front of them and comes out without harming him at all. Astonishment falls on everyone. They say to one another, “What is this word? With authority and power he commands the unclean spirits and they come out!” And the report about him spreads to every corner of the surrounding region.
Simon’s Mother-in-law and the Evening Healings · 4:38–41

He gets up from the synagogue and enters Simon’s house. Simon’s mother-in-law is in the grip of a severe fever, and they ask him about her. And standing over her, he rebukes the fever — and it releases her. She gets up at once and begins to serve them. When the sun sets, everyone who has people sick with various diseases brings them to him. And laying his hands on each one of them, he heals them. Demons also come out of many people, shouting, “You are the Son of God!” But he rebukes them and will not let them speak — because they know he is the Messiah.
Departing for Other Towns · 4:42–44
When day comes, he goes out to a deserted place. And the crowds search for him. They find him and try to hold him back — to keep him from leaving them.
“I must proclaim the good news of the kingdom of God to the other towns too,” he tells them. “That is what I was sent to do.” And he keeps on proclaiming in the synagogues of Judea.
The Catch of Fish · 5:1–11

One day the crowd is pressing in on Jesus to hear the word of God — and he is standing at the edge of Lake Gennesaret. He sees two boats pulled up on the shore. The fishermen have left them and are washing their nets. He gets into one of the boats — Simon’s — and asks him to push out a little from the shore. Then he sits down and teaches the crowd from the boat. When he has finished speaking, he says to Simon, “Put out into the deep water and let down your nets for a catch.”

“Master,” Simon answers, “we worked through the whole night and caught nothing. But — on your word — I’ll let down the nets.” And when they do, they catch such a huge number of fish that their nets begin to tear. They wave to their partners in the other boat to come and help them. And they come — and they fill both boats so full they begin to sink. When Simon Peter sees this, he falls down at Jesus’ knees and says, “Go away from me, Lord — I’m a sinful man.”
For astonishment had seized him — and everyone with him — at the catch of fish they had taken. And the same with James and John, the sons of Zebedee, who were partners with Simon.
“Don’t be afraid,” Jesus says to Simon. “From now on you will be catching people.” And when they bring the boats to shore, they leave everything and follow him.
The Man Covered in Leprosy · 5:12–16

And it happens — while he is in one of the towns — that there is a man covered all over with leprosy. When he sees Jesus, he falls on his face and begs him: “Lord, if you are willing — you can make me clean.” And reaching out his hand, Jesus touches him. “I am willing,” he says. “Be clean.” And immediately the leprosy leaves him. And Jesus orders him to tell no one. “But go,” he says, “show yourself to the priest, and offer what Moses commanded for your cleansing — as a testimony to them.”
But the word about him spreads all the more. Great crowds gather to hear him and to be healed of their illnesses. And he himself withdraws to deserted places and prays.
The Man Let Down Through The Roof · 5:17–26

One day Jesus is teaching. Pharisees and teachers of the Law are sitting there — they have come from every village in Galilee and Judea, and from Jerusalem. And the power of the Lord is present for him to heal. And some men come carrying a paralyzed man on a mat. They are trying to bring him in and set him down before Jesus. But they can’t find a way to get him in because of the crowd. So they go up on the roof, take off the tiles, and lower him down on his mat — right into the middle of the room, in front of Jesus.

When Jesus sees their faith, he says, “Friend — your sins are released.” The scribes and Pharisees begin to argue among themselves: “Who is this, speaking blasphemies? Who can release sins but God alone?” Jesus knows what they are thinking. “Why are you turning this over in your hearts?” he says to them.

“Which is easier — to say ‘Your sins are released,’ or to say ‘Get up and walk’? But so that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to release sins —” he turns to the paralyzed man and says, “I tell you: get up, pick up your mat, and go home.” At once he gets up in front of them. He picks up what he had been lying on, and goes home glorifying God. Amazement seizes everyone. They glorify God, and they are filled with fear. “We’ve seen extraordinary things today,” they say.
The Calling of Levi · 5:27–32
After this, Jesus goes out and notices a tax collector named Levi sitting at the tax booth.

“Follow me,” he says to him. And Levi leaves everything, gets up, and follows him. And Levi throws a great banquet for him at his house. There is a large crowd of tax collectors and others reclining at the table with them. The Pharisees and their scribes grumble at his disciples: “Why do you eat and drink with tax collectors and sinners?”
“It’s not the healthy who need a doctor,” Jesus answers them, “but the sick. I haven’t come to call the righteous. I’ve come to call sinners — to repentance.”
The Question About Fasting · 5:33–39
“John’s disciples fast often and offer prayers,” they say to him, “and so do the disciples of the Pharisees. But yours — they eat and drink.”
“Can you make the wedding guests fast while the bridegroom is still with them?” Jesus asks.

“But the days will come — when the bridegroom is taken away from them. They will fast in those days.” And he gives them this illustration: “Nobody tears a patch from a new garment and sews it on an old one. If they do, they will have torn the new garment, and the patch from the new won’t match the old. And nobody pours new wine into old wineskins. If they do, the new wine will burst the skins, it will spill out, and the skins will be ruined.
No — new wine must go into fresh wineskins. And nobody who has been drinking old wine wants new. They say, ‘The old is good.’”
Lord of the Sabbath · 6:1–5

One Sabbath Jesus is going through the grain fields. His disciples are plucking heads of grain, rubbing them in their hands, and eating. Some of the Pharisees say, “Why are you doing what is not lawful on the Sabbath?”

“Haven’t you read what David did,” Jesus answers, “when he and his companions were hungry — how he entered the house of God, took the bread of the Presence, and ate it — and gave it to his companions too? Which is not lawful for anyone to eat except the priests.” And he says to them, “The Son of Man is Lord of the Sabbath.”
The Man with The Withered Hand · 6:6–11

On another Sabbath he enters the synagogue and teaches. There is a man there whose right hand is withered. The scribes and Pharisees are watching him closely — will he heal on the Sabbath? — so they can find grounds to accuse him. But he knows what they are thinking. He says to the man with the withered hand, “Get up and stand in the middle.” And he gets up and stands there.

“I ask you,” Jesus says to them: “is it lawful on the Sabbath to do good or to do harm? To save a life or to destroy it?” And he looks around at all of them, then says to the man, “Stretch out your hand.” He does — and his hand is restored. But they are filled with fury and begin discussing with one another what they might do to Jesus.
The Choosing of The Twelve · 6:12–16

In those days he goes out to the mountain to pray, and spends the whole night in prayer to God. And when day comes, he calls his disciples and chooses twelve of them — whom he also names apostles: Simon, whom he also names Peter; and his brother Andrew; and James and John; and Philip and Bartholomew; and Matthew and Thomas; and James the son of Alphaeus; and Simon called the Zealot; and Judas the son of James; and Judas Iscariot, who becomes a traitor.
The Crowd on The Plain · 6:17–19

He comes down with them and stands on a level place. A large crowd of his disciples is there, and a great multitude of people from all over Judea and Jerusalem and the coastal region of Tyre and Sidon — who had come to hear him and to be healed of their diseases. And those troubled by unclean spirits are cured. And the whole crowd is trying to touch him — because power is going out from him and healing everyone.
The Beatitudes and Woes · 6:20–26
And he lifts his eyes to his disciples and says:
“Blessed are you who are poor —
for the kingdom of God is yours.
Blessed are you who are hungry now —
for you will be filled.
Blessed are you who weep now —
for you will laugh.
Blessed are you when people hate you,
and when they shut you out and insult you
and throw your name out as evil
on account of the Son of Man.
Rejoice in that day and leap for joy —
for your reward is great in heaven.
For that is how their ancestors treated the prophets.
But woe to you who are rich —
for you have received your comfort in full.
Woe to you who are full now —
for you will be hungry.
Woe to you who laugh now —
for you will mourn and weep.
Woe to you when everyone speaks well of you —
for that is how their ancestors treated the false prophets.
Love Your Enemies · 6:27–36

“But I say to you who are listening: love your enemies. Do good to those who hate you. Bless those who curse you. Pray for those who mistreat you. To the one who strikes you on the cheek, offer the other also. And from the one who takes your cloak, don’t hold back your shirt either. Give to everyone who asks you. And from the one who takes what is yours, don’t demand it back. And just as you want people to treat you — treat them the same way.

If you love only those who love you, what credit is that to you? Even sinners love those who love them. And if you do good only to those who do good to you, what credit is that to you? Even sinners do the same. And if you lend only to those you expect to get something back from, what credit is that to you? Even sinners lend to sinners, expecting to get back as much. But — love your enemies. Do good. Lend without expecting anything back. And your reward will be great, and you will be sons of the Most High — because he is kind to the ungrateful and the evil.
Be compassionate, just as your Father is compassionate.
On Judging · 6:37–42

“Don’t judge — and you won’t be judged. Don’t condemn — and you won’t be condemned. Release — and you will be released. Give, and it will be given to you. A good measure — pressed down, shaken together, running over — will be poured into your lap. Because the measure you use is the measure that will be used back on you.” And he gives them an illustration: “Can a blind man lead a blind man? Won’t they both fall into a ditch?

A student is not above his teacher. But everyone who is fully trained will be like his teacher. Why do you see the splinter in your brother’s eye but don’t notice the beam in your own? How can you say to your brother, ‘Brother, let me take out the splinter in your eye,’ when you yourself don’t see the beam in your own? Hypocrite — first take the beam out of your own eye. Then you’ll see clearly enough to take out the splinter in your brother’s.”
Tree and Fruit · 6:43–45

“A good tree doesn’t produce rotten fruit, and a rotten tree doesn’t produce good fruit. Each tree is known by its own fruit. You don’t pick figs from thornbushes, or gather grapes from a briar patch. A good person brings good things out of the good stored up in their heart. And an evil person brings evil things out of evil. Because the mouth speaks from what overflows in the heart.”
The Two Builders · 6:46–49

“Why do you call me ‘Lord, Lord’ and not do what I say? Everyone who comes to me and hears my words and does them — I’ll show you what they are like. They are like a man building a house who dug down deep and laid the foundation on rock. When a flood came, the river burst against that house — and could not shake it, because it was well built. But the one who hears and does not do — is like a man who built a house on the ground without a foundation. The river burst against it, and immediately it collapsed. And the ruin of that house was great.”
The Centurion’s Servant · 7:1–10

When he has finished saying all this to the people, he enters Capernaum. A centurion there has a servant who is dear to him — gravely ill, and close to death. When the centurion hears about Jesus, he sends some Jewish elders to ask him to come and save his servant. When they come to Jesus, they urge him earnestly: “He deserves this from you — he loves our people, and he himself built our synagogue.” So Jesus goes with them. And when he is not far from the house, the centurion sends friends with a message: “Lord, don’t trouble yourself — I am not worthy to have you come under my roof.

That is why I didn’t presume to come to you myself. But say the word, and my servant will be healed. For I too am a man under authority, with soldiers under me. I say to one, ‘Go,’ and he goes. And to another, ‘Come,’ and he comes. And to my servant, ‘Do this,’ and he does it.” When Jesus hears this, he is astonished at him. And turning to the crowd following him, he says, “I tell you — not even in Israel have I found faith like this.”
And when the messengers return to the house, they find the servant well.
The Widow of Nain · 7:11–17

Soon after, he travels to a town called Nain. His disciples and a large crowd go with him. As he approaches the town gate, a dead man is being carried out — the only son of his mother, and she is a widow. A considerable crowd from the town is with her. When the Lord sees her, his heart breaks for her. “Don’t weep,” he says to her. And he comes forward and touches the bier. The pallbearers stop.

“Young man,” he says, “I tell you — get up.” And the dead man sits up and begins to speak. And Jesus gives him back to his mother. Fear seizes everyone. And they glorify God: “A great prophet has risen among us!” they say. “God has visited his people!” And this word about him spreads through all of Judea and the surrounding countryside.
John’s Question from Prison · 7:18–35

John’s disciples report all these things to him. And calling two of them, John sends them to the Lord to ask: “Are you the one who is to come — or should we look for someone else?” When the men come to him, they say, “John the Baptist has sent us to ask: are you the one who is to come, or should we look for someone else?” In that very hour he heals many people of diseases and afflictions and evil spirits, and gives sight to many who are blind.

And he answers them: “Go and report to John what you have seen and heard — the blind see, the lame walk, lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead are raised, and the poor have the good news proclaimed to them. And blessed is the one who is not tripped up by me.” When John’s messengers have gone, Jesus begins to speak to the crowds about John: “What did you go out into the wilderness to see? A reed shaken by the wind?

If not that — what did you go out to see? A man dressed in fine clothes? Look — those who wear splendid clothing and live in luxury are in royal palaces. So what did you go out to see? A prophet? Yes — I tell you, and more than a prophet. This is the one about whom it is written: ‘Look — I am sending my messenger ahead of you, who will prepare your way before you.’ I tell you — among those born of women, no one is greater than John. And yet the least in the kingdom of God is greater than he.”

All the people who heard — and the tax collectors — acknowledged the justice of God, having been baptized with John’s baptism. But the Pharisees and the lawyers rejected the purpose of God for themselves, having refused to be baptized by him.

“To what then shall I compare the people of this generation? What are they like? They are like children sitting in the marketplace and calling to each other: ‘We played the flute for you and you didn’t dance. We sang a lament and you didn’t weep.’ For John the Baptist came neither eating bread nor drinking wine, and you say, ‘He has a demon.’ The Son of Man came eating and drinking, and you say, ‘Look at him — a glutton and a drunk, a friend of tax collectors and sinners.’
And yet wisdom is vindicated by all her children.”
The Woman with The Alabaster Jar · 7:36–50

One of the Pharisees asks Jesus to eat with him. And going into the Pharisee’s house, he reclines at the table. And there is a woman in the town who is a sinner. When she finds out that Jesus is reclining at the Pharisee’s table, she brings an alabaster jar of perfume. And standing behind him at his feet, weeping, she begins to wet his feet with her tears. She wipes them with her hair, kisses his feet, and anoints them with the perfume.
When the Pharisee who had invited him sees this, he says to himself, “If this man were a prophet, he would know what kind of woman is touching him — that she is a sinner.”
“Simon,” Jesus says to him, “I have something to say to you.”
“Teacher,” he says, “say it.”
“A moneylender had two debtors. One owed five hundred denarii, the other fifty. When neither of them had anything to pay with, he canceled both debts. So which of them will love him more?”
“I suppose,” Simon answers, “the one he canceled more for.”

“You have judged rightly,” he says. And turning toward the woman, he says to Simon: “Do you see this woman? I came into your house — you gave me no water for my feet. But she has wet my feet with her tears and wiped them with her hair. You gave me no kiss. But from the moment I came in, she has not stopped kissing my feet. You did not anoint my head with oil. But she has anointed my feet with perfume. For this reason I tell you — her many sins have been released, because she loved much. But the one who is released little, loves little.”

And he says to her, “Your sins are released.” And those reclining at the table with him begin to say among themselves, “Who is this, that he even releases sins?” And he says to the woman, “Your faith has saved you. Go in peace.”
The Women Who Followed · 8:1–3

Soon after, he makes his way through town after town and village after village, proclaiming and announcing the good news of the kingdom of God. The Twelve are with him, and also some women who had been healed of evil spirits and diseases — Mary called Magdalene, from whom seven demons had gone out, and Joanna the wife of Chuza, Herod’s household manager, and Susanna, and many others. They were providing for them out of their own means.
The Parable of The Sower · 8:4–8
And when a large crowd gathers — with people streaming to him from town after town — he speaks through a parable:

“A sower goes out to sow his seed. And as he sows, some falls along the path and gets trampled, and the birds of the sky devour it. Some falls on rock, and when it sprouts it withers — because it has no moisture. Some falls among thorns, and the thorns grow up with it and choke it. And some falls into good soil, and grows up and produces a hundredfold.” As he says this, he calls out: “Whoever has ears to hear — let them hear.”
Why Parables · 8:9–10
His disciples ask him what this parable means.
“To you,” he says, “it has been given to know the mysteries of the kingdom of God. But to the rest — in parables — so that seeing they may not see, and hearing they may not understand.
The Parable Explained · 8:11–15

“This is what the parable means: the seed is the word of God. The ones along the path are those who hear — then the devil comes and takes the word away from their heart, so they won’t believe and be saved. The ones on the rock are those who receive the word with joy when they hear it — but these have no root. They believe for a while, and in a time of testing they fall away. And what fell among the thorns — these are the ones who hear, but as they go on their way they are choked by the cares and riches and pleasures of life, and their fruit never matures.
But the ones in the good soil — these are the ones who hear the word and hold it in an honest and good heart, and bear fruit with patient endurance.”
The Lamp · 8:16–18

“Nobody lights a lamp and covers it with a jar or puts it under a bed. They put it on a stand, so that those who come in can see the light. For there is nothing hidden that will not be revealed, nothing concealed that will not be known and brought into the open. So pay attention to how you hear. Because whoever has — more will be given. And whoever does not have — even what they think they have will be taken from them.”
The True Family of Jesus · 8:19–21
His mother and brothers come to him, but they can’t get to him because of the crowd. Someone tells him: “Your mother and your brothers are standing outside — they want to see you.”
“My mother and my brothers,” he answers, “are those who hear the word of God and do it.”

One day he gets into a boat with his disciples and says to them, “Let’s cross to the other side of the lake.” And they set out. And as they sail, he falls asleep. And a squall comes down on the lake. They are taking on water and are in danger. They come and wake him: “Master! Master! We’re dying!” He wakes up, rebukes the wind and the surging water — and they stop. And there is calm.
“Where is your faith?” he says to them. And they are afraid and astonished. “Who then is this,” they say to one another, “that he commands even the wind and the water — and they obey him?”

They sail to the region of the Gerasenes, which is across the lake from Galilee. When Jesus steps ashore, he is met by a man from the town who has demons. For a long time he has worn no clothes and lived not in a house but in the tombs. When he sees Jesus, he cries out and falls before him and shouts at the top of his voice: “What do you want with me, Jesus, Son of the Most High God? I beg you — don’t torment me!” For Jesus had been commanding the unclean spirit to come out of the man. Many times it had seized him; and even when he was kept under guard, bound with chains and shackles, he would break the bonds and be driven by the demon into the wilderness.
“What is your name?” Jesus asks him.

“Legion,” he says — because many demons had entered him. And they begged him not to command them to go away into the abyss. Now a large herd of pigs is feeding there on the hillside. And the demons beg him to let them enter the pigs. And he gives them permission. The demons come out of the man and enter the pigs, and the herd rushes down the steep bank into the lake and drowns. When the herdsmen see what has happened, they run off and report it in the town and in the countryside.

People come out to see for themselves. They come to Jesus and find the man from whom the demons had gone out — sitting at Jesus’ feet, clothed and in his right mind. And they are afraid. Those who had seen it tell them how the demon-possessed man had been saved. And the whole crowd of the Gerasene region asks Jesus to leave them — because they are gripped with great fear. So he gets into the boat and returns. The man from whom the demons had gone out begs to go with him. But Jesus sends him away:
“Go back home and tell what God has done for you.” And he goes off, proclaiming through the whole town what Jesus had done for him.
Jairus’s Daughter and the Woman Who Touched His Cloak · 8:40–56

When Jesus returns, the crowd welcomes him — they were all waiting for him. And a man named Jairus comes — a ruler of the synagogue. He falls at Jesus’ feet and begs him to come to his house, because he has an only daughter, about twelve years old, and she is dying. And as he goes, the crowd presses in on him. A woman who has had a discharge of blood for twelve years — and though she had spent all she had on doctors, could not be healed by anyone —
comes up behind him and touches the fringe of his garment. And immediately her flow of blood stops.
“Who touched me?” Jesus asks. When everyone denies it, Peter says, “Master, the crowd is surrounding you and pressing in on you.”

“Someone touched me,” Jesus says. “I know that power has gone out from me.” When the woman sees that she has not gone unnoticed, she comes trembling and falls before him. And in front of all the people she tells why she touched him, and how she was instantly healed.

“Daughter,” he says to her, “your faith has saved you. Go in peace.” While he is still speaking, someone comes from the ruler’s house: “Your daughter has died — don’t trouble the teacher anymore.” When Jesus hears this, he answers him: “Don’t be afraid — just believe, and she will be saved.” When he comes to the house, he allows no one to go in with him except Peter and John and James, and the child’s father and mother.
And everyone is weeping and mourning for her.

“Stop weeping,” he says. “She hasn’t died — she is sleeping.” They laugh at him — they know she is dead. But he takes her by the hand and calls out: “Child — get up.” And her spirit returns, and she gets up at once. And he orders that something be given to her to eat. Her parents are overwhelmed. But he instructs them to tell no one what had happened.
The Sending of The Twelve · 9:1–6
And calling the Twelve together, he gives them power and authority over all demons and to heal diseases. And he sends them out to proclaim the kingdom of God and to heal.

“Take nothing for the road,” he says to them. “No staff, no bag, no bread, no silver — and don’t have two tunics apiece. Whatever house you enter, stay there — and leave from there. And wherever they don’t receive you — when you leave that town, shake the dust off your feet as a testimony against them.” And going out, they travel through village after village, proclaiming the good news and healing everywhere.
Herod’s Perplexity · 9:7–9

Now Herod the tetrarch hears about everything that is happening. And he is deeply perplexed — because some are saying that John has been raised from the dead, and some that Elijah has appeared, and others that one of the ancient prophets has risen.
“John I beheaded,” Herod says. “But who is this I keep hearing about?” And he keeps trying to see him.
The Feeding of The Five Thousand · 9:10–17

When the apostles return, they report to Jesus everything they have done. And taking them with him, he withdraws privately to a town called Bethsaida. But the crowds find out and follow him. And he welcomes them and speaks to them about the kingdom of God, and heals those who need healing. The day begins to draw to a close. The Twelve come to him and say, “Send the crowd away, so they can go to the surrounding villages and countryside and find food and lodging — because we’re in a deserted place here.”
“You give them something to eat,” he says to them.
“We have no more than five loaves and two fish,” they say, “unless we go and buy food for all these people.” There are about five thousand men.

“Have them sit down in groups of about fifty,” he says to his disciples. And they do — they have everyone sit down. And taking the five loaves and the two fish, he looks up to heaven, blesses them, breaks them, and gives them to the disciples to set before the crowd. And they all eat and are satisfied. And twelve baskets of leftover pieces are gathered up.
Peter’s Confession · 9:18–22
And it happens that while he is praying alone — the disciples are with him — he asks them: “Who do the crowds say I am?”
“John the Baptist,” they answer. “But others say Elijah. And others — that one of the ancient prophets has come back.”

“And you,” he says to them, “who do you say I am?” Peter answers: “The Messiah of God.” And he sternly charges them to tell this to no one, saying: “The Son of Man must suffer many things and be rejected by the elders and chief priests and scribes, and be killed — and on the third day be raised.”
The Cost of Following · 9:23–27

And he says to all of them: “If anyone wants to come after me, let them deny themselves and take up their cross every day — and follow me. For whoever wants to save their life will lose it. But whoever loses their life for my sake — that person will save it. What does it profit a person to gain the whole world but lose or forfeit themselves? For whoever is ashamed of me and my words — the Son of Man will be ashamed of that person when he comes in his glory and the glory of the Father and the holy angels.
But I tell you truly — there are some standing here who will not taste death before they see the kingdom of God.”
The Transfiguration · 9:28–36

About eight days after these words, he takes Peter and John and James and goes up the mountain to pray. And while he is praying, the appearance of his face becomes different, and his clothing turns dazzling white. And suddenly two men are talking with him — Moses and Elijah, who appear in glory and speak of his departure, which he is about to accomplish at Jerusalem. Peter and those with him are heavy with sleep. But when they wake fully, they see his glory — and the two men standing with him.

As the men are leaving him, Peter says to Jesus, “Master, it is good for us to be here. Let us make three shelters — one for you and one for Moses and one for Elijah.” He does not know what he is saying. And while he is saying this, a cloud comes and overshadows them. And they are afraid as the men enter the cloud. And a voice comes out of the cloud:
“This is my Son — my Chosen. Listen to him.” When the voice has spoken, Jesus is found alone. And they keep silent and in those days tell no one anything of what they have seen.
The Boy with The Unclean Spirit · 9:37–43

The next day, when they come down from the mountain, a large crowd meets him. And a man from the crowd cries out: “Teacher — I beg you, look at my son. He is my only child. A spirit seizes him, and suddenly he cries out. It convulses him and makes him foam at the mouth, and it hardly ever leaves him — and it is destroying him. I begged your disciples to drive it out, but they couldn’t.”

“O faithless and twisted generation,” Jesus answers, “how long am I to be with you and put up with you? Bring your son here.” Even as the boy is coming, the demon throws him down and convulses him. But Jesus rebukes the unclean spirit, heals the boy, and gives him back to his father. And everyone is astonished at the majesty of God.
The Second Passion Prediction · 9:43–45
And while everyone is marveling at everything he is doing, he says to his disciples:

“Listen carefully — let these words sink into your ears: the Son of Man is going to be delivered into the hands of men.” But they do not understand this saying. It is hidden from them so they cannot grasp it. And they are afraid to ask him about it.
Who is the Greatest · 9:46–48

An argument rises among them — which of them is the greatest. Jesus knows the argument in their hearts. He takes a child and places him by his side and says to them, “Whoever receives this child in my name receives me. And whoever receives me receives the one who sent me. For the one who is least among all of you — that person is great.”
The One Who is Not Against You · 9:49–50
“Master,” John says, “we saw someone driving out demons in your name, and we tried to stop him — because he doesn’t follow with us.”
“Don’t stop him,” Jesus says. “For the one who is not against you is for you.”

And it happens — when the days are being completed for his being taken up — that he sets his face resolutely to go to Jerusalem. And he sends messengers ahead of him. And going on their way, they enter a Samaritan village to make preparations for him. But the people there do not receive him — because his face is set toward Jerusalem. When the disciples James and John see this, they say, “Lord — do you want us to call fire down from heaven to consume them?”
But he turns and rebukes them. And they go on to another village. And as they are going along the road, someone says to him, “I will follow you wherever you go.”
“Foxes have holes,” Jesus says to him, “and the birds of the sky have nests. But the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head.” To another he says, “Follow me.”
“Lord,” the man says, “let me first go and bury my father.”

“Leave the dead to bury their own dead,” Jesus says to him. “But you — go and proclaim the kingdom of God.” Another also says, “I will follow you, Lord. But first let me say goodbye to the people at my house.”
“No one who puts their hand to the plow and looks back,” Jesus says, “is fit for the kingdom of God.”

After this, the Lord appoints seventy-two others and sends them out two by two ahead of him into every town and place he himself is about to go.

“The harvest is plentiful,” he says to them, “but the workers are few. Pray therefore to the Lord of the harvest to send out workers into his harvest. Go. Look — I am sending you out like lambs among wolves. Carry no money bag, no pack, no sandals. And greet no one on the road. Whatever house you enter, first say, ‘Peace to this house.’ And if a son of peace is there, your peace will rest on him. If not, it will return to you.

Stay in that same house — eating and drinking what they give you. For the worker deserves his wages. Don’t move from house to house. And whatever town you enter and they receive you — eat what is set before you, heal the sick in it, and say to them, ‘The kingdom of God has come near to you.’ But whatever town you enter and they don’t receive you — go out into its streets and say, ‘Even the dust of your town that clings to our feet we wipe off against you. But know this: the kingdom of God has come near.’
I tell you — on that day it will be more bearable for Sodom than for that town.

“Woe to you, Chorazin! Woe to you, Bethsaida! For if the miracles done in you had been done in Tyre and Sidon, they would have repented long ago — sitting in sackcloth and ashes. But it will be more bearable for Tyre and Sidon at the judgment than for you. And you, Capernaum — will you be lifted to heaven? You will go down to Hades.
“Whoever listens to you listens to me. Whoever rejects you rejects me. And whoever rejects me rejects the one who sent me.”

The seventy-two return with joy. “Lord,” they say, “even the demons submit to us in your name!”
“I was watching Satan fall like lightning from heaven,” he says to them.

“Look — I have given you authority to tread on snakes and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy. And nothing will harm you. Nevertheless — don’t rejoice that the spirits submit to you. Rejoice that your names are written in heaven.” In that same hour he rejoices in the Holy Spirit and says: “I praise you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and understanding and revealed them to little children. Yes, Father — for this is what was pleasing in your sight.

Everything has been handed over to me by my Father. And no one knows who the Son is except the Father, or who the Father is except the Son — and anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him.” And turning to the disciples privately, he says, “Blessed are the eyes that see what you see. For I tell you — many prophets and kings wanted to see what you see and did not see it, and to hear what you hear and did not hear it.”
The Good Samaritan · 10:25–37
And a lawyer stands up to test him. “Teacher,” he says, “what must I do to inherit eternal life?”
“What is written in the Law?” Jesus asks him. “How do you read it?”
“Love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your strength and with all your mind,” he answers. “And love your neighbor as yourself.”

“You have answered correctly,” Jesus says. “Do this and you will live.” But wanting to justify himself, he says to Jesus, “And who is my neighbor?” Jesus takes up the question: “A man is going down from Jerusalem to Jericho. And he falls among robbers — who strip him, beat him, and go off leaving him half dead. Now by chance a priest is going down that road. When he sees him, he passes by on the other side. And likewise a Levite — when he comes to the place and sees him, he passes by on the other side.

But a Samaritan traveling that way comes to him. And when he sees him, his heart breaks for him. He goes to him and bandages his wounds, pouring on oil and wine. He puts him on his own animal, brings him to an inn, and takes care of him. The next day he takes out two denarii and gives them to the innkeeper. ‘Take care of him,’ he says, ‘and whatever more you spend, I will repay you when I come back.’
“Which of these three do you think proved to be a neighbor to the man who fell among the robbers?”
“The one who showed him mercy,” he says.
“Go,” Jesus tells him, “and do the same.”
Mary and Martha · 10:38–42

As they go on their way, he enters a village. And a woman named Martha welcomes him into her home. She has a sister named Mary, who sits at the Lord’s feet and listens to his teaching. But Martha is pulled in every direction by all the serving. She comes to him and says, “Lord — don’t you care that my sister has left me to serve alone? Tell her to help me.”
“Martha, Martha,” the Lord answers her. “You are anxious and troubled about many things. But one thing is necessary. Mary has chosen the good part — and it will not be taken from her.”
The Lord’s Prayer · 11:1–4
One day he is praying in a certain place. When he finishes, one of his disciples says to him, “Lord — teach us to pray, just as John taught his disciples.”
“When you pray,” he says to them, “say:
Father — may your name be hallowed.
May your kingdom come.
Give us each day our bread for the coming day.
And release us from our sins —
for we ourselves release everyone who is indebted to us.
And do not bring us into testing.”
The Persistent Neighbor · 11:5–13

And he says to them, “Suppose one of you has a friend, and you go to him at midnight and say, ‘Friend — lend me three loaves, because a friend of mine has arrived at my house from a journey and I have nothing to set before him.’ And suppose he answers from inside, ‘Don’t bother me. The door is already locked, and my children are in bed with me. I can’t get up and give you anything.’ I tell you — even if he won’t get up and give him anything because he is his friend, yet because of his shamelessness he will get up and give him whatever he needs.

“And I say to you: ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find; knock, and the door will be opened to you. For everyone who asks receives; and the one who seeks finds; and to the one who knocks, the door will be opened. What father among you — if his son asks for a fish, will give him a snake instead? Or if he asks for an egg, will give him a scorpion? If you then, being evil, know how to give good gifts to your children — how much more will the Father from heaven give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him?”

He is driving out a demon that was mute. When the demon comes out, the mute man speaks. And the crowds are amazed. But some of them say, “By Beelzebul, the ruler of the demons, he drives out demons.” And others, testing him, demand a sign from heaven. But he knows their thoughts and says to them: “Every kingdom divided against itself is laid waste, and a divided household falls. And if Satan is divided against himself — how will his kingdom stand? For you say I drive out demons by Beelzebul.

And if I drive out demons by Beelzebul — by whom do your sons drive them out? They will be your judges. But if I drive out demons by the finger of God — then the kingdom of God has come upon you. When a strong man, fully armed, guards his own house — his possessions are safe. But when someone stronger than him attacks and overpowers him, he strips away the armor the man trusted in and divides the spoils.
“Whoever is not with me is against me. And whoever does not gather with me scatters.

“When an unclean spirit goes out of a person, it passes through waterless places looking for rest. And finding none, it says, ‘I’ll go back to the house I left.’ And when it comes back, it finds the house swept and set in order. Then it goes and brings seven other spirits more evil than itself, and they move in and settle there. And the final state of that person is worse than the first.”
True Blessedness · 11:27–28
While he is saying these things, a woman in the crowd raises her voice and calls out: “Blessed is the womb that carried you and the breasts that nursed you!”
“Blessed rather,” he says, “are those who hear the word of God and keep it.”
The Sign of Jonah · 11:29–32

As the crowds press around him, he begins to say: “This generation is an evil generation. It demands a sign. But no sign will be given to it except the sign of Jonah. For just as Jonah became a sign to the people of Nineveh — so the Son of Man will be to this generation. The queen of the South will rise up at the judgment with the men of this generation and condemn them — because she came from the ends of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon, and look — something greater than Solomon is here.
The men of Nineveh will rise up at the judgment with this generation and condemn it — because they repented at the preaching of Jonah, and look — something greater than Jonah is here.
The Lamp of The Body · 11:33–36

“Nobody lights a lamp and puts it in a cellar or under a basket. They put it on a stand, so that those who come in may see the light. Your eye is the lamp of your body. When your eye is clear, your whole body is full of light. But when it is bad, your body is full of darkness. So watch out — that the light in you is not darkness. If then your whole body is full of light, with no part of it in darkness — it will be completely radiant, as when a lamp illuminates you with its beam.”
