While he is speaking, a Pharisee asks him to eat with him. So he goes in and reclines at the table. The Pharisee is astonished when he sees that Jesus does not first wash before the meal.

“You Pharisees,” the Lord says to him, “clean the outside of the cup and the dish — but inside you are full of greed and wickedness. You fools! Did not the one who made the outside also make the inside? But give what is inside as generosity — and look, everything is clean for you.
“But woe to you Pharisees! You tithe mint and rue and every herb — but you pass over justice and the love of God. These you ought to have done, without neglecting the others.
“Woe to you Pharisees! You love the best seats in the synagogues and greetings in the marketplaces.
“Woe to you! You are like unmarked graves — people walk over them without knowing it.” One of the lawyers answers him: “Teacher — when you say these things, you are insulting us too.”
“Woe to you lawyers as well!” he says. “You load people down with burdens that are hard to carry — and you yourselves won’t touch those burdens with one of your fingers.

“Woe to you! You build the tombs of the prophets — and your ancestors killed them. So you are witnesses and you approve of what your ancestors did: they killed them, and you build their tombs. For this reason the Wisdom of God said, ‘I will send them prophets and apostles — some of whom they will kill and persecute,’ so that the blood of all the prophets — shed from the foundation of the world — may be charged to this generation:
from the blood of Abel to the blood of Zechariah, who was killed between the altar and the sanctuary. Yes, I tell you — it will be charged to this generation.

“Woe to you lawyers! You have taken away the key of knowledge. You didn’t enter yourselves — and you blocked those who were trying to enter.” When he goes out from there, the scribes and Pharisees begin to press him hard and to question him about many things, lying in wait for him — trying to catch something from his own mouth.
Fear God, Not People · 12:1–12

In the meantime, with a crowd of many thousands pressing in so that they are trampling one another, he begins to say to his disciples first: “Guard yourselves from the yeast of the Pharisees — which is hypocrisy. There is nothing covered up that will not be uncovered, nothing hidden that will not be made known. Therefore whatever you have said in the dark will be heard in the light, and what you have whispered in private rooms will be proclaimed from the rooftops.

“I tell you, my friends — don’t be afraid of those who kill the body and after that have nothing more they can do. But I will show you whom to fear: fear the one who, after killing, has authority to throw into Gehenna. Yes — I tell you, fear this one. Aren’t five sparrows sold for two pennies? And not one of them is forgotten before God. Why — even the hairs of your head are all numbered. Don’t be afraid. You are worth more than many sparrows.

“I tell you — everyone who acknowledges me before people, the Son of Man will also acknowledge before the angels of God. But whoever denies me before people will be denied before the angels of God. And everyone who speaks a word against the Son of Man — it will be released for them. But for the one who blasphemes against the Holy Spirit — it will not be released. And when they bring you before synagogues and rulers and authorities, don’t worry about how you will defend yourselves or what you will say.
For the Holy Spirit will teach you in that very hour what you ought to say.”
The Rich Fool · 12:13–21
Someone in the crowd says to him, “Teacher — tell my brother to divide the inheritance with me.”

“Man,” he answers, “who appointed me a judge or arbitrator over you?” And he says to them, “Watch out — be on your guard against every form of greed. Because a person’s life does not consist in the abundance of their possessions.” And he tells them a parable: “A rich man’s land produced abundantly. And he reasoned to himself, ‘What shall I do? I have nowhere to store my crops.’ Then he said, ‘This is what I’ll do: I’ll tear down my barns and build bigger ones, and store all my grain and goods there.
And I’ll say to my soul: Soul — you have plenty of goods laid up for many years. Take your ease. Eat, drink, be merry.’
“But God said to him, ‘Fool — this very night your soul is being demanded of you. And the things you have prepared — whose will they be?’
“So it is with the one who stores up treasure for himself — and is not rich toward God.”
Do Not Be Anxious · 12:22–34

And he says to his disciples: “For this reason I tell you — don’t be anxious about your life, what you will eat, nor about your body, what you will wear. For life is more than food, and the body more than clothing. Consider the ravens: they don’t sow or reap, they have no storehouse or barn, and God feeds them. How much more valuable are you than birds! And which of you by being anxious can add a single hour to their lifespan?

If then you cannot do even the smallest thing, why are you anxious about the rest? Consider the lilies — how they grow. They don’t toil or spin. Yet I tell you — not even Solomon in all his glory was dressed like one of these. But if God clothes the grass in the field this way — grass that is here today and thrown into the oven tomorrow — how much more will he clothe you? You of little faith! And don’t keep seeking what you will eat and what you will drink — and don’t be in suspense.
For the nations of the world chase after all these things. But your Father knows you need them. Instead — seek his kingdom, and these things will be added to you.

“Don’t be afraid, little flock — for your Father has been pleased to give you the kingdom. Sell your possessions and give to the poor. Make yourselves purses that don’t wear out — an inexhaustible treasure in heaven, where no thief comes near and no moth destroys. For where your treasure is — there your heart will be also.”
Watchful Servants · 12:35–48

“Let your loins be girded and your lamps burning. And be like people waiting for their master to come home from a wedding feast — so that when he comes and knocks, they can open the door for him at once. Blessed are those servants whom the master finds awake when he comes. Truly I tell you — he will gird himself and have them recline at table, and he will come and serve them. If he comes in the second watch of the night, or the third — and finds them awake — blessed are those servants.

But know this: if the master of the house had known what hour the thief was coming, he would not have let his house be broken into. You also must be ready — because the Son of Man is coming at an hour you don’t expect.”

“Lord,” Peter says, “are you telling this parable for us — or for everyone?” The Lord says, “Who then is the faithful and wise manager whom the master will set over his household, to give them their portion of food at the right time? Blessed is that servant whom his master finds doing this when he comes. Truly I tell you — he will set him over all his possessions. But if that servant says to himself, ‘My master is taking a long time in coming,’ and begins to beat the menservants and maidservants, and to eat and drink and get drunk —
the master of that servant will come on a day he doesn’t expect, at an hour he doesn’t know, and will cut him to pieces and assign him a place with the unfaithful.

“That servant who knew his master’s will but did not prepare or act according to it will be beaten with many blows. But the one who did not know, and did what deserved a beating, will be beaten with few. From everyone to whom much is given, much will be required. And from the one entrusted with much, even more will be asked.”
Fire and Division · 12:49–53

“I came to cast fire on the earth — and how I wish it were already kindled! I have a baptism to be baptized with — and how I am hemmed in until it is accomplished! Do you think I have come to give peace on earth? No, I tell you — but rather division. From now on, five in one household will be divided — three against two, and two against three. Father against son and son against father, mother against daughter and daughter against mother, mother-in-law against her daughter-in-law and daughter-in-law against mother-in-law.”
Reading the Times · 12:54–59

And he also says to the crowds: “When you see a cloud rising in the west, you say at once, ‘A shower is coming’ — and so it happens. And when the south wind blows, you say, ‘It’s going to be hot’ — and it is. Hypocrites! You know how to read the face of the earth and sky. Why don’t you know how to read this present time?

“And why don’t you judge for yourselves what is right? As you go with your accuser to the magistrate, make an effort to settle with him on the way — so that he doesn’t drag you before the judge, and the judge hand you over to the officer, and the officer throw you into prison. I tell you — you will not get out until you have paid back the very last penny.”
Repent or Perish · 13:1–9
At that very time some people bring him news about the Galileans whose blood Pilate had mixed with their sacrifices.

“Do you think,” he answers, “that these Galileans were worse sinners than all the other Galileans because they suffered this? No, I tell you. But unless you repent — you will all perish in the same way. Or those eighteen who were killed when the tower of Siloam fell on them — do you think they were worse offenders than all the others living in Jerusalem? No, I tell you. But unless you repent — you will all perish in the same way.”

And he tells this parable: “A man had a fig tree planted in his vineyard. He comes looking for fruit on it and finds none. So he says to the vinedresser, ‘Look — for three years now I’ve been coming to look for fruit on this fig tree and I find none. Cut it down. Why should it keep wasting the soil?’ ‘Master,’ he answers, ‘leave it one more year. I’ll dig around it and put on manure. And if it bears fruit next year, good. But if not — then cut it down.’”
The Crippled Woman · 13:10–17

He is teaching in one of the synagogues on the Sabbath. And there is a woman there who has had a spirit of weakness for eighteen years. She is bent over and cannot straighten up at all. When Jesus sees her, he calls her over and says, “Woman — you are released from your weakness.” And he lays his hands on her. And immediately she straightens up and glorifies God. But the ruler of the synagogue — indignant because Jesus had healed on the Sabbath — says to the crowd, “There are six days in which work ought to be done. Come and be healed on those days, not on the Sabbath day.”

“You hypocrites!” the Lord answers him. “Does not each of you on the Sabbath untie his ox or his donkey from the stall and lead it away to water? And this woman — a daughter of Abraham, whom Satan has kept bound for eighteen long years — should she not be released from this bond on the Sabbath day?” As he says this, all his opponents are put to shame. And the entire crowd rejoices at all the glorious things being done by him.
The Mustard Seed and The Leaven · 13:18–21

He says therefore, “What is the kingdom of God like? What shall I compare it to? It is like a mustard seed that a man takes and throws into his garden. And it grows and becomes a tree — and the birds of the sky nest in its branches.” And again he says, “What shall I compare the kingdom of God to? It is like leaven that a woman takes and hides in three measures of flour — until the whole batch is leavened.”
The Narrow Door · 13:22–30
He makes his way through town after town and village after village, teaching and journeying toward Jerusalem.
“Lord,” someone asks him, “are only a few people going to be saved?”

“Strive to enter through the narrow door,” he says to them, “because many, I tell you, will try to enter and will not be able to. Once the master of the house has got up and shut the door, you will stand outside and begin to knock on the door, saying, ‘Lord, open up for us.’ And he will answer you, ‘I don’t know where you are from.’ Then you will start saying, ‘We ate and drank in your presence, and you taught in our streets.’

And he will say, ‘I tell you, I don’t know where you are from. Away from me, all you workers of unrighteousness.’ There will be weeping and grinding of teeth when you see Abraham and Isaac and Jacob and all the prophets in the kingdom of God — and yourselves thrown out. And they will come from east and west, from north and south, and recline at table in the kingdom of God. And look — some who are last will be first, and some who are first will be last.”
Herod the Fox · 13:31–33
At that very hour some Pharisees come to him and say, “Leave and go from here — because Herod wants to kill you.”

“Go and tell that fox,” he says, “I am driving out demons and performing cures today and tomorrow, and on the third day I reach my goal. But I must go on my way today and tomorrow and the day after — because it cannot be that a prophet should perish away from Jerusalem.”
The Lament Over Jerusalem · 13:34–35
“Jerusalem, Jerusalem —
the city that kills the prophets
and stones those sent to her!
How many times I have longed to gather your children together
the way a hen gathers her chicks under her wings —
and you were not willing.
Look — your house is left to you desolate.
And I tell you — you will not see me
until you say:
‘Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord.’”
Healing on the Sabbath · 14:1–6

One Sabbath he goes to eat at the house of a leading Pharisee — and they are watching him carefully. And right there in front of him is a man whose body is swollen with fluid. Jesus speaks to the lawyers and Pharisees: “Is it lawful to heal on the Sabbath — or not?” They stay silent. So he takes hold of the man, heals him, and sends him on his way. And he says to them, “Which of you, if your son or your ox falls into a well on the Sabbath day — will not immediately pull him out?”
And they have no answer to this.
On Choosing Seats · 14:7–11
He notices how the guests are choosing the places of honor. And he tells them a parable:

“When you are invited to a wedding feast, don’t recline in the place of honor — in case someone more distinguished than you has been invited, and the one who invited both of you comes and says to you, ‘Give this person your place.’ And then in shame you would have to take the lowest seat. But when you are invited — go and sit in the lowest place. So that when your host comes, he will say to you, ‘Friend, move up higher.’ Then you will have honor in front of all the others at the table.
For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and everyone who humbles himself will be exalted.”
On Choosing Guests · 14:12–14

And he says to the man who had invited him: “When you give a lunch or a dinner, don’t invite your friends or your brothers or your relatives or your rich neighbors — in case they also invite you back, and it becomes repayment. But when you give a feast — invite the poor, the crippled, the lame, the blind. And you will be blessed, because they cannot repay you. For you will be repaid at the resurrection of the righteous.”
The Parable of The Great Banquet · 14:15–24

When one of those at the table hears this, he says to him, “Blessed is the one who will eat bread in the kingdom of God!” Jesus says to him: “A man gives a great banquet and invites many. At the time of the banquet he sends his servant to say to those who had been invited, ‘Come — everything is ready now.’ But they all begin to make excuses, one after another. The first says to him, ‘I have bought a field and I need to go out and see it. Please consider me excused.’

Another says, ‘I have bought five pairs of oxen and I’m going to examine them. Please consider me excused.’ And another says, ‘I have just got married — and so I can’t come.’ The servant comes back and reports all this to his master. Then the master of the house is angry and says to his servant, ‘Go out quickly into the streets and lanes of the city and bring in the poor and the crippled and the blind and the lame.’ ‘Master,’ the servant says, ‘what you ordered has been done — and there is still room.’
‘Go out to the roads and hedges,’ the master says, ‘and compel them to come in, so that my house may be filled. For I tell you — not one of those who were invited will taste my banquet.’”
The Cost of Discipleship · 14:25–35
Now large crowds are traveling with him. And he turns and says to them:

“If anyone comes to me and does not hate his own father and mother and wife and children and brothers and sisters — yes, and even his own life — he cannot be my disciple. Whoever does not carry their own cross and come after me cannot be my disciple.

“For which of you, wanting to build a tower, doesn’t first sit down and count the cost — to see whether he has enough to complete it? Otherwise, when he has laid the foundation and is not able to finish, everyone who sees it will begin to mock him, saying, ‘This man started to build and wasn’t able to finish.’

“Or what king, going to war against another king, won’t first sit down and consider whether he is able with ten thousand men to meet the one coming against him with twenty thousand? And if not — while the other is still far away, he sends a delegation and asks for terms of peace.
“So then — any one of you who does not give up everything he has cannot be my disciple.

“Salt is good. But if even salt has lost its taste — how will it be made salty again? It is fit neither for the soil nor for the manure pile. People throw it out. Whoever has ears to hear — let them hear.”
The Setting · 15:1–2
Now all the tax collectors and sinners are drawing near to hear him. And the Pharisees and scribes are grumbling: “This man welcomes sinners and eats with them.”
The Lost Sheep · 15:3–7
And he tells them this parable:

“Which man among you who has a hundred sheep and loses one of them — does not leave the ninety-nine in the open country and go after the lost one until he finds it? And when he finds it, he lays it on his shoulders, rejoicing. And coming home, he calls together his friends and neighbors: ‘Rejoice with me — I have found my sheep that was lost!’ I tell you — in the same way there will be more joy in heaven over one sinner who repents than over ninety-nine righteous people who have no need of repentance.”
The Lost Coin · 15:8–10

“Or what woman who has ten silver coins, if she loses one, does not light a lamp and sweep the house and search carefully until she finds it? And when she finds it, she calls together her friends and neighbors: ‘Rejoice with me — I have found the coin I lost!’ In the same way, I tell you — there is joy in the presence of the angels of God over one sinner who repents.”
The Lost Son · 15:11–32

And he says: “A man has two sons. The younger one says to his father, ‘Father — give me my share of the estate.’ So the father divides his property between them. Not many days later, the younger son gathers everything together and sets off for a distant country. There he squanders his wealth in reckless living. When he has spent everything, a severe famine comes over that country — and he begins to be in need. So he goes and hires himself out to one of the citizens of that country, who sends him into his fields to feed pigs.

And he longs to fill his stomach with the pods the pigs are eating — and no one gives him anything. And coming to himself, he says, ‘How many of my father’s hired servants have more than enough bread — and here I am dying of hunger! I will get up and go to my father, and I will say to him: Father — I have sinned against heaven and before you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son. Make me like one of your hired servants.’

And he gets up and comes to his father. But while he is still a long way off, his father sees him — and his heart breaks for him — and he runs and falls on his neck and kisses him again and again. ‘Father,’ the son says, ‘I have sinned against heaven and before you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son.’ But the father says to his servants, ‘Quick — bring out the best robe and put it on him. Put a ring on his hand and sandals on his feet.

And bring the fattened calf — slaughter it, and let’s eat and celebrate. Because this son of mine was dead and has come back to life — he was lost and has been found.’ And they begin to celebrate. Now the older son is in the field. And as he comes and draws near to the house, he hears music and dancing. He calls over one of the servants and asks what is going on. ‘Your brother has come,’ the servant tells him, ‘and your father has slaughtered the fattened calf — because he has him back safe and sound.’

The older son is furious and will not go in. His father comes out and pleads with him. But he answers his father: ‘Look — I have been serving you all these years and I never once disobeyed your orders. And you never gave me even a young goat so I could celebrate with my friends. But when this son of yours comes back — the one who devoured your property with prostitutes — you slaughter the fattened calf for him!’ ‘Son,’ the father says to him, ‘you are always with me — and everything I have is yours.
But we had to celebrate and rejoice — because this brother of yours was dead and has come back to life, he was lost and has been found.’”
The Shrewd Manager · 16:1–13

He also says to the disciples: “A rich man has a manager, and reports come to him that this manager is squandering his possessions. So he calls him in and says, ‘What is this I hear about you? Give an account of your management — you can no longer be manager.’

“What am I going to do?” the manager says to himself. “My master is taking away my position. I’m not strong enough to dig, and I’m ashamed to beg. I know what I’ll do — so that when I’m removed from management, people will welcome me into their homes.’ And calling in each of his master’s debtors one by one, he says to the first, ‘How much do you owe my master?’ ‘A hundred measures of olive oil,’ he says. ‘Take your bill,’ he tells him. ‘Sit down quickly and write fifty.’

Then he says to another, ‘And how much do you owe?’ ‘A hundred measures of wheat,’ he says. ‘Take your bill and write eighty.’ And the master commends the dishonest manager because he acted shrewdly. For the children of this age are shrewder in dealing with their own generation than the children of light.

“And I tell you — make friends for yourselves by means of dishonest wealth, so that when it gives out, they will welcome you into the eternal dwellings. The one who is faithful in a very little is also faithful in much. And the one who is dishonest in a very little is also dishonest in much. If then you have not been faithful with dishonest wealth, who will entrust you with true wealth? And if you have not been faithful with what belongs to another, who will give you what is your own?
No servant can serve two masters. For either he will hate the one and love the other, or he will be devoted to the one and despise the other. You cannot serve God and money.”
The Law, The Kingdom, and Divorce · 16:14–18
The Pharisees — who are lovers of money — hear all this and sneer at him.
“You are the ones who justify yourselves before people,” he says to them, “but God knows your hearts. For what is exalted among people is an abomination before God.

“The Law and the Prophets were until John. Since then the kingdom of God is being proclaimed as good news — and everyone is pressing forcefully into it. But it is easier for heaven and earth to pass away than for one stroke of a letter of the Law to drop out.
“Every man who divorces his wife and marries another commits adultery, and the man who marries a woman divorced from her husband commits adultery.”
The Rich Man and Lazarus · 16:19–31

“There is a rich man who dresses in purple and fine linen and feasts in splendor every day. And at his gate there is laid a poor man named Lazarus, covered with sores, who longs to be fed from what falls from the rich man’s table. Even the dogs come and lick his sores. And it happens that the poor man dies and is carried by the angels to Abraham’s side. The rich man also dies and is buried. And in Hades, being in torment, he lifts up his eyes and sees Abraham far off — and Lazarus at his side.

‘Father Abraham,’ he calls out, ‘have mercy on me and send Lazarus to dip the tip of his finger in water and cool my tongue — because I am in agony in this flame.’ ‘Child,’ Abraham says, ‘remember that in your lifetime you received your good things, and Lazarus likewise received bad things. But now he is comforted here, and you are in agony. And besides all this, between us and you a great chasm has been fixed — so that those who want to pass from here to you cannot, and none may cross from there to us.’

‘Then I beg you, father,’ he says, ‘send him to my father’s house — for I have five brothers — so that he may warn them, lest they also come to this place of torment.’ ‘They have Moses and the Prophets,’ Abraham says. ‘Let them listen to them.’ ‘No, father Abraham,’ he says. ‘But if someone goes to them from the dead, they will repent.’ ‘If they do not listen to Moses and the Prophets,’ he says to him, ‘they will not be persuaded even if someone rises from the dead.’”
On Stumbling Blocks, Forgiveness, and Faith · 17:1–6

He says to his disciples: “Stumbling blocks are bound to come — but woe to the one through whom they come. It would be better for him if a millstone were hung around his neck and he were thrown into the sea, than that he should cause one of these little ones to stumble. Watch yourselves. If your brother sins, rebuke him — and if he repents, forgive him. And if he sins against you seven times in a day and comes back to you seven times saying, ‘I repent’ — you must forgive him.”
The apostles say to the Lord, “Increase our faith!”
“If you had faith like a grain of mustard seed,” the Lord says, “you could say to this mulberry tree, ‘Be uprooted and planted in the sea’ — and it would obey you.”
The Servant’s Duty · 17:7–10

“Which of you who has a servant plowing or tending sheep will say to him when he comes in from the field, ‘Come at once and sit down to eat’? Won’t he instead say, ‘Prepare my supper, get yourself ready, and serve me while I eat and drink — and after that, you can eat and drink’? Does he thank the servant for doing what he was told? I don’t think so. In the same way — when you have done everything you were told to do, say, ‘We are unworthy servants. We have only done what was our duty.’”
The Ten Lepers · 17:11–19

And it happens that as he is going to Jerusalem, he is passing along the border between Samaria and Galilee. And as he enters a village, ten men with leprosy meet him. They are standing at a distance and they lift their voices and call out: “Jesus, Master — have mercy on us!” When he sees them, he says, “Go and show yourselves to the priests.” And as they are going, they are cleansed. But one of them — seeing that he is healed — turns back, glorifying God at the top of his voice.
And he falls on his face at Jesus’ feet, giving him thanks. And he is a Samaritan.
“Were not ten cleansed?” Jesus asks. “Where are the nine? Was no one found to return and give glory to God except this foreigner?” And he says to him, “Get up and go — your faith has saved you.”
The Coming of The Kingdom · 17:20–37

Being asked by the Pharisees when the kingdom of God is coming, he answers them: “The kingdom of God does not come with things to be observed, nor will people say, ‘Look, here it is!’ or ‘There!’ — for look, the kingdom of God is in your midst.” And he says to the disciples, “Days are coming when you will long to see one of the days of the Son of Man, and you will not see it. And they will say to you, ‘Look, there he is!’ or ‘Look, here!’ Don’t go off, don’t follow.
For just as lightning flashes and lights up the sky from one side to the other — so will the Son of Man be in his day. But first he must suffer many things and be rejected by this generation.

“Just as it was in the days of Noah — so it will be in the days of the Son of Man. They were eating and drinking, marrying and being given in marriage, right up to the day Noah entered the ark. Then the flood came and destroyed them all. It was the same in the days of Lot: they were eating and drinking, buying and selling, planting and building. But on the day Lot left Sodom, fire and sulphur rained from heaven and destroyed them all.

It will be like that on the day the Son of Man is revealed. On that day, if someone is on the rooftop and their belongings are in the house — let them not come down to get them. And likewise the person in the field — let them not turn back. Remember Lot’s wife. Whoever tries to preserve their life will lose it, and whoever loses it will keep it. I tell you — on that night there will be two people in one bed: one will be taken and the other left.
Two women will be grinding together: one will be taken and the other left.”
“Where, Lord?” they ask him.
“Where the body is,” he says, “there the vultures will gather.”
The Persistent Widow · 18:1–8
He tells them a parable about the need to pray always and not lose heart.

“In a certain city there is a judge who does not fear God and has no respect for people. And there is a widow in that city who keeps coming to him and saying, ‘Give me justice against my adversary.’ For a time he refuses. But afterward he says to himself, ‘Even though I don’t fear God or care about people — yet because this widow keeps bothering me, I will give her justice. Otherwise she will wear me out by her continual coming.’”
“Listen to what the unjust judge says,” the Lord says.

“And will not God bring about justice for his chosen ones who cry out to him day and night? Will he keep putting them off? I tell you — he will bring about justice for them quickly. Nevertheless — when the Son of Man comes, will he find faith on the earth?”
The Pharisee and The Tax Collector · 18:9–14
He also tells this parable to some who are confident in their own righteousness and look down on everyone else:

“Two men go up to the temple to pray — one a Pharisee and the other a tax collector. The Pharisee stands and prays about himself like this: ‘God, I thank you that I am not like other people — swindlers, unrighteous, adulterers — or even like this tax collector. I fast twice a week. I give tithes of everything I get.’ But the tax collector, standing far off, will not even lift his eyes to heaven. He beats his chest and says, ‘God — have mercy on me, a sinner.’
I tell you — this man goes home justified rather than the other. For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and everyone who humbles himself will be exalted.”
Let the Children Come · 18:15–17

People are bringing even infants to him so that he might touch them. When the disciples see it, they rebuke them. But Jesus calls them to him and says, “Let the children come to me and don’t stop them — for the kingdom of God belongs to such as these. Truly I tell you — whoever does not receive the kingdom of God like a child will never enter it.”
The Rich Ruler · 18:18–30
A certain ruler asks him, “Good Teacher — what must I do to inherit eternal life?”

“Why do you call me good?” Jesus says to him. “No one is good except God alone. You know the commandments: ‘Do not commit adultery. Do not murder. Do not steal. Do not bear false witness. Honor your father and mother.’”

“All these I have kept from my youth,” he says. When Jesus hears this, he says to him, “One thing you still lack. Sell everything you have and distribute it to the poor — and you will have treasure in heaven. Then come and follow me.” But when he hears this, he becomes very sad — for he is extremely rich. Jesus looks at him and says, “How hard it is for those who have wealth to enter the kingdom of God! It is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich person to enter the kingdom of God.”
“Then who can be saved?” those who hear it ask.
“What is impossible with people is possible with God,” he says.
“Look,” Peter says, “we have left everything we had and followed you.”

“Truly I tell you,” he says to them, “there is no one who has left house or wife or brothers or parents or children for the sake of the kingdom of God who will not receive many times more in this age — and in the age to come, eternal life.”
The Third Passion Prediction · 18:31–34

Taking the Twelve aside, he says to them, “Look — we are going up to Jerusalem, and everything that is written about the Son of Man by the prophets will be fulfilled. For he will be handed over to the Gentiles and will be mocked and insulted and spat on. And after flogging him they will kill him. And on the third day he will rise.” But they understand none of this. The meaning is hidden from them — and they do not grasp what is being said.
The Blind Beggar at Jericho · 18:35–43
As he draws near to Jericho, a blind man is sitting by the road begging.
Hearing a crowd going by, he asks what is happening.
“Jesus of Nazareth is passing by,” they tell him.
And he cries out: “Jesus — Son of David — have mercy on me!”
Those going ahead rebuke him and tell him to be quiet. But he cries out all the more: “Son of David — have mercy on me!”
Jesus stops and orders the man to be brought to him. When he comes near, he asks him,
“What do you want me to do for you?”
“Lord — let me see again,” he says.
“Receive your sight,” Jesus says to him. “Your faith has saved you.”
And immediately he receives his sight and follows him, glorifying God. And all the people, when they see it, give praise to God.
Zacchaeus · 19:1–10

He enters Jericho and is passing through. And there is a man named Zacchaeus — he is a chief tax collector and he is rich. And he is trying to see who Jesus is — but he cannot, because of the crowd, since he is small in stature. So he runs ahead and climbs up into a sycamore tree to see him — because he is about to pass that way. And when Jesus comes to the place, he looks up and says to him, “Zacchaeus — come down quickly. I must stay at your house today.”

And he comes down quickly and welcomes him with joy. And when they see it, everyone grumbles: “He has gone in to be the guest of a man who is a sinner.” But Zacchaeus stands there and says to the Lord: “Look, Lord — half of my possessions I give to the poor. And if I have extorted anything from anyone, I pay it back fourfold.”
“Today salvation has come to this house,” Jesus says to him, “because he too is a son of Abraham. For the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost.”
The Parable of The Ten Minas · 19:11–27
As they are listening to this, he goes on to tell a parable — because he is near Jerusalem and they suppose that the kingdom of God is about to appear at once.

“A nobleman goes to a distant country to receive a kingdom for himself and then return. Calling ten of his servants, he gives them ten minas and says, ‘Do business with these until I come back.’ But his citizens hate him and send a delegation after him, saying, ‘We don’t want this man to reign over us.’ When he returns, having received the kingdom, he orders the servants to whom he had given the money to be called in — so he could find out what they had gained by trading.

The first comes and says, ‘Master — your mina has made ten more minas.’ ‘Well done, good servant!’ he says. ‘Because you have been faithful in a very little, you shall have authority over ten cities.’ The second comes and says, ‘Master — your mina has made five minas.’ And he says to this one too, ‘You shall be over five cities.’ Then another comes and says, ‘Master — here is your mina. I kept it laid away in a cloth,

because I was afraid of you. You are a severe man — you collect what you didn’t deposit, and reap what you didn’t sow.’ ‘I will judge you by your own words, you wicked servant!’ he says. ‘You knew I was a severe man, collecting what I didn’t deposit and reaping what I didn’t sow? Why then didn’t you put my money in the bank — so that when I came back I could have collected it with interest?’ And he says to those standing there, ‘Take the mina from him and give it to the one who has ten.’

‘But Master — he already has ten minas!’ they say. ‘I tell you — to everyone who has, more will be given. But from the one who has nothing, even what he has will be taken away. As for those enemies of mine who did not want me to reign over them — bring them here and slaughter them in front of me.’”
The Triumphal Entry · 19:28–40
Having said this, he goes on ahead, going up to Jerusalem.
And when he draws near to Bethphage and Bethany, at the mount called Olivet, he sends two of the disciples,
saying, “Go into the village ahead. As you enter it you will find a colt tied, on which no one has ever sat. Untie it and bring it here.
And if anyone asks, ‘Why are you untying it?’ say this: ‘The Lord has need of it.’”
Those who are sent go and find it just as he told them.
And as they are untying the colt, its owners say to them, “Why are you untying the colt?”
“The Lord has need of it,” they say.
And they bring it to Jesus. And throwing their cloaks on the colt, they set Jesus on it.
And as he is riding along, people spread their cloaks on the road.
As he draws near — already at the descent of the Mount of Olives — the whole crowd of disciples begins to rejoice and praise God with a loud voice for all the mighty works they have seen,
saying:
“Blessed is the King who comes in the name of the Lord!
Peace in heaven and glory in the highest!”
And some of the Pharisees in the crowd say to him, “Teacher — rebuke your disciples.”
“I tell you,” he answers, “if these are silent, the stones will cry out.”
The Weeping Over Jerusalem · 19:41–44
And as he draws near and sees the city, he weeps over it,
saying:
“If you — even you — had known on this day
the things that make for peace.
But now they are hidden from your eyes.
For days are coming upon you
when your enemies will throw up a barricade against you
and surround you and hem you in on every side.
And they will tear you down to the ground,
you and your children within you.
And they will not leave one stone upon another in you —
because you did not know the time of your visitation.”
The Cleansing of The Temple · 19:45–48

And he enters the temple and begins to drive out those who are selling, saying to them, “It is written: ‘My house shall be a house of prayer.’ But you have made it a den of robbers.” And he is teaching every day in the temple. The chief priests and the scribes and the leading men of the people are seeking to destroy him, but they cannot find anything they can do — for all the people are hanging on his words.
The Question of Authority · 20:1–8

One day, as he is teaching the people in the temple and proclaiming the good news, the chief priests and the scribes come up, together with the elders, and say to him, “Tell us — by what authority are you doing these things? Or who is it that gave you this authority?”

“I will also ask you a question,” he answers them. “Tell me: the baptism of John — was it from heaven or from human beings?” And they discuss it among themselves: “If we say ‘from heaven,’ he will say, ‘Why didn’t you believe him?’ And if we say ‘from human beings,’ all the people will stone us — for they are convinced that John was a prophet.” So they answer that they don’t know where it was from.
“Neither will I tell you by what authority I do these things,” Jesus says to them.
The Parable of The Wicked Tenants · 20:9–19

And he goes on to tell the people this parable: “A man plants a vineyard and lets it out to tenants and goes abroad for a long time. When the time comes, he sends a servant to the tenants to get his share of the fruit from the vineyard. But the tenants beat him and send him away empty-handed. And he sends another servant. But they beat him too and treat him shamefully and send him away empty-handed. And he sends a third. This one they wound and throw out.

Then the owner of the vineyard says, ‘What shall I do? I will send my beloved son. Perhaps they will respect him.’ But when the tenants see him, they discuss it among themselves and say, ‘This is the heir. Let’s kill him, so that the inheritance may be ours.’ And they throw him out of the vineyard and kill him. What then will the owner of the vineyard do to them? He will come and destroy those tenants and give the vineyard to others.”

When they hear this, they say, “May it never be!” But he looks directly at them and says, “What then is this that is written: ‘The stone the builders rejected — this has become the cornerstone’? Everyone who falls on that stone will be broken to pieces. And when it falls on anyone, it will crush them.” The scribes and chief priests want to lay hands on him at that very hour — but they are afraid of the people. For they understand that he has told this parable against them.
The Question About Taxes · 20:20–26

Watching him carefully, they send spies who pretend to be sincere — to catch him in his words, so as to hand him over to the authority and jurisdiction of the governor. And they ask him, “Teacher, we know that you speak and teach rightly, and show no partiality, but truly teach the way of God. Is it lawful for us to pay taxes to Caesar — or not?” But he sees through their cunning and says to them,
“Show me a denarius. Whose image and inscription does it have?”
“Caesar’s,” they say.

“Then give back to Caesar what belongs to Caesar,” he says to them, “and to God what belongs to God.” And they are unable to catch him in his words in front of the people. They are astonished at his answer and fall silent.
The Question About The Resurrection · 20:27–40

Some Sadducees — those who say there is no resurrection — come to him and ask him a question, saying, “Teacher, Moses wrote for us that if a man’s brother dies, having a wife but no children, the man must take the wife and raise up offspring for his brother. Now there were seven brothers. The first took a wife and died without children. And the second and the third took her, and likewise all seven left no children and died.
Afterward the woman also died. In the resurrection, therefore, whose wife will the woman be? For all seven had her as wife.”

“The children of this age marry and are given in marriage,” Jesus says to them. But those who are considered worthy to attain to that age and to the resurrection from the dead neither marry nor are given in marriage. For they cannot die any more — because they are equal to angels and are sons of God, being sons of the resurrection. But that the dead are raised — even Moses showed, in the passage about the burning bush, when he calls the Lord the God of Abraham and the God of Isaac and the God of Jacob.
Now he is not the God of the dead but of the living — for all are alive to him.” And some of the scribes answer, “Teacher, you have spoken well.” For they no longer dare to ask him anything.
Whose Son is the Messiah · 20:41–44
And he says to them, “How can they say that the Messiah is David’s son?
For David himself says in the book of Psalms:
‘The Lord said to my Lord:
“Sit at my right hand,
until I make your enemies your footstool.”’
David therefore calls him ‘Lord’ — so how is he his son?”
Warning About the Scribes · 20:45–47
And while all the people are listening, he says to his disciples:

“Beware of the scribes, who like to walk around in long robes and love greetings in the marketplaces and the best seats in the synagogues and the places of honor at feasts — who devour widows’ houses and for a show make lengthy prayers. These will receive a heavier judgment.”
The Widow’s Offering · 21:1–4
He looks up and sees the rich putting their gifts into the offering box. And he sees a poor widow putting in two small copper coins.
“Truly I tell you,” he says, “this poor widow has put in more than all of them. For all of these gave out of their abundance. But she — out of her poverty — has put in everything she had to live on.”
The Temple Will Be Destroyed · 21:5–6
And while some are speaking about the temple — how it is adorned with beautiful stones and offerings — he says,
“As for these things you are looking at — days are coming when not one stone will be left on another that will not be thrown down.”
Signs of the End · 21:7–19
“Teacher,” they ask him, “when will these things be? And what will be the sign when these things are about to take place?”

“Watch out that you are not led astray,” he says. “For many will come in my name, saying, ‘I am he’ and ‘The time is at hand.’ Don’t follow them. And when you hear of wars and uprisings, don’t be terrified. These things must happen first — but the end will not come right away.” Then he says to them: “Nation will rise against nation, and kingdom against kingdom. There will be great earthquakes and in various places famines and plagues. And there will be terrifying things and great signs from heaven.

“But before all this — they will lay hands on you and persecute you, handing you over to synagogues and prisons, and bringing you before kings and governors, for my name’s sake. This will be your opportunity to bear witness. Settle it in your hearts, then, not to prepare your defense beforehand. For I will give you words and wisdom that none of your adversaries will be able to withstand or contradict. You will be delivered up even by parents and brothers and relatives and friends, and some of you will be put to death.
And you will be hated by all because of my name. But not a hair of your head will perish. By your endurance you will gain your lives.”
The Destruction of Jerusalem · 21:20–24

“When you see Jerusalem surrounded by armies — then know that its desolation has come near. Then let those who are in Judea flee to the mountains, and let those who are inside the city get out, and let those who are in the country not enter it. For these are days of vengeance — a fulfillment of everything that is written. How terrible it will be in those days for women who are pregnant and for those who are nursing infants! For there will be great distress across the land and wrath against this people.
They will fall by the edge of the sword and be taken captive among all nations. And Jerusalem will be trampled down by the Gentiles, until the times of the Gentiles are fulfilled.”
The Coming of The Son of Man · 21:25–28

“And there will be signs in sun and moon and stars. And on the earth distress of nations in perplexity at the roaring of the sea and the waves, people fainting from fear and foreboding of what is coming on the world. For the powers of the heavens will be shaken. And then they will see the Son of Man coming in a cloud with power and great glory. Now when these things begin to take place — stand up and lift your heads, because your redemption is drawing near.”
The Parable of The Fig Tree · 21:29–33

And he tells them a parable: “Look at the fig tree and all the trees. When they sprout leaves, you see for yourselves and know that summer is already near. So also, when you see these things taking place, know that the kingdom of God is near. Truly I tell you — this generation will not pass away until all these things have taken place. Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will never pass away.”
The Call to Watchfulness · 21:34–38

“But watch yourselves — that your hearts are not weighed down with dissipation and drunkenness and the anxieties of life, and that day catch you off guard like a trap. For it will come upon all who dwell on the face of the whole earth. But stay awake at all times, praying that you may have strength to escape all these things that are going to take place, and to stand before the Son of Man.” Every day he is teaching in the temple. And every night he goes out and lodges on the mount called Olivet.
And all the people come to him early in the morning in the temple to hear him.
The Plot and Judas · 22:1–6

Now the Feast of Unleavened Bread was drawing near — the feast called Passover. And the chief priests and the scribes are looking for a way to put him to death — for they are afraid of the people. Then Satan enters into Judas, the one called Iscariot, who is numbered among the Twelve. And he goes off and discusses with the chief priests and the temple officers how he might hand him over to them. They are delighted and agree to give him money.
And he consents and begins looking for a good opportunity to hand him over to them without a crowd being present.
Preparation for the Passover · 22:7–13
Then the Day of Unleavened Bread comes — the day when the Passover lamb must be sacrificed. And he sends Peter and John, saying, “Go and prepare the Passover for us, so that we may eat it.”
“Where do you want us to prepare it?” they ask him.

“Listen,” he says to them. “When you enter the city, a man carrying a jar of water will meet you. Follow him into the house he enters and say to the owner of the house, ‘The Teacher says to you: Where is the guest room, where I may eat the Passover with my disciples?’ And he will show you a large upper room, furnished. Prepare it there.” And they go and find it just as he told them. And they prepare the Passover.
The Last Supper · 22:14–23
And when the hour comes, he reclines at table, and the apostles with him.
“I have longed and longed to eat this Passover with you before I suffer,” he says to them.

“For I tell you — I will not eat it again until it is fulfilled in the kingdom of God.” And taking a cup, he gives thanks and says, “Take this and divide it among yourselves. For I tell you — from now on I will not drink of the fruit of the vine until the kingdom of God comes.” And taking bread, he gives thanks and breaks it and gives it to them, saying, “This is my body, which is given for you. Do this in remembrance of me.”
And likewise the cup after supper, saying, “This cup is the new covenant in my blood, which is poured out for you.

“But look — the hand of the one who betrays me is with mine on the table. For the Son of Man goes as it has been determined — but woe to that man by whom he is betrayed!” And they begin to question one another which of them it could be who was going to do this.
Dispute About Greatness · 22:24–30
A dispute also arises among them — which of them is to be regarded as the greatest.

“The kings of the Gentiles lord it over them,” he says to them, “and those in authority over them are called Benefactors. But it must not be so with you. Rather, let the greatest among you become like the youngest, and the leader like the one who serves. For who is the greater — the one who reclines at table or the one who serves? Isn’t it the one who reclines? But I am among you as the one who serves.

“You are the ones who have stood by me in my trials. And I assign to you — just as my Father assigned to me — a kingdom, so that you may eat and drink at my table in my kingdom and sit on thrones judging the twelve tribes of Israel.”
Peter’s Denial Foretold · 22:31–34

“Simon, Simon — listen. Satan has demanded to have you all, to sift you like wheat. But I have prayed for you — for you specifically — that your faith may not fail. And when you have turned back, strengthen your brothers.”
“Lord,” he says to him, “I am ready to go with you both to prison and to death.”
“I tell you, Peter,” he says, “the rooster will not crow today until you have denied three times that you know me.”
Purse and Sword · 22:35–38
And he says to them, “When I sent you out without purse or bag or sandals, did you lack anything?”
“Nothing,” they say.

“But now,” he says, “let the one who has a purse take it, and likewise a bag. And let the one who has no sword sell his cloak and buy one. For I tell you — this scripture must be fulfilled in me: ‘And he was counted among the lawless.’ For what is written about me is reaching its end.”
“Lord — look, here are two swords,” they say.
“Enough of that,” he says.
Gethsemane · 22:39–46

And going out, he makes his way, as was his custom, to the Mount of Olives. And the disciples follow him. When he arrives at the place, he says to them, “Pray that you may not enter into testing.” And he withdraws from them about a stone’s throw, and kneeling down, he prays,

“Father — if you are willing, remove this cup from me. Nevertheless — not my will but yours be done.” And an angel from heaven appears to him, strengthening him. And being in agony he prays more earnestly. And his sweat becomes like drops of blood falling to the ground. And rising from prayer, he comes to the disciples and finds them sleeping from grief.
“Why are you sleeping?” he says to them. “Get up and pray that you may not enter into testing.”
The Arrest · 22:47–53
While he is still speaking, a crowd arrives. And the one called Judas, one of the Twelve, is leading them. He draws near to Jesus to kiss him.

“Judas — are you betraying the Son of Man with a kiss?” Jesus says to him. When those around him see what is about to happen, they say, “Lord — shall we strike with the sword?” And one of them strikes the high priest’s servant and cuts off his right ear.

“No more of this!” Jesus says. And he touches his ear and heals him. Then Jesus says to the chief priests and temple officers and elders who have come for him, “Have you come out with swords and clubs as if against a robber? When I was with you every day in the temple you did not lay hands on me. But this is your hour — and the power of darkness.”
Peter’s Denial · 22:54–62
Then they seize him and lead him away, bringing him into the high priest’s house. Peter is following at a distance.
And when they kindle a fire in the middle of the courtyard and sit down together, Peter sits down among them.
A servant girl sees him sitting in the firelight. She stares at him and says, “This man was with him too.”
But he denies it. “Woman, I don’t know him,” he says.
A little later someone else sees him and says, “You’re one of them too.”
“Man, I am not,” Peter says.
And about an hour later, another man insists: “This man was certainly with him — he’s a Galilean.”
“Man, I don’t know what you’re talking about!” Peter says.
And immediately, while he is still speaking, the rooster crows.
And the Lord turns and looks at Peter. And Peter remembers the word of the Lord — how he said to him, “Before the rooster crows today, you will deny me three times.”
And he goes outside and weeps bitterly.
Mocking and the Trial Before the Council · 22:63–71
The men who are holding Jesus mock him and beat him.
They blindfold him and demand: “Prophesy! Who is it that struck you?”
And they say many other things against him, blaspheming.
When day comes, the council of elders of the people gathers — both chief priests and scribes. And they lead him into their council chamber.
“If you are the Messiah,” they say, “tell us.”
“If I tell you, you will not believe,” he says to them.
“And if I ask you, you will not answer.
But from now on the Son of Man will be seated at the right hand of the power of God.”
“So you are the Son of God?” they all say.
“You say that I am,” he says to them.
“What further testimony do we need?” they say. “We have heard it ourselves from his own mouth.”
Before Pilate · 23:1–7

The whole assembly rises and brings him before Pilate. And they begin to accuse him: “We found this man misleading our nation, forbidding us to pay taxes to Caesar, and saying that he himself is Christ, a king.”
“Are you the King of the Jews?” Pilate asks him.
“You say so,” he answers.

“I find no guilt in this man,” Pilate says to the chief priests and the crowds. But they insist: “He is stirring up the people, teaching throughout all Judea — from Galilee all the way here.” When Pilate hears this, he asks whether the man is a Galilean. And learning that he belongs to Herod’s jurisdiction, he sends him to Herod, who is himself in Jerusalem at that time.
Before Herod · 23:8–12

When Herod sees Jesus, he is very glad — for he has been wanting to see him for a long time, because he has heard about him and is hoping to see some sign performed by him. So he questions him at length — but he gives him no answer. The chief priests and the scribes stand there and accuse him vehemently. And Herod, with his soldiers, treats him with contempt and mocks him. Dressing him in splendid clothing, he sends him back to Pilate.
And Herod and Pilate become friends with each other that very day — for before this they had been enemies.
The Verdict · 23:13–25

Pilate calls together the chief priests and the rulers and the people and says to them, “You brought me this man as one who was misleading the people. And look — having examined him before you, I found no guilt in this man in regard to your charges against him. Neither did Herod — for he sent him back to us. Look — nothing deserving death has been done by him. I will therefore have him flogged and release him.” But they all cry out together: “Away with this man! Release Barabbas for us!”

(He was a man who had been thrown into prison for an insurrection that had taken place in the city, and for murder.) Pilate addresses them again, wanting to release Jesus. But they keep shouting: “Crucify him! Crucify him!” A third time he says to them, “What evil has this man done? I have found no grounds for the death sentence in him. I will have him flogged and release him.” But they press on with loud voices, demanding that he be crucified. And their voices prevail.

And Pilate decides that their demand should be granted. He releases the man who had been thrown into prison for insurrection and murder — the one they are asking for — and he hands Jesus over to their will.
The Way to The Cross · 23:26–32

And as they lead him away, they seize a man named Simon of Cyrene, coming in from the country, and they lay the cross on him to carry it behind Jesus. A large crowd of people follows him, including women who are mourning and lamenting for him. But turning to them, Jesus says, “Daughters of Jerusalem — don’t weep for me. Weep for yourselves and for your children. For look — days are coming when they will say, ‘Blessed are the barren, the wombs that never bore and the breasts that never nursed.’

Then they will begin to say to the mountains, ‘Fall on us,’ and to the hills, ‘Cover us.’ For if they do these things when the wood is green — what will happen when it is dry?” Two others — criminals — are also led away with him to be executed.
The Crucifixion · 23:33–43
And when they come to the place called The Skull, they crucify him there — along with the criminals, one on his right and one on his left.

“Father — forgive them, for they don’t know what they are doing.” And they cast lots to divide his clothing. The people stand watching. The rulers sneer at him: “He saved others — let him save himself, if he is the Messiah of God, the Chosen One!” The soldiers also mock him, coming up and offering him sour wine and saying, “If you are the King of the Jews — save yourself!” And there is an inscription over him: THIS IS THE KING OF THE JEWS.

One of the criminals hanging there hurls insults at him: “Aren’t you the Messiah? Save yourself — and us!” But the other rebukes him: “Don’t you fear God? You are under the same sentence. And we justly — for we are receiving what our deeds deserve. But this man has done nothing wrong.” And he says, “Jesus — remember me when you come into your kingdom.”
“Truly I tell you,” he says to him, “today you will be with me in paradise.”
The Death of Jesus · 23:44–49

It is now about the sixth hour. And darkness comes over the whole land until the ninth hour, the sun failing. And the curtain of the temple is torn in two. And crying out with a loud voice, Jesus says, “Father — into your hands I commit my spirit.” And having said this, he breathes his last. When the centurion sees what has happened, he glorifies God and says, “Certainly this man was righteous.” And all the crowds who have gathered for this spectacle — when they see what has happened — return home beating their chests.
And all his acquaintances are standing at a distance, including the women who had followed him from Galilee, watching these things.
The Burial · 23:50–56

And there is a man named Joseph, a member of the council, a good and righteous man who had not agreed with their decision and action. He is from Arimathea, a town in Judea, and he is waiting for the kingdom of God. He goes to Pilate and asks for the body of Jesus. And taking it down, he wraps it in a linen cloth and lays it in a tomb cut from rock, where no one had yet been laid. It is the day of Preparation, and the Sabbath is beginning to dawn.

The women who had come with him from Galilee follow and see the tomb and how his body is laid. Then they return and prepare spices and ointments. And on the Sabbath they rest according to the commandment.
The Empty Tomb · 24:1–12

But on the first day of the week, at early dawn, they come to the tomb, bringing the spices they have prepared. And they find the stone rolled away from the tomb. And going in, they do not find the body of the Lord Jesus. And while they are perplexed about this, two men in dazzling clothes suddenly stand beside them. And as the women are terrified and bow their faces to the ground, the men say to them:

“Why are you looking for the living among the dead? He is not here — he has risen. Remember how he told you, while he was still in Galilee, that the Son of Man must be delivered into the hands of sinful men and be crucified and on the third day rise.” And they remember his words. And returning from the tomb, they report all these things to the Eleven and to all the rest. It is Mary Magdalene and Joanna and Mary the mother of James, and the other women with them — they tell these things to the apostles.

But these words seem to them like nonsense, and they do not believe them. But Peter gets up and runs to the tomb. Bending down, he looks in and sees only the linen cloths lying there. And he goes home marveling at what has happened.
The Road to Emmaus · 24:13–35

And look — that very day, two of them are traveling to a village called Emmaus, about seven miles from Jerusalem. And they are talking with each other about all these things that have happened. And while they are talking and discussing, Jesus himself draws near and goes along with them. But their eyes are kept from recognizing him.

“What is this conversation you are holding with each other as you walk?” he asks them. And they stop, their faces downcast. Then one of them, named Cleopas, answers him: “Are you the only visitor to Jerusalem who doesn’t know the things that have happened there in these days?”
“What things?” he asks them.

“The things about Jesus of Nazareth,” they say, “a man who was a prophet, powerful in deed and word before God and all the people. And how our chief priests and rulers handed him over to be condemned to death, and crucified him. But we were hoping that he was the one who was going to redeem Israel. And on top of all this, it is now the third day since these things happened. And some women from our group astonished us — they were at the tomb early this morning

and didn’t find his body. They came back saying they had even seen a vision of angels, who said he was alive. And some of those who were with us went to the tomb and found it just as the women had said. But him they did not see.”

“Oh, how foolish you are,” he says to them, “and how slow of heart to believe all that the prophets have spoken! Was it not necessary for the Messiah to suffer these things and enter into his glory?” And beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, he interprets to them in all the scriptures the things concerning himself. As they draw near to the village they are heading to, he acts as though he is going on further. But they urge him strongly: “Stay with us — for it is toward evening and the day is now far spent.”

So he goes in to stay with them. And when he is at table with them, he takes the bread and blesses and breaks it and gives it to them. And their eyes are opened — and they recognize him. And he vanishes from their sight.

“Weren’t our hearts burning within us,” they say to each other, “while he talked to us on the road, while he opened the scriptures to us?” And they get up that very hour and return to Jerusalem. And they find the Eleven gathered together, with those who are with them, saying, “The Lord has risen indeed — and has appeared to Simon!” And they tell what happened on the road, and how he is made known to them in the breaking of the bread.
Jesus Appears to the Disciples · 24:36–49
And as they are saying these things, he himself stands among them and says to them, “Peace to you.” But they are startled and terrified and think they are seeing a ghost.

“Why are you troubled,” he says to them, “and why do doubts rise in your hearts? See my hands and my feet — it is I myself. Touch me and see. For a ghost does not have flesh and bones as you see that I have.” And having said this, he shows them his hands and his feet. And while they still cannot believe for joy — and are marveling — he says to them, “Do you have anything here to eat?” They give him a piece of broiled fish,

and he takes it and eats it before them. And he says to them, “These are my words that I spoke to you while I was still with you — that everything written about me in the Law of Moses and the Prophets and the Psalms must be fulfilled.” Then he opens their minds to understand the scriptures, and says to them, “This is what is written: the Messiah is to suffer and to rise from the dead on the third day, and repentance for the release of sins is to be proclaimed in his name to all nations — beginning from Jerusalem.
You are witnesses of these things. And look — I am sending the promise of my Father upon you. But stay in the city until you are clothed with power from on high.”
