And he leads them out as far as Bethany. And lifting up his hands, he blesses them. And while he is blessing them, he parts from them and is carried up into heaven. And they worship him and return to Jerusalem with great joy. And they are continually in the temple, blessing God.
The Prologue · 1:1–18
In the beginning, the Word already was.
The Word was face to face with God,
and the Word was God.
From the very start he was there, with God.
Everything came to be through him;
not one thing that exists came to be apart from him.
Life was in him,
and his life was light for every human being.
And the light keeps on shining in the dark,
and the dark has never put it out,
never even understood it.

A man comes along, sent from God. His name is John. He comes as a witness, to testify about the light, so that through him everyone might come to trust. John himself isn’t the light. He comes to point people to the light.
The true light,
the one that shines on every person,
is on its way into the world.
He is in the world,
and the world came to be through him,
and still the world doesn’t know who he is.
He comes home to what is his,
and his own people won’t take him in.
But to all who do take him in,
all who trust in his name,
he gives the right to become God’s own children:
born not from bloodlines,
not from the body’s wanting or a man’s choosing,
but born from God himself.
The Word becomes flesh
and pitches his tent among us,
and we gaze on his glory,
glory like that of a one-of-a-kind Son from his Father,
brimming with grace and truth.
John testifies about him. He cries out, “This is the one I was talking about when I said, ‘The one who comes after me ranks ahead of me, because he was before me.’”
From the overflow of all he is,
every one of us has received grace upon grace.
The law came to us through Moses,
but grace and truth arrive in Jesus the Messiah.
Nobody has ever laid eyes on God.
But the one-of-a-kind, who is God himself,
who lies close against the Father’s heart,
he is the one who has told us the Father’s story.
The Testimony of John · 1:19–28

This is what John says when the Judean leaders send priests and Levites down from Jerusalem to ask him, “Who are you?” He doesn’t dodge the question. He states it plainly: “I’m not the Messiah.” “Then what? Are you Elijah?” they ask. “I am not,” he says. “Are you the Prophet?” “No.” So they press him. “Then who are you? Give us an answer to take back to the ones who sent us. What do you say about yourself?” He says, “I am the voice of someone shouting in the wilderness, ‘Make the Lord’s road straight,’ just as the prophet Isaiah said.”

Now these messengers have been sent by the Pharisees, and they ask him, “Then why are you baptizing, if you aren’t the Messiah, or Elijah, or the Prophet?” John answers them, “I baptize in water. But someone is standing right here among you, someone you don’t know. He is the one coming after me, and I’m not worthy to untie the strap of his sandal.” All this happens at Bethany, on the far side of the Jordan, where John is baptizing.
The Lamb of God · 1:29–34

The next day John sees Jesus walking toward him, and he says, “Look! There is God’s Lamb, the one who carries away the sin of the world! He’s the one I meant when I said, ‘A man is coming after me who ranks ahead of me, because he was before me.’ I didn’t know him myself. But this is the reason I came baptizing in water: so that he would be shown to Israel.”

Then John gives his testimony: “I watched the Spirit coming down out of heaven like a dove, and it stayed on him. I didn’t know him. But the one who sent me to baptize in water told me, ‘The man you see the Spirit come down on and stay on, he’s the one who baptizes in the Holy Spirit.’ And I have seen it. I give my testimony: this is the Son of God.”
The First Disciples · 1:35–51

The next day John is standing there again with two of his disciples. He watches Jesus walk past and says, “Look! God’s Lamb!” The two disciples hear him say it, and they go after Jesus. Jesus turns around and sees them following. “What are you looking for?” he asks. They say, “Rabbi” (that means Teacher), “where are you staying?” “Come and see,” he tells them. So they come, and they see where he is staying, and they stay with him the rest of that day. It is about four in the afternoon.

One of the two who heard John and followed Jesus is Andrew, Simon Peter’s brother. The first thing Andrew does is find his own brother Simon. “We’ve found the Messiah!” he tells him. (Messiah is the Hebrew word for the Anointed One, the Christ.) He brings Simon to Jesus. Jesus looks hard at him and says, “You are Simon, son of John. You will be called Cephas” (that means Rock, Peter in Greek).

The next day Jesus makes up his mind to head out for Galilee. He finds Philip and says to him, “Follow me.” Philip comes from Bethsaida, the hometown of Andrew and Peter. Philip goes and finds Nathanael. “We’ve found him!” he says. “The one Moses wrote about in the law, the one the prophets wrote about: Jesus of Nazareth, Joseph’s son.” “Nazareth?” says Nathanael. “Has anything good ever come out of Nazareth?” Philip says, “Come and see.”

Jesus sees Nathanael coming toward him and says of him, “Look, here’s a true Israelite, with not a crooked bone in him!” “How do you know me?” Nathanael asks. Jesus answers, “Before Philip ever called you, while you were sitting under the fig tree, I saw you.” Nathanael says, “Rabbi, you’re the Son of God! You’re Israel’s King!” Jesus answers him, “You believe because I told you I saw you under the fig tree? You’ll see far greater things than that.” Then he says, “Truly, truly, I tell you all: you will see heaven standing open, and the angels of God going up and coming down on the Son of Man.”
The Wedding at Cana · 2:1–12

On the third day there is a wedding at Cana in Galilee, and the mother of Jesus is there. Jesus and his disciples have been invited to the wedding too. Then the wine runs out. Jesus’ mother says to him, “They’re out of wine.” Jesus says to her, “Woman, what does that have to do with you and me? My hour hasn’t come yet.” His mother turns to the servants. “Whatever he tells you,” she says, “do it.”

Six stone water jars are standing there, the kind the Jews use for washing and purifying. Each one holds twenty or thirty gallons. Jesus tells the servants, “Fill the jars with water.” And they fill them right up to the brim. Then he tells them, “Now dip some out and take it to the master of the feast.” So they do. The master of the feast tastes the water, which has now become wine. He has no idea where it came from, though the servants who drew the water know. He calls the bridegroom over and says, “Everybody brings out the good wine first, and the cheaper stuff after the guests have had plenty. But you have saved the good wine until now!” This is the first of the signs Jesus does, there at Cana in Galilee. It lets his glory shine out, and his disciples put their trust in him.
After this he goes down to Capernaum with his mother, his brothers, and his disciples, and they stay there a few days.
The Cleansing of the Temple · 2:13–25

The Jewish Passover is near, so Jesus goes up to Jerusalem. In the temple courts he finds people selling cattle and sheep and doves, and money changers sitting at their tables. He braids a whip out of cords and drives them all out of the temple, sheep and cattle alike. He dumps out the money changers’ coins and flips their tables over. To the dove sellers he says, “Take all this out of here! My Father’s house is no marketplace!” And his disciples remember that it is written, “Zeal for your house will eat me up.”

So the Judean leaders challenge him. “What sign can you show us,” they say, “to prove you have the right to do this?” Jesus answers them, “Tear this temple down, and in three days I’ll raise it up again.” “Forty-six years it has taken to build this temple,” they say, “and you’re going to raise it up in three days?” But the temple he means is his own body. Later, after he is raised from the dead, his disciples remember that he said this, and they trust both the Scripture and what Jesus said.

While he is in Jerusalem for the Passover festival, many people see the signs he is doing and put their trust in his name. But Jesus does not put his trust in them, because he knows them all. He doesn’t need anyone to tell him about people, because he knows what is inside a person.
Nicodemus · 3:1–21

Now there is a man among the Pharisees named Nicodemus, one of the leaders of the Jewish people. He comes to Jesus at night and says to him, “Rabbi, we know you’re a teacher who has come from God. Nobody could do the signs you’re doing unless God were with him.” Jesus answers him, “Truly, truly, I tell you, unless someone is born anew, from above, he can’t see God’s kingdom.” Nicodemus says, “How can a man be born when he’s already old? He can’t climb back into his mother’s womb a second time and be born, can he?”

Jesus answers, “Truly, truly, I tell you, unless someone is born of water and Spirit, he can’t enter God’s kingdom. What is born of flesh is flesh, and what is born of the Spirit is spirit. Don’t be surprised that I told you, ‘You must be born anew, from above.’ The wind blows wherever it likes. (In the Greek, wind and Spirit are the same word.) You hear the sound of it, but you can’t tell where it’s coming from or where it’s headed. That’s how it is with everyone born of the Spirit.” “How can this be?” Nicodemus asks.

Jesus answers him, “You’re the teacher of Israel, and you don’t understand these things? Truly, truly, I tell you, we speak about what we know, and we testify to what we’ve seen, and still you people won’t accept our testimony. I’ve told you about earthly things and you don’t believe. How will you believe if I tell you about heavenly things? No one has gone up into heaven except the one who came down out of heaven: the Son of Man. Moses lifted up the snake on a pole in the wilderness, and the Son of Man has to be lifted up the same way, so that everyone who trusts may have eternal life in him.

This is how God loved the world: he gave his one-of-a-kind Son, so that everyone who trusts in him won’t be lost, but will have eternal life. God didn’t send the Son into the world to pass sentence on the world. He sent him so the world could be rescued through him. Whoever trusts in him is not condemned. Whoever won’t trust is condemned already, for refusing to trust in the name of God’s one-of-a-kind Son. And this is the verdict: light has come into the world, and people loved the dark more than the light, because the things they were doing were evil. Everyone who does wicked things hates the light and stays away from it, afraid their deeds will be dragged out into the open. But whoever lives by the truth walks into the light, so it can be plain to see that what they have done was done in God.”
The Last Testimony of John · 3:22–36

After this, Jesus and his disciples go out into the Judean countryside. He spends time there with them and baptizes. John is baptizing too, at Aenon near Salim, because there is plenty of water there, and people keep coming to be baptized. (This is before John is thrown into prison.)

An argument breaks out between some of John’s disciples and a certain Jewish man about the washing rituals. So they come to John and say, “Rabbi, that man who was with you on the other side of the Jordan, the one you testified about: look, now he’s baptizing, and everyone is going to him!” John answers, “Nobody can receive anything unless it’s given to him from heaven. You yourselves heard me say, ‘I’m not the Messiah. I’ve been sent ahead of him.’ The bride belongs to the bridegroom. The bridegroom’s friend stands near and listens for him, and when he hears the bridegroom’s voice, his joy runs over. That’s my joy, and now it’s full to the brim. He has to grow greater, and I have to grow smaller.

The one who comes from above is over everyone. Whoever is from the earth belongs to the earth and talks the way the earth talks. The one who comes from heaven is over everyone. He tells what he has seen and heard, and yet nobody accepts his testimony. Whoever does accept it puts his own seal on this: God is true. The one God sent speaks God’s own words, for he gives the Spirit without measuring it out. The Father loves the Son and has put everything into his hands. Whoever trusts in the Son has eternal life. Whoever refuses to obey the Son won’t see life; God’s anger stays on him.”
The Woman at the Well · 4:1–26

Word reaches the Pharisees that Jesus is making and baptizing more disciples than John. (Jesus himself doesn’t baptize anyone; his disciples do.) When Jesus learns that they have heard this, he leaves Judea and heads back to Galilee. His road has to take him through Samaria.

So he comes to a Samaritan town called Sychar, near the piece of land Jacob gave to his son Joseph. Jacob’s well is there. Jesus is worn out from the journey, so he sits down by the well. It is about noon. A Samaritan woman comes to draw water, and Jesus says to her, “Give me a drink.” (His disciples have gone into town to buy food.) The Samaritan woman says to him, “How is it that you, a Jew, are asking me for a drink? I’m a Samaritan woman!” (Jews don’t share anything with Samaritans.)

Jesus answers her, “If you knew the gift God gives, and who it is asking you for a drink, you’d have asked him, and he’d have given you living water.” “Sir,” the woman says, “you don’t even have a bucket, and the well is deep. Where are you going to get this living water? You’re not greater than our father Jacob, are you? He gave us this well. He drank from it himself, and so did his sons and his flocks.” Jesus answers her, “Everyone who drinks this water will get thirsty again. But whoever drinks the water I give will never be thirsty again. The water I give will become a spring inside that person, bubbling up into eternal life.” “Sir,” the woman says, “give me this water! Then I won’t get thirsty, and I won’t have to keep coming all the way out here to draw water.”

Jesus tells her, “Go call your husband and come back here.” “I don’t have a husband,” the woman answers. Jesus says, “You’re right to say, ‘I don’t have a husband.’ You’ve had five husbands, and the man you have now isn’t your husband. What you said is true.” “Sir,” the woman says, “I can see you’re a prophet. Our ancestors worshiped on this mountain, but you Jews say Jerusalem is the place where people have to worship.”

Jesus says to her, “Woman, believe me, the hour is coming when you won’t worship the Father on this mountain or in Jerusalem. You Samaritans worship what you don’t know. We worship what we do know, because salvation comes from the Jews. But the hour is coming, and it’s already here, when people who truly worship will bow before the Father in spirit and in truth. Those are the worshipers the Father is looking for. God is spirit. So the ones who worship him must do it in spirit and in truth.” The woman says to him, “I know the Messiah is coming, the one they call the Christ. When he comes, he’ll explain everything to us.” Jesus says to her, “I AM, the one who’s talking with you right now.”
The Disciples Return; the Woman Witnesses · 4:27–42

Just then his disciples come back. They’re astonished to find him talking with a woman, but none of them asks, “What do you want with her?” or “Why are you talking to her?” The woman leaves her water jar behind, hurries back to town, and tells the people, “Come and see a man who told me everything I’ve ever done! He couldn’t be the Messiah, could he?” So they come streaming out of town toward him.

Meanwhile his disciples keep urging him, “Rabbi, eat something.” But he tells them, “I have food to eat that you know nothing about.” The disciples ask each other, “Did somebody bring him something to eat?” Jesus says to them, “My food is doing the will of the one who sent me, and finishing the work he gave me. Don’t you have a saying, ‘Four more months, and then the harvest’? Well, I tell you, lift your eyes and look at the fields. They’re already white and ready to harvest. The reaper is already drawing his wages and gathering a crop for eternal life, so that the sower and the reaper can celebrate together. That’s where the saying holds true: ‘One plants, another harvests.’ I sent you to reap a field you didn’t work. Other people did the hard labor, and you’ve stepped in to enjoy the fruit of it.”

Many of the Samaritans from that town put their trust in him because of the woman’s testimony: “He told me everything I’ve ever done.” So when the Samaritans reach him, they beg him to stay with them, and he stays there two days. And many more come to trust because of what he himself says. They tell the woman, “We don’t believe just because of what you said anymore. We’ve heard him for ourselves, and we know this man really is the Savior of the world.”
The Official’s Son · 4:43–54

After those two days he leaves there for Galilee. (Jesus himself has said that a prophet gets no honor in his own hometown.) When he arrives in Galilee, the Galileans welcome him. They have seen everything he did in Jerusalem at the festival, because they were at the festival too.

So he comes once more to Cana in Galilee, where he turned the water into wine. There is a royal official there whose son lies sick in Capernaum. When this man hears that Jesus has come from Judea into Galilee, he goes to him and begs him to come down and heal his son, because the boy is dying. Jesus says to him, “You people won’t ever believe unless you see signs and wonders.” The official says, “Sir, come down before my little boy dies!” Jesus tells him, “Go on home. Your son is alive.” The man takes Jesus at his word and starts for home.

While he’s still on the road down, his servants meet him with the news: “Your boy is alive!” He asks them what time the boy started to get better. They tell him, “Yesterday, about one in the afternoon, the fever left him.” Then the father realizes that was the very hour Jesus told him, “Your son is alive.” And he and his whole household put their trust in him. This is the second sign Jesus does after coming from Judea into Galilee.
The Healing at the Pool · 5:1–18

Some time later there is a Jewish festival, and Jesus goes up to Jerusalem. Now in Jerusalem, near the Sheep Gate, there is a pool called in Aramaic Bethzatha, ringed by five covered porches. Under those porches lie crowds of sick people: the blind, the lame, the withered. One man there has been ill for thirty-eight years. Jesus sees him lying there, and knows he has been that way a long, long time. He asks him, “Do you want to be made well?”

The sick man answers, “Sir, I don’t have anybody to put me into the pool when the water is stirred. While I’m still trying to get there, somebody else gets down in ahead of me.” Jesus says to him, “Get up, take your mat, and walk.” And at once the man is well. He picks up his mat and walks. Now that day is a Sabbath.

So the Judean leaders say to the man who has been healed, “It’s the Sabbath! The law doesn’t allow you to carry your mat.” He answers them, “The man who made me well is the one who told me, ‘Pick up your mat and walk.’” They ask him, “Who is this man who told you to pick it up and walk?” But the healed man has no idea who it was, because Jesus has slipped away into the crowd that fills the place.

Later Jesus finds him in the temple and says to him, “Look, you’re healed now. Don’t go on sinning, or something worse could come on you.” The man goes off and tells the Judean leaders that Jesus is the one who made him well. And that is why they start hounding Jesus: because he is doing these things on the Sabbath. But Jesus answers them, “My Father has never stopped working, right up to this moment, and I’m working too.” This makes them even more determined to kill him, because he isn’t just breaking the Sabbath; he is calling God his own Father, making himself equal with God.
The Authority of the Son · 5:19–30

So Jesus answers them, “Truly, truly, I tell you, the Son can’t do a thing on his own. He only does what he sees the Father doing. Whatever the Father does, the Son does too. The Father loves the Son dearly and shows him everything he is doing. And he’ll show him even greater works than these, and you’ll be amazed. Just as the Father raises the dead and gives them life, the Son gives life to anyone he chooses. The Father doesn’t judge anyone. He has handed all judging over to the Son, so that everyone will honor the Son the way they honor the Father. Whoever won’t honor the Son won’t honor the Father who sent him.

Truly, truly, I tell you, whoever hears what I say and trusts the one who sent me has eternal life. That person won’t come under judgment. They have already crossed over, out of death and into life. Truly, truly, I tell you, the hour is coming, and it’s already here, when the dead will hear the voice of the Son of God, and the ones who hear it will live. The Father has life in himself, and in the same way he has granted the Son to have life in himself. And he has given him the authority to judge, because he is the Son of Man. Don’t be amazed at this. The hour is coming when everyone lying in the tombs will hear his voice and come out. Those who have done good will rise to life. Those who have done evil will rise to be judged. I can’t do a thing on my own. I judge just as I hear, and my judgment is fair, because I’m not after what I want, but what the one who sent me wants.
Witnesses to the Son · 5:31–47

If I’m the only one testifying about myself, my testimony doesn’t count. But there is someone else testifying about me, and I know that what he says about me is true. You sent messengers to John, and he gave testimony to the truth. Not that I depend on human testimony. I’m telling you this so that you can be saved. John was a lamp, burning and shining, and for a while you were glad to enjoy his light. But I have testimony weightier than John’s. The works the Father gave me to finish, the very works I’m doing, they testify that the Father has sent me. And the Father who sent me has testified about me himself. You’ve never heard his voice. You’ve never seen his form. And his word doesn’t live in you, because you won’t trust the one he sent.

You dig through the Scriptures, because you think you’ll find eternal life in them. And those very Scriptures are testifying about me! Yet you refuse to come to me so you can have life. I’m not looking for praise from people. But I know you. I know you don’t have the love of God inside you. I’ve come in my Father’s name, and you won’t accept me. If somebody else comes in his own name, him you’ll accept. How could you ever believe, when you trade praise with each other and don’t even look for the praise that comes from the only God?

Don’t think I’m going to be the one accusing you before the Father. Your accuser is Moses, the very one you’ve pinned your hopes on. If you really believed Moses, you’d believe me, because he wrote about me. But if you don’t believe what he wrote, how are you going to believe what I say?”
The Feeding of Five Thousand · 6:1–15

After this, Jesus crosses to the far side of the Sea of Galilee, which is also called the Sea of Tiberias. A huge crowd keeps following him, because they have seen the signs he does for the sick. Jesus goes up onto the mountain and sits down there with his disciples. The Passover, the Jewish festival, is near.

Jesus looks up and sees a great crowd coming toward him, and he says to Philip, “Where can we buy bread for all these people to eat?” He says this to test Philip, because he already knows what he is going to do. Philip answers him, “Two hundred denarii worth of bread wouldn’t be enough for each of them to get even a bite!” (That is more than half a year’s wages.) One of his disciples, Andrew, Simon Peter’s brother, speaks up: “There’s a boy here with five barley loaves and two little fish. But what good is that with this many people?”

Jesus says, “Have the people sit down.” There is plenty of grass in that place, so they sit down, about five thousand men. Jesus takes the loaves, gives thanks, and hands them out to the people sitting there. He does the same with the fish, as much as anyone wants. When they’ve all eaten their fill, he tells his disciples, “Gather up the pieces that are left over, so nothing goes to waste.” So they gather them up, and from the five barley loaves they fill twelve baskets with the leftover pieces.

When the people see the sign Jesus has done, they start saying, “This must be the Prophet, the one who’s coming into the world!” Jesus knows they are about to come and grab him and make him king by force, so he slips away again to the mountain, all by himself.
Walking on Water · 6:16–21

When evening comes, his disciples go down to the sea, climb into a boat, and start across toward Capernaum. By now it is dark, and Jesus still hasn’t come to them. A strong wind is blowing, and the sea is getting rough. When they’ve rowed three or four miles, they see Jesus walking on the sea, coming closer to the boat, and they’re terrified. But he says to them, “I AM. Don’t be afraid.” Then they’re glad to take him into the boat, and right away the boat reaches the shore where they were heading.

The next day, the crowd still standing on the far shore realizes there had been only one boat there. They know Jesus didn’t get into it with his disciples; the disciples went off alone. Then some other boats from Tiberias come in near the place where they ate the bread after the Lord gave thanks. So when the crowd sees that neither Jesus nor his disciples are there, they climb into those boats and head for Capernaum, looking for Jesus. They find him on the other side of the sea and ask him, “Rabbi, when did you get here?”

Jesus answers them, “Truly, truly, I tell you, you’re not looking for me because you saw signs. You’re looking for me because you ate the loaves and got full. Don’t work so hard for food that spoils. Work for the food that lasts, into eternal life, the food the Son of Man will give you. God the Father has stamped him with his seal.” So they ask him, “What do we have to do to be doing the works God wants?” Jesus answers them, “This is the work God wants: that you trust in the one he has sent.”

They say to him, “Then what sign will you do, so we can see it and believe you? What work are you going to do? Our ancestors ate the manna in the wilderness. Just as it is written, ‘He gave them bread from heaven to eat.’” Jesus says to them, “Truly, truly, I tell you, it wasn’t Moses who gave you the bread from heaven. It’s my Father who is giving you the true bread from heaven. God’s bread is the one who comes down out of heaven and gives the world life.” “Sir,” they say to him, “give us this bread from now on.”

Jesus tells them, “I am the bread of life. Anyone who comes to me won’t ever go hungry again, and anyone who trusts in me won’t ever be thirsty again. But as I told you, you have seen me, and still you won’t believe. Everyone the Father gives me will come to me, and I will never, ever turn away anyone who comes to me. I haven’t come down from heaven to do what I want. I’ve come to do what the one who sent me wants. Whoever chews on my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life, and I’ll raise him up on the last day. My flesh is food indeed, and my blood is drink indeed. Whoever chews on my flesh and drinks my blood stays in me, and I stay in him. The living Father sent me, and I live because of the Father. In the same way, whoever feeds on me will live because of me. This is the bread that came down from heaven. It’s not like the manna your ancestors ate, and then died. Whoever chews on this bread will live forever.” He says these things while he is teaching in the synagogue at Capernaum.
The Words of Eternal Life · 6:60–71

When they hear it, many of his disciples say, “This teaching is hard! Who can stand to listen to it?” Jesus knows, deep inside, that his disciples are grumbling about it, and he says to them, “Does this trip you up? Then what if you see the Son of Man going up to where he was before? Life comes from the Spirit; flesh can’t do a thing for you. These words I’ve been speaking to you are Spirit, and they are life. But some of you don’t believe.” (Jesus has known from the beginning which of them don’t believe, and which one will betray him.) And he says, “That’s why I told you that no one can come to me unless the Father grants it to him.”

After that, many of his disciples drift away and no longer walk with him. So Jesus says to the Twelve, “What about you? Do you want to go too?” Simon Peter answers him, “Lord, who else would we go to? The words you speak are the words of eternal life. We’ve put our trust in you, and we’re sure of it now: you are God’s Holy One.”
Jesus answers them, “Didn’t I choose you, the Twelve? And yet one of you is a devil.” He means Judas, son of Simon Iscariot. Judas, one of the Twelve, is the one who is going to betray him.
Jesus and His Brothers · 7:1–13

After this, Jesus goes about in Galilee. He keeps away from Judea, because the Judean leaders are looking for a chance to kill him. Now the Jewish Festival of Shelters is near. So his brothers say to him, “Get out of here and go to Judea, so your disciples there can see the works you’re doing. Nobody who wants to be known does things in secret. If you’re doing these things, show yourself to the world!” (Not even his own brothers believe in him.)

Jesus tells them, “My time hasn’t come yet. For you, any time will do. The world can’t hate you. But it hates me, because I keep testifying that what it does is evil. You go on up to the festival. I’m not going up to this festival, because my time hasn’t fully come yet.” After telling them this, he stays on in Galilee.

But once his brothers have gone up to the festival, he goes up too, not openly but quietly, as if in secret. At the festival the Judean leaders keep watching for him. “Where is he?” they ask. And there is a lot of whispering about him in the crowds. Some say, “He’s a good man.” Others say, “No, he’s leading the people astray.” But nobody says anything about him out loud, because they are afraid of the Judean leaders.
Teaching in the Temple · 7:14–36

About halfway through the festival, Jesus goes up into the temple and begins to teach. The Judean leaders are amazed. “How does this man know so much about the Scriptures,” they say, “when he’s never been schooled?” Jesus answers them, “My teaching isn’t mine. It belongs to the one who sent me. If anyone is set on doing God’s will, he’ll know whether my teaching comes from God or whether I’m just speaking on my own. A man who speaks on his own is out for his own glory. But a man who is out for the glory of the one who sent him is true, and there’s nothing crooked in him. Didn’t Moses give you the law? Yet not one of you keeps the law. Why are you trying to kill me?” The crowd answers, “You’ve got a demon! Who’s trying to kill you?”

Jesus answers them, “I did one work, and you’re all astonished. Moses gave you circumcision (not that it started with Moses; it goes back to the patriarchs), and so you circumcise a boy even on the Sabbath. If a boy can be circumcised on the Sabbath so the law of Moses isn’t broken, why are you furious with me for making a whole man well on the Sabbath? Quit judging by how things look on the surface. Judge what is truly right.”

Some of the people of Jerusalem start saying, “Isn’t this the man they’re trying to kill? And look, here he is, speaking right out in the open, and they don’t say a word to him! Could it be the leaders have actually decided he’s the Messiah? But we know where this man comes from. When the Messiah comes, nobody will know where he’s from.”

Then Jesus, still teaching in the temple, cries out, “So you know me, and you know where I’m from? I haven’t come on my own. The one who sent me is true, and you don’t know him. I know him, because I come from him, and he is the one who sent me.” At this they try to seize him, but nobody lays a hand on him, because his hour hasn’t come yet. Still, many in the crowd put their trust in him. “When the Messiah comes,” they say, “he won’t do more signs than this man has done, will he?”

The Pharisees hear the crowd whispering these things about him, and the chief priests and Pharisees send temple guards to arrest him. So Jesus says, “I’m with you only a little while longer, and then I’m going to the one who sent me. You’ll look for me, and you won’t find me. Where I am, you can’t come.” The Judean leaders say to each other, “Where is he planning to go that we won’t be able to find him? Is he going off to our people scattered among the Greeks, to teach the Greeks? What does he mean by saying, ‘You’ll look for me, and you won’t find me. Where I am, you can’t come’?”
Rivers of Living Water · 7:37–44

On the last day of the festival, the great day, Jesus stands up and cries out, “Anyone who’s thirsty, come to me and drink! Whoever trusts in me, just as the Scripture says: rivers of living water will pour out from deep inside him.” (He means the Spirit, whom those who trust in him are about to receive. The Spirit hasn’t come yet, because Jesus hasn’t yet been glorified.)

When they hear these words, some of the crowd say, “This man really is the Prophet.” Others say, “He’s the Messiah.” But others say, “Surely the Messiah doesn’t come from Galilee! Doesn’t the Scripture say that the Messiah comes from David’s line, and from Bethlehem, the village where David lived?” So the crowd is split down the middle because of him. Some of them want to arrest him, but nobody lays a hand on him.
The Officers Return Empty-handed · 7:45–52

So the temple guards go back to the chief priests and Pharisees, who ask them, “Why didn’t you bring him in?” The guards answer, “Nobody has ever talked like this!” “You haven’t been fooled too, have you?” the Pharisees answer. “Has a single one of the leaders believed in him? Or any of the Pharisees? No! But this rabble that doesn’t know the law, they’re under a curse.”

Nicodemus, the one who went to Jesus earlier and who is one of them, speaks up: “Does our law condemn a man without first giving him a hearing and finding out what he’s done?” They answer him, “Are you from Galilee too? Look it up, and you’ll see: no prophet comes out of Galilee.”
The Woman Caught in Adultery · 7:53–8:11
Then they all go home,
The Woman Caught in Adultery · 8:1–11

but Jesus goes out to the Mount of Olives. At dawn he comes back into the temple, and all the people gather around him. He sits down and teaches them. Then the scribes and the Pharisees bring in a woman who has been caught in adultery. They stand her in the middle of everyone and say to him, “Teacher, this woman was caught in the very act of adultery. In the law, Moses commanded us to stone women like this. So what do you say?” They say this to trap him, so they’ll have something to accuse him of. But Jesus bends down and starts writing on the ground with his finger.

When they keep on pressing him, he straightens up and says to them, “Whichever one of you has never sinned, you throw the first stone at her.” And he bends down again and goes on writing on the ground.

When they hear this, they begin to drift away one at a time, the oldest first, until Jesus is left alone, with the woman still standing there in the middle. Jesus straightens up and says to her, “Woman, where are they? Hasn’t anyone condemned you?” “No one, sir,” she says. And Jesus says, “Then I don’t condemn you either. Go, and from now on, don’t sin anymore.”
The Light of the World · 8:12–20

Jesus speaks to the people again. “I am the light of the world,” he says. “Anyone who follows me won’t go stumbling around in the dark. He’ll have the light that gives life.” The Pharisees say to him, “You’re testifying on your own behalf. Your testimony doesn’t count.” Jesus answers them, “Even if I do testify on my own behalf, my testimony is true, because I know where I came from and where I’m going. But you have no idea where I come from or where I’m going. You judge by human standards. I don’t judge anyone. But even if I do judge, my judgment is true, because I’m not alone in it. The Father who sent me is with me. Your own law says that the testimony of two witnesses holds up. I testify about myself, and the Father who sent me testifies about me too.”

“Where is this Father of yours?” they ask him. Jesus answers, “You don’t know me, and you don’t know my Father. If you knew me, you’d know my Father too.” He says these things while he is teaching in the temple, near the treasury. And still nobody arrests him, because his hour hasn’t come yet.
Where I Am Going · 8:21–30

Again Jesus says to them, “I’m going away. You’ll look for me, and you’ll die in your sin. Where I’m going, you can’t come.” So the Judean leaders say, “Is he going to kill himself? Is that why he says, ‘Where I’m going, you can’t come’?” He tells them, “You’re from below. I’m from above. You belong to this world. I don’t belong to this world. That’s why I told you you’d die in your sins. Unless you believe that I AM, you will die in your sins.”

“Who are you?” they ask him. Jesus says, “Just what I’ve been telling you from the beginning. I have a great deal to say about you and to judge in you. But the one who sent me is true, and what I’ve heard from him, that’s what I tell the world.” They don’t grasp that he is talking to them about the Father. So Jesus says, “When you have lifted up the Son of Man, then you will know that I AM, and that I do nothing on my own. I say just what the Father has taught me. And the one who sent me is with me. He hasn’t left me on my own, because I always do what pleases him.” As he is saying these things, many people put their trust in him.
The Truth Will Set You Free · 8:31–47

So Jesus says to the Jews who have believed him, “If you stay in my word, you’re truly my disciples. You’ll come to know the truth, and the truth will make you free.” They answer him, “We’re Abraham’s descendants. We’ve never been slaves to anybody. How can you say, ‘You’ll be made free’?”

Jesus answers them, “Truly, truly, I tell you, everyone who keeps on sinning is a slave to sin. A slave doesn’t have a permanent place in the household. A son belongs there forever. So if the Son sets you free, you’ll be free through and through. I know you’re Abraham’s descendants. Yet you’re trying to kill me, because my word finds no room in you. I tell you what I’ve seen at my Father’s side, and you do what you’ve heard from your father.”

“Abraham is our father,” they answer. Jesus tells them, “If you were Abraham’s children, you’d be doing what Abraham did. But instead you’re trying to kill me, a man who has told you the truth I heard from God. Abraham never did anything like that. You’re doing what your own father does.” “We weren’t born of sexual immorality!” they say. “We have one Father: God himself.”

Jesus says to them, “If God were your Father, you’d love me, because I came out from God, and here I am. I didn’t come on my own. He sent me. Why can’t you understand what I’m saying? Because you can’t bear to hear my word. Your father is the devil, and you want to do what your father craves. From the very beginning he has been a killer of people. He has never stood in the truth, because there is no truth in him. When he lies, he’s talking in his own voice, because lying is what he is, and he is the father of lies. But because I tell the truth, you won’t believe me. Can any of you prove me guilty of sin? If I’m telling the truth, why won’t you believe me? Whoever belongs to God hears what God says. The reason you don’t hear is that you don’t belong to God.”
Before Abraham Was, I Am · 8:48–59

The Judean leaders answer him, “Aren’t we right when we say you’re a Samaritan and you’ve got a demon?” Jesus answers, “I don’t have a demon. I honor my Father, and you dishonor me. I’m not out for my own glory. There is one who looks after that, and he is the judge. Truly, truly, I tell you, whoever keeps my word will never see death.”

The Judean leaders say to him, “Now we know you’ve got a demon! Abraham died, and so did the prophets. And you say, ‘Whoever keeps my word will never taste death.’ You’re not greater than our father Abraham, are you? He died! The prophets died! Who do you think you are?” Jesus answers, “If I glorify myself, my glory is worth nothing. The one who glorifies me is my Father, the one you say is your God. You’ve never known him, but I know him. If I said I didn’t know him, I’d be a liar like you. But I do know him, and I keep his word. Your father Abraham was thrilled at the thought of seeing my day. He saw it, and he was glad.”

“You’re not even fifty years old,” the Judean leaders say to him, “and you’ve seen Abraham?” Jesus says to them, “Truly, truly, I tell you, before Abraham ever came to be, I AM.” At that they pick up stones to throw at him. But Jesus is hidden from them, and he goes out of the temple.
The Man Born Blind · 9:1–12

As Jesus walks along, he sees a man who has been blind since the day he was born. His disciples ask him, “Rabbi, whose sin was it that he was born blind? His own, or his parents’?” Jesus answers, “It wasn’t his sin, and it wasn’t his parents’. This happened so that God’s works could be put on display in him. We have to do the works of the one who sent me while it’s still daytime. Night is on its way, and then nobody can work. As long as I’m in the world, I’m the world’s light.”

After saying this, he spits on the ground, makes some mud with the spit, and smears the mud on the man’s eyes. “Go and wash in the Pool of Siloam,” he tells him (Siloam means Sent). Off the man goes, he washes, and he comes back able to see.

His neighbors, and the people who used to see him begging, start saying, “Isn’t this the man who used to sit and beg?” Some say, “That’s him.” Others say, “No, he just looks like him.” But the man himself keeps saying, “I’m the one!” “Then how were your eyes opened?” they ask him. He answers, “The man they call Jesus made mud and smeared it on my eyes and told me, ‘Go to Siloam and wash.’ So I went and washed, and now I can see.” “Where is he?” they ask him. “I don’t know,” he says.
The First Interrogation by the Pharisees · 9:13–17

They bring the man who used to be blind to the Pharisees. Now the day Jesus made the mud and opened his eyes was a Sabbath. So the Pharisees ask him too how he came to see. He tells them, “He put mud on my eyes. I washed. And I see.” Some of the Pharisees say, “This man can’t be from God; he breaks the Sabbath.” But others say, “How could a sinful man do signs like these?” And they are split down the middle. So they turn to the blind man again. “What do you say about him? It was your eyes he opened.” “He’s a prophet,” the man says.
The Parents Questioned · 9:18–23

The Judean leaders still won’t believe he was blind and has gained his sight, not until they call in the parents of the man who can now see. They ask them, “Is this your son, the one you say was born blind? Then how is it that he can see now?” His parents answer, “We know he’s our son, and we know he was born blind. But how he can see now, we don’t know. Or who opened his eyes, we don’t know. Ask him. He’s old enough. He can speak for himself.” His parents say this because they’re afraid of the Judean leaders, who have already agreed that anyone who confesses Jesus as the Messiah will be thrown out of the synagogue. That’s why his parents say, “He’s old enough. Ask him.”
The Second Interrogation · 9:24–34

So for the second time they call in the man who had been blind. “Give glory to God,” they tell him. “We know this man is a sinner.” He answers, “Whether he’s a sinner, I don’t know. Here’s the one thing I know: I used to be blind, and now I can see.” They say to him, “What did he do to you? How did he open your eyes?” He answers them, “I’ve told you already, and you didn’t listen. Why do you want to hear it all over again? You don’t want to become his disciples too, do you?”

Then they heap insults on him. “You’re that man’s disciple,” they say. “We’re disciples of Moses. We know God spoke to Moses. But this fellow, we don’t even know where he comes from.” The man answers them, “Well, that’s astonishing! You don’t know where he comes from, and yet he opened my eyes! We know God doesn’t listen to sinners. But if someone honors God and does his will, God listens to him. Since the world began, nobody has ever heard of anyone opening the eyes of a man born blind. If this man weren’t from God, he couldn’t do anything at all.” They answer him, “You were born steeped in sin from head to toe, and you’re trying to teach us?” And they throw him out.
The Third Interrogation: Jesus Finds Him · 9:35–41

Jesus hears that they have thrown him out. He goes and finds him and says, “Do you trust in the Son of Man?” The man answers, “Who is he, sir? Tell me, so I can trust in him.” Jesus says to him, “You’ve seen him. He’s the one talking with you right now.” “Lord, I believe,” the man says, and he kneels down and worships him.

Jesus says, “I came into this world for judgment, so that people who can’t see will see, and people who can see will go blind.” Some Pharisees who are with him hear this and say to him, “We’re not blind too, are we?” Jesus tells them, “If you were blind, you wouldn’t be guilty of sin. But now that you say, ‘We see,’ your sin stays put.”
I Am the Gate · 10:1–10

“Truly, truly, I tell you, anyone who doesn’t come into the sheepfold through the gate, but climbs in some other way, is a thief and a bandit. The one who comes in through the gate is the shepherd of the sheep. The gatekeeper opens the gate for him, and the sheep listen for his voice. He calls his own sheep by name, one by one, and leads them out. When he has brought out all his own, he walks on ahead of them, and the sheep come along behind him; they know his voice. They’ll never follow a stranger. They’ll run away from him, because a stranger’s voice is a voice they don’t know.” Jesus tells them this picture-story, but they don’t understand what he is talking about.

So Jesus says to them again, “Truly, truly, I tell you, I am the gate for the sheep. All who came before me are thieves and bandits, but the sheep never listened to them. I am the gate. Anyone who comes in through me will be safe. He’ll come in and go out and find good grass. The thief comes for one reason: to steal, to kill, to destroy. I came so they can have life, life overflowing.
I Am the Good Shepherd · 10:11–21

I am the good shepherd. A good shepherd will lay his own life down for the sheep. A hired man isn’t the shepherd. The sheep aren’t his. So when he sees the wolf coming, he leaves the sheep and runs, and the wolf snatches them and scatters the flock. He runs because he’s only a hired man, and the sheep don’t matter to him. I am the good shepherd. I know the ones who are mine, and they know me, the way the Father knows me and I know him. And for the sheep I lay my life down. I have other sheep too, sheep that aren’t from this fold. I have to bring them in as well. They’ll listen to my voice, and there will be one flock, with one shepherd. This is why the Father loves me: because I lay down my life, so that I can take it up again. Nobody takes it away from me. I lay it down of my own free will. I have the right to lay it down, and I have the right to take it up again. This is the command I received from my Father.”

Once again the people are split over what he says. Many of them say, “He’s got a demon. He’s out of his mind! Why listen to him?” Others say, “These aren’t the words of a man with a demon. Can a demon open blind people’s eyes?”
I and the Father are One · 10:22–42

Then comes the Festival of Dedication in Jerusalem, the feast of lights. It is winter, and Jesus is walking in the temple, in Solomon’s Porch. The Judean leaders gather around him and say, “How long are you going to keep us in suspense? If you’re the Messiah, tell us straight out.”

Jesus answers them, “I’ve told you, and you don’t believe. The works I do in my Father’s name, they testify about me. But you don’t believe, because you aren’t my sheep. My sheep listen for my voice. I know each one, and they follow where I go. I give them eternal life. They’ll never be lost, and no one is going to tear them out of my hand. What my Father has given me is greater than everything, and no one can tear anything out of the Father’s hand. The Father and I are one.”

Once again the Judean leaders pick up stones to stone him. Jesus answers them, “I’ve done one good work after another in front of you, all from the Father. Which one of them are you stoning me for?” The Judean leaders answer him, “We’re not stoning you for any good work. We’re stoning you for blasphemy, because you, a mere man, are making yourself God.”

Jesus answers them, “Isn’t it written in your own law, ‘I said, you are gods’? If he called them gods, the people the word of God came to, and the Scripture can’t be broken, then what about the one the Father set apart and sent into the world? Do you tell him, ‘You’re blaspheming,’ because I said, ‘I am God’s Son’? If I’m not doing my Father’s works, then don’t believe me. But if I am doing them, then even if you won’t believe me, believe the works. Then you’ll come to know, and go on knowing, that the Father is in me and I am in the Father.” Again they try to seize him, but he slips out of their grasp.

He goes away again across the Jordan, to the place where John first baptized, and he stays there. And many people come to him. “John never did a single sign,” they say, “but everything John said about this man was true.” And many people there put their trust in him.
Lazarus is Ill · 11:1–16

Now a man named Lazarus is sick. He is from Bethany, the village where Mary and her sister Martha live. (This is the Mary who anointed the Lord with perfume and wiped his feet with her hair. Her brother Lazarus is the one who is sick.) So the sisters send word to Jesus: “Lord, look, the one you love so dearly is sick.” When Jesus hears it, he says, “This sickness isn’t headed for death. It is for God’s glory, so that through it the Son of God will be glorified.” Jesus loves Martha, and her sister, and Lazarus. So when he hears that Lazarus is sick, he stays where he is two more days. Then, after that, he says to the disciples, “Let’s go back to Judea.”

“Rabbi,” the disciples say to him, “the Judean leaders were just now trying to stone you, and you’re going back there?” Jesus answers, “Aren’t there twelve hours of daylight? Anyone who walks around in the daytime doesn’t stumble, because he sees by the light of this world. But anyone who walks around at night does stumble, because the light isn’t in him.” After he says this, he tells them, “Our friend Lazarus is asleep, and I’m on my way to wake him.” The disciples say to him, “Lord, if he’s asleep, he’ll get better.” Jesus has been talking about his death, but they think he means ordinary sleep. So then Jesus tells them plainly, “Lazarus has died. And for your sake I’m glad I wasn’t there, so that you can come to believe. But let’s go to him.” Then Thomas, the one called the Twin, says to the other disciples, “Let’s go too, so we can die with him.”
I Am the Resurrection and the Life · 11:17–27

When Jesus arrives, he finds that Lazarus has already been in the tomb four days. Bethany is close to Jerusalem, less than two miles away, and many of the Judean people have come out to Martha and Mary to comfort them about their brother. When Martha hears that Jesus is coming, she goes out to meet him, but Mary stays sitting in the house. Martha says to Jesus, “Lord, if only you’d been here, my brother would still be alive. But even now I know that whatever you ask of God, God will give you.” Jesus says to her, “Your brother will rise again.” Martha says to him, “I know he’ll rise again in the resurrection on the last day.”

Jesus says to her, “I am the resurrection and the life. Whoever trusts in me will live, even if he dies. And everyone who is alive and trusts in me will never, ever die. Do you believe this?” “Yes, Lord,” she tells him. “I’ve come to believe it: you’re the Messiah, God’s Son, the one who is coming into the world.”
Jesus Weeps · 11:28–37

After saying this, she goes back and calls her sister Mary aside. “The Teacher is here,” she says quietly, “and he’s asking for you.” As soon as Mary hears it, she gets up quickly and goes to him. Jesus still hasn’t come into the village. He is still at the place where Martha met him. The people who are in the house with Mary, comforting her, see her get up quickly and go out. So they follow her, thinking she is going to the tomb to weep there.

When Mary comes to where Jesus is and sees him, she falls at his feet. “Lord,” she says, “if only you’d been here, my brother would still be alive.” Jesus sees her sobbing, and he sees the people who have come with her sobbing too, and something rises up hot inside him. He is shaken to the core. “Where have you laid him?” he asks. They say to him, “Lord, come and see.” Jesus weeps.
So the people say, “See how much he loved him!” But some of them say, “This man opened a blind man’s eyes. Couldn’t he have kept this man from dying too?”
Lazarus Raised · 11:38–44

Then Jesus, again churning hot inside, comes to the tomb. It is a cave, with a stone lying across the entrance. “Take the stone away,” Jesus says. Martha, the dead man’s sister, says to him, “Lord, by now he’ll smell. He’s been dead four days.” Jesus says to her, “Didn’t I tell you? If you believe, you’ll see God’s glory.” So they take the stone away. And Jesus lifts his eyes upward and says, “Father, thank you for hearing me. I know you always hear me. But I’m saying this for the sake of the crowd standing here, so that they will believe you sent me.” And when he has said this, he shouts in a great voice, “Lazarus, come out!” And the dead man comes out, his hands and feet wrapped in strips of linen, and a cloth wound around his face. Jesus tells them, “Unwrap him, and let him go.”
The Council’s Decision · 11:45–57

Many of the Judean people who came to Mary and saw what Jesus did put their trust in him. But some of them go off to the Pharisees and tell them what Jesus has done. So the chief priests and the Pharisees call the council together. “What are we going to do?” they say. “This man is doing a lot of signs. If we let him carry on like this, everybody will believe in him, and then the Romans will come and take away both our holy place and our nation.”

But one of them, Caiaphas, who is high priest that year, says to them, “You don’t know anything at all! Don’t you see? You’re better off with one man dying for the people than with the whole nation wiped out.” He doesn’t say this on his own. As high priest that year, he is prophesying that Jesus is going to die for the nation, and not only for the nation, but to gather into one all of God’s children scattered far and wide. So from that day on, they plot to kill him. That is why Jesus no longer walks about openly among the Judean people. He goes away from there to the country near the wilderness, to a town called Ephraim, and stays there with his disciples.

Now the Jewish Passover is near, and many people go up from the countryside to Jerusalem before the Passover to purify themselves. They keep looking for Jesus, and as they stand in the temple they say to one another, “What do you think? Surely he won’t come to the festival?” Now the chief priests and the Pharisees have given orders that anyone who knows where he is must report it, so they can arrest him.
Mary Anoints Jesus · 12:1–8

Six days before the Passover, Jesus comes to Bethany, where Lazarus lives, the man Jesus raised from the dead. They give a dinner for him there. Martha serves, and Lazarus is one of the people at the table with him. Then Mary takes a whole pound of perfume, pure nard, very costly, and anoints Jesus’ feet and wipes his feet with her hair. And the whole house fills with the scent of the perfume. Jesus answers, “You would have no power at all against me, unless it were given to you from above. Therefore he who delivered me to you has greater sin.”
At this, Pilate is seeking to release him, but the Jews cry out, saying, “If you release this man, you aren’t Caesar’s friend! Everyone who makes himself a king speaks against Caesar!”

When Pilate therefore hears these words, he brings Jesus out, and sits down on the judgment seat at a place called “The Pavement”, but in Hebrew, “Gabbatha.” Now it is the Preparation Day of the Passover, at about the sixth hour. He says to the Jews, “Look, your King!”
They cry out, “Away with him! Away with him! Crucify him!”
Pilate says to them, “Should I crucify your King?”
The chief priests answer, “We have no king but Caesar!”
So then he delivers him to them to be crucified. So they take Jesus and lead him away.
The Crucifixion · 19:17–27

He goes out, bearing his cross, to the place called “The Place of a Skull”, which is called in Hebrew, “Golgotha”, where they crucify him, and with him two others, on either side one, and Jesus in the middle. Pilate writes a title also, and puts it on the cross. There is written, “JESUS OF NAZARETH, THE KING OF THE JEWS.” Therefore many of the Jews read this title, for the place where Jesus is crucified are near the city; and it is written in Hebrew, in Latin, and in Greek. The chief priests of the Jews therefore say to Pilate, “Don’t write, ‘The King of the Jews,’ but, ‘he said, “I am King of the Jews.”’”
Pilate answers, “What I have written, I have written.”

Then the soldiers, when they have crucified Jesus, take his garments and make four parts, to every soldier a part; and also the coat. Now the coat is without seam, woven from the top throughout. Then they say to one another, “Let’s not tear it, but cast lots for it to decide whose it will be,” that the Scripture might be fulfilled, which says,
“They parted my garments among them.
For my cloak they cast lots.”

Therefore the soldiers do these things. But there are standing by the cross of Jesus his mother, and his mother’s sister, Mary the wife of Clopas, and Mary Magdalene. Therefore when Jesus sees his mother, and the disciple whom he loves standing there, he says to his mother, “Woman, look, your son!” Then he says to the disciple, “Look, your mother!” From that hour, the disciple takes her to his own home.
It is Finished · 19:28–37

After this, Jesus, seeing that all things are now finished, that the Scripture might be fulfilled, says, “I am thirsty.” Now a vessel full of vinegar is set there; so they put a sponge full of the vinegar on hyssop, and hold it at his mouth. When Jesus therefore has received the vinegar, he says, “It is finished.” He bows his head, and gives up his spirit.

Therefore the Jews, because it is the Preparation Day, so that the bodies wouldn’t remain on the cross on the Sabbath (for that Sabbath are a special one), asked of Pilate that their legs might be broken, and that they might be taken away. Therefore the soldiers come, and break the legs of the first, and of the other who is crucified with him; but when they come to Jesus, and see that he is already dead, they don’t break his legs. However one of the soldiers pierces his side with a spear, and immediately blood and water come out. He who has seen has testified, and his testimony is true. He knows that he tells the truth, that you may believe. For these things happen, that the Scripture might be fulfilled, “A bone of him will not be broken.” Again another Scripture says, “They will look on him whom they pierced.”
The Burial · 19:38–42

After these things, Joseph of Arimathaea, being a disciple of Jesus, but secretly for fear of the Jews, asked of Pilate that he might take away Jesus’ body. Pilate gives him permission. He comes therefore and takes away his body. Nicodemus, who at first comes to Jesus by night, also comes bringing a mixture of myrrh and aloes, about a hundred Roman pounds. So they take Jesus’ body, and bind it in linen cloths with the spices, as the custom of the Jews is to bury. Now in the place where he is crucified there is a garden. In the garden is a new tomb in which no man has ever yet been laid. Then because of the Jews’ Preparation Day (for the tomb is near at hand) they lay Jesus there.
The Empty Tomb · 20:1–10

Now on the first day of the week, Mary Magdalene goes early, while it is still dark, to the tomb, and sees the stone taken away from the tomb. Therefore she runs and comes to Simon Peter, and to the other disciple whom Jesus loves, and says to them, “They have taken away the Lord out of the tomb, and we don’t know where they have laid him!”

Therefore Peter and the other disciple go out, and they go toward the tomb. They both run together. The other disciple outran Peter, and comes to the tomb first. Stooping and looking in, he sees the linen cloths lying, yet he doesn’t enter in. Then Simon Peter comes, following him, and enters into the tomb. He sees the linen cloths lying, and the cloth that has been on his head, not lying with the linen cloths, but rolls up in a place by itself. So then the other disciple who comes first to the tomb also enters in, and he sees and believes. For as yet they don’t know the Scripture, that he must rise from the dead. So the disciples go away again to their own homes.
Mary Magdalene Meets the Risen Jesus · 20:11–18

But Mary is standing outside at the tomb weeping. So, as she weeps, she stoops and looks into the tomb, and she sees two angels in white sitting, one at the head, and one at the feet, where the body of Jesus has lain. They tell her, “Woman, why are you weeping?”

She says to them, “Because they have taken away my Lord, and I don’t know where they have laid him.” When she has said this, she turns around and sees Jesus standing, and doesn’t know that it is Jesus.
Jesus says to her, “Woman, why are you weeping? Who are you looking for?”
She, supposing him to be the gardener, says to him, “Sir, if you have carried him away, tell me where you have laid him, and I will take him away.”
Jesus says to her, “Mary.”
She turns and says to him, “Rabboni!” which is to say, “Teacher!”
Jesus says to her, “Don’t hold me, for I haven’t yet ascended to my Father; but go to my brothers, and tell them, ‘I am ascending to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God.’”
Mary Magdalene comes and tells the disciples that she has seen the Lord, and that he has said these things to her.
The Risen Jesus Appears to the Disciples · 20:19–23

When therefore it is evening, on that day, the first day of the week, and when the doors are locked where the disciples are assembled, for fear of the Jews, Jesus comes and stands in the middle, and says to them, “Peace be to you.”

When he has said this, he shows them his hands and his side. The disciples therefore are glad when they see the Lord. Jesus therefore says to them again, “Peace be to you. As the Father has sent me, even so I send you.” When he has said this, he breathes on them, and says to them, “Receive the Holy Spirit! If you forgive anyone’s sins, they have been forgiven them. If you retain anyone’s sins, they have been retained.”
Thomas · 20:24–29
But Thomas, one of the twelve, called Didymus, isn’t with them when Jesus comes. The other disciples therefore say to him, “We have seen the Lord!”
But he says to them, “Unless I see in his hands the print of the nails, put my finger into the print of the nails, and put my hand into his side, I will not believe.”

After eight days again his disciples are inside, and Thomas is with them. Jesus comes, the doors being locked, and stands in the middle, and says, “Peace be to you.” Then he says to Thomas, “Reach here your finger, and see my hands. Reach here your hand, and put it into my side. Don’t be unbelieving, but believing.”
Thomas answers him, “My Lord and my God!”
Jesus says to him, “Because you have seen me, you have believed. Blessed are those who have not seen, and have believed.”
The Purpose of the Gospel · 20:30–31

Therefore Jesus does many other signs in the presence of his disciples, which are not written in this book; but these are written, that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that believing you may have life in his name.
The Lakeside Appearance · 21:1–14

After these things, Jesus reveals himself again to the disciples at the sea of Tiberias. He reveals himself this way. Simon Peter, Thomas calls Didymus, Nathanael of Cana in Galilee, and the sons of Zebedee, and two others of his disciples are together. Simon Peter says to them, “I’m going fishing.”

They tell him, “We are also coming with you.” They immediately go out, and enter into the boat. That night, they catch nothing. But when day has already come, Jesus stands on the beach, yet the disciples don’t know that it is Jesus. Jesus therefore says to them, “Children, have you anything to eat?”
They answer him, “No.”
He says to them, “Cast the net on the right side of the boat, and you will find some.”
They cast it therefore, and now they aren’t able to draw it in for the multitude of fish. That disciple therefore whom Jesus loves says to Peter, “It’s the Lord!”

So when Simon Peter hears that it is the Lord, he wraps his coat around him (for he is naked), and throws himself into the sea. But the other disciples come in the little boat (for they are not far from the land, but about two hundred cubits away), dragging the net full of fish. So when they get out on the land, they see a fire of coals there, and fish lays on it, and bread. Jesus says to them, “Bring some of the fish which you have just caught.”
Simon Peter goes up, and draws the net to land, full of great fish, one hundred fifty-three; and even though there are so many, the net isn’t torn.
Jesus says to them, “Come and eat breakfast.”
None of the disciples dares inquire of him, “Who are you?” knowing that it is the Lord.
Then Jesus comes and takes the bread, gives it to them, and the fish likewise. This is now the third time that Jesus is revealed to his disciples, after he has risen from the dead.
The Restoration of Peter · 21:15–19
So when they have eaten their breakfast, Jesus says to Simon Peter, “Simon, son of Jonah, do you love me more than these?”
He says to him, “Yes, Lord; you know that I have affection for you.”
He says to him, “Feed my lambs.” He says to him again a second time, “Simon, son of Jonah, do you love me?”
He says to him, “Yes, Lord; you know that I have affection for you.”
He says to him, “Tend my sheep.” He says to him the third time, “Simon, son of Jonah, do you have affection for me?”
Peter is grieved because he asks him the third time, “Do you have affection for me?” He says to him, “Lord, you know everything. You know that I have affection for you.”

Jesus says to him, “Feed my sheep. Truly I tell you, when you were young, you dressed yourself, and walked where you wanted to. But when you are old, you will stretch out your hands, and another will dress you, and carry you where you don’t want to go.”
Now he says this, signifying by what kind of death he would glorify God. When he has said this, he says to him, “Follow me.”
The Beloved Disciple · 21:20–25

Then Peter, turning around, sees a disciple following. This is the disciple whom Jesus loves, the one who has also leaned on Jesus’ breast at the supper and asks, “Lord, who is going to betray You?” Peter seeing him, says to Jesus, “Lord, what about this man?”

Jesus says to him, “If I desire that he stay until I come, what is that to you? You follow me.” This saying therefore goes out among the brothers, that this disciple wouldn’t die. Yet Jesus doesn’t say to him that he wouldn’t die, but, “If I desire that he stay until I come, what is that to you?” This is the disciple who testifies about these things, and writes these things. We know that his witness is true. There are also many other things which Jesus does, which if they would all be written, I suppose that even the world itself wouldn’t have room for the books that would be written.
Prologue · 1:1–5

The first book I write, Theophilus, concerned all that Jesus begins both to do and to teach, until the day in which he is received up, after he has given commandment through the Holy Spirit to the apostles whom he has chosen. To these he also shows himself alive after he suffers, by many proofs, appearing to them over a period of forty days, and speaking about God’s Kingdom. Being assembled together with them, he commands them, “Don’t depart from Jerusalem, but wait for the promise of the Father, which you heard from me. For John indeed baptized in water, but you will be baptized in the Holy Spirit not many days from now.”
The Ascension · 1:6–11
Therefore when they have come together, they ask him, “Lord, are you now restoring the kingdom to Israel?”

He says to them, “It isn’t for you to know times or seasons which the Father has set within his own authority. But you will receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you. You will be witnesses to me in Jerusalem, in all Judea and Samaria, and to the uttermost parts of the earth.”

When he has said these things, as they are looking, he is taken up, and a cloud receives him out of their sight. While they are looking steadfastly into the sky as he goes, look, two men stand by them in white clothing, who also says, “You men of Galilee, why do you stand looking into the sky? This Jesus, who was received up from you into the sky, will come back in the same way as you saw him going into the sky.”
Return to Jerusalem · 1:12–14

Then they return to Jerusalem from the mountain called Olivet, which is near Jerusalem, a Sabbath day’s journey away. When they have come in, they go up into the upper room, where they are staying; that is Peter, John, James, Andrew, Philip, Thomas, Bartholomew, Matthew, James the son of Alphaeus, Simon the Zealot, and Judas the son of James. All these with one accord continued steadfastly in prayer and supplication, along with the women, and Mary the mother of Jesus, and with his brothers.
Matthias Chosen · 1:15–26

In these days, Peter stands up in the middle of the disciples (and the number of names is about one hundred twenty), and says, “Brothers, it was necessary that this Scripture should be fulfilled, which the Holy Spirit spoke before by the mouth of David concerning Judas, who was guide to those who took Jesus. For he was counted with us, and received his portion in this ministry. Now this man obtained a field with the reward for his wickedness, and falling headlong, his body burst open, and all his intestines gushed out. It became known to everyone who lived in Jerusalem that in their language that field was called ‘Akeldama,’ that is, ‘The field of blood.’ For it is written in the book of Psalms,
‘Let his habitation be made desolate.
Let no one dwell therein;’
and,
‘Let another take his office.’

“Of the men therefore who have accompanied us all the time that the Lord Jesus went in and out among us, beginning from the baptism of John, to the day that he was received up from us, of these one must become a witness with us of his resurrection.”

They put forward two, Joseph calls Barsabbas, who is also called Justus, and Matthias. They pray, and say, “You, Lord, who know the hearts of all men, show which one of these two you have chosen to take part in this ministry and apostleship from which Judas fell away, that he might go to his own place.” They draw lots for them, and the lot falls on Matthias, and he is counted with the eleven apostles.
The Day of Pentecost · 2:1–13

Now when the day of Pentecost has come, they are all with one accord in one place. Suddenly there comes from the sky a sound like the rushing of a mighty wind, and it fills all the house where they are sitting. Tongues like fire appear and are distributed to them, and one sits on each of them. They are all filled with the Holy Spirit, and begin to speak with other languages, as the Spirit gives them the ability to speak. Now there are dwelling in Jerusalem Jews, devout men, from every nation under the sky. When this sound is heard, the multitude comes together, and are bewildered, because everyone hears them speaking in his own language. They are all amazed and marvel, saying to one another, “Look, aren’t all these who speak Galileans? How do we hear, everyone in our own native language? Parthians, Medes, Elamites, and people from Mesopotamia, Judea, Cappadocia, Pontus, Asia, Phrygia, Pamphylia, Egypt, the parts of Libya around Cyrene, visitors from Rome, both Jews and proselytes, Cretans and Arabians: we hear them speaking in our languages the mighty works of God!” They are all amazed, and are perplexed, saying to one another, “What does this mean?” Others, mocking, say, “They are filled with new wine.”
Peter’s Sermon · 2:14–36

But Peter, standing up with the eleven, lifts up his voice, and speaks out to them, “You men of Judea, and all you who dwell at Jerusalem, let this be known to you, and listen to my words. For these aren’t drunken, as you suppose, seeing it is only the third hour of the day. But this is what has been spoken through the prophet Joel:
‘It will be in the last days, says God,
that I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh.
Your sons and your daughters will prophesy.
Your young men will see visions.
Your old men will dream dreams.
Yes, and on my servants and on my handmaidens in those days,
I will pour out my Spirit, and they will prophesy.
I will show wonders in the sky above,
and signs on the earth beneath;
blood, and fire, and billows of smoke.
The sun will be turned into darkness,
and the moon into blood,
before the great and glorious day of the Lord comes.
It will be that whoever will call on the name of the Lord will be saved.’

“Men of Israel, hear these words! Jesus of Nazareth, a man approved by God to you by mighty works and wonders and signs which God did by him among you, even as you yourselves know, him, being delivered up by the determined counsel and foreknowledge of God, you have taken by the hand of lawless men, crucified and killed; whom God raised up, having freed him from the agony of death, because it was not possible that he should be held by it. For David says concerning him,
‘I saw the Lord always before my face,
For he is on my right hand, that I should not be moved.
Therefore my heart was glad, and my tongue rejoiced.
Moreover my flesh also will dwell in hope;
because you will not leave my soul in Hades,
neither will you allow your Holy One to see decay.
You made known to me the ways of life.
You will make me full of gladness with your presence.’

“Brothers, I may tell you freely of the patriarch David, that he both died and was buried, and his tomb is with us to this day. Therefore, being a prophet, and knowing that God had sworn with an oath to him that of the fruit of his body, according to the flesh, he would raise up the Christ to sit on his throne, he foreseeing this spoke about the resurrection of the Christ, that his soul wasn’t left in Hades, and his flesh didn’t see decay. This Jesus God raised up, to which we all are witnesses. Being therefore exalted by the right hand of God, and having received from the Father the promise of the Holy Spirit, he has poured out this, which you now see and hear. For David didn’t ascend into the heavens, but he says himself,
‘The Lord said to my Lord, “Sit by my right hand,
until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet.”’
“Let all the house of Israel therefore know certainly that God has made him both Lord and Christ, this Jesus whom you crucified.”
Three Thousand Added · 2:37–41
Now when they hear this, they are cut to the heart, and say to Peter and the rest of the apostles, “Brothers, what should we do?”

Peter says to them, “Repent, and be baptized, every one of you, in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of sins, and you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit. For the promise is to you, and to your children, and to all who are far off, even as many as the Lord our God will call to himself.” With many other words he testifies, and exhorts them, saying, “Save yourselves from this crooked generation!”
Then those who gladly receive his word are baptized. There are added that day about three thousand souls.
Life Together · 2:42–47

They continue steadfastly in the apostles’ teaching and fellowship, in the breaking of bread, and prayer. Fear comes on every soul, and many wonders and signs are done through the apostles. All who believe are together, and have all things in common. They sell their possessions and goods, and distribute them to all, according as anyone has need. Day by day, continuing steadfastly with one accord in the temple, and breaking bread at home, they take their food with gladness and singleness of heart, praising God, and having favor with all the people. The Lord adds to the assembly day by day those who are being saved.
Healing at the Beautiful Gate · 3:1–10

Peter and John are going up into the temple at the hour of prayer, the ninth hour. A certain man who is lame from his mother’s womb is being carried, whom they lay daily at the door of the temple which is called Beautiful, to ask gifts for the needy of those who enter into the temple. Seeing Peter and John about to go into the temple, he asks to receive gifts for the needy. Peter, fastening his eyes on him, with John, says, “Look at us.” He listens to them, expecting to receive something from them. But Peter says, “I have no silver or gold, but what I have, that I give you. In the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, get up and walk!” He takes him by the right hand, and raises him up. Immediately his feet and his ankle bones receive strength. Leaping up, he stands, and begins to walk. He enters with them into the temple, walking, leaping, and praising God. All the people see him walking and praising God. They recognize him, that it is he who uses to sit begging for gifts for the needy at the Beautiful Gate of the temple. They are filled with wonder and amazement at what has happened to him.
Peter’s Speech at Solomon’s Portico · 3:11–26
As the lame man who is healed held on to Peter and John, all the people run together to them in the porch that is called Solomon’s, greatly wondering.

When Peter sees it, he responds to the people, “You men of Israel, why do you marvel at this man? Why do you fasten your eyes on us, as though by our own power or godliness we had made him walk? The God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, the God of our fathers, has glorified his Servant Jesus, whom you delivered up, and denied in the presence of Pilate, when he had determined to release him. But you denied the Holy and Righteous One, and asked for a murderer to be granted to you, and killed the Prince of life, whom God raised from the dead, to which we are witnesses. By faith in his name, his name has made this man strong, whom you see and know. Yes, the faith which is through him has given him this perfect soundness in the presence of you all.
“Now, brothers, I know that you did this in ignorance, as did also your rulers. But the things which God announced by the mouth of all his prophets, that Christ should suffer, he thus fulfilled.

“Repent therefore, and turn again, that your sins may be blotted out, so that there may come times of refreshing from the presence of the Lord, and that he may send Christ Jesus, who was ordained for you before, whom heaven must receive until the times of restoration of all things, which God spoke long ago by the mouth of his holy prophets.
