For Moses indeed said to the fathers, ‘The Lord God will raise up a prophet for you from among your brothers, like me. You will listen to him in all things whatever he says to you. It will be that every soul that will not listen to that prophet will be utterly destroyed from among the people.’ Yes, and all the prophets from Samuel and those who followed after, as many as have spoken, they also told of these days. You are the children of the prophets, and of the covenant which God made with our fathers, saying to Abraham, ‘In your offspring will all the families of the earth be blessed.’ God, having raised up his servant Jesus, sent him to you first to bless you, in turning away every one of you from your wickedness.”
Peter and John Before the Council · 4:1–22

As they speak to the people, the priests and the captain of the temple and the Sadducees come to them, being upset because they teach the people and proclaim in Jesus the resurrection from the dead. They lay hands on them, and put them in custody until the next day, for it is now evening. But many of those who hear the word believes, and the number of the men come to be about five thousand.

In the morning, their rulers, elders, and scribes are gathered together in Jerusalem. Annas the high priest is there, with Caiaphas, John, Alexander, and as many as were relatives of the high priest. When they have stood Peter and John in the middle of them, they inquire, “By what power, or in what name, have you done this?”

Then Peter, filled with the Holy Spirit, says to them, “You rulers of the people, and elders of Israel, if we are examined today concerning a good deed done to a crippled man, by what means this man has been healed, be it known to you all, and to all the people of Israel, that in the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, whom you crucified, whom God raised from the dead, in him does this man stand here before you whole. He is ‘the stone which was regarded as worthless by you, the builders, which has become the head of the corner.’ There is salvation in none other, for neither is there any other name under heaven, that is given among men, by which we must be saved!”

Now when they see the boldness of Peter and John, and have perceived that they are unlearned and ignorant men, they marvel. They recognize that they have been with Jesus. Seeing the man who is healed standing with them, they can say nothing against it. But when they have commanded them to go aside out of the council, they confer among themselves, saying, “What should we do to these men? Because indeed a notable miracle has been done through them, as can be plainly seen by all who dwell in Jerusalem, and we can’t deny it. But so that this spreads no further among the people, let’s threaten them, that from now on they don’t speak to anyone in this name.” They call them, and command them not to speak at all nor teach in the name of Jesus.
But Peter and John answer them, “Whether it is right in the sight of God to listen to you rather than to God, judge for yourselves, for we can’t help telling the things which we saw and heard.”

When they have further threatened them, they let them go, finding no way to punish them, because of the people; for everyone glorifies God for that which is done. For the man on whom this miracle of healing is performed is more than forty years old.
The Believers’ Prayer · 4:23–31

Being let go, they come to their own company, and report all that the chief priests and the elders have said to them. When they hear it, they lift up their voice to God with one accord, and say, “O Lord, you are God, who made the heaven, the earth, the sea, and all that is in them; who by the mouth of your servant, David, said,
‘Why do the nations rage,
and the peoples plot a vain thing?
The kings of the earth take a stand,
and the rulers take council together,
against the Lord, and against his Christ.’

“For truly, in this city against your holy servant, Jesus, whom you anointed, both Herod and Pontius Pilate, with the Gentiles and the people of Israel, were gathered together to do whatever your hand and your council foreordained to happen. Now, Lord, look at their threats, and grant to your servants to speak your word with all boldness, while you stretch out your hand to heal; and that signs and wonders may be done through the name of your holy Servant Jesus.”
When they have prayed, the place is shaken where they are gathered together. They are all filled with the Holy Spirit, and they speak the word of God with boldness.
All Things in Common · 4:32–37

The multitude of those who believe are of one heart and soul. Not one of them claims that anything of the things which he possesses is his own, but they have all things in common. With great power, the apostles give their testimony of the resurrection of the Lord Jesus. Great grace is on them all. For neither is there among them any who lacks, for as many as were owners of lands or houses sells them, and brings the proceeds of the things that are sold, and lay them at the apostles’ feet, and distribution is made to each, according as anyone has need. Joses, who by the apostles is also called Barnabas (which is, being interpreted, Son of Encouragement), a Levite, a man of Cyprus by race, having a field, sells it, and brings the money and lays it at the apostles’ feet.
Ananias and Sapphira · 5:1–11

But a certain man named Ananias, with Sapphira, his wife, sells a possession, and keeps back part of the price, his wife also being aware of it, and brings a certain part, and lays it at the apostles’ feet. But Peter says, “Ananias, why has Satan filled your heart to lie to the Holy Spirit, and to keep back part of the price of the land? While you kept it, didn’t it remain your own? After it was sold, wasn’t it in your power? How is it that you have conceived this thing in your heart? You haven’t lied to men, but to God.”

Ananias, hearing these words, falls down and dies. Great fear comes on all who hear these things. The young men arise and wrap him up, and they carry him out and bury him. About three hours later, his wife, not knowing what has happened, come in. Peter answers her, “Tell me whether you sold the land for so much.”
She says, “Yes, for so much.”
But Peter asks her, “How is it that you have agreed together to tempt the Spirit of the Lord? Look, the feet of those who have buried your husband are at the door, and they will carry you out.”

She falls down immediately at his feet, and dies. The young men come in and find her dead, and they carry her out and bury her by her husband. Great fear comes on the whole assembly, and on all who hear these things.
Signs and Wonders · 5:12–16

By the hands of the apostles many signs and wonders are done among the people. They are all with one accord in Solomon’s porch. None of the rest dares to join them, however the people honor them. More believers are added to the Lord, multitudes of both men and women. They even carry out the sick into the streets, and lay them on cots and mattresses, so that as Peter comes by, at the least his shadow might overshadow some of them. The multitude also comes together from the cities around Jerusalem, bringing sick people, and those who are tormented by unclean spirits: and they are all healed.
The Apostles Arrested Again · 5:17–42

But the high priest rises up, and all those who are with him (which is the sect of the Sadducees), and they are filled with jealousy, and lay hands on the apostles, and put them in public custody. But an angel of the Lord opens the prison doors by night, and brings them out, and says, “Go stand and speak in the temple to the people all the words of this life.”

When they hear this, they enter into the temple about daybreak, and taught. But the high priest comes, and those who are with him, and calls the council together, and all the senate of the children of Israel, and sends to the prison to have them brought. But the officers who come don’t find them in the prison. They return and report, “We found the prison shut and locked, and the guards standing before the doors, but when we opened them, we found no one inside!”

Now when the high priest, the captain of the temple, and the chief priests hears these words, they are very perplexed about them and what might become of this. One comes and tells them, “Look, the men whom you put in prison are in the temple, standing and teaching the people.” Then the captain goes with the officers, and brings them without violence, for they are afraid that the people might stone them.

When they have brought them, they set them before the council. The high priest questions them, saying, “Didn’t we strictly command you not to teach in this name? Look, you have filled Jerusalem with your teaching, and intend to bring this man’s blood on us.”

But Peter and the apostles answer, “We must obey God rather than men. The God of our fathers raised up Jesus, whom you killed, hanging him on a tree. God exalted him with his right hand to be a Prince and a Savior, to give repentance to Israel, and remission of sins. We are His witnesses of these things; and so also is the Holy Spirit, whom God has given to those who obey him.”

But they, when they hear this, are cut to the heart, and are determined to kill them. But one stands up in the council, a Pharisee named Gamaliel, a teacher of the law, honored by all the people, and commands to put the apostles out for a little while. He says to them, “You men of Israel, be careful concerning these men, what you are about to do. For before these days Theudas rose up, making himself out to be somebody; to whom a number of men, about four hundred, joined themselves: who was slain; and all, as many as obeyed him, were dispersed, and came to nothing. After this man, Judas of Galilee rose up in the days of the enrollment, and drew away some people after him. He also perished, and all, as many as obeyed him, were scattered abroad. Now I tell you, withdraw from these men, and leave them alone. For if this counsel or this work is of men, it will be overthrown. But if it is of God, you will not be able to overthrow it, and you would be found even to be fighting against God!”

They agree with him. Summoning the apostles, they beat them and command them not to speak in the name of Jesus, and let them go. They therefore depart from the presence of the council, rejoicing that they are counted worthy to suffer dishonor for Jesus’ name.
Every day, in the temple and at home, they never stop teaching and preaching Jesus, the Christ.
The Seven Chosen · 6:1–7

Now in those days, when the number of the disciples is multiplying, a complaint arises from the Hellenists against the Hebrews, because their widows are neglected in the daily service. The twelve summons the multitude of the disciples and says, “It is not appropriate for us to forsake the word of God and serve tables. Therefore select from among you, brothers, seven men of good report, full of the Holy Spirit and of wisdom, whom we may appoint over this business. But we will continue steadfastly in prayer and in the ministry of the word.”

These words please the whole multitude. They choose Stephen, a man full of faith and of the Holy Spirit, Philip, Prochorus, Nicanor, Timon, Parmenas, and Nicolaus, a proselyte of Antioch; whom they set before the apostles. When they have prayed, they lay their hands on them. The word of God increases and the number of the disciples multiplied in Jerusalem exceedingly. A great company of the priests are obedient to the faith.
Stephen Arrested · 6:8–15

Stephen, full of faith and power, performs great wonders and signs among the people. But some of those who are of the synagogue call “The Libertines”, and of the Cyrenians, of the Alexandrians, and of those of Cilicia and Asia arises, disputing with Stephen. They aren’t able to withstand the wisdom and the Spirit by which he speaks. Then they secretly induce men to say, “We have heard him speak blasphemous words against Moses and God.” They stir up the people, the elders, and the scribes, and come against him and seize him, and bring him in to the council, and set up false witnesses who say, “This man never stops speaking blasphemous words against this holy place and the law. For we have heard him say that this Jesus of Nazareth will destroy this place, and will change the customs which Moses delivered to us.” All who sit in the council, fastening their eyes on him, see his face like it is the face of an angel.
Stephen’s Defense: Abraham and the Patriarchs · 7:1–22
The high priest says, “Are these things so?”

He says, “Brothers and fathers, listen. The God of glory appeared to our father Abraham, when he was in Mesopotamia, before he lived in Haran, and said to him, ‘Get out of your land, and from your relatives, and come into a land which I will show you.’ Then he came out of the land of the Chaldaeans, and lived in Haran. From there, when his father was dead, God moved him into this land, where you are now living. He gave him no inheritance in it, no, not so much as to set his foot on. He promised that he would give it to him for a possession, and to his offspring after him, when he still had no child. God spoke in this way: that his offspring would live as aliens in a strange land, and that they would be enslaved and mistreated for four hundred years. ‘I will judge the nation to which they will be in bondage,’ said God, ‘and after that will they come out, and serve me in this place.’ He gave him the covenant of circumcision. So Abraham became the father of Isaac, and circumcised him the eighth day. Isaac became the father of Jacob, and Jacob became the father of the twelve patriarchs.

“The patriarchs, moved with jealousy against Joseph, sold him into Egypt. God was with him, and delivered him out of all his afflictions, and gave him favor and wisdom before Pharaoh, king of Egypt. He made him governor over Egypt and all his house. Now a famine came over all the land of Egypt and Canaan, and great affliction. Our fathers found no food. But when Jacob heard that there was grain in Egypt, he sent out our fathers the first time. On the second time Joseph was made known to his brothers, and Joseph’s race was revealed to Pharaoh. Joseph sent, and summoned Jacob, his father, and all his relatives, seventy-five souls. Jacob went down into Egypt, and he died, himself and our fathers, and they were brought back to Shechem, and laid in the tomb that Abraham bought for a price in silver from the children of Hamor of Shechem.

“But as the time of the promise came close which God had sworn to Abraham, the people grew and multiplied in Egypt, until there arose a different king, who didn’t know Joseph. The same took advantage of our race, and mistreated our fathers, and forced them to throw out their babies, so that they wouldn’t stay alive. At that time Moses was born, and was exceedingly handsome. He was nourished three months in his father’s house. When he was thrown out, Pharaoh’s daughter took him up, and reared him as her own son. Moses was instructed in all the wisdom of the Egyptians. He was mighty in his words and works.
Moses, the Rejected Deliverer · 7:23–43

But when he was forty years old, it came into his heart to visit his brothers, the children of Israel. Seeing one of them suffer wrong, he defended him, and avenged him who was oppressed, striking the Egyptian. He supposed that his brothers understood that God, by his hand, was giving them deliverance; but they didn’t understand.

“The day following, he appeared to them as they fought, and urged them to be at peace again, saying, ‘Sirs, you are brothers. Why do you wrong one another?’ But he who did his neighbor wrong pushed him away, saying, ‘Who made you a ruler and a judge over us? Do you want to kill me, as you killed the Egyptian yesterday?’ Moses fled at this saying, and became a stranger in the land of Midian, where he became the father of two sons.

“When forty years were fulfilled, an angel of the Lord appeared to him in the wilderness of Mount Sinai, in a flame of fire in a bush. When Moses saw it, he wondered at the sight. As he came close to see, a voice of the Lord came to him, ‘I am the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob.’ Moses trembled, and dared not look. The Lord said to him, ‘Take off your sandals, for the place where you stand is holy ground. I have surely seen the affliction of my people that is in Egypt, and have heard their groaning. I have come down to deliver them. Now come, I will send you into Egypt.’

“This Moses, whom they refused, saying, ‘Who made you a ruler and a judge?’—God has sent him as both a ruler and a deliverer by the hand of the angel who appeared to him in the bush. This man led them out, having worked wonders and signs in Egypt, in the Red Sea, and in the wilderness for forty years. This is that Moses, who said to the children of Israel, ‘The Lord our God will raise up a prophet for you from among your brothers, like me.’ This is he who was in the assembly in the wilderness with the angel that spoke to him on Mount Sinai, and with our fathers, who received living revelations to give to us, to whom our fathers wouldn’t be obedient, but rejected him, and turned back in their hearts to Egypt, saying to Aaron, ‘Make us gods that will go before us, for as for this Moses, who led us out of the land of Egypt, we don’t know what has become of him.’ They made a calf in those days, and brought a sacrifice to the idol, and rejoiced in the works of their hands. But God turned, and gave them up to serve the army of the sky, as it is written in the book of the prophets,
‘Did you offer to me slain animals and sacrifices
forty years in the wilderness, O house of Israel?
You took up the tabernacle of Moloch,
the star of your god Rephan,
the figures which you made to worship.
I will carry you away beyond Babylon.’
The Temple and Its Limits · 7:44–53

“Our fathers had the tabernacle of the testimony in the wilderness, even as he who spoke to Moses commanded him to make it according to the pattern that he had seen; which also our fathers, in their turn, brought in with Joshua when they entered into the possession of the nations, whom God drove out before the face of our fathers, to the days of David, who found favor in the sight of God, and asked to find a habitation for the God of Jacob. But Solomon built him a house. However, the Most High doesn’t dwell in temples made with hands, as the prophet says,
‘heaven is my throne,
and the earth a footstool for my feet.
What kind of house will you build me?’ says the Lord.
‘Or what is the place of my rest?
Didn’t my hand make all these things?’

“You stiff-necked and uncircumcised in heart and ears, you always resist the Holy Spirit! As your fathers did, so you do. Which of the prophets didn’t your fathers persecute? They killed those who foretold the coming of the Righteous One, of whom you have now become betrayers and murderers. You received the law as it was ordained by angels, and didn’t keep it!”
The Stoning of Stephen · 7:54–60

Now when they hear these things, they are cut to the heart, and they gnash at him with their teeth. But he, being full of the Holy Spirit, looks up steadfastly into heaven, and sees the glory of God, and Jesus standing on the right hand of God, and says, “Look, I see the heavens opened, and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God!”

But they cry out with a loud voice, and stop their ears, and rush at him with one accord. They throw him out of the city, and stone him. The witnesses place their garments at the feet of a young man named Saul. They stone Stephen as he calls out, saying, “Lord Jesus, receive my spirit!” He kneels down, and cries with a loud voice, “Lord, don’t hold this sin against them!” When he has said this, he falls asleep.
Saul and the Scattering · 8:1–3

Saul is consenting to his death. A great persecution arises against the assembly which is in Jerusalem in that day. They are all scattered abroad throughout the regions of Judea and Samaria, except for the apostles. Devout men bury Stephen, and lament greatly over him. But Saul ravages the assembly, entering into every house, and drags both men and women off to prison.
Philip in Samaria · 8:4–25

Therefore those who are scattered abroad go around preaching the word. Philip goes down to the city of Samaria, and proclaims to them the Christ. The multitudes listen with one accord to the things that are spoken by Philip, when they hear and see the signs which he does. For unclean spirits comes out of many of those who have them. They come out, crying with a loud voice. Many who have been paralyzed and lame are healed. There is great joy in that city.

But there is a certain man, Simon by name, who uses to practice sorcery in the city, and amazes the people of Samaria, making himself out to be some great one, to whom they all listen, from the least to the greatest, saying, “This man is that great power of God.” They listen to him, because for a long time he has amazed them with his sorceries. But when they believe Philip preaching good news concerning God’s Kingdom and the name of Jesus Christ, they are baptized, both men and women. Simon himself also believes. Being baptized, he continues with Philip. Seeing signs and great miracles occurring, he is amazed.

Now when the apostles who are at Jerusalem hear that Samaria has received the word of God, they send Peter and John to them, who, when they have come down, prays for them, that they might receive the Holy Spirit; for as yet he has fallen on none of them. They have only been baptized in the name of Christ Jesus. Then they lay their hands on them, and they receive the Holy Spirit. Now when Simon sees that the Holy Spirit is given through the laying on of the apostles’ hands, he offers them money, saying, “Give me also this power, that whomever I lay my hands on may receive the Holy Spirit.” But Peter says to him, “May your silver perish with you, because you thought you could obtain the gift of God with money! You have neither part nor lot in this matter, for your heart isn’t right before God. Repent therefore of this, your wickedness, and ask God if perhaps the thought of your heart may be forgiven you. For I see that you are in the poison of bitterness and in the bondage of iniquity.”
Simon answers, “Pray for me to the Lord, that none of the things which you have spoken happen to me.”
They therefore, when they have testified and spoken the word of the Lord, return to Jerusalem, and preach the Good News to many villages of the Samaritans.
Philip and the Ethiopian Official · 8:26–40
But an angel of the Lord speaks to Philip, saying, “Arise, and go toward the south to the way that goes down from Jerusalem to Gaza. This is a desert.”

He arises and goes; and look, there is a man of Ethiopia, a eunuch of great authority under Candace, queen of the Ethiopians, who are over all her treasure, who has come to Jerusalem to worship. He is returning and sitting in his chariot, and is reading the prophet Isaiah.
The Spirit says to Philip, “Go near, and join yourself to this chariot.”
Philip runs to him, and hears him reading Isaiah the prophet, and says, “Do you understand what you are reading?”
He says, “How can I, unless someone explains it to me?” He begs Philip to come up and sit with him. Now the passage of the Scripture which he is reading is this,
“He was led as a sheep to the slaughter.
As a lamb before his shearer is silent,
so he doesn’t open his mouth.
In his humiliation, his judgment was taken away.
Who will declare His generation?
For his life is taken from the earth.”
The eunuch answers Philip, “Who is the prophet talking about? About himself, or about someone else?”

Philip opens his mouth, and beginning from this Scripture, preaches to him about Jesus. As they go on the way, they come to some water, and the eunuch says, “Look, here is water. What is keeping me from being baptized?”
He commands the chariot to stand still, and they both go down into the water, both Philip and the eunuch, and he baptizes him.

When they come up out of the water, the Spirit of the Lord catches Philip away, and the eunuch doesn’t see him any more, for he goes on his way rejoicing. But Philip is found at Azotus. Passing through, he preaches the Good News to all the cities, until he comes to Caesarea.
The Conversion of Saul · 9:1–19

But Saul, still breathing threats and slaughter against the disciples of the Lord, goes to the high priest, and asks for letters from him to the synagogues of Damascus, that if he finds any who are of the Way, whether men or women, he might bring them bound to Jerusalem. As he travels, he gets close to Damascus, and suddenly a light from the sky shines around him. He falls on the earth, and hears a voice saying to him, “Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?”
He says, “Who are you, Lord?”
The Lord says, “I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting. But rise up, and enter into the city, and you will be told what you must do.”

The men who travel with him stand speechless, hearing the sound, but seeing no one. Saul arises from the ground, and when his eyes are opened, he sees no one. They lead him by the hand, and bring him into Damascus. He is without sight for three days, and neither ate nor drank.
Now there is a certain disciple at Damascus named Ananias. The Lord says to him in a vision, “Ananias!”
He says, “Look, it’s me, Lord.”

The Lord says to him, “Arise, and go to the street which is called Straight, and inquire in the house of Judah for one named Saul, a man of Tarsus. For look, he is praying, and in a vision he has seen a man named Ananias coming in, and laying his hands on him, that he might receive his sight.”
But Ananias answers, “Lord, I have heard from many about this man, how much evil he did to your saints at Jerusalem. Here he has authority from the chief priests to bind all who call on your name.”

But the Lord says to him, “Go your way, for he is my chosen vessel to bear my name before the nations and kings, and the children of Israel. For I will show him how many things he must suffer for my name’s sake.”

Ananias departs, and enters into the house. Laying his hands on him, he says, “Brother Saul, the Lord, who appeared to you on the road by which you came, has sent me, that you may receive your sight, and be filled with the Holy Spirit.” Immediately something like scales fall from his eyes, and he receives his sight. He arises and is baptized. He takes food and is strengthened. Saul stays several days with the disciples who are at Damascus.
Saul Preaches and Escapes · 9:20–31

Immediately in the synagogues he proclaims the Christ, that he is the Son of God. All who hear him are amazed, and say, “Isn’t this he who in Jerusalem made havoc of those who called on this name? And he had come here intending to bring them bound before the chief priests!”

But Saul increases more in strength, and confounds the Jews who live at Damascus, proving that this is the Christ. When many days are fulfilled, the Jews conspire together to kill him, but their plot becomes known to Saul. They watch the gates both day and night that they might kill him, but his disciples take him by night, and let him down through the wall, lowering him in a basket. When Saul has come to Jerusalem, he tries to join himself to the disciples; but they are all afraid of him, not believing that he is a disciple. But Barnabas takes him, and brings him to the apostles, and declares to them how he has seen the Lord on the way, and that he has spoken to him, and how at Damascus he has preached boldly in the name of Jesus. He is with them entering into Jerusalem, preaching boldly in the name of the Lord Jesus. He speaks and disputed against the Hellenists, but they are seeking to kill him. When the brothers know it, they bring him down to Caesarea, and send him off to Tarsus. So the assemblies throughout all Judea and Galilee and Samaria have peace, and are built up. They are multiplied, walking in the fear of the Lord and in the comfort of the Holy Spirit.
Aeneas Healed, Tabitha Raised · 9:32–43

As Peter goes throughout all those parts, he comes down also to the saints who live at Lydda. There he finds a certain man named Aeneas, who has been bedridden for eight years, because he is paralyzed. Peter says to him, “Aeneas, Jesus Christ heals you. Get up and make your bed!” Immediately he arises. All who live at Lydda and in Sharon see him, and they turn to the Lord.

Now there is at Joppa a certain disciple named Tabitha, which when translated, means Dorcas. This woman is full of good works and acts of mercy which she does. In those days, she becomes sick, and dies. When they have washed her, they lay her in an upper room. As Lydda is near Joppa, the disciples, hearing that Peter is there, sends two men to him, imploring him not to delay in coming to them. Peter gets up and goes with them. When he has come, they bring him into the upper room. All the widows stand by him weeping, and showing the coats and garments which Dorcas has made while she is with them. Peter sends them all out, and kneels down and prays. Turning to the body, he says, “Tabitha, get up!” She opens her eyes, and when she sees Peter, she sits up. He gives her his hand, and raises her up. Calling the saints and widows, he presents her alive. And it becames known throughout all Joppa, and many believe in the Lord. He stays many days in Joppa with a tanner named Simon.
Cornelius’s Vision · 10:1–8

Now there is a certain man in Caesarea, Cornelius by name, a centurion of what is called the Italian Regiment, a devout man, and one who fears God with all his house, who gives gifts for the needy generously to the people, and always prays to God. At about the ninth hour of the day, he clearly sees in a vision an angel of God coming to him, and saying to him, “Cornelius!”
He, fastening his eyes on him, and being frightened, says, “What is it, Lord?”

He says to him, “Your prayers and your gifts to the needy have gone up for a memorial before God. Now send men to Joppa, and get Simon, who is also called Peter. He lodges with a tanner named Simon, whose house is by the seaside.

When the angel who spoke to him had departed, Cornelius called two of his household servants and a devout soldier of those who waited on him continually. Having explained everything to them, he sent them to Joppa.
Peter’s Vision · 10:9–23

Now on the next day as they were on their journey, and got close to the city, Peter went up on the housetop to pray at about noon. He became hungry and desired to eat, but while they were preparing, he fell into a trance. He saw heaven opened and a certain container descending to him, like a great sheet let down by four corners on the earth, in which were all kinds of four-footed animals of the earth, wild animals, reptiles, and birds of the sky. A voice came to him, “Rise, Peter, kill and eat!”
But Peter says, “Not so, Lord; for I have never eaten anything that is common or unclean.”

A voice comes to him again the second time, “What God has cleansed, you must not call unclean.” This is done three times, and immediately the vessel is received up into heaven. Now while Peter is very perplexed in himself what the vision which he has seen might mean, look, the men who are sent by Cornelius, having made inquiry for Simon’s house, stand before the gate, and call and ask whether Simon, who is also called Peter, is lodging there. While Peter is pondering the vision, the Spirit says to him, “Look, three men seek you. But arise, get down, and go with them, doubting nothing; for I have sent them.”
Peter goes down to the men, and says, “Look, I am he whom you seek. Why have you come?”

They say, “Cornelius, a centurion, a righteous man and one who fears God, and well spoken of by all the nation of the Jews, was directed by a holy angel to invite you to his house, and to listen to what you say.” So he calls them in and provides a place to stay. On the next day Peter arises and goes out with them, and some of the brothers from Joppa accompanies him.
Peter at Cornelius’s House · 10:24–48

On the next day they enter into Caesarea. Cornelius is waiting for them, having called together his relatives and his near friends. When Peter enters, Cornelius meets him, falls down at his feet, and worships him. But Peter raises him up, saying, “Stand up! I myself am also a man.” As he talks with him, he goes in and finds many gathered together. He says to them, “You yourselves know how it is an unlawful thing for a man who is a Jew to join himself or come to one of another nation, but God has shown me that I shouldn’t call any man unholy or unclean. Therefore also I came without complaint when I was sent for. I ask therefore, why did you send for me?”

Cornelius says, “Four days ago, I was fasting until this hour, and at the ninth hour, I prayed in my house, and look, a man stood before me in bright clothing, and said, ‘Cornelius, your prayer is heard, and your gifts to the needy are remembered in the sight of God. Send therefore to Joppa, and summon Simon, who is also called Peter. He lodges in the house of a tanner named Simon, by the seaside. When he comes, he will speak to you.’ Therefore I sent to you at once, and it was good of you to come. Now therefore we are all here present in the sight of God to hear all things that have been commanded you by God.”

Peter opens his mouth and says, “Truly I perceive that God doesn’t show favoritism; but in every nation he who fears him and works righteousness is acceptable to him. The word which he sent to the children of Israel, preaching good news of peace by Jesus Christ—he is Lord of all— you yourselves know what happened, which was proclaimed throughout all Judea, beginning from Galilee, after the baptism which John preached; even Jesus of Nazareth, how God anointed him with the Holy Spirit and with power, who went about doing good and healing all who were oppressed by the devil, for God was with him. We are witnesses of everything he did both in the country of the Jews, and in Jerusalem; whom they also killed, hanging him on a tree. God raised him up the third day, and gave him to be revealed, not to all the people, but to witnesses who were chosen before by God, to us, who ate and drank with him after he rose from the dead. He commanded us to preach to the people and to testify that this is he who is appointed by God as the Judge of the living and the dead. All the prophets testify about him, that through his name everyone who believes in him will receive remission of sins.”

While Peter is still speaking these words, the Holy Spirit falls on all those who hear the word. They of the circumcision who believes are amazed, as many as come with Peter, because the gift of the Holy Spirit is also poured out on the Gentiles. For they hear them speaking in other languages and magnifying God.

Then Peter answers, “Can anyone forbid these people from being baptized with water? They have received the Holy Spirit just like us.” He commands them to be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ. Then they ask him to stay some days.
Peter’s Report in Jerusalem · 11:1–18

Now the apostles and the brothers who are in Judea hear that the Gentiles has also received the word of God. When Peter has come up to Jerusalem, those who are of the circumcision contend with him, saying, “You went in to uncircumcised men, and ate with them!”

But Peter begins, and explains to them in order, saying, “I was in the city of Joppa praying, and in a trance I saw a vision: a certain container descending, like it was a great sheet let down from heaven by four corners. It came as far as me. When I had looked intently at it, I considered, and saw the four-footed animals of the earth, wild animals, creeping things, and birds of the sky. I also heard a voice saying to me, ‘Rise, Peter, kill and eat!’ But I said, ‘Not so, Lord, for nothing unholy or unclean has ever entered into my mouth.’ But a voice answered me the second time out of heaven, ‘What God has cleansed, don’t you call unclean.’ This was done three times, and all were drawn up again into heaven. Look, immediately three men stood before the house where I was, having been sent from Caesarea to me. The Spirit told me to go with them, without discriminating. These six brothers also accompanied me, and we entered into the man’s house. He told us how he had seen the angel standing in his house, and saying to him, ‘Send to Joppa, and get Simon, who is called Peter, who will speak to you words by which you will be saved, you and all your house.’ As I began to speak, the Holy Spirit fell on them, even as on us at the beginning. I remembered the word of the Lord, how he said, ‘John indeed baptized in water, but you will be baptized in the Holy Spirit.’ If then God gave to them the same gift as us, when we believed in the Lord Jesus Christ, who was I, that I could withstand God?”
When they hear these things, they hold their peace, and glorify God, saying, “Then God has also granted to the Gentiles repentance to life!”
The Church at Antioch · 11:19–30

They therefore who are scattered abroad by the oppression that arises about Stephen travels as far as Phoenicia, Cyprus, and Antioch, speaking the word to no one except to Jews only. But there are some of them, men of Cyprus and Cyrene, who, when they have come to Antioch, speak to the Hellenists, preaching the Lord Jesus. The hand of the Lord is with them, and a great number believed and turns to the Lord. The report concerning them comes to the ears of the assembly which are in Jerusalem. They send out Barnabas to go as far as Antioch, who, when he has come, and has seen the grace of God, is glad. He exhorts them all, that with purpose of heart they should remain near to the Lord. For he is a good man, and full of the Holy Spirit and of faith, and many people are added to the Lord.

Barnabas goes out to Tarsus to look for Saul. When he has found him, he brings him to Antioch. For a whole year they are gathered together with the assembly, and teach many people. The disciples are first called Christians in Antioch.

Now in these days, prophets come down from Jerusalem to Antioch. One of them named Agabus stands up, and indicated by the Spirit that there should be a great famine all over the world, which also happens in the days of Claudius. As any of the disciples has plenty, each determines to send relief to the brothers who live in Judea; which they also do, sending it to the elders by the hands of Barnabas and Saul.
James Killed, Peter Imprisoned · 12:1–19

Now about that time, King Herod stretches out his hands to oppress some of the assembly. He kills James, the brother of John, with the sword. When he sees that it pleases the Jews, he proceeds to seize Peter also. This is during the days of unleavened bread. When he has arrested him, he puts him in prison, and delivers him to four squads of four soldiers each to guard him, intending to bring him out to the people after the Passover. Peter therefore is kept in the prison, but constant prayer is made by the assembly to God for him. The same night when Herod is about to bring him out, Peter is sleeping between two soldiers, bound with two chains. Guards in front of the door keep the prison.

And look, an angel of the Lord stands by him, and a light shone in the cell. He strikes Peter on the side, and wakes him up, saying, “Stand up quickly!” His chains fall off from his hands. The angel says to him, “Get dressed and put on your sandals.” He does so. He says to him, “Put on your cloak, and follow me.” And he goes out and follows him. He doesn’t know that what is being done by the angel is real, but thinks he sees a vision. When they are past the first and the second guard, they come to the iron gate that leads into the city, which opens to them by itself. They go out, and go down one street, and immediately the angel departs from him.

When Peter has come to himself, he says, “Now I truly know that the Lord has sent out his angel and delivered me out of the hand of Herod, and from everything the Jewish people were expecting.” Thinking about that, he comes to the house of Mary, the mother of John who is called Mark, where many are gathered together and are praying. When Peter knocks at the door of the gate, a maid named Rhoda comes to answer. When she recognizes Peter’s voice, she doesn’t open the gate for joy, but runs in, and reports that Peter is standing in front of the gate.

They say to her, “You are crazy!” But she insists that it is so. They say, “It is his angel.” But Peter continues knocking. When they have opened, they see him, and are amazed. But he, beckoning to them with his hand to be silent, declares to them how the Lord has brought him out of the prison. He says, “Tell these things to James, and to the brothers.” Then he departs, and goes to another place.

Now as soon as it is day, there is no small stir among the soldiers about what has become of Peter. When Herod has sought for him, and doesn’t find him, he examines the guards, and commands that they should be put to death. He goes down from Judea to Caesarea, and stays there.
The Death of Herod · 12:20–25

Now Herod is very angry with the people of Tyre and Sidon. They come with one accord to him, and, having made Blastus, the king’s personal aide, their friend, they ask for peace, because their country depends on the king’s country for food. On an appointed day, Herod dresses himself in royal clothing, sits on the throne, and gives a speech to them. The people shout, “The voice of a god, and not of a man!” Immediately an angel of the Lord strikes him, because he doesn’t give God the glory, and he is eaten by worms and dies.
But the word of God grows and multiplied. Barnabas and Saul return to Jerusalem, when they have fulfilled their service, also taking with them John who is called Mark.
Barnabas and Saul Sent Out · 13:1–3

Now in the assembly that is at Antioch there are some prophets and teachers: Barnabas, Simeon who is called Niger, Lucius of Cyrene, Manaen the foster brother of Herod the tetrarch, and Saul. As they serve the Lord and fast, the Holy Spirit says, “Separate Barnabas and Saul for me, for the work to which I have called them.”
Then, when they have fasted and pray and lay their hands on them, they send them away.
Cyprus · 13:4–12

So, being sent out by the Holy Spirit, they go down to Seleucia. From there they sail to Cyprus. When they are at Salamis, they proclaim God’s word in the Jewish synagogues. They have also John as their attendant. When they have gone through the island to Paphos, they find a certain sorcerer, a false prophet, a Jew, whose name is Bar Jesus, who is with the proconsul, Sergius Paulus, a man of understanding. This man summons Barnabas and Saul, and seeks to hear the word of God. But Elymas the sorcerer (for so is his name by interpretation) withstands them, seeking to turn the proconsul away from the faith. But Saul, who is also called Paul, filled with the Holy Spirit, fastens his eyes on him, and says, “Full of all deceit and all cunning, you son of the devil, you enemy of all righteousness, will you not cease to pervert the right ways of the Lord? Now, look, the hand of the Lord is on you, and you will be blind, not seeing the sun for a season!”

Immediately a mist and darkness fall on him. He goes around seeking someone to lead him by the hand. Then the proconsul, when he sees what is done, believed, being astonished at the teaching of the Lord.
Pisidian Antioch: the Sermon in the Synagogue · 13:13–41

Now Paul and his company set sail from Paphos, and come to Perga in Pamphylia. John departs from them and returns to Jerusalem. But they, passing on from Perga, come to Antioch of Pisidia. They go into the synagogue on the Sabbath day, and sit down. After the reading of the law and the prophets, the rulers of the synagogue sent to them, saying, “Brothers, if you have any word of exhortation for the people, speak.”

Paul stands up, and beckoning with his hand says, “Men of Israel, and you who fear God, listen. The God of this people chose our fathers, and exalted the people when they stayed as aliens in the land of Egypt, and with an uplifted arm, he led them out of it. For a period of about forty years he put up with them in the wilderness. When he had destroyed seven nations in the land of Canaan, he gave them their land for an inheritance, for about four hundred fifty years. After these things he gave them judges until Samuel the prophet. Afterward they asked for a king, and God gave to them Saul the son of Kish, a man of the tribe of Benjamin, for forty years. When he had removed him, he raised up David to be their king, to whom he also testified, ‘I have found David the son of Jesse, a man after my heart, who will do all my will.’ From this man’s offspring, God has brought salvation to Israel according to his promise, before his coming, when John had first preached the baptism of repentance to Israel. As John was fulfilling his course, he said, ‘What do you suppose that I am? I am not he. But look, one comes after me, the sandals of whose feet I am not worthy to untie.’ Brothers, children of the stock of Abraham, and those among you who fear God, the word of this salvation is sent out to you. For those who dwell in Jerusalem, and their rulers, because they didn’t know him, nor the voices of the prophets which are read every Sabbath, fulfilled them by condemning him. Though they found no cause for death, they still asked Pilate to have him killed. When they had fulfilled all things that were written about him, they took him down from the tree, and laid him in a tomb. But God raised him from the dead, and he was seen for many days by those who came up with him from Galilee to Jerusalem, who are his witnesses to the people. We bring you good news of the promise made to the fathers, that God has fulfilled the same to us, their children, in that he raised up Jesus. As it is also written in the second psalm,
‘You are my Son.
Today I have become your father.’

“Concerning that he raised him up from the dead, now no more to return to corruption, he has spoken thus: ‘I will give you the holy and sure blessings of David.’ Therefore he says also in another psalm, ‘You will not allow your Holy One to see decay.’ For David, after he had in his own generation served the counsel of God, fell asleep, and was laid with his fathers, and saw decay. But he whom God raised up saw no decay. Be it known to you therefore, brothers, that through this man is proclaimed to you remission of sins, and by him everyone who believes is justified from all things, from which you could not be justified by the law of Moses. Beware therefore, lest that come on you which is spoken in the prophets:
‘Look, you scoffers, and wonder, and perish;
for I work a work in your days,
a work which you will in no way believe, if one declares it to you.’”
Response and Second Sabbath · 13:42–52

So when the Jews go out of the synagogue, the Gentiles begs that these words might be preached to them the next Sabbath. Now when the synagogue breaks up, many of the Jews and of the devout proselytes follow Paul and Barnabas; who, speaking to them, urges them to continue in the grace of God. The next Sabbath, almost the whole city is gathered together to hear the word of God. But when the Jews see the multitudes, they are filled with jealousy, and contradict the things which are spoken by Paul, and blasphemed.

Paul and Barnabas speak out boldly, and say, “It was necessary that God’s word should be spoken to you first. Since indeed you thrust it from you, and judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life, look, we turn to the Gentiles. For so has the Lord commanded us, saying,
‘I have set you as a light for the Gentiles,
that you should bring salvation to the uttermost parts of the earth.’”

As the Gentiles hears this, they are glad, and glorify the word of God. As many as were appointed to eternal life believed. The Lord’s word is spread abroad throughout all the region. But the Jews stir up the devout and prominent women and the chief men of the city, and stir up a persecution against Paul and Barnabas, and throw them out of their borders. But they shake off the dust of their feet against them, and come to Iconium. The disciples are filled with joy and with the Holy Spirit.
Iconium · 14:1–7

In Iconium, they enter together into the synagogue of the Jews, and so speak that a great multitude both of Jews and of Greeks believe. But the disbelieving Jews stir up and embittered the souls of the Gentiles against the brothers. Therefore they stay there a long time, speaking boldly in the Lord, who testifies to the word of his grace, granting signs and wonders to be done by their hands. But the multitude of the city is divided. Part sides with the Jews, and part with the apostles. When some of both the Gentiles and the Jews, with their rulers, makes a violent attempt to mistreat and stone them, they become aware of it, and flee to the cities of Lycaonia, Lystra, Derbe, and the surrounding region. There they preach the Good News.
Lystra: Healing and Its Aftermath · 14:8–20

At Lystra a certain man sits, impotent in his feet, a cripple from his mother’s womb, who never has walked. He is listening to Paul speaking, who, fastening eyes on him, and seeing that he has faith to be made whole, says with a loud voice, “Stand upright on your feet!” He leaps up and walks. When the multitude sees what Paul has done, they lift up their voice, saying in the language of Lycaonia, “The gods have come down to us in the likeness of men!” They call Barnabas “Jupiter”, and Paul “Mercury”, because he is the chief speaker. The priest of Jupiter, whose temple is in front of their city, brings oxen and garlands to the gates, and would have made a sacrifice along with the multitudes. But when the apostles, Barnabas and Paul, hear of it, they tear their clothes, and spring into the multitude, crying out, “Men, why are you doing these things? We also are men of like passions with you, and bring you good news, that you should turn from these vain things to the living God, who made the sky, the earth, the sea, and all that is in them; who in the generations gone by allowed all the nations to walk in their own ways. Yet he didn’t leave himself without witness, in that he did good and gave you rains from the sky and fruitful seasons, filling our hearts with food and gladness.”

Even saying these things, they hardly stop the multitudes from making a sacrifice to them. But some Jews from Antioch and Iconium come there, and having persuaded the multitudes, they stone Paul, and drag him out of the city, supposing that he is dead.
But as the disciples stand around him, he rises up, and enters into the city. On the next day he goes out with Barnabas to Derbe.
The Return Journey · 14:21–28

When they have preached the Good News to that city, and have made many disciples, they return to Lystra, Iconium, and Antioch, confirming the souls of the disciples, exhorting them to continue in the faith, and that through many afflictions we must enter into God’s Kingdom. When they have appointed elders for them in every assembly, and have prayed with fasting, they commend them to the Lord, on whom they have believed.

They pass through Pisidia, and come to Pamphylia. When they have spoken the word in Perga, they go down to Attalia. From there they sail to Antioch, from where they have been committed to the grace of God for the work which they have fulfilled. When they have arrived, and have gathered the assembly together, they report all the things that God has done with them, and that he has opened a door of faith to the nations. They stay there with the disciples for a long time.
The Jerusalem Council · 15:1–21

Some men come down from Judea and teach the brothers, “Unless you are circumcised after the custom of Moses, you can’t be saved.” Therefore when Paul and Barnabas have no small discord and discussion with them, they appoint Paul and Barnabas, and some others of them, to go up to Jerusalem to the apostles and elders about this question. They, being sent on their way by the assembly, pass through both Phoenicia and Samaria, declaring the conversion of the Gentiles. They cause great joy to all the brothers. When they have come to Jerusalem, they are received by the assembly and the apostles and the elders, and they report all things that God has done with them.
But some of the sect of the Pharisees who believe rises up, saying, “It is necessary to circumcise them, and to command them to keep the law of Moses.”

The apostles and the elders are gathered together to see about this matter. When there has been much discussion, Peter rises up and says to them, “Brothers, you know that a good while ago God made a choice among you, that by my mouth the nations should hear the word of the Good News, and believe. God, who knows the heart, testified about them, giving them the Holy Spirit, just like he did to us. He made no distinction between us and them, cleansing their hearts by faith. Now therefore why do you tempt God, that you should put a yoke on the neck of the disciples which neither our fathers nor we were able to bear? But we believe that we are saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus, just as they are.”

All the multitude keeps silence, and they listen to Barnabas and Paul reporting what signs and wonders God has done among the nations through them. After they are silent, James answers, “Brothers, listen to me. Simeon has reported how God first visited the nations, to take out of them a people for his name. This agrees with the words of the prophets. As it is written,
‘After these things I will return.
I will again build the tabernacle of David, which has fallen.
I will again build its ruins.
I will set it up,
That the rest of men may seek after the Lord;
all the Gentiles who are called by my name,
says the Lord, who does all these things.
All of God’s works are known to him from eternity.’

“Therefore my judgment is that we don’t trouble those from among the Gentiles who turn to God, but that we write to them that they abstain from the pollution of idols, from sexual immorality, from what is strangled, and from blood. For Moses from generations of old has in every city those who preach him, being read in the synagogues every Sabbath.”
The Council’s Letter · 15:22–35

Then it seems good to the apostles and the elders, with the whole assembly, to choose men out of their company, and send them to Antioch with Paul and Barnabas: Judas calls Barsabbas, and Silas, chief men among the brothers. They write these things by their hand:

“The apostles, the elders, and the brothers, to the brothers who are of the Gentiles in Antioch, Syria, and Cilicia: greetings. Because we have heard that some who went out from us have troubled you with words, unsettling your souls, saying, ‘You must be circumcised and keep the law,’ to whom we gave no commandment; it seemed good to us, having come to one accord, to choose out men and send them to you with our beloved Barnabas and Paul, men who have risked their lives for the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. We have sent therefore Judas and Silas, who themselves will also tell you the same things by word of mouth. For it seemed good to the Holy Spirit, and to us, to lay no greater burden on you than these necessary things: that you abstain from things sacrificed to idols, from blood, from things strangled, and from sexual immorality, from which if you keep yourselves, it will be well with you. Farewell.”

So, when they are sent off, they come to Antioch. Having gathered the multitude together, they deliver the letter. When they have read it, they rejoice over the encouragement. Judas and Silas, also being prophets themselves, encourage the brothers with many words, and strengthen them. After they have spent some time there, they are sent back with greetings from the brothers to the apostles. But Paul and Barnabas stay in Antioch, teaching and preaching the word of the Lord, with many others also.
Paul and Barnabas Part Ways · 15:36–41

After some days Paul says to Barnabas, “Let’s return now and visit our brothers in every city in which we proclaimed the word of the Lord, to see how they are doing.” Barnabas plans to take John, who is called Mark, with them also. But Paul doesn’t think that it is a good idea to take with them someone who has withdrawn from them in Pamphylia, and doesn’t go with them to do the work. Then the contention grows so sharp that they separate from each other. Barnabas takes Mark with him, and sails away to Cyprus, but Paul chooses Silas, and goes out, being commended by the brothers to the grace of God. He goes through Syria and Cilicia, strengthening the assemblies.
Timothy Joins Paul · 16:1–5

He comes to Derbe and Lystra: and look, a certain disciple is there, named Timothy, the son of a Jewess who believes; but his father is a Greek. The brothers who are at Lystra and Iconium give a good testimony about him. Paul wants to have him go out with him, and he takes and circumcises him because of the Jews who are in those parts; for they all know that his father is a Greek. As they go on their way through the cities, they deliver the decrees to them to keep which has been ordained by the apostles and elders who are at Jerusalem. So the assemblies are strengthened in the faith, and increase in number daily.
The Macedonian Call · 16:6–10

When they have gone through the region of Phrygia and Galatia, they are forbidden by the Holy Spirit to speak the word in Asia. When they have come opposite Mysia, they try to go into Bithynia, but the Spirit doesn’t allow them. Passing by Mysia, they come down to Troas. A vision appears to Paul in the night. There is a man of Macedonia standing, begging him, and saying, “Come over into Macedonia and help us.” When he has seen the vision, immediately we seek to go out to Macedonia, concluding that the Lord has called us to preach the Good News to them.
Lydia in Philippi · 16:11–15

Setting sail therefore from Troas, we make a straight course to Samothrace, and the day following to Neapolis; and from there to Philippi, which is a city of Macedonia, the foremost of the district, a Roman colony. We are staying some days in this city.

On the Sabbath day we go outside of the city by a riverside, where we suppose there is a place of prayer, and we sit down, and speak to the women who have come together. A certain woman named Lydia, a seller of purple, of the city of Thyatira, one who worships God, hears us; whose heart the Lord opens to listen to the things which are spoken by Paul. When she and her household are baptized, she begs us, saying, “If you have judged me to be faithful to the Lord, come into my house, and stay.” So she persuades us.
Paul and Silas in Prison · 16:16–40

As we are going to prayer, a certain girl having a spirit of divination meets us, who brings her masters much gain by fortune telling. Following Paul and us, she cries out, “These men are servants of the Most High God, who proclaim to us a way of salvation!” She is doing this for many days.

But Paul, becoming greatly annoyed, turns and says to the spirit, “I command you in the name of Jesus Christ to come out of her!” It comes out that very hour. But when her masters see that the hope of their gain is gone, they seize Paul and Silas, and drag them into the marketplace before the rulers. When they have brought them to the magistrates, they say, “These men, being Jews, are agitating our city, and advocate customs which it is not lawful for us to accept or to observe, being Romans.”

The multitude rises up together against them, and the magistrates tear their clothes from them, and command them to be beaten with rods. When they have laid many stripes on them, they throw them into prison, charging the jailer to keep them safely, who, having received such a command, throws them into the inner prison, and secures their feet in the stocks.

But about midnight Paul and Silas are praying and singing hymns to God, and the prisoners are listening to them. Suddenly there is a great earthquake, so that the foundations of the prison are shaken; and immediately all the doors are opened, and everyone’s bonds are loosened. The jailer, being roused out of sleep and seeing the prison doors open, draws his sword and is about to kill himself, supposing that the prisoners have escaped. But Paul cries with a loud voice, saying, “Don’t harm yourself, for we are all here!”
He calls for lights, springs in, falls down trembling before Paul and Silas, brings them out, and says, “Sirs, what must I do to be saved?”
They say, “Believe in the Lord Jesus Christ, and you will be saved, you and your household.” They speak the word of the Lord to him, and to all who are in his house.

He takes them the same hour of the night, and washes their stripes, and is immediately baptized, he and all his household. He brings them up into his house, and sets food before them, and rejoices greatly, with all his household, having believed in God.
But when it is day, the magistrates send the sergeants, saying, “Let those men go.”
The jailer reports these words to Paul, saying, “The magistrates have sent to let you go; now therefore come out, and go in peace.”

But Paul says to them, “They have beaten us publicly, without a trial, men who are Romans, and have cast us into prison! Do they now release us secretly? No, most certainly, but let them come themselves and bring us out!”

The sergeants report these words to the magistrates, and they are afraid when they hear that they are Romans, and they come and beg them. When they have brought them out, they ask them to depart from the city. They go out of the prison, and enter into Lydia’s house. When they have seen the brothers, they encourage them, and depart.
Thessalonica and Berea · 17:1–15

Now when they have passed through Amphipolis and Apollonia, they come to Thessalonica, where there is a Jewish synagogue. Paul, as is his custom, goes in to them, and for three Sabbath days reasoned with them from the Scriptures, explaining and demonstrating that the Christ has to suffer and rise again from the dead, and saying, “This Jesus, whom I proclaim to you, is the Christ.”

Some of them are persuaded, and joins Paul and Silas, of the devout Greeks a great multitude, and not a few of the chief women. But the unpersuaded Jews take along some wicked men from the marketplace, and gathering a crowd, set the city in an uproar. Assaulting the house of Jason, they seek to bring them out to the people. When they don’t find them, they drag Jason and certain brothers before the rulers of the city, crying, “These who have turned the world upside down have come here also, whom Jason has received. These all act contrary to the decrees of Caesar, saying that there is another king, Jesus!” The multitude and the rulers of the city are troubled when they hear these things. When they have taken security from Jason and the rest, they let them go. The brothers immediately send Paul and Silas away by night to Beroea. When they arrive, they go into the Jewish synagogue.

Now these are more noble than those in Thessalonica, in that they receive the word with all readiness of mind, examining the Scriptures daily to see whether these things are so. Many of them therefore believe; also of the prominent Greek women, and not a few men. But when the Jews of Thessalonica have knowledge that the word of God is proclaimed by Paul at Beroea also, they come there likewise, agitating the multitudes. Then the brothers immediately send out Paul to go as far as to the sea, and Silas and Timothy still stay there. But those who escort Paul bring him as far as Athens. Receiving a commandment to Silas and Timothy that they should come to him very quickly, they depart.
Paul in Athens · 17:16–34

Now while Paul waits for them at Athens, his spirit is provoked within him as he sees the city full of idols. So he reasons in the synagogue with the Jews and the devout persons, and in the marketplace every day with those who meet him. Some of the Epicurean and Stoic philosophers also are conversing with him. Some says, “What does this babbler want to say?”
Others say, “He seems to be advocating foreign deities,” because he preaches Jesus and the resurrection.

They take hold of him, and bring him to the Areopagus, saying, “May we know what this new teaching is, which is spoken by you? For you bring certain strange things to our ears. We want to know therefore what these things mean.” Now all the Athenians and the strangers living there spend their time in nothing else, but either to tell or to hear some new thing.

Paul stands in the middle of the Areopagus, and says, “You men of Athens, I perceive that you are very religious in all things. For as I passed along, and observed the objects of your worship, I found also an altar with this inscription: ‘TO AN UNKNOWN GOD.’ What therefore you worship in ignorance, this I announce to you. The God who made the world and all things in it, he, being Lord of heaven and earth, doesn’t dwell in temples made with hands, neither is he served by men’s hands, as though he needed anything, seeing he himself gives to all life and breath, and all things. He made from one blood every nation of men to dwell on all the surface of the earth, having determined appointed seasons, and the boundaries of their dwellings, that they should seek the Lord, if perhaps they might reach out for him and find him, though he is not far from each one of us. ‘For in him we live, and move, and have our being.’ As some of your own poets have said, ‘For we are also his offspring.’ Being then the offspring of God, we ought not to think that the Divine Nature is like gold, or silver, or stone, engraved by art and design of man. The times of ignorance therefore God overlooked. But now he commands that all people everywhere should repent, because he has appointed a day in which he will judge the world in righteousness by the man whom he has ordained; of which he has given assurance to all men, in that he has raised him from the dead.”
Now when they hear of the resurrection of the dead, some mocks; but others say, “We want to hear you again concerning this.”
Thus Paul goes out from among them. But certain men join with him, and believe, among whom also is Dionysius the Areopagite, and a woman named Damaris, and others with them.
Corinth: Priscilla, Aquila, and Crispus · 18:1–17

After these things Paul departs from Athens, and comes to Corinth. He finds a certain Jew named Aquila, a man of Pontus by race, who has recently come from Italy, with his wife Priscilla, because Claudius has commanded all the Jews to depart from Rome. He comes to them, and because he practices the same trade, he lives with them and works, for by trade they are tent makers. He reasons in the synagogue every Sabbath, and persuades Jews and Greeks. But when Silas and Timothy come down from Macedonia, Paul is compelled by the Spirit, testifying to the Jews that Jesus is the Christ. When they oppose him and blaspheme, he shakes out his clothing and says to them, “Your blood be on your own heads! I am clean. From now on, I will go to the Gentiles!”

He departs there, and goes into the house of a certain man named Justus, one who worships God, whose house is next door to the synagogue. Crispus, the ruler of the synagogue, believes in the Lord with all his house. Many of the Corinthians, when they hear, believe and are baptized. The Lord says to Paul in the night by a vision, “Don’t be afraid, but speak and don’t be silent; for I am with you, and no one will attack you to harm you, for I have many people in this city.”

He lives there a year and six months, teaching the word of God among them. But when Gallio is proconsul of Achaia, the Jews with one accord rise up against Paul and bring him before the judgment seat, saying, “This man persuades men to worship God contrary to the law.”

But when Paul is about to open his mouth, Gallio says to the Jews, “If indeed it were a matter of wrong or of wicked crime, you Jews, it would be reasonable that I should bear with you; but if they are questions about words and names and your own law, look to it yourselves. For I don’t want to be a judge of these matters.” So he drives them from the judgment seat.
Then all the Greeks lay hold on Sosthenes, the ruler of the synagogue, and beat him before the judgment seat. Gallio doesn’t care about any of these things.
Return and Third Journey Begins · 18:18–23

Paul, having stayed after this many more days, takes his leave of the brothers, and sails from there for Syria, together with Priscilla and Aquila. He shaves his head in Cenchreae, for he has a vow. He comes to Ephesus, and he leaves them there; but he himself enters into the synagogue, and reasons with the Jews. When they ask him to stay with them a longer time, he declines; but taking his leave of them, he says, “I must by all means keep this coming feast in Jerusalem, but I will return again to you if God wills.” Then he sets sail from Ephesus.

When he has landed at Caesarea, he goes up and greets the assembly, and goes down to Antioch. Having spent some time there, he departs, and goes through the region of Galatia, and Phrygia, in order, establishing all the disciples.
Apollos · 18:24–28

Now a certain Jew named Apollos, an Alexandrian by race, an eloquent man, comes to Ephesus. He is mighty in the Scriptures. This man has been instructed in the way of the Lord; and being fervent in spirit, he speaks and teaches accurately the things concerning Jesus, although he knows only the baptism of John. He begins to speak boldly in the synagogue. But when Priscilla and Aquila hear him, they take him aside, and explain to him the way of God more accurately.

When he has determined to pass over into Achaia, the brothers encourage him, and write to the disciples to receive him. When he has come, he greatly helps those who have believed through grace; for he powerfully refutes the Jews, publicly showing by the Scriptures that Jesus is the Christ.
Disciples of John in Ephesus · 19:1–7
While Apollos is at Corinth, Paul, having passed through the upper country, comes to Ephesus, and finds certain disciples. He says to them, “Did you receive the Holy Spirit when you believed?”
They say to him, “No, we haven’t even heard that there is a Holy Spirit.”
He says, “Into what then were you baptized?”
They say, “Into John’s baptism.”
Paul says, “John indeed baptized with the baptism of repentance, saying to the people that they should believe in the one who would come after him, that is, in Jesus.”

When they hear this, they are baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus. When Paul has laid his hands on them, the Holy Spirit comes on them, and they speak with other languages and prophesy. They are about twelve men in all.
Two Years in Ephesus · 19:8–22
He enters into the synagogue, and speaks boldly for a period of three months, reasoning and persuading about the things concerning God’s Kingdom.

But when some are hardened and disobedient, speaking evil of the Way before the multitude, he departs from them, and separates the disciples, reasoning daily in the school of Tyrannus. This continues for two years, so that all those who live in Asia hear the word of the Lord Jesus, both Jews and Greeks.

God works special miracles by the hands of Paul, so that even handkerchiefs or aprons are carried away from his body to the sick, and the diseases depart from them, and the evil spirits go out. But some of the itinerant Jews, exorcists, takes on themselves to invoke over those who have the evil spirits the name of the Lord Jesus, saying, “We adjure you by Jesus whom Paul preaches.” There are seven sons of one Sceva, a Jewish chief priest, who does this.

The evil spirit answers, “Jesus I know, and Paul I know, but who are you?” The man in whom the evil spirit is leaped on them, overpowers them, and prevails against them, so that they flee out of that house naked and wounded. This becomes known to all, both Jews and Greeks, who live at Ephesus. Fear falls on them all, and the name of the Lord Jesus is magnified. Many also of those who have believed come, confessing, and declaring their deeds. Many of those who practice magical arts bring their books together and burn them in the sight of all. They count their price, and find it to be fifty thousand pieces of silver. So the word of the Lord is growing and becoming mighty.
Now after these things have ended, Paul determines in the spirit, when he has passed through Macedonia and Achaia, to go to Jerusalem, saying, “After I have been there, I must also see Rome.”
Having sent into Macedonia two of those who serve him, Timothy and Erastus, he himself stays in Asia for a while.
The Riot in Ephesus · 19:23–41

About that time there arises no small stir concerning the Way. For a certain man named Demetrius, a silversmith, who makes silver shrines of Artemis, brings no little business to the craftsmen, whom he gathers together, with the workmen of like occupation, and says, “Sirs, you know that by this business we have our wealth. You see and hear, that not at Ephesus alone, but almost throughout all Asia, this Paul has persuaded and turned away many people, saying that they are no gods, that are made with hands. Not only is there danger that this our trade come into disrepute, but also that the temple of the great goddess Artemis will be counted as nothing, and her majesty destroyed, whom all Asia and the world worships.”

When they hear this they are filled with anger, and cry out, saying, “Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!” The whole city is filled with confusion, and they rush with one accord into the theater, having seized Gaius and Aristarchus, men of Macedonia, Paul’s companions in travel. When Paul wants to enter in to the people, the disciples don’t allow him. Certain also of the Asiarchs, being his friends, sent to him and beg him not to venture into the theater. Some therefore cries one thing, and some another, for the assembly is in confusion. Most of them doesn’t know why they have come together. They bring Alexander out of the multitude, the Jews putting him forward. Alexander beckoned with his hand, and would have made a defense to the people. But when they perceive that he is a Jew, all with one voice for a time of about two hours cries out, “Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!”

When the town clerk has quieted the multitude, he says, “You men of Ephesus, what man is there who doesn’t know that the city of the Ephesians is temple keeper of the great goddess Artemis, and of the image which fell down from Zeus? Seeing then that these things can’t be denied, you ought to be quiet, and to do nothing rash. For you have brought these men here, who are neither robbers of temples nor blasphemers of your goddess. If therefore Demetrius and the craftsmen who are with him have a matter against anyone, the courts are open, and there are proconsuls. Let them press charges against one another. But if you seek anything about other matters, it will be settled in the regular assembly. For indeed we are in danger of being accused concerning today’s riot, there being no cause. Concerning it, we wouldn’t be able to give an account of this commotion.” When he has thus spoken, he dismisses the assembly.
Through Macedonia to Troas · 20:1–12

After the uproar has ceased, Paul sends for the disciples, takes leave of them, and departs to go into Macedonia. When he has gone through those parts, and has encouraged them with many words, he comes into Greece. When he has spent three months there, and a plot is made against him by Jews as he is about to set sail for Syria, he determines to return through Macedonia. These accompany him as far as Asia: Sopater of Beroea; Aristarchus and Secundus of the Thessalonians; Gaius of Derbe; Timothy; and Tychicus and Trophimus of Asia. But these have gone ahead, and are waiting for us at Troas. We sail away from Philippi after the days of Unleavened Bread, and come to them at Troas in five days, where we stay seven days.

On the first day of the week, when the disciples are gathered together to break bread, Paul talks with them, intending to depart on the next day, and continues his speech until midnight. There are many lights in the upper room where we are gathered together. A certain young man named Eutychus sits in the window, weighs down with deep sleep. As Paul speaks still longer, being weighed down by his sleep, he falls down from the third floor, and is taken up dead. Paul goes down, and falls upon him, and embracing him says, “Don’t be troubled, for his life is in him.”
When he has gone up, and has broken bread, and eats, and has talked with them a long while, even until break of day, he departs. They bring the boy in alive, and are greatly comforted.
Miletus: Paul’s Farewell to the Ephesian Elders · 20:13–38

But we, going ahead to the ship, set sail for Assos, intending to take Paul aboard there; for he has so arranged, intending himself to go by land. When he meets us at Assos, we take him aboard, and come to Mitylene. Sailing from there, we come the following day opposite Chios. The next day we touch at Samos and stay at Trogyllium, and the day after we come to Miletus. For Paul has determined to sail past Ephesus, that he might not have to spend time in Asia; for he is hastening, if it were possible for him, to be in Jerusalem on the day of Pentecost.

From Miletus he sends to Ephesus, and calls to himself the elders of the assembly. When they have come to him, he says to them, “You yourselves know, from the first day that I set foot in Asia, how I was with you all the time, serving the Lord with all humility, with many tears, and with trials which happened to me by the plots of the Jews; how I didn’t shrink from declaring to you anything that was profitable, teaching you publicly and from house to house, testifying both to Jews and to Greeks repentance toward God, and faith toward our Lord Jesus. Now, look, I go bound by the Spirit to Jerusalem, not knowing what will happen to me there; except that the Holy Spirit testifies in every city, saying that bonds and afflictions wait for me. But these things don’t count; nor do I hold my life dear to myself, so that I may finish my race with joy, and the ministry which I received from the Lord Jesus, to fully testify to the Good News of the grace of God.

“Now, look, I know that you all, among whom I went about preaching God’s Kingdom, will see my face no more. Therefore I testify to you today that I am clean from the blood of all men, for I didn’t shrink from declaring to you the whole counsel of God. Take heed, therefore, to yourselves, and to all the flock, in which the Holy Spirit has made you overseers, to shepherd the assembly of the Lord and God which he purchased with his own blood. For I know that after my departure, vicious wolves will enter in among you, not sparing the flock. Men will arise from among your own selves, speaking perverse things, to draw away the disciples after them. Therefore watch, remembering that for a period of three years I didn’t cease to admonish everyone night and day with tears. Now, brothers, I entrust you to God, and to the word of his grace, which is able to build up, and to give you the inheritance among all those who are sanctified. I coveted no one’s silver, or gold, or clothing. You yourselves know that these hands served my necessities, and those who were with me.
